class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Programming questions"><h2>Programming</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming"></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET"><h3>NET</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is targeting .NET Standard still justified?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Targeting .NET Standard is justified when one library build must be usable on more than one .NET implementation, which in practice usually means .NET Framework consumers remain. <code>netstandard2.0</code> is the highest version .NET Framework can consume, so it is the target that keeps that reach. When every consumer runs modern .NET, a modern <code>netX.0</code> target is the better default.</p>
<p dir="auto">.NET Standard is a versioned API contract, not a runtime, and meeting the contract does not by itself guarantee that a library runs on a given host. Targeting a version fixes the baseline reference API surface the library compiles against. Each .NET implementation supports particular .NET Standard versions starting from particular releases, so a consumer can use the library only on an implementation release that supports the targeted version. Compatible NuGet packages can add APIs beyond that baseline, and every package dependency must then also support the consumer's platform. After .NET 5 unified the target frameworks, no new .NET Standard versions are planned beyond 2.1.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Target</th>
<th>Consumers that can use it</th>
<th>Cost</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>netstandard2.0</code> only</td>
<td>Releases of .NET Framework, .NET Core, Mono, Xamarin and modern .NET that implement 2.0</td>
<td>Limited to the 2.0 baseline plus APIs from compatible packages, with no modern-target APIs or optimizations</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>netstandard2.1</code></td>
<td>Implementations and releases that support 2.1, including modern .NET, but not .NET Framework</td>
<td>Gives up .NET Framework reach without the full modern API set</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Modern <code>netX.0</code> only</td>
<td>Apps on that .NET version or later</td>
<td>.NET Framework and older runtimes cannot load it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Multi-target, such as <code>net8.0;netstandard2.0</code></td>
<td>Both groups, each receiving the assembly built for it</td>
<td>More builds, tests, conditional code and package metadata, justified only when distinct consumer groups need distinct assets</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Modern .NET implements .NET Standard 2.1 and earlier, so an existing <code>netstandard2.0</code> library can keep serving modern consumers, provided its package dependencies also support those runtimes. Retargeting is worthwhile when the library needs APIs or features that only a newer target provides.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/net-standard" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/net-standard" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: .NET Standard</a> · <a href="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET Blog: The future of .NET Standard</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/NET Standart.md" class="internal-link">NET Standart</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What are the main layers of .NET, and why does it help to separate them?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A practical model splits .NET into languages and compilers, SDK tooling, the runtime, the base libraries and application frameworks. Separating them helps because each owns different behavior, so naming the owning layer turns a vague symptom into a testable hypothesis.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Layer</th>
<th>What it owns</th>
<th>Example of a problem it owns</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Languages and compilers</td>
<td>Translate C#, F# or Visual Basic source into IL stored in assemblies.</td>
<td>A compile error, or unexpected behavior of a language feature.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>SDK and tools</td>
<td>Restore packages, then build, test and publish projects, mainly through the <code>dotnet</code> CLI.</td>
<td>A package-restore, build or publish failure.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Runtime (CLR)</td>
<td>Load assemblies and run managed code: JIT compilation, garbage collection, exception handling and threading.</td>
<td>GC pauses, or slow startup while methods are compiled.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Base libraries</td>
<td>Shared APIs such as collections, I/O, networking and threading primitives.</td>
<td>The behavior or cost of a specific API, such as a collection or stream.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Application frameworks</td>
<td>Application models such as ASP.NET Core, WPF or .NET MAUI, including pipelines like HTTP middleware.</td>
<td>A slow or misordered request pipeline.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A symptom often appears in a different layer from its cause. Rising memory shows up as garbage-collection activity in the runtime even when application code is keeping objects reachable. A slow HTTP request can come from the framework pipeline, synchronous I/O in application code or the generated machine code. “.NET is slow” is not a useful hypothesis until the owning part is named.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is a conceptual map rather than an official fixed taxonomy, and component and version boundaries change between releases.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/introduction" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/introduction" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Introduction to .NET</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/clr" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/clr" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Common Language Runtime overview</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/NET.md" class="internal-link">NET</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API"><h4>ASP NET Web API</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What must an API establish before it trusts a bearer JWT?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Before trusting a bearer JWT, an API must confirm all of the following against its own configured trust settings:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Signature:</strong> the token was signed with a key the API accepts, so its contents were not changed after signing.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Issuer:</strong> the authority the API expects issued it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Audience:</strong> it was issued for this API rather than for another service.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Lifetime:</strong> it has not expired.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Each check answers a different question, so none can stand in for another. A valid signature proves only that an accepted key signed the token. It does not show that the expected authority issued the token, that this API was the intended recipient, or that the token is still valid. Any further claims the API requires depend on its own trust configuration.</p>
<p dir="auto">In ASP.NET Core, the JWT bearer handler performs these checks according to its <code>TokenValidationParameters</code>. Disabling issuer, audience or lifetime validation because the token is signed removes the protection that check provides.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/configure-jwt-bearer-authentication?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/configure-jwt-bearer-authentication?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Configure JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Authentication.md" class="internal-link">Authentication</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between <code>GetService&lt;T&gt;</code> and <code>GetRequiredService&lt;T&gt;</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>GetService&lt;T&gt;</code> returns <code>null</code> when the requested registration is absent. <code>GetRequiredService&lt;T&gt;</code> throws <code>InvalidOperationException</code> at resolution. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.serviceproviderserviceextensions.getrequiredservice?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.serviceproviderserviceextensions.getrequiredservice?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: GetRequiredService</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: service lifetimes</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: DI guidelines</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Dependency Injection.md" class="internal-link">Dependency Injection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the normal execution order of ASP.NET Core MVC filter types?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">After routing selects an MVC action, the filter stages run in this order: authorization, resource, action, then result. Exception filters are not a sequential stage; they run only when an unhandled exception occurs.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Authorization filters</strong> run first and can short-circuit an unauthorized request.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Resource filters</strong> run their before logic next, ahead of model binding, and their after logic last, once the rest of the pipeline has completed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Action filters</strong> run immediately before and after the action method.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Result filters</strong> run immediately before and after the action result executes.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Full flow: authorization → resource (before) → action (before) → action method → action (after) → result (before) → result execution → result (after) → resource (after).</p>
<p dir="auto">Action filters finish before result filters start, so an action filter's after logic can still replace the result. Only resource filters wrap both the action and the result stages.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Filters.md" class="internal-link">Filters</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which exceptions can ASP.NET Core MVC exception filters handle, and what happens after they run?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">MVC exception filters handle only unhandled exceptions raised while MVC creates the controller, binds the model, runs action filters or runs the action method. They are not a before-and-after stage; they run only when such an exception occurs.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Not covered:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Exceptions from authorization filters and resource filters, which run outside that part of the pipeline.</li>
<li dir="auto">Exceptions from result filters or from executing the action result.</li>
<li dir="auto">Exceptions from middleware, routing or non-MVC endpoints, which run outside MVC.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>After an exception filter runs:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Handled:</strong> the filter sets <code>ExceptionHandled</code> to <code>true</code> or assigns a <code>Result</code>, and the exception stops propagating. A supplied <code>Result</code> is executed as the response. Ordinary result filters do not run around it; only always-run result filters, such as <code>IAlwaysRunResultFilter</code> implementations, do.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Not handled:</strong> the exception leaves the MVC pipeline and continues to outer middleware, such as exception-handling middleware.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Because of these gaps, exception-handling middleware is the broader boundary for a uniform API error response.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Filters.md" class="internal-link">Filters</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Within one ASP.NET Core MVC filter type, how do scope and the <code>Order</code> property determine execution order?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">By default, scope decides the order among filters of one type: global filters wrap controller filters, which wrap action filters. An explicit <code>Order</code> value, exposed through <code>IOrderedFilter</code>, takes precedence over scope.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Equal <code>Order</code> values:</strong> before logic runs global → controller → action, and after logic runs action → controller → global.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Different <code>Order</code> values:</strong> filters are sorted by <code>Order</code> first and by scope second. A lower value runs its before logic earlier and its after logic later, so it wraps filters with higher values regardless of their scope.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For example, an action-level action filter with <code>Order</code> 0 runs its before logic ahead of a global action filter with <code>Order</code> 1.</p>
<p dir="auto">This ordering only arranges filters of the same type. It cannot move an action filter ahead of an authorization filter, because each filter type runs at its own stage of the MVC pipeline.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Filters.md" class="internal-link">Filters</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does middleware differ from an MVC action filter?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Middleware runs in the general ASP.NET Core request pipeline for every request that reaches it, and it can run before an endpoint is selected. An MVC action filter runs only inside MVC, around a controller action after that action has been selected. It can read and change the action's arguments and result.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Middleware</th>
<th>MVC action filter</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Position</td>
<td>A pipeline component that runs in registration order and can run before routing selects an endpoint.</td>
<td>Runs inside MVC after action selection, immediately before and after the action method.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Requests covered</td>
<td>Every request that reaches it, including static files, Minimal API endpoints and requests that never enter MVC. An earlier component that short-circuits, or a branch that bypasses it, removes that coverage.</td>
<td>Only the controller actions the filter is applied to.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Context</td>
<td><code>HttpContext</code> and the rest of the pipeline. It has no model-bound arguments or action result.</td>
<td>Action context: model-bound arguments, which it can read or replace before the action runs, and the result, which it can inspect or replace afterward.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fits</td>
<td>Concerns that span endpoint types, such as exception handling, request logging, CORS and authentication.</td>
<td>Behavior that depends on action arguments or results for a set of controllers or actions.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Minimal API endpoints do not run MVC action filters. Their endpoint-scoped equivalent is endpoint filters.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/middleware?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/middleware?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Middleware in Minimal API apps</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Middlewares.md" class="internal-link">Middlewares</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can an ASP.NET Core application handle unhandled exceptions consistently?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A single exception-handling middleware, such as <code>UseExceptionHandler</code>, is registered near the start of the pipeline so that it wraps every later component. It turns any unhandled exception from those components into one safe, consistent error response. In ASP.NET Core 8 and later, a registered <code>IExceptionHandler</code> implementation can keep the mapping from exception to response in one place.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">A later component or the endpoint throws. The exception propagates back out through each <code>next</code> call until it reaches the handler.</li>
<li dir="auto">A safe server-side diagnostic records the failure. This diagnostic is arranged deliberately, not assumed. In ASP.NET Core 10, when an <code>IExceptionHandler</code> reports an exception as handled, the middleware's own diagnostics are suppressed by default. The handler therefore records what an investigation needs.</li>
<li dir="auto">The handler writes the application's error contract: an error status code and a body. With <code>AddProblemDetails()</code> registered, that body can be a standard Problem Details response.</li>
<li dir="auto">Production responses omit stack traces and other sensitive details.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Limits:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Coverage:</strong> components registered before the handler are outside it, so their exceptions are not caught.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Started responses:</strong> once the response has started, the status code and headers may already be sent. The handler then cannot reliably replace them with an error response.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Swallowing:</strong> logging the exception but returning a success status hides the failure from clients. The boundary either writes a real error response or lets the exception continue.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Handle errors in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Middlewares.md" class="internal-link">Middlewares</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does a request move through the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A request passes inward through middleware in registration order until something produces a response, normally the endpoint. The response then passes back outward through the same components in reverse order.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Each component receives <code>HttpContext</code> and a <code>next</code> delegate. Code before <code>await next(context)</code> runs on the way in.</li>
<li dir="auto">A component either calls <code>next</code> to pass control inward, or returns without calling it to short-circuit. After a short-circuit, later components and the endpoint do not run.</li>
<li dir="auto">In a typical API pipeline, routing selects the endpoint. Authentication then tries to establish <code>HttpContext.User</code> and normally continues even without a valid credential. Authorization evaluates the endpoint's policy. If the caller fails it, authorization triggers the scheme's challenge for an unauthenticated caller, or forbid for an authenticated one. The scheme decides the response, for example <code>401</code> or <code>403</code> for bearer tokens, or a redirect for cookies.</li>
<li dir="auto">The endpoint runs and produces the response.</li>
<li dir="auto">Control returns through earlier components in reverse order, so code after <code>next</code> runs on the way out.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Code after <code>next</code> can change the status code or headers only while the response has not started. Once <code>Response.HasStarted</code> is true, they may already be on the wire. Branches such as <code>Map</code> and <code>UseWhen</code> change which components a request passes through, so order within a branch matters as well.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/middleware?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/middleware?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Middleware in Minimal API apps</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ASP.NET Core authentication overview</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Handle errors in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/ASP NET Web API/Middlewares.md" class="internal-link">Middlewares</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET/CSharp"><h4>CSharp</h4></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism"><h5>Concurrency and Parallelism</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do asynchronous waiting and multithreading differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Asynchronous waiting is about not occupying a thread while an operation is pending; multithreading is about running work on more than one thread. An <code>async</code> method does not create a thread by itself.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Asynchronous waiting</th>
<th>Multithreading</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it addresses</td>
<td>Time spent waiting for I/O or another pending operation.</td>
<td>Executing several pieces of work on separate threads.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Thread use</td>
<td>While true asynchronous I/O is pending, the method is suspended and no thread runs it. A thread is needed again only when completion makes the continuation runnable.</td>
<td>Each piece of work occupies its thread while it runs. The threads run in parallel only when enough processors are available; otherwise the scheduler interleaves them.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>CPU-bound work</td>
<td>No gain by itself, because computation still needs a thread to execute.</td>
<td>Several pieces of CPU-bound work can make progress at the same time when processors allow.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The two ideas are independent: asynchronous code can wait without extra threads, and multithreaded code can still block its threads while waiting.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/await" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/await" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>await</code> operator</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ASP.NET Core best practices</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Async Await.md" class="internal-link">Async Await</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What changes when an incomplete task is consumed with <code>await</code> instead of <code>Task.Result</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>await</code> suspends the method and frees the current thread until the task completes, while <code>Task.Result</code> blocks the calling thread for the entire wait. That difference also changes deadlock risk and how failures surface.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th><code>await</code></th>
<th><code>Task.Result</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Calling thread</td>
<td>Returns to its caller while the task is pending, so the thread can run other work.</td>
<td>Stays blocked and idle until the task completes.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Resumption</td>
<td>Runs the rest of the method later as a continuation, through the captured <code>SynchronizationContext</code> or non-default <code>TaskScheduler</code> when one applies.</td>
<td>Continues on the same thread once it is released; no continuation is involved.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Deadlock risk</td>
<td>Avoids the context deadlock, because the waiting code does not hold the context's thread.</td>
<td>Can deadlock when the task's continuation needs a single-threaded context, such as a UI thread, that the blocked caller occupies. Each side then waits for the other.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Failures</td>
<td>Rethrows the task's exception itself; when a task holds several exceptions, <code>await</code> rethrows one of them.</td>
<td>Throws an <code>AggregateException</code> that wraps the task's exception or exceptions.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/synchronous-wrappers-for-asynchronous-methods" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/synchronous-wrappers-for-asynchronous-methods" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Synchronous wrappers for asynchronous methods</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task-1.result" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task-1.result" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>Task&lt;TResult&gt;.Result</code></a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Async Await.md" class="internal-link">Async Await</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does <code>ConfigureAwait(false)</code> change, and when is it useful?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>ConfigureAwait(false)</code> tells an <code>await</code> that its continuation does not need to resume through the captured <code>SynchronizationContext</code> or non-default <code>TaskScheduler</code>. It is mainly useful in general-purpose library code that never needs its caller's context.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What changes:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">By default, awaiting an incomplete task captures the current <code>SynchronizationContext</code>, or a non-default current <code>TaskScheduler</code>, and resumes through it. In a UI app, that returns the continuation to the UI thread.</li>
<li dir="auto">With <code>ConfigureAwait(false)</code>, that scheduling context is not captured. The continuation can run on a ThreadPool thread or directly on the thread that completed the operation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What it does not do:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">It does not force a thread switch. If the awaited task has already completed, the method continues synchronously on the current thread, still inside the original context.</li>
<li dir="auto">It does not stop <code>ExecutionContext</code> flow. Ambient state such as <code>AsyncLocal&lt;T&gt;</code> values still reaches the continuation by default.</li>
<li dir="auto">It is not a reliable fix for code that blocks on asynchronous work. Every <code>await</code> along the path would need it; keeping the call chain asynchronous is the durable fix.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Where it fits:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Reusable libraries:</strong> library code stays independent of whatever context its caller has and avoids the cost of queuing back to it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>UI code:</strong> usually keeps the default, because code after the <code>await</code> often updates controls that belong to the UI thread.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>ASP.NET Core:</strong> normally has no custom <code>SynchronizationContext</code>, so the setting usually changes little. <code>HttpContext</code> lifetime and thread safety remain separate concerns: <code>HttpContext</code> is not thread-safe and is unsafe to use outside the processing of its request, whichever thread resumes the method.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.configureawait?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.configureawait?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task.ConfigureAwait</a> · <a href="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET Blog: ConfigureAwait FAQ</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/use-http-context?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/use-http-context?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: HttpContext in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Async Await.md" class="internal-link">Async Await</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can true asynchronous I/O improve server concurrency without keeping a thread for every wait?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Asynchronous I/O improves concurrency because a pending operation needs no thread. At the <code>await</code>, the request code gives its worker thread back to the ThreadPool, and a thread is needed again only to run the continuation after the I/O completes.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Request code starts an I/O operation, such as a database query, and awaits the incomplete task.</li>
<li dir="auto">The method suspends and returns, and the worker thread goes back to the pool.</li>
<li dir="auto">While the I/O is pending, that thread can serve other requests.</li>
<li dir="auto">When the I/O completes, the continuation becomes runnable and a thread resumes the method. Whether the continuation is queued or runs directly on the completing thread depends on completion timing and the scheduling context.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">A synchronous blocking call instead keeps its thread idle for the entire wait. Under load, blocked threads pile up, the ThreadPool runs short of free threads, and response times degrade.</p>
<p dir="auto">Async I/O removes threads as the limit on how many waits can be in flight. It does not guarantee a particular capacity or throughput: CPU work, remaining blocking calls, connection pools, downstream services and other resource limits still constrain the system.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/await" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/await" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>await</code> operator</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ASP.NET Core best practices</a> · <a href="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET Blog: ConfigureAwait FAQ</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Async Await.md" class="internal-link">Async Await</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>Task.Run</code> useful, and why is it usually wrong around asynchronous I/O?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>Task.Run</code> is useful for moving CPU-bound work off a thread that must stay responsive, typically a UI thread. Around an API that is already asynchronous it gains nothing: the I/O does not finish sooner, and the wrapper only adds a ThreadPool scheduling hop.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it does:</strong> queues a delegate to the ThreadPool and returns a task that represents that work.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Useful case:</strong> a UI event handler awaits <code>Task.Run(() =&gt; BuildReport(data))</code>, so the UI thread keeps handling input during a long calculation. The calculation still consumes CPU and occupies a pool thread while it runs.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Already-asynchronous I/O:</strong> <code>await Task.Run(() =&gt; client.GetStringAsync(url))</code> only starts the same request from a pool thread. The wait was already threadless, so awaiting <code>client.GetStringAsync(url)</code> directly gives the same result with less overhead.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Synchronous blocking I/O:</strong> wrapping a blocking call does not make it asynchronous. The block moves to a pool thread, which stays occupied for the whole wait.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">On a server, request code already runs on ThreadPool threads, so wrapping work in <code>Task.Run</code> and immediately awaiting it frees nothing and adds scheduling and pool pressure.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ASP.NET Core best practices</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Async Await.md" class="internal-link">Async Await</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a <code>Channel&lt;T&gt;</code>, and what reliability does it provide?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>Channel&lt;T&gt;</code> is an in-process, in-memory queue that hands items from producers to consumers, with asynchronous waiting on both sides. Its reliability ends at the process boundary. Queued items are not persisted, so a crash loses them, and code on other hosts cannot read them.</p>
<p dir="auto">How it works:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Writer and reader:</strong> producers write through <code>channel.Writer</code>, for example with <code>WriteAsync</code>. Consumers read through <code>channel.Reader</code>, often with <code>await foreach</code> over <code>ReadAllAsync()</code>. A reader waiting on an empty channel, or a writer waiting on a full bounded channel, waits without blocking a thread.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Capacity:</strong> <code>Channel.CreateBounded&lt;T&gt;(capacity)</code> has a fixed buffer and a full-mode policy that either makes producers wait or drops an item. <code>Channel.CreateUnbounded&lt;T&gt;()</code> keeps growing.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Completion:</strong> <code>Writer.Complete()</code> signals that no more items will arrive, so readers drain the buffer and their read loop ends.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A typical use is an HTTP endpoint that queues a job while a <code>BackgroundService</code> in the same process handles it.</p>
<p dir="auto">Reliability limits:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No persistence:</strong> buffered items exist only in that process's memory and are lost if it crashes.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No cross-host delivery:</strong> only code inside the same process can read the channel.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No durable retry:</strong> reading an item removes it from the channel, and nothing redelivers it if processing then fails.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Work that must survive a crash or be retried durably needs a database, message broker or other persistent store.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Channels</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/hosted-services?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/hosted-services?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Queued background tasks</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Channels.md" class="internal-link">Channels</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does a bounded <code>Channel&lt;T&gt;</code> provide that <code>SemaphoreSlim</code> does not?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A bounded <code>Channel&lt;T&gt;</code> stores the work itself and hands it to separate consumers, using a fixed buffer and an overload policy. <code>SemaphoreSlim</code> stores no work. It only counts permits, which limits how many callers run an operation at the same time.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Bounded <code>Channel&lt;T&gt;</code></th>
<th><code>SemaphoreSlim</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it holds</td>
<td>Up to <code>capacity</code> queued items</td>
<td>Only a count of free permits</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Who does the work</td>
<td>A producer writes an item and continues; a consumer reads and processes it later</td>
<td>The caller that gets a permit runs the operation itself, then releases the permit</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>At the limit</td>
<td>In <code>Wait</code> mode, <code>WriteAsync</code> waits for buffer space, which slows producers; drop modes discard an item instead</td>
<td><code>WaitAsync</code> waits for a permit; nothing is stored or dropped</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Order</td>
<td>Items are read in the order they were queued; with several consumers, they can finish in a different order</td>
<td>Waiting callers have no guaranteed order, such as FIFO, for receiving permits</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A channel therefore fits producer-consumer handoff, such as a request queuing a job for a background worker. A semaphore fits admission control, such as capping concurrent calls to a dependency.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Channels</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SemaphoreSlim API</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Channels.md" class="internal-link">Channels</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is <code>Channel.CreateUnbounded&lt;T&gt;()</code> a risky default?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An unbounded channel does not apply capacity backpressure. If producers continue to outpace consumers, queued items accumulate and consume memory until the process is pressured. A bounded channel forces an explicit overload choice: wait for capacity or drop according to a chosen policy. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Channels</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Channels.md" class="internal-link">Channels</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest</code> a reasonable policy?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>DropOldest</code> is reasonable when each newer item makes older buffered items obsolete, so only the latest values matter. Examples are progress snapshots, current status updates and sampled metrics.</p>
<p dir="auto">When the buffer is full, the channel removes the oldest buffered item and accepts the incoming one. The write still succeeds, so the producer is not slowed, and the write result does not report the discard; only an <code>itemDropped</code> callback, when configured for the channel, signals that an item was discarded. Losing a stale snapshot is harmless when a newer one is already queued, but counting or logging drops keeps unexpected loss visible.</p>
<p dir="auto">It is the wrong policy for independent jobs, commands or business events that must each be processed. Dropping one of those silently loses work. The default <code>Wait</code> mode instead makes producers wait for space and discards nothing.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Channels</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Channels.md" class="internal-link">Channels</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism in practice?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Concurrency means several operations are in progress during the same period, even if only one runs at any instant. Parallelism means several operations run at the same instant on different cores. Parallel execution is always concurrent, but concurrent work need not be parallel.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Concurrency</th>
<th>Parallelism</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it describes</td>
<td>How work is structured: operations overlap in time, and their steps can interleave</td>
<td>How work executes: operations run simultaneously</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hardware required</td>
<td>Possible on a single thread or core</td>
<td>Requires multiple cores</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical .NET use</td>
<td>Asynchronous I/O: a thread starts an operation, yields at <code>await</code> and runs other work while the operating system waits</td>
<td>CPU-bound work split across cores, such as <code>Parallel.For</code> over independent items</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it improves</td>
<td>Progress continues during waits, without a thread held for each wait</td>
<td>Elapsed time of computation that divides into independent parts</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">For example, one thread can start two HTTP requests, yield at each <code>await</code> and resume each request when its response arrives. Both requests are in flight together, yet the thread runs one continuation at a time. Extra threads would not make the remote service respond sooner. Parallelism pays off only when there is enough independent CPU work to repay the cost of partitioning and scheduling it.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Asynchronous programming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Parallel programming in .NET</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Concurrency and Parallelism.md" class="internal-link">Concurrency and Parallelism</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What should be checked before choosing <code>Task</code>, <code>lock</code>, <code>Parallel</code>, or <code>Channel</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Three checks drive the choice: whether the work waits on I/O or uses CPU, whether threads share mutable state, and which code owns completion, cancellation and failure.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Check</th>
<th>Fits</th>
<th>Reason</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>The work mostly waits on I/O</td>
<td><code>Task</code> with <code>await</code></td>
<td>The thread is released while the operation waits; more threads would not make the I/O finish sooner</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>The work is independent CPU computation large enough to split</td>
<td><code>Parallel</code> with a measured degree of parallelism</td>
<td>Several cores compute at once, but small or contended work may not repay partitioning and scheduling</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Threads change shared mutable state in a short synchronous step</td>
<td><code>lock</code></td>
<td>Only one thread at a time performs the change; a <code>lock</code> cannot be held across <code>await</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Producers hand work to separate consumers</td>
<td>Bounded <code>Channel&lt;T&gt;</code></td>
<td>It buffers items and fixes an overload policy: producers wait or items are dropped</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Ownership applies to every option. Some code must await or otherwise observe each task so that its exceptions surface. That code also passes a cancellation token into the operation and, for a channel, calls <code>Complete</code> after the last write. Without such an owner, a task can fail unnoticed and a channel reader can wait forever for items that will never arrive.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Asynchronous programming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Parallel programming in .NET</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Channels</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Concurrency and Parallelism.md" class="internal-link">Concurrency and Parallelism</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What are the four Coffman conditions for a resource deadlock?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. A classical resource deadlock occurs only when all four hold at the same time.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Mutual exclusion:</strong> a resource can be held by only one participant at a time, as with a lock.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Hold and wait:</strong> a participant keeps the resources it holds while waiting for another.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No preemption:</strong> a resource cannot be taken from its holder; only the holder can release it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Circular wait:</strong> the waiting participants form a closed chain, each waiting for a resource held by the next.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">For example, thread T1 holds lock A and waits for lock B, while T2 holds B and waits for A. Both locks are exclusive, each thread holds one while waiting, neither lock can be taken away, and the two waits close a cycle.</p>
<p dir="auto">Because all four conditions are required, breaking any one prevents this kind of deadlock. Which condition is practical to break depends on the resources and design. For locks, a single global acquisition order that every code path follows makes circular wait impossible.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/356586.356588" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://doi.org/10.1145/356586.356588" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani: System Deadlocks</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/Dlls/dynamic-link-library-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/Dlls/dynamic-link-library-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Dynamic-link library best practices</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Deadlocks.md" class="internal-link">Deadlocks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can lock-based deadlocks be prevented in .NET code?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Lock-based deadlocks are prevented by making a closed wait cycle impossible, or by ensuring that a thread does not wait forever while it holds locks.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>One global lock order:</strong> every code path that needs several locks acquires them in the same order, such as A before B. No thread can then hold B while waiting for A, so circular wait cannot form.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Bounded acquisition:</strong> a timed <code>Monitor.TryEnter</code> lets a thread give up instead of waiting forever. On failure, the thread releases any locks it already holds, then reports an error or retries after a randomized delay. The timeout does not take the lock from its owner, and identical retry timing could make two threads keep colliding (livelock).</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Short critical sections:</strong> I/O, blocking waits and calls into unknown library code stay outside the lock. Code called while a lock is held may take its own locks, which adds an ordering dependency that is hard to see.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Private lock objects:</strong> a <code>private readonly</code> lock object keeps the lock under the component's control. Locking on <code>this</code>, a <code>Type</code> or a string lets unrelated code take the same lock and join the ordering.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For example, if <code>First</code> locks A then B while <code>Second</code> locks B then A, two threads can each hold one lock and wait for the other. Changing <code>Second</code> to lock A then B removes the cycle.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/Dlls/dynamic-link-library-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/Dlls/dynamic-link-library-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Dynamic-link library best practices</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Deadlocks.md" class="internal-link">Deadlocks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does blocking on an incomplete task deadlock a UI thread?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Blocking deadlocks a UI thread when the task cannot complete without running code on that same UI thread. This happens when an <code>await</code> inside the task captured the UI <code>SynchronizationContext</code>, which runs continuations only on the UI thread.</p>
<p dir="auto">The cycle forms in five steps:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">A UI event handler calls an async method, such as <code>LoadDataAsync()</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Inside it, <code>await</code> on incomplete I/O captures the UI context, and the method returns an incomplete task.</li>
<li dir="auto">The handler calls <code>.Result</code> or <code>.Wait()</code> on that task, blocking the UI thread.</li>
<li dir="auto">The I/O completes, and the rest of <code>LoadDataAsync()</code> is queued to run on the UI thread.</li>
<li dir="auto">The UI thread waits for the task, while the task waits for the UI thread. Neither can proceed.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Awaiting through the whole call chain breaks the cycle, because the handler yields the UI thread instead of blocking it. <code>ConfigureAwait(false)</code> in library code avoids capturing the context for those awaits, but it does not make blocking on asynchronous code a safe general bridge.</p>
<p dir="auto">Without a single-threaded context, as in ASP.NET Core, this particular cycle does not form. Blocking still holds a thread-pool thread for each waiting call and can starve the pool under load.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/common-async-bugs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/common-async-bugs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Common async bugs</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/synchronous-wrappers-for-asynchronous-methods" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/synchronous-wrappers-for-asynchronous-methods" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Synchronous wrappers for async methods</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Deadlocks.md" class="internal-link">Deadlocks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can a production .NET deadlock be diagnosed?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A production deadlock is diagnosed from a process dump by finding a closed wait-for cycle, in which each blocked thread or task waits for something that another member of the cycle holds or must run.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Dump:</strong> <code>dotnet-dump collect</code> saves the memory and thread state of the hung process.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Blocked threads:</strong> in <code>dotnet-dump analyze</code>, <code>clrstack -all</code> shows every managed stack. Deadlocked threads sit in lock acquisitions such as <code>Monitor.Enter</code>, or in synchronous task waits such as <code>.Result</code> or <code>.Wait()</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Monitor owners:</strong> <code>syncblk</code> lists which thread owns each monitor. Matching each waiting thread to the lock it wants, and that lock to its owner, shows whether the waits close a cycle.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Async waits:</strong> for a thread blocked on a task, the analysis also needs the task's pending continuation and the context or scheduler it must run on. For example, a continuation bound to the UI context cannot run while the UI thread itself is blocked on that task.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The cycle is the evidence. A high thread count, or many blocked threads without a cycle, points to a different problem such as thread-pool starvation.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-deadlock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-deadlock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Debug a .NET deadlock</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/dotnet-dump" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/dotnet-dump" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: dotnet-dump</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Deadlocks.md" class="internal-link">Deadlocks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a race condition, and how does <code>lock</code> prevent it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
