<p dir="auto">A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of threads that access shared state concurrently. <code>lock</code> prevents it by letting only one thread at a time run code protected by the same lock object, so one protected update cannot interleave with another.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, two threads run <code>_count++</code> on a shared field. The increment is three steps: read the value, add one and write the result back.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Thread A reads 5.</li>
<li dir="auto">Thread B reads 5 before A writes.</li>
<li dir="auto">A writes 6.</li>
<li dir="auto">B writes 6.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Two increments ran, but one was lost. With <code>lock (_gate) { _count++; }</code> in both threads, B cannot read until A has written and released the lock, so the result is 7.</p>
<p dir="auto">The protection covers only code that takes the same lock. Every read and write of the shared state must use that lock object; an unprotected access elsewhere can still interleave with a protected update.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/managed-threading-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/managed-threading-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Managed threading best practices</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Locking.md" class="internal-link">Locking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When <code>lock</code> targets an ordinary object, what does the compiler ensure around the critical section?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The compiler acquires the monitor with <code>Monitor.Enter(obj, ref lockTaken)</code>, runs the body inside <code>try</code>, and exits in <code>finally</code> only if acquisition succeeded. This releases ownership on normal and exceptional exits without exiting a monitor the thread never acquired. The specialized <code>System.Threading.Lock</code> path in C# 13 uses <code>EnterScope</code> instead. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Monitor.Enter</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Locking.md" class="internal-link">Locking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can’t a <code>lock</code> block contain <code>await</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>Monitor</code> ownership belongs to the thread that entered it, and only that thread can exit it. An awaited continuation may resume on a different thread, which would then try to release a monitor it does not own. The C# compiler therefore rejects <code>await</code> inside a <code>lock</code> block.</p>
<p dir="auto">Holding a lock across <code>await</code> would also make other threads wait for the whole asynchronous operation, turning I/O latency into lock contention.</p>
<p dir="auto">Two alternatives remain:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Restructure:</strong> the awaited work runs outside the lock, and only the resulting state change runs inside a short <code>lock</code>. This fits most cases.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Async-aware gate:</strong> when an invariant must stay protected across an <code>await</code>, a <code>SemaphoreSlim</code> with one permit and <code>await WaitAsync()</code> provides the gate. It has no thread ownership, so a continuation on another thread can release it. <code>Release()</code> belongs in <code>finally</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Monitor.Enter</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SemaphoreSlim API</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Locking.md" class="internal-link">Locking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does <code>System.Threading.Lock</code> change about <code>lock</code> in C# 13 and .NET 9+?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>System.Threading.Lock</code> gives the compiler a dedicated synchronization type instead of an arbitrary object. In C# 13, <code>lock</code> on that type lowers to an <code>EnterScope()</code> guard that releases when the scope exits, rather than the ordinary <code>Monitor.Enter</code>/<code>Exit</code> pattern. It remains synchronous and cannot span <code>await</code>; the type does not promise a universal speedup. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Locking.md" class="internal-link">Locking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does reentrancy differ between <code>lock</code>/<code>Monitor</code> and <code>SemaphoreSlim</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>lock</code>/<code>Monitor</code> is reentrant for its owning thread. <code>SemaphoreSlim</code> is not reentrant, because it has no owner.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>lock</code>/<code>Monitor</code>:</strong> records which thread owns the monitor and how many times it has entered. The owner can enter again without blocking, and other threads can acquire the monitor only after the owner has exited the same number of times.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>SemaphoreSlim</code>:</strong> records only how many permits remain, not which thread or asynchronous flow holds them. A second wait from the same code is just another request for a permit.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">With a one-permit <code>SemaphoreSlim</code>, a method that holds the permit and then calls code that waits on the same semaphore ends up waiting for itself. Without a timeout or cancellation, <code>Wait()</code> blocks forever and <code>WaitAsync()</code> never completes. The permit therefore belongs at one boundary in the call chain, with <code>Release()</code> in <code>finally</code> so that each acquisition is released exactly once.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>lock</code> statement</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.monitor.enter?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Monitor.Enter</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SemaphoreSlim API</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Locking.md" class="internal-link">Locking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a named <code>Mutex</code> appropriate in .NET?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A named <code>Mutex</code> fits when separate processes on the same machine must not run a critical section at the same time. Examples are a single-instance application guard and several processes writing one local file. Every process that opens the same name shares one operating-system mutex, and only one thread across those processes can own it at a time.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Thread ownership:</strong> the thread that acquires the mutex must release it with <code>ReleaseMutex</code>; a call from any other thread throws. Acquisition and release therefore stay in one synchronous scope, not around an <code>await</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Inside one process:</strong> <code>lock</code> for synchronous code, or <code>SemaphoreSlim</code> for asynchronous code, provides exclusion without an operating-system mutex.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Across machines:</strong> a named mutex cannot coordinate them. Ownership across machines needs a lease or lock managed by a shared database or coordination service.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Platform:</strong> name visibility and access rules depend on the operating system. On Windows, the <code>Global\</code> and <code>Local\</code> prefixes control whether other Terminal Services sessions see the name.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/mutexes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/mutexes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Mutexes</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.mutex?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.mutex?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Mutex API</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SemaphoreSlim API</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Mutex.md" class="internal-link">Mutex</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does <code>AbandonedMutexException</code> signal?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The previous owner thread terminated without releasing the mutex. The waiting thread receives <code>AbandonedMutexException</code> but acquires ownership, so it must still release the mutex. The protected state may have been left halfway through an update and should be validated or recovered before other threads enter. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.mutex?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.mutex?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Mutex class</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/mutexes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/mutexes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Mutexes</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Mutex.md" class="internal-link">Mutex</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can adding more parallel workers reduce performance?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Extra workers help only while there is independent work for them and spare capacity to run it. Past that point, each added worker contributes more overhead and contention than useful work, so throughput can fall and latency can rise.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>More CPU-bound workers than cores:</strong> the extra workers cannot run at the same time. The operating system time-slices them, which adds switching overhead without adding compute.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Contention on shared resources:</strong> locks, shared writes and thread-safe collections make workers wait for one another. Memory bandwidth and caches are shared as well, so memory-heavy workers slow each other down.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Coordination overhead:</strong> partitioning the input, scheduling the pieces and merging the results cost more as work is spread across more workers.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Downstream limits:</strong> when each worker calls a database or remote service, extra workers queue on that dependency's connections or rate limits, adding waiting and possibly timeouts.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Worker count is therefore a value to measure against the real workload, not a direct measure of speed.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/potential-pitfalls-with-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/potential-pitfalls-with-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Potential pitfalls with PLINQ</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Understanding speedup in PLINQ</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Parallelism.md" class="internal-link">Parallelism</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should <code>MaxDegreeOfParallelism</code> be chosen?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The limit should come from the resource that actually constrains the work and be confirmed by measurement under representative load. <code>Environment.ProcessorCount</code> is a reasonable starting point for CPU-bound work, not a universal default.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>CPU-bound work:</strong> values near the core count are a starting point. Higher values add time-slicing overhead without adding compute.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Memory- or cache-heavy work:</strong> memory bandwidth can saturate before every core is busy, so the best value can be lower than the core count.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Work that waits on I/O or a dependency:</strong> the limit follows what the database or remote service can handle, such as its connection pool or rate limits. It can be higher or lower than the core count.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The chosen value is the one that meets throughput and tail-latency goals without exhausting those resources. <code>MaxDegreeOfParallelism</code> is only an upper bound on concurrent operations. It does not force that many to run.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.paralleloptions.maxdegreeofparallelism?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.paralleloptions.maxdegreeofparallelism?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ParallelOptions.MaxDegreeOfParallelism</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/introduction-to-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/introduction-to-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Introduction to PLINQ</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Understanding speedup in PLINQ</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Parallelism.md" class="internal-link">Parallelism</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is PLINQ a poor fit?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">PLINQ is a poor fit when the query's work is not independent and large enough per element, or when running its delegates concurrently would break correctness.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared mutable state:</strong> delegates that write to shared variables or call non-thread-safe code can corrupt data. Locks or thread-safe calls that prevent this make workers wait on each other and can erase the speedup.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Order-dependent side effects:</strong> elements are processed on several threads, so side effects happen in no predictable order. <code>AsOrdered()</code> only preserves the order of the query's results, at extra merge cost.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Thread-affine code:</strong> work that must run on a specific thread, such as Windows Forms or WPF UI access or single-threaded-apartment COM objects, cannot safely run inside PLINQ delegates.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Too little work per element:</strong> partitioning and merging overhead can outweigh the parallel gain.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">PLINQ fits pure, CPU-bound transforms over in-memory data, where each element does enough work and measurement shows a speedup.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/potential-pitfalls-with-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/potential-pitfalls-with-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Potential pitfalls with PLINQ</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/introduction-to-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/introduction-to-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Introduction to PLINQ</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Understanding speedup in PLINQ</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Parallelism.md" class="internal-link">Parallelism</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can a parallel query be slower than a sequential query for small inputs?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Parallel execution pays to partition input, schedule work, and merge results. With few items or little work per item, the sequential loop can finish before those fixed costs are repaid. Parallel execution is useful only when independent work is large enough to outweigh the setup and coordination. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/understanding-speedup-in-plinq" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Understanding speedup in PLINQ</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Parallelism.md" class="internal-link">Parallelism</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>SemaphoreSlim</code> a better fit than <code>lock</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>SemaphoreSlim</code> is the better fit when waiting must be asynchronous, such as protected work that contains <code>await</code>, or when up to N callers may proceed at once. <code>lock</code> remains the simpler fit for a short synchronous section that one thread at a time may enter.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th><code>lock</code></th>
<th><code>SemaphoreSlim</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Callers inside at once</td>
<td>One thread, so it only provides mutual exclusion.</td>
<td>Up to the configured count. A count of 1 gives mutual exclusion, and a higher count throttles concurrency.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How a caller waits</td>
<td>The waiting thread blocks until the lock is free.</td>
<td><code>WaitAsync</code> returns a task, so the caller waits without holding a thread. <code>Wait</code> blocks like a lock.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>await</code> inside the section</td>
<td>Not allowed by the compiler, because the lock belongs to the thread that entered it.</td>
<td>Allowed, because a permit is not tied to any thread.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Release</td>
<td>Automatic when the block exits, including after an exception.</td>
<td>Only through an explicit <code>Release</code> call, which any code can make.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Because a semaphore tracks no owner, each successful wait is paired with exactly one <code>Release</code>, normally in a <code>finally</code> block. A missed release permanently removes a permit. An extra release adds a permit beyond the intended limit. A <code>maxCount</code> does not reliably prevent this: <code>Release</code> throws <code>SemaphoreFullException</code> only when it would raise the count above that maximum, so an extra release made while permits are still held succeeds silently.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: SemaphoreSlim</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim.release?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.semaphoreslim.release?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: SemaphoreSlim.Release</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/lock" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: C# lock statement</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Semaphore.md" class="internal-link">Semaphore</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is <code>Task</code> not equivalent to a thread?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A <code>Task</code> is an object that represents an operation and its eventual outcome: a result, a failure or cancellation. A thread is an execution resource that runs code. A task uses a thread only while code belonging to it is actually running.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>CPU-bound tasks:</strong> with the default scheduler, which <code>Task.Run</code> uses, their delegates are queued to the ThreadPool, where a limited set of reusable threads runs many tasks over time instead of one thread per task. A custom <code>TaskScheduler</code> decides for itself where its tasks run, and the <code>LongRunning</code> hint typically leads the default scheduler to use a separate non-pool thread.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>I/O-bound tasks:</strong> while the operating system performs the I/O, the pending task holds no managed thread. A thread is needed only to start the operation and to run the code that processes its completion.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Creating many tasks therefore does not mean one thread per task, and the number of pending tasks does not show how many threads are busy.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.taskscheduler?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.taskscheduler?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: TaskScheduler</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/implementing-the-task-based-asynchronous-pattern#io-bound-tasks" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/implementing-the-task-based-asynchronous-pattern#io-bound-tasks" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: TAP I/O-bound tasks</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Tasks.md" class="internal-link">Tasks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does awaiting <code>Task.Run</code> inside an ASP.NET Core request usually not help?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">ASP.NET Core already runs request code on ThreadPool threads. When the request awaits <code>Task.Run</code>, its own thread returns to the pool while another pool thread runs the work. The request therefore gains no CPU capacity and frees no net thread. It only adds a scheduling hop.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Blocking work:</strong> inside <code>Task.Run</code> it still blocks a pool thread, just a different one. Synchronous I/O does not become asynchronous I/O.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Already asynchronous APIs:</strong> awaiting them directly gives the same non-blocking wait without the extra hop.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Long-running or CPU-heavy work:</strong> it competes with other requests for the same pool threads. It belongs outside the request path, for example in a background service or an out-of-process worker fed by a queue, with the result reported to the client asynchronously.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ASP.NET Core best practices</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Tasks.md" class="internal-link">Tasks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can <code>Task.WhenAll</code> reduce elapsed time for independent asynchronous calls?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The time saving comes from starting the calls before waiting, so their waits overlap. Awaiting each call in turn makes the total roughly the sum of the call times. Starting all of them first and then awaiting <code>Task.WhenAll</code> makes the total approach the slowest call.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token comment">// Sequential: the second call starts only after the first finishes</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> user <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">await</span> <span class="token function">GetUserAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>id<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> orders <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">await</span> <span class="token function">GetOrdersAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>id<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>

<span class="token comment">// Overlapped: both calls are in flight before the wait</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> userTask <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token function">GetUserAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>id<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> ordersTask <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token function">GetOrdersAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>id<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token keyword">await</span> Task<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">WhenAll</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>userTask<span class="token punctuation">,</span> ordersTask<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<p dir="auto"><code>Task.WhenAll</code> itself only returns a task that completes when every supplied task has completed. It does not start tasks that were never started, and it does not make synchronous work run in parallel. Awaiting the already-started tasks one by one would also overlap them. <code>WhenAll</code> adds one wait for all of them that also records every failure.</p>
<p dir="auto">The gain also requires the calls to be independent and the downstream service to handle them concurrently. If it queues or throttles them, the total moves back toward the sum.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenall?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenall?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task.WhenAll</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-based-asynchronous-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task-based asynchronous programming</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Tasks.md" class="internal-link">Tasks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does <code>Task.WhenAll</code> report failures when several of its tasks fail?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The task returned by <code>Task.WhenAll</code> completes only after every supplied task has finished. If any of them faulted, it ends faulted, and its <code>Exception</code> holds an <code>AggregateException</code> with the failures from all faulted tasks. Awaiting it, however, rethrows only one of those exceptions.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The other failures:</strong> after <code>await</code> throws, the full set is still available on the combined task's <code>Exception.InnerExceptions</code> and on each input task's own <code>Exception</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No early exit:</strong> one failure does not stop or cancel the remaining tasks, and <code>WhenAll</code> still waits for all of them.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cancellation:</strong> when no task faulted but at least one was canceled, the combined task ends canceled.</li>
</ul>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name">Task</span> all <span class="token operator">=</span> Task<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">WhenAll</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>a<span class="token punctuation">,</span> b<span class="token punctuation">,</span> c<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token keyword">try</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token keyword">await</span> all<span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
<span class="token keyword">catch</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name">Exception</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token comment">// await rethrew one failure; the combined task keeps all of them</span>
    <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> failures <span class="token operator">=</span> all<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Exception<span class="token punctuation">?.</span>InnerExceptions<span class="token punctuation">;</span>
    <span class="token function">Log</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>failures<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
    <span class="token keyword">throw</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenall?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenall?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Task.WhenAll</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Tasks.md" class="internal-link">Tasks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>ValueTask</code> worth using instead of <code>Task</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>ValueTask</code> is worth it only when profiling shows that <code>Task</code> allocations on a hot path matter. The typical case is a method called very often that usually completes synchronously, such as a read served from an internal buffer. <code>Task</code> remains the default.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it saves:</strong> when the result is already available, <code>ValueTask&lt;T&gt;</code> carries it directly instead of allocating a <code>Task&lt;T&gt;</code>. It can also wrap a reusable <code>IValueTaskSource</code>, so some asynchronous completions avoid an allocation too.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it costs:</strong> the struct holds more fields than a single <code>Task</code> reference, so returning and copying it costs more. It also has stricter consumption rules: it is awaited only once, never awaited concurrently, and its <code>Result</code> is not read before it completes. A pooled source can be reused for another operation after the first consumption, so breaking these rules gives undefined behavior, such as reading another operation's result.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A caller that must store, share or await the result more than once calls <code>AsTask()</code> once and uses the resulting <code>Task</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.valuetask?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.valuetask?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ValueTask</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/Tasks.md" class="internal-link">Tasks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the .NET ThreadPool for, and what work does it not suit?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The ThreadPool is a per-process set of reusable background worker threads that runs short pieces of queued work, such as Task Parallel Library tasks, timer callbacks and asynchronous I/O completions. Reusing threads avoids creating and destroying a thread for each small job, and the runtime adjusts the number of workers to optimize throughput.</p>
<p dir="auto">Pool threads are shared and interchangeable, so the pool does not suit work that holds a thread for a long time or needs control over the thread:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Long blocking work:</strong> the pool has a maximum size and, above its minimum, may wait before adding threads. Many blocked workers can keep queued work from starting, which is ThreadPool starvation.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Thread-specific needs:</strong> a foreground thread that keeps the process alive, a particular priority, a single-threaded apartment for COM, or a stable thread identity.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A long-lived dedicated job:</strong> a component that owns a loop for the process's lifetime fits a dedicated <code>Thread</code> better than a borrowed pool worker.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: The managed thread pool</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/ThreadPool.md" class="internal-link">ThreadPool</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is ThreadPool starvation, and how does it usually start?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">ThreadPool starvation is a state in which queued work items and continuations wait because no pool worker is available to run them. It usually starts when workers are blocked rather than busy, through synchronous blocking on pool threads: most often sync-over-async calls such as <code>.Result</code> or <code>.Wait()</code> on a task, or synchronous I/O in request code.</p>
<p dir="auto">A typical progression:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Many pool threads each block, waiting for an asynchronous operation to finish.</li>
<li dir="auto">When an operation's I/O completes, its continuation, the code that finishes the operation, is queued to the ThreadPool.</li>
<li dir="auto">All workers are blocked, so that continuation stays queued while the blocked workers keep waiting for it.</li>
<li dir="auto">Above its minimum, the pool may wait before adding workers, so the queue can grow faster than new workers arrive.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">In this blocking-driven case, the typical symptoms are a growing queue and rising latency or timeouts while CPU stays well below saturation. That pattern separates it from CPU saturation, where every core is busy with real work and more threads do not help.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-threadpool-starvation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-threadpool-starvation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Debug ThreadPool starvation</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: The managed thread pool</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/ThreadPool.md" class="internal-link">ThreadPool</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is it appropriate to call <code>ThreadPool.SetMinThreads</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Raising the minimum is appropriate only after measurements show that the pool's gradual thread injection is delaying work. That covers a burst of work arriving faster than the pool adds workers. It also covers blocking-related starvation, where a higher minimum can serve as a temporary mitigation while the blocking code is fixed. It is a late tuning step: it does not remove the cause of blocking, and it does not help when the CPU is already saturated.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it changes:</strong> the minimum is the number of workers the pool creates on demand without its usual injection delay. It does not create those threads in advance, and an idle pool can stay below it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it costs:</strong> the pool can create many threads quickly, which adds memory use, contention and context switching, and can oversubscribe the CPU.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it does not fix:</strong> when workers block on synchronous waits, extra threads can relieve the backlog for a while, but the blocking remains the cause, and enough load can block the new threads too. When all cores are already busy, extra threads add switching overhead rather than throughput.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Queue length, thread count, CPU and latency compared before and after the change show whether it helped.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.threadpool.setminthreads?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.threadpool.setminthreads?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ThreadPool.SetMinThreads</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: The managed thread pool</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Concurrency and Parallelism/ThreadPool.md" class="internal-link">ThreadPool</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals"><h5>Fundamentals</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a .NET method throw an exception instead of returning a failure result?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A method throws when it cannot deliver what it promises and callers are not expected to branch on that outcome in normal flow. It returns a failure result when the outcome is common and expected, so callers routinely check it.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Throwing an exception</th>
<th>Returning a failure result</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Fits when</td>
<td>The failure is unexpected for this call, such as an invalid argument, an invalid object state or an unavailable dependency.</td>
<td>The outcome is part of normal flow, such as a cache miss, unparsable user input or a rejected validation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>If the caller ignores it</td>
<td>A synchronous throw propagates up the call stack until a handler catches it, so the caller cannot skip it by not checking. A <code>Task</code>-returning async method stores the exception on that <code>Task</code>; it surfaces only when the code that owns the task awaits or otherwise observes it, so an ignored faulted task can go unnoticed.</td>
<td>The failure can be silently ignored if the caller never checks the result.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost when it happens</td>
<td>Throwing and unwinding are expensive, which matters when the outcome occurs on every request.</td>
<td>Reporting the outcome costs about the same as success.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical .NET shape</td>
<td>A specific exception type such as <code>ArgumentException</code> or <code>InvalidOperationException</code>.</td>
<td>A <code>Try</code> method such as <code>int.TryParse</code> returning <code>bool</code>, <code>null</code> or default for a common miss, or an explicit result type.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Many APIs offer both forms: <code>int.Parse</code> throws on bad input, while <code>int.TryParse</code> returns <code>false</code>. The caller then picks the form that matches how often failure is expected.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Best practices for exceptions</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.taskscheduler.unobservedtaskexception?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.taskscheduler.unobservedtaskexception?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Exception Handling.md" class="internal-link">Exception Handling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between <code>throw;</code> and <code>throw ex;</code> inside a <code>catch</code> block?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>throw;</code> rethrows the current exception while preserving its original stack trace. <code>throw ex;</code> starts the visible stack at the rethrow site and loses the original path. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: exception handling statements</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Exception Handling.md" class="internal-link">Exception Handling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should an exception be wrapped instead of rethrown directly?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An exception should be wrapped when a boundary must add meaning that the original lacks: context about the operation that failed, or translation into a stable failure type that callers of that layer are expected to handle. The original goes into the new exception's <code>InnerException</code>, so its type, message and stack trace stay available.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, a data-access layer can translate a database provider's exception into a domain-level <code>OrderStoreUnavailableException</code>. Callers then handle one stable type and do not depend on the provider.</p>
<p dir="auto">When the catch block only logs, cleans up or decides it cannot handle the failure, <code>throw;</code> rethrows the original with its stack trace intact. Wrapping without adding meaning only lengthens the exception chain. It can also change which outer handlers match. A <code>catch</code> matches its declared type and types derived from it, so a handler that caught the original stops matching when the wrapper's type is neither that type nor derived from it.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Best practices for exceptions</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Exception-handling statements</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Exception Handling.md" class="internal-link">Exception Handling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is throwing from <code>finally</code> dangerous?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An exception that escapes <code>finally</code> while another exception is already propagating replaces that exception. The original stops propagating, so callers, outer handlers and any later logging see only the cleanup error, which usually says little about the real cause.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, a <code>try</code> block fails with a timeout, and closing a connection in <code>finally</code> then throws an exception that escapes the block. The caller receives the close failure, and the timeout no longer appears in the propagated exception.</p>
<p dir="auto">Cleanup in <code>finally</code> is therefore kept simple, and any failure it can raise is caught and logged inside the <code>finally</code> block so the original exception keeps propagating.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Exception-handling statements</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Best practices for exceptions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Exception Handling.md" class="internal-link">Exception Handling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When might <code>finally</code> not execute?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>finally</code> runs when control leaves its <code>try</code> block while the process keeps executing: normal completion, a jump such as <code>return</code> or <code>break</code>, or an exception unwinding through it. It does not run when the process ends without unwinding or when control never leaves the <code>try</code> block.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Immediate process termination:</strong> <code>Environment.FailFast</code> ends the process without running pending <code>finally</code> blocks or finalizers. A stack overflow, or the process being killed by the operating system or an orchestrator, ends it just as abruptly.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unhandled exceptions:</strong> cleanup is reliable when a handler exists and the stack unwinds to it. If no handler is found, whether <code>finally</code> blocks run depends on how the runtime and operating system end the process.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Control never leaves the <code>try</code> block:</strong> an infinite loop or a deadlock inside it means <code>finally</code> is never reached.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><code>finally</code> is therefore in-process cleanup, not crash recovery. State that must survive a crash relies on durable mechanisms such as transactions or recovery logic that runs on restart.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Exception-handling statements</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.environment.failfast?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.environment.failfast?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Environment.FailFast</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Exception Handling.md" class="internal-link">Exception Handling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What must a type provide to work with <code>foreach</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A type works with <code>foreach</code> in either of two ways. It implements <code>IEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code> or <code>IEnumerable</code>, or it matches the enumerator pattern that the compiler looks for. The interface is the usual reusable contract, but it is not required.</p>
<p dir="auto">The pattern has two parts:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The source</strong> has a public parameterless <code>GetEnumerator()</code> method. That method can also be an extension method.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The returned enumerator</strong> has a public <code>Current</code> property and a public parameterless <code>MoveNext()</code> method that returns <code>bool</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The compiler binds to these members rather than to an interface, so a type can be iterated without implementing either interface. Arrays also receive specialized compiler handling.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: iteration statements</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Foreach.md" class="internal-link">Foreach</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does <code>foreach</code> work under the hood?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The compiler rewrites <code>foreach</code> into lower-level code, and the result depends on the source type. For the general enumerator pattern, the rewrite is roughly:</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> enumerator <span class="token operator">=</span> source<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">GetEnumerator</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token keyword">try</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token keyword">while</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span>enumerator<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">MoveNext</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span>
    <span class="token punctuation">{</span>
        <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> item <span class="token operator">=</span> enumerator<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Current<span class="token punctuation">;</span>
        <span class="token comment">// loop body</span>
    <span class="token punctuation">}</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
<span class="token keyword">finally</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token comment">// Disposes the enumerator when it requires disposal.</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><code>GetEnumerator()</code> is called once, before the first element.</li>
<li dir="auto">Each <code>MoveNext()</code> call advances to the next element and returns <code>false</code> when the sequence is exhausted.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>Current</code> supplies that element, which is assigned to the iteration variable before the body runs.</li>
<li dir="auto">When the enumerator requires disposal, the <code>finally</code> block disposes it, including after <code>break</code> or an exception. A handwritten <code>while (MoveNext())</code> loop has to provide that cleanup itself, or the enumerator's cleanup does not run.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">No single generated shape fits every source. Arrays, for example, can be lowered to index-based code without an enumerator.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: iteration statements</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Foreach.md" class="internal-link">Foreach</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>yield return</code> useful compared with a materialized collection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>yield return</code> produces values on demand, so a consumer can stop early without first building the whole result. The iterator body runs during enumeration; enumerating again runs it again and may observe changed state. A materialized collection is preferable when a stable snapshot or repeated traversal is needed. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/yield" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/yield" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: yield statement</a></p>
