</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Foreach.md" class="internal-link">Foreach</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What do generics add to a C# API?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Generics let one implementation take a type as a parameter. The same code then works with many types, while the compiler still checks the type of every value that goes in or comes out.</p>
<p dir="auto">Compared with an API that accepts <code>object</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Type safety:</strong> an <code>object</code>-based API needs casts on the way out, so a wrong type fails only at runtime. A <code>List&lt;string&gt;</code> instead rejects an <code>int</code> at compile time and returns strings without casts.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No storage boxing for value types:</strong> an <code>object</code>-based collection boxes each <code>int</code> it stores, while <code>List&lt;int&gt;</code> stores the integers directly. Generic code can still box a value-type <code>T</code> through conversions, such as converting it to <code>object</code> or to an interface type.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Constraints</strong> such as <code>where T : IComparable&lt;T&gt;</code> narrow which type arguments are allowed. In return, the generic code may use the members that the constraint guarantees, such as <code>CompareTo</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: generic types and methods</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: constraints on type parameters</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/conversions#1029-boxing-conversions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/conversions#1029-boxing-conversions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: boxing conversions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Generics.md" class="internal-link">Generics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does <code>IEnumerable&lt;string&gt;</code> assign to <code>IEnumerable&lt;object&gt;</code>, but <code>List&lt;string&gt;</code> does not assign to <code>List&lt;object&gt;</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>IEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code> declares its type parameter covariant (<code>out T</code>), so the conversion is allowed. <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code> is invariant, so it is not.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>IEnumerable&lt;string&gt;</code> as <code>IEnumerable&lt;object&gt;</code>:</strong> the interface only hands <code>T</code> values out. Every string read from the sequence is also an object, so reading strings as objects is safe.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>List&lt;string&gt;</code> as <code>List&lt;object&gt;</code>:</strong> <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code> also takes <code>T</code> values in, for example through <code>Add</code>. If the conversion were allowed, code could add an <code>int</code> through the <code>List&lt;object&gt;</code> reference, and the original <code>List&lt;string&gt;</code> would then hold a non-string.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Variance also has to be declared, and C# allows it only on generic interfaces and delegates. A generic class such as <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code> is therefore always invariant, whatever its members do.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: covariance and contravariance</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Generics.md" class="internal-link">Generics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a generic interface type parameter be marked <code>out</code> or <code>in</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A type parameter can be marked <code>out</code> when the interface only produces <code>T</code>, and <code>in</code> when it only consumes <code>T</code>. When <code>T</code> flows both in and out, it stays invariant.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Marking</th>
<th>Where <code>T</code> may appear</th>
<th>Conversion it enables</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>out</code> (covariant)</td>
<td>Only in output positions, such as method return types</td>
<td>A more derived type argument can stand in for a less derived one: <code>IEnumerable&lt;string&gt;</code> converts to <code>IEnumerable&lt;object&gt;</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>in</code> (contravariant)</td>
<td>Only in input positions, such as method parameter types</td>
<td>A less derived type argument can stand in for a more derived one: <code>IComparer&lt;object&gt;</code> converts to <code>IComparer&lt;string&gt;</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>None (invariant)</td>
<td>In both input and output positions</td>
<td>No conversion, because either direction would allow an unsafe read or write</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The compiler enforces these positions, so it accepts a variant marking only when the interface's members keep it safe.</p>
<p dir="auto">Variance conversions work only when the type arguments are reference types. <code>IEnumerable&lt;int&gt;</code> does not convert to <code>IEnumerable&lt;object&gt;</code>, because a value-type argument makes the constructed type invariant.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: covariance and contravariance</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Generics.md" class="internal-link">Generics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">A generic method uses <code>default(T)</code> as a fallback. Why can this be dangerous?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>default(T)</code> is not one fixed value. It is <code>null</code> when <code>T</code> is a reference type, and a zero-initialized value such as <code>0</code> or <code>false</code> when <code>T</code> is a value type. Those values can also be legitimate data, so returning <code>default(T)</code> to signal that nothing was found or that something failed makes absence look like a real result.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, a <code>GetOrDefault&lt;T&gt;</code> method that returns <code>default(T)</code> for a missing key returns <code>0</code> when <code>T</code> is <code>int</code>. A caller then cannot tell a missing entry from a stored <code>0</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">When that distinction matters, the API reports absence separately from the value:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>Try</code> method:</strong> returns <code>bool</code> for success and the value through an <code>out T</code> parameter.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Result type:</strong> carries the success or failure state together with the value.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Nullable contract:</strong> returns <code>T?</code>, with <code>null</code> meaning absence. This works only when <code>null</code> is never legitimate data and the return type can actually hold <code>null</code> for the type argument. For a value type that requires <code>Nullable&lt;T&gt;</code>, for example <code>T?</code> under a <code>where T : struct</code> constraint, whose <code>HasValue</code> separates a missing entry from a stored <code>0</code>. With an unconstrained <code>T</code>, <code>T?</code> adds no null state for a value-type argument, so <code>GetOrDefault&lt;int&gt;</code> would still return <code>0</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/default" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/default" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: default keyword</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: nullable value types</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Generics.md" class="internal-link">Generics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do <code>ref</code>, <code>out</code>, and <code>in</code> parameters differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">All three pass the argument by reference instead of copying its value. For <code>ref</code> and <code>out</code>, the parameter always aliases the caller's variable. For <code>in</code>, it aliases the caller's variable when the argument is a variable of the parameter's type. An <code>in</code> argument that is not a variable, or that needs a conversion, can instead be copied into a temporary, and the parameter then refers to that temporary. The three modifiers differ in which direction data may flow through the reference.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Modifier</th>
<th>How data flows through the reference</th>
<th>Typical use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>ref</code></td>
<td>Both ways. The caller must initialize the variable, and the method can read it and assign it. The caller sees any assignment</td>
<td>Updating or replacing the caller's variable</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>out</code></td>
<td>Outward. The caller can pass an unassigned variable. The method cannot read it before assigning it and must assign it before every normal return</td>
<td>Returning an extra result, as in <code>Try</code> methods such as <code>Dictionary.TryGetValue</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>in</code></td>
<td>Inward and readonly. The caller must initialize the argument, and the method can read the parameter but cannot assign it</td>
<td>Avoiding copies of a large struct on a measured hot path</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Without a modifier, the parameter is a copy, so assigning it never changes the caller's variable.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: method parameters</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods.md" class="internal-link">Methods</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why would a method need <code>ref</code> when the argument is already a reference type?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A reference-type argument passes a copy of the reference. The method can mutate the shared object through that copy, but assigning a different object changes only its local copy. <code>ref</code> aliases the caller’s variable, allowing the method to replace the reference stored there. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: method parameters</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods.md" class="internal-link">Methods</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does an <code>in</code> parameter do, and when is it useful?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An <code>in</code> parameter passes a value by readonly reference, so the method cannot assign through that parameter. It may avoid copying a large struct in a measured hot path, but conversions and non-variable arguments can still require a temporary. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: method parameters</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods.md" class="internal-link">Methods</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does C# apply an optional parameter's default value, and why can already-compiled callers keep an old default?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The default is applied at the call site. When an ordinary compiled call omits an optional argument, the compiler inserts the declared default value into the caller's code, and the method receives it like any other argument.</p>
<p dir="auto">The declaration rules fit that mechanism:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The default must be a compile-time value:</strong> a constant expression, <code>default(S)</code>, or <code>new S()</code> where <code>S</code> is a value type. The compiler has to be able to write the value into each call.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Optional parameters come after all required parameters.</strong> Named arguments let a call supply a later optional argument while omitting earlier ones.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Versioning consequence:</strong> the default lives in each caller's compiled code. If a library changes a default, callers compiled against the old version keep passing the old value until they are recompiled. A public default value is therefore part of the library's compatibility contract.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/named-and-optional-arguments" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/named-and-optional-arguments" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: named and optional arguments</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#12623-run-time-evaluation-of-argument-lists" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#12623-run-time-evaluation-of-argument-lists" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C#: 12.6.2.3 Run-time evaluation of argument lists</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods.md" class="internal-link">Methods</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When <code>Animal a = new Dog();</code> calls <code>a.Category()</code>, what makes the call run <code>Dog</code>'s implementation, and what does that commit the <code>Animal</code> API to?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>Animal.Category()</code> must be declared <code>virtual</code>, and <code>Dog</code> must implement <code>Category()</code> with <code>override</code>. The call is then resolved by the runtime type of the object, <code>Dog</code>, rather than by the declared type of the variable, <code>Animal</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Methods are non-virtual by default. A non-virtual <code>a.Category()</code> binds to <code>Animal.Category()</code> because <code>a</code> is declared as <code>Animal</code>, even when <code>Dog</code> declares its own <code>Category()</code> with <code>new</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Commitment for the base API:</strong> a virtual member is an extension point. Derived classes can replace its behavior, unless an override along the hierarchy is marked <code>sealed</code>, which stops classes below it from overriding the member again. Ordinary calls to the member on such an object run the most-derived override, including calls made from code inside <code>Animal</code>. An explicit <code>base.Category()</code> call in a derived class is the exception: it runs the base class's implementation rather than the most-derived override. <code>Animal</code> can therefore no longer assume that its own implementation of that member is the one that runs.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: virtual keyword</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: new modifier</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/base" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/base" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: base keyword</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/sealed" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/sealed" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: sealed modifier</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods.md" class="internal-link">Methods</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">A base method is not virtual, but a derived class needs different behavior. What are the options, and which ones work through a base-class reference?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Only virtual dispatch makes a call through a base-class reference run derived code. Making the base member <code>virtual</code> and overriding it is therefore the only option that works through such a reference. Hiding with <code>new</code> affects only derived-typed references, and composition moves the variation out of inheritance.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Option</th>
<th>Call through a base reference</th>
<th>Fits when</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Base member made <code>virtual</code>, derived member marked <code>override</code></td>
<td>Runs the derived implementation, chosen by the object's runtime type</td>
<td>The base type can be changed and derived objects are meant to substitute for base objects</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Derived member declared with <code>new</code> (hiding)</td>
<td>Still runs the base implementation. Only references typed as the derived class reach the new member</td>
<td>Hiding itself is the intended behavior, such as a deliberate compatibility split, not polymorphism</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Composition</td>
<td>No inheritance dispatch is involved. The class delegates the varying step to an object it holds</td>
<td>The base cannot be changed, or the variation is not a natural subtype relationship</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Hiding is the common trap. The same object behaves differently depending on whether it is referenced as the derived type or as the base type.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: virtual keyword</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: new modifier</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods.md" class="internal-link">Methods</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What do a C# namespace, an assembly, and an access modifier control?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A namespace organizes qualified names, an assembly is a compiled unit used for deployment and loading, and access modifiers control which code can see a type or member. These are separate boundaries: sharing a namespace does not place types in one assembly or grant access. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/program-structure/namespaces" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/program-structure/namespaces" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: namespaces</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/assembly/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/assembly/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: assemblies</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/access-modifiers" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/access-modifiers" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: access modifiers</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Namespaces.md" class="internal-link">Namespaces</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is reflection in .NET, and what is it used for?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Reflection is the ability of running code to inspect .NET metadata, such as assemblies, types, members and attributes, and to use that metadata to create objects or call members that the calling code does not name at compile time.</p>
<p dir="auto">It works in two phases:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Inspect:</strong> code obtains a <code>Type</code>, for example through <code>typeof(T)</code>, an object's <code>GetType()</code> or a loaded assembly. Objects such as <code>MethodInfo</code>, <code>PropertyInfo</code> and <code>ConstructorInfo</code> then describe its members, signatures and attributes.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Act (optional):</strong> code creates an instance of a discovered type or invokes a discovered member late-bound, for example with <code>Activator.CreateInstance</code> or <code>MethodInfo.Invoke</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Typical uses are reading custom attributes, examining and instantiating types from an assembly, such as plug-ins that implement a known interface, and late binding to members selected at runtime.</p>
<p dir="auto">The trade-off is a weaker contract. A misspelled member name or an incompatible signature is discovered only when the code runs, not by the compiler.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/reflection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/reflection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: reflection overview</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: attributes and reflection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Reflection.md" class="internal-link">Reflection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is reflection often a poor default in performance-critical code?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Reflection replaces a call that the compiler binds once with work done while the program runs. A direct call is resolved during compilation. Reflection finds a member by inspecting metadata, often by name, and <code>MethodInfo.Invoke</code> then receives its arguments as an <code>object[]</code> and checks them against the member's signature on each call.</p>
<p dir="auto">On a hot path, repeating that lookup and late-bound invocation adds work to every call. The cost depends on the operation and how often it runs, so there is no universal threshold.</p>
<p dir="auto">When reflection is needed on a repeated path, the usual mitigation is to discover the member once, cache it, and bind it to a strongly typed delegate. Later calls then go through the delegate without per-call reflection. Measurement shows whether that setup cost pays off.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/reflection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/reflection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: reflection overview</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Reflection.md" class="internal-link">Reflection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do attributes become behavior at runtime?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An attribute does nothing by itself. The compiler stores it as metadata on the marked type or member, and it affects runtime behavior only when some code reads that metadata and acts on it.</p>
<p dir="auto">At runtime the flow is:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The attribute and its arguments were recorded in the assembly's metadata when the code was compiled.</li>
<li dir="auto">A framework or the application inspects the type or member through reflection, for example with <code>GetCustomAttribute&lt;T&gt;()</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">The consumer acts on what it finds, such as registering a handler or selecting a method to invoke.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">An attribute that no code reads has no runtime effect. A source generator is the build-time alternative. It reads attributes during compilation and emits ordinary code, so the behavior no longer depends on runtime reflection.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: attributes and reflection</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: source generators overview</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Reflection.md" class="internal-link">Reflection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When do interfaces or generics, source generators, and reflection each fit best?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The deciding question is whether the code can depend on a compile-time contract or has to work from metadata. Interfaces and generics fit when the code can name the types or operations it needs. When the work is driven by metadata instead, timing separates the other two: a source generator reads metadata visible during compilation and emits ordinary code, while reflection reads metadata while the program runs. Reflection therefore covers both types that are unknown until runtime and runtime inspection of known types, such as reading their attributes.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Mechanism</th>
<th>Fits when</th>
<th>Consequence</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Interface or generic contract</td>
<td>The calling code can state the types or operations it needs</td>
<td>The compiler checks every use against the contract, and trimming can see what is used. An interface or virtual call can still select its implementation at runtime, but only among types that satisfy the compiled contract</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Source generator</td>
<td>Repetitive code can be derived from types and attributes in the compilation, such as registration code for the project's own attributed types</td>
<td>The work moves to build time, and the generated code is compiled, checked and trimmed like handwritten code. Types that appear only at runtime, such as plug-ins loaded later, are invisible to it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reflection</td>
<td>Code has to discover or read metadata at runtime, such as plug-ins loaded from a folder, members named by data, or attributes that a framework reads from known types</td>
<td>It is the most flexible option, but mistakes surface at runtime and repeated lookup and invocation cost more. In trimmed deployments, which include Native AOT, members reached only dynamically can be removed unless annotations such as <code>DynamicallyAccessedMembers</code> or explicit registration preserve them</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/reflection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/reflection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: reflection overview</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: attributes and reflection</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: source generators overview</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/trimming/prepare-libraries-for-trimming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/trimming/prepare-libraries-for-trimming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: prepare libraries for trimming</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#1266-function-member-invocation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#1266-function-member-invocation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: function member invocation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Reflection.md" class="internal-link">Reflection</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types"><h6>Types</h6><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface with default members, and when is an abstract class a better fit?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An abstract class is a partial implementation that derived classes extend through single inheritance, and it can hold per-object state. An interface is a contract that a type can implement alongside any number of other interfaces. Default members let it supply behavior, but not instance state. An abstract class is the better fit when the derived types genuinely share instance state, construction rules or <code>protected</code> extension points.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Abstract class</th>
<th>Interface with default members</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Inheritance limit</td>
<td>A class can derive from only one base class, so an abstract base uses that single slot.</td>
<td>A class or struct can implement many interfaces, so independent capabilities combine freely.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Instance state</td>
<td>Can declare fields and auto-implemented properties that every derived object carries.</td>
<td>Cannot declare instance fields or auto-implemented properties, so default members can build only on other members, not on stored per-object data.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Construction and hooks</td>
<td>Can declare constructors and <code>protected</code> members, so the base controls how derived objects are initialized and which extension points they get.</td>
<td>Cannot declare instance constructors, so it cannot control how implementers are initialized.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Coupling</td>
<td>Derived classes depend on the base's constructors, protected members and the order in which it calls them, so changes to the base can break them.</td>
<td>Implementers depend only on the contract, which is easier to evolve when no shared state is needed.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">For example, a <code>Shape</code> base that stores a <code>Color</code> and declares an abstract <code>Area()</code> shares state across all shapes, so an abstract class fits. A capability such as <code>IComparable&lt;T&gt;</code>, implemented by otherwise unrelated types, fits an interface.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/abstract" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/abstract" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: abstract</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/interface" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/interface" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: interface</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: classes</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Classes.md" class="internal-link">Classes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can’t a static class implement an interface?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A static class never has instances, but an interface's instance members are always reached through an object. A variable, parameter or field of the interface type must refer to something that implements it. A static class can supply no such object, so C# forbids a static class declaration from listing a base class or any implemented interfaces.</p>
<p dir="auto">As a result, behavior that callers must reach through an interface has to live on an instance type rather than in a static class. A test that substitutes a fake is one such caller.</p>
<p dir="auto">Static abstract interface members, available from C# 11 and .NET 7, do not change this. A non-static class or struct implements them. Generic code calls them on a type parameter constrained to the interface, as in <code>T.Create()</code> with <code>where T : IFactory&lt;T&gt;</code>, rather than through an instance.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/static" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/static" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: static</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: classes (static classes)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/interface-implementation/static-virtual-interface-members" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/interface-implementation/static-virtual-interface-members" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: static abstract interface members</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Classes.md" class="internal-link">Classes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">A <code>sealed override</code> stops further overriding. Can a derived class use <code>new</code> to hide it, and what happens at runtime?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Yes. <code>new</code> can declare a separate hidden member, but it does not reopen the sealed virtual slot. A call through the derived type can select the hidden member by compile-time lookup; a call through the base type still dispatches to the sealed override. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: class types</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Classes.md" class="internal-link">Classes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does a <code>partial</code> type let a source generator add code to a handwritten class?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">All declarations of a type marked <code>partial</code> are parts of a single type, and at compile time the compiler combines every part into one type. A source generator adds a new source file to the compilation containing another <code>partial</code> declaration of the class. The members, interfaces and attributes in that generated part become part of the handwritten class, while the handwritten file stays unchanged.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token comment">// Order.cs (handwritten)</span>
<span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">partial</span> <span class="token keyword">class</span> <span class="token class-name">Order</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">int</span></span> Id <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token keyword">get</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token keyword">set</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>

<span class="token comment">// Order.g.cs (generated)</span> <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">partial</span> <span class="token keyword">class</span> <span class="token class-name">Order</span> <span class="token punctuation">:</span> <span class="token type-list"><span class="token class-name">IValidatable</span></span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">bool</span></span> <span class="token function">Validate</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=></span> Id <span class="token operator">></span> <span class="token number">0</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<p dir="auto">Consequences of the parts forming one type:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>One member set:</strong> members declared in any part are available to all parts. If the handwritten and generated parts both declare <code>Validate()</code> with the same signature, compilation fails with a duplicate-member error.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Combined declaration:</strong> the type implements the interfaces listed on every part, and <code>abstract</code> or <code>sealed</code> on any part applies to the whole type.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Matching parts:</strong> every part must use <code>partial</code>, have the same accessibility and be compiled into the same assembly and module.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Additive generation:</strong> the generator contributes new source instead of editing the handwritten file. Generated members are still part of the type's behavior, so they need the same review and tests as handwritten members.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/partial-classes-and-methods" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/partial-classes-and-methods" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: partial classes and members</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/partial-type" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/partial-type" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: partial types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: source generators</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Classes.md" class="internal-link">Classes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does the C# compiler remove a partial method and the calls to it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The compiler removes a partial method, together with every call to it, when no part of the type supplies an implementing declaration and the method qualifies as optional. It qualifies only if its declaration has:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">no access modifier, not even an explicit <code>private</code>;</li>
<li dir="auto">a <code>void</code> return type;</li>
<li dir="auto">no <code>out</code> parameters;</li>
<li dir="auto">none of the modifiers <code>virtual</code>, <code>override</code>, <code>sealed</code>, <code>new</code> or <code>extern</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Partial methods gained access modifiers, non-<code>void</code> returns and <code>out</code> parameters in C# 9. Those extended forms, such as <code>public partial bool Validate();</code>, always require an implementation, so leaving it out is a compile error rather than a silent removal.</p>
<p dir="auto">Optional partial methods suit hooks in generated code. A generator can declare <code>partial void OnNameChanged();</code> and call it, and the handwritten part may implement it. When no part implements it, the calls are removed at compile time, including evaluation of their argument expressions, so behavior expected from the hook never runs.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/partial-member" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/partial-member" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: partial members</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: classes (partial methods)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Classes.md" class="internal-link">Classes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When a class does not overload <code>==</code>, why do two separately created instances with equal fields compare unequal, and how can value equality be added?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">For a class, <code>==</code> without an overload compares references: it is <code>true</code> only when both operands refer to the same object. Two separately created instances are two objects, so they compare unequal even when every field matches. <code>Equals(object)</code> compares references in the same way only when neither the class nor any of its base classes overrides it, so the implementation inherited from <code>Object</code> applies; the absence of an <code>==</code> overload alone does not guarantee this.</p>
<p dir="auto">Value equality is added by deciding which fields make two instances equal and applying that rule consistently:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">implement <code>IEquatable&lt;T&gt;.Equals(T)</code> and override <code>Equals(object)</code> to compare those fields;</li>
<li dir="auto">override <code>GetHashCode</code> from the same fields, so equal instances produce equal hash codes and hash-based collections such as <code>Dictionary&lt;TKey,TValue&gt;</code> and <code>HashSet&lt;T&gt;</code> treat them as the same key;</li>
<li dir="auto">overload <code>==</code> and <code>!=</code> to call <code>Equals</code> when operator comparison belongs to the type's API. Overriding <code>Equals</code> alone leaves <code>==</code> comparing references.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A <code>record class</code> generates all of these members, comparing the runtime type and every field, so it is the shorter choice when that generated equality matches the domain.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/how-to-define-value-equality-for-a-type" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/how-to-define-value-equality-for-a-type" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: define value equality</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Classes.md" class="internal-link">Classes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a delegate, and what does a delegate value carry?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A delegate is a type that represents references to methods with a particular signature. The delegate type fixes the parameter and return types. A delegate value packages a compatible method so it can be stored, passed and invoked later like any other value.</p>
<p dir="auto">A delegate value carries:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Method:</strong> the method to call, which must be compatible with the delegate's signature.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Target (optional):</strong> a delegate closed over an instance method also stores the object the method runs on. A delegate with no bound object, such as one created from an ordinary static method, has no target. Reflection through <code>Delegate.CreateDelegate</code> can also create open instance delegates, which receive the instance as an argument, and static delegates closed over their first argument.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Invocation list:</strong> a delegate can combine several methods, for example with <code>+=</code>. Invoking it calls each in order.</li>
</ul>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> tenPercent <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Discount</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">0.10m</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token class-name">PriceCalculator</span> calc <span class="token operator">=</span> tenPercent<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Apply<span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token comment">// closed instance delegate: method Apply, target tenPercent</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> total <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token function">calc</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">3</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token number">20m</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>            <span class="token comment">// runs tenPercent.Apply: 54.00</span>

<span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">delegate</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> <span class="token function">PriceCalculator</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">int</span></span> quantity<span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> unitPrice<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>

<span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">sealed</span> <span class="token keyword">class</span> <span class="token class-name">Discount</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token keyword">private</span> <span class="token keyword">readonly</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> \_rate<span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token function">Discount</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> rate<span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=></span> \_rate <span class="token operator">=</span> rate<span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> <span class="token function">Apply</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">int</span></span> quantity<span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">decimal</span></span> unitPrice<span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=></span> quantity <span class="token operator">_</span> unitPrice <span class="token operator">_</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">1</span> <span class="token operator">-</span> \_rate<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<p dir="auto">Delegate values are immutable: adding or removing a method produces a new delegate. Lambdas and method groups convert to delegate types, which is how callbacks, LINQ operators and events pass behavior around.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/delegates/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/delegates/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: delegates</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/delegates" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/delegates" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: delegates</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.delegate.createdelegate?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.delegate.createdelegate?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Delegate.CreateDelegate</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Delegates.md" class="internal-link">Delegates</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When a multicast delegate is invoked, in what order do its methods run, and what happens to return values and exceptions?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Its methods run synchronously, one after another, in invocation-list order, which is the order in which they were combined. For a non-<code>void</code> delegate, the caller receives only the last method's return value. If any method throws, the exception propagates to the caller and the remaining methods are not invoked.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name">Func<span class="token punctuation">&lt;</span><span class="token keyword">int</span><span class="token punctuation">&gt;</span></span> f <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=&gt;</span> <span class="token number">1</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
f <span class="token operator">+=</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=&gt;</span> <span class="token number">2</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
f <span class="token operator">+=</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=&gt;</span> <span class="token number">3</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">int</span></span> result <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token function">f</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token comment">// 3; the results 1 and 2 are discarded</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">Consequences:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Lost results:</strong> every result is available only by enumerating <code>GetInvocationList()</code> and invoking each delegate separately.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>One failure skips later handlers:</strong> an event raised with a single call stops at the first subscriber that throws. Isolating subscribers requires invoking each entry from <code>GetInvocationList()</code> inside its own <code>try</code>/<code>catch</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/delegates" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/delegates" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: delegates (delegate invocation)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Delegates.md" class="internal-link">Delegates</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between an event and a public delegate field?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Outside code can only subscribe to and unsubscribe from an event, and the declaring type alone decides when it is raised. A public delegate field exposes the delegate value itself, so any outside code can also invoke it, overwrite it or clear it.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>What outside code does</th>
<th><code>public event EventHandler? Changed;</code></th>
<th><code>public EventHandler? Changed;</code> (field)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Add or remove a handler: <code>feed.Changed += OnChanged;</code></td>
<td>Allowed, through the event's <code>add</code> and <code>remove</code> accessors.</td>
<td>Allowed, by storing a new combined delegate in the field.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Raise it: <code>feed.Changed?.Invoke(feed, EventArgs.Empty);</code></td>
<td>Compile error, so only the publisher can announce the change.</td>
<td>Allowed, so any caller can send a notification for a change that never happened.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Overwrite it: <code>feed.Changed = OnChanged;</code> or <code>= null</code></td>
<td>Compile error.</td>
<td>Allowed, so one careless <code>=</code> silently removes every other subscriber.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Inside the declaring type, a field-like event behaves like its backing delegate, so the publisher can still invoke it and check it for <code>null</code>. The <code>event</code> keyword therefore restricts access to the same delegate mechanism rather than introducing a different one.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: events</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: classes (events)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Events.md" class="internal-link">Events</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can event subscriptions keep an otherwise unused object alive?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Subscribing stores a delegate in the publisher, and a delegate for an instance method keeps a reference to the subscriber as its target. The garbage collector reclaims only objects that are unreachable from roots. As long as the publisher is reachable, the subscriber is reachable through it, even when nothing else uses the subscriber.</p>
<p dir="auto">Reference path: GC root → publisher → event delegate → subscriber.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Long-lived publisher:</strong> a static event or an application-wide service stays reachable for the life of the process. Every subscriber that never unsubscribes stays in memory, and its handler keeps being called.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Short-lived publisher:</strong> references point from the publisher to its subscribers, not the reverse. Once the publisher becomes unreachable, it no longer keeps its subscribers alive.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The fix is to unsubscribe with <code>-=</code> when the subscriber's lifetime ends, commonly in <code>Dispose</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/how-to-subscribe-to-and-unsubscribe-from-events" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/how-to-subscribe-to-and-unsubscribe-from-events" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: subscribe to and unsubscribe from events</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: events</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: GC fundamentals</a></p>
