</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Events.md" class="internal-link">Events</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a C# record, and what does the compiler generate for it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A record is a class or struct declared with <code>record</code>, whose equality is based on its data rather than its identity. The compiler generates the members that make it behave as a data value:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Value equality:</strong> <code>Equals</code>, <code>GetHashCode</code>, <code>==</code> and <code>!=</code> treat two records as equal when they have the same runtime type and equal field values, each field compared with its own type's equality. Two separately created <code>record class</code> instances with equal data compare equal, unlike two ordinary class instances.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Nondestructive mutation:</strong> <code>p with { Age = 31 }</code> copies the record and changes the listed members. The copy is shallow, so referenced objects are shared.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Readable <code>ToString</code>:</strong> prints the type name and public members, such as <code>Person { Name = Alice, Age = 30 }</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Positional members:</strong> <code>record Person(string Name, int Age)</code> also generates a primary constructor, a public property for each parameter and <code>Deconstruct</code>. These properties are init-only for <code>record class</code> and <code>readonly record struct</code>, but settable for a plain <code>record struct</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><code>record</code> alone means <code>record class</code>, a reference type that can inherit from another record class, while <code>record struct</code> is a value type. Records fit DTOs, messages and value objects. Types whose identity matters more than their current data, such as Entity Framework Core entities, fit ordinary classes better.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In <code>record Wrapper(List&lt;int&gt; Items)</code>, if <code>var b = a with { };</code> and an item is added to <code>b.Items</code>, does <code>a</code> observe the change, and why?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Yes. A <code>with</code> expression makes a shallow copy: it copies each field of <code>a</code> into the new record, and for a reference-type field that copies the reference, not the object it points to. <code>a.Items</code> and <code>b.Items</code> therefore refer to the same <code>List&lt;int&gt;</code>, so an item added through <code>b.Items</code> is visible through <code>a.Items</code>.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> a <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Wrapper</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">List<span class="token punctuation">&lt;</span><span class="token keyword">int</span><span class="token punctuation">&gt;</span></span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token number">1</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token number">2</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> b <span class="token operator">=</span> a <span class="token keyword">with</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
b<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Items<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">Add</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">3</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
Console<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">WriteLine</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>a<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Items<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Count<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token comment">// 3</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">An independent copy needs its own list, for example <code>a with { Items = new List&lt;int&gt;(a.Items) }</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Given <code>record Wrapper(List&lt;int&gt; Items)</code> and <code>var b = a with { };</code>, are <code>a</code> and <code>b</code> equal before and after an item is added to <code>b.Items</code>? Why?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They are equal both before and after the item is added. Generated record equality compares the runtime type and each field using that field's own equality, and <code>List&lt;int&gt;</code> compares by reference. Because <code>with</code> copied the reference, <code>a.Items</code> and <code>b.Items</code> refer to the same list. Adding an item changes that list in place without replacing it. The comparison therefore sees the same reference both times and never looks at the list's contents.</p>
<p dir="auto">The converse follows from the same rule: two <code>Wrapper</code> instances holding separate lists with identical items compare unequal.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can a record compare a collection member by its elements instead of by reference?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">There are two ways: override the record's equality so it compares the collection's elements, or store the elements in a type whose own <code>Equals</code> compares elements. Generated record equality compares each field with that field type's equality, and <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code> compares references, so the default never looks at the elements.</p>
<p dir="auto">Overriding equality in the record replaces the generated <code>Equals(T?)</code> and keeps <code>GetHashCode</code> consistent with it:</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">sealed</span> <span class="token keyword">record</span> <span class="token class-name">Basket</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">string</span></span> Owner<span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token class-name">List<span class="token punctuation">&lt;</span><span class="token keyword">string</span><span class="token punctuation">&gt;</span></span> Items<span class="token punctuation">)</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">bool</span></span> <span class="token function">Equals</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name">Basket<span class="token punctuation">?</span></span> other<span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=&gt;</span>
        other <span class="token keyword">is</span> <span class="token keyword">not</span> <span class="token keyword">null</span>
        <span class="token operator">&amp;&amp;</span> Owner <span class="token operator">==</span> other<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Owner
        <span class="token operator">&amp;&amp;</span> Items<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">SequenceEqual</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>other<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Items<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token comment">// element-wise and order-sensitive</span>

```
<span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">override</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">int</span></span> <span class="token function">GetHashCode</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> hash <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">HashCode</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
    hash<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">Add</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>Owner<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
    <span class="token keyword">foreach</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> item <span class="token keyword">in</span> Items<span class="token punctuation">)</span> hash<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">Add</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>item<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
    <span class="token keyword">return</span> hash<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">ToHashCode</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
```

<span class="token punctuation">}</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<p dir="auto">The generated <code>==</code> and <code>!=</code> call this <code>Equals</code>, so they also compare elements. <code>GetHashCode</code> hashes the same components that <code>Equals</code> compares, so records that compare equal produce equal hash codes, as hash-based collections require.</p>
<p dir="auto">Trade-offs:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost:</strong> <code>SequenceEqual</code> compares elements pairwise in order and stops at the first mismatch, so a comparison examines up to all n items, O(n), instead of comparing one reference. The <code>GetHashCode</code> shown always visits every item, so it is O(n).</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Mutation:</strong> this equality and hash read the list's current contents. If the list changes while the record is stored in a <code>HashSet&lt;T&gt;</code> or used as a dictionary key, the record's current hash can stop matching the hash the collection recorded, and its equality can change, so lookups become unreliable. A different hash and a failed lookup are both possible but not guaranteed, because different contents can produce the same hash code. This equality therefore fits collections that are not changed while the record serves as a key.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Immutability alone is not enough:</strong> an immutable collection prevents such changes, but its type's own <code>Equals</code> still decides whether elements are compared.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/how-to-define-value-equality-for-a-type" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/how-to-define-value-equality-for-a-type" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: define value equality</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Object.GetHashCode</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Dictionary&lt;TKey,TValue&gt;</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/dotnet/blob/b0f34d51fccc69fd334253924abd8d6853fad7aa/src/runtime/src/libraries/System.Linq/src/System/Linq/SequenceEqual.cs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/dotnet/blob/b0f34d51fccc69fd334253924abd8d6853fad7aa/src/runtime/src/libraries/System.Linq/src/System/Linq/SequenceEqual.cs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET runtime: SequenceEqual source</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>record class</code> a better choice than <code>readonly record struct</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A <code>record class</code> is the better choice when the value is large, needs inheritance, uses <code>null</code> as an ordinary 'no value' state, or is frequently handled as <code>object</code> or an interface. A <code>readonly record struct</code> fits small immutable values where avoiding a separate heap object matters more than those features. Both generate value equality and support <code>with</code>, so equality alone does not decide.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th><code>record class</code></th>
<th><code>readonly record struct</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Assignment and passing</td>
<td>Copies a reference, so the cost is the same however many fields the record has.</td>
<td>Copies every field, which is cheap for a few small fields and grows with the size of the value.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Storage</td>
<td>Each instance is a separate heap object that the garbage collector must track.</td>
<td>Stored inline in its variable, field or array element. Converting it to <code>object</code> or an interface boxes it into a heap copy.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Absence</td>
<td>A variable of the type can be <code>null</code>.</td>
<td>Needs <code>Nullable&lt;T&gt;</code> (<code>T?</code>) to represent a missing value.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Inheritance</td>
<td>Can derive from another record class, and equality accounts for the runtime type.</td>
<td>Cannot take part in inheritance: it neither derives from a record nor can be derived from.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">When inheritance or <code>null</code> as absence decides the choice, no measurement is needed. When the justification rests on performance, the size at which copying outweighs allocation depends on the workload, so allocation and copy costs drive the decision only when measurement shows they matter.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: value types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: boxing</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">If record equality is customized, why must <code>GetHashCode</code> stay consistent with it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Hash-based collections such as <code>Dictionary&lt;TKey,TValue&gt;</code> and <code>HashSet&lt;T&gt;</code> use <code>GetHashCode</code> to decide where to look, and then call <code>Equals</code> only on entries with a matching hash code. Objects that are equal must therefore return the same hash code. Otherwise a lookup never reaches <code>Equals</code> for the matching entry.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, suppose a custom <code>Equals</code> ignores an <code>UpdatedAt</code> property, but the generated <code>GetHashCode</code> still includes every field:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Record <code>a</code> is added to a <code>HashSet</code> under a hash code that includes <code>a.UpdatedAt</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Record <code>b</code> differs only in <code>UpdatedAt</code>, so <code>a.Equals(b)</code> is <code>true</code>, but <code>b</code>'s hash code is computed from a different <code>UpdatedAt</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">A lookup for <code>b</code> searches by <code>b</code>'s hash code and never compares it with <code>a</code>. <code>Contains(b)</code> returns <code>false</code>, and <code>Add(b)</code> stores a second entry equal to the first, unless the two hash codes happen to collide.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><code>GetHashCode</code> therefore must not depend on anything that can differ between two equal records, such as a property that <code>Equals</code> ignores. Hashing exactly the components that <code>Equals</code> compares is the usual choice. A coarser hash over a subset of them is also valid, because equal records agree on that subset; it only causes more collisions. The reverse is not required: unequal objects may share a hash code, which only costs extra <code>Equals</code> calls. For records, the compiler reports CS8851 when a record defines its own <code>Equals</code> but not <code>GetHashCode</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Object.GetHashCode</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/compiler-messages/record-declaration-errors" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/compiler-messages/record-declaration-errors" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: record declaration errors</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/how-to-define-value-equality-for-a-type" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/how-to-define-value-equality-for-a-type" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: define value equality</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Can a record struct be used safely as a <code>Dictionary</code> key, and what can make it unsafe?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Yes, as long as the equality and hash code the dictionary actually uses cannot change while the key is stored. That is either the key type's own equality or the <code>IEqualityComparer&lt;TKey&gt;</code> supplied to the dictionary. A dictionary stores its own copy of a struct key, so later assignments to the original variable do not affect the stored key. The risk comes from referenced objects: copying a struct copies references, not the objects they point to. Suppose the effective equality or a supplied comparer observes a referenced object's mutable state. Changing that object can make the key's current hash differ from the hash the dictionary recorded and can change its equality. The dictionary does not notice, so lookups for the entry can fail.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> tag <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Tag</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> Name <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token string">"a"</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> map <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Dictionary<span class="token punctuation">&lt;</span>Key<span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token keyword">string</span><span class="token punctuation">&gt;</span></span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token punctuation">[</span><span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Key</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">1</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> tag<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">]</span> <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token string">"x"</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>

tag<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Name <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token string">"b"</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>                                       <span class="token comment">// changes state inside the stored key</span>
map<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">ContainsKey</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Key</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">1</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> tag<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>                    <span class="token comment">// false unless the "a" and "b" key hashes collide</span>
map<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">ContainsKey</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Key</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">1</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">Tag</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> Name <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token string">"a"</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token comment">// false: Equals now sees "b"</span>

<span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">record</span> <span class="token class-name">Tag</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token return-type class-name"><span class="token keyword">string</span></span> Name <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token keyword">get</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token keyword">set</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span> <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token string">""</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span> <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">readonly</span> <span class="token keyword">record</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">struct</span></span> <span class="token function">Key</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">int</span></span> Id<span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token class-name">Tag</span> Label<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<p dir="auto"><code>readonly</code> prevents reassigning the struct's own fields but does not freeze the objects they reference. A reference member compared by reference, such as a <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code> under the default comparer, stays stable when its contents change, because its identity does not. That holds only while the effective comparer also compares it by reference. A supplied comparer that compares the list's elements makes the key depend on mutable state again. A record struct key is therefore safe when every component that the effective equality and hash observe is immutable or compared by reference.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: records</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: value types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Dictionary&lt;TKey,TValue&gt;</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Object.GetHashCode</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Records.md" class="internal-link">Records</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is <code>StringBuilder</code> a better choice than string concatenation?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>StringBuilder</code> is the better choice when text is built through many appends, especially in a loop or another frequently executed path where allocations matter. For a small, fixed expression, interpolation or concatenation is clearer.</p>
<p dir="auto">The difference comes from string immutability:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Repeated concatenation:</strong> a <code>string</code> cannot change, so each <code>result += part</code> allocates a new string holding the accumulated text plus the new part. Each loop step leaves behind an intermediate string, and the growing text is copied again every time.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>StringBuilder</code>:</strong> each append writes into a mutable buffer, and <code>ToString()</code> creates the final string once. The buffer reallocates only when it runs out of capacity, so an initial capacity close to the expected final size avoids that growth.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">No fixed number of appends marks the switch point. The signal for a builder is repeated construction in code where measured allocation cost matters.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/stringbuilder" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/stringbuilder" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Using the StringBuilder class</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Strings.md" class="internal-link">Strings</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can <code>ReferenceEquals(a, b)</code> be false when <code>a == b</code> is true for strings?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They test different things. For strings, <code>==</code> compares contents: it returns true when both strings hold the same characters in the same order, using an ordinal, case-sensitive comparison. <code>ReferenceEquals</code> returns true only when both references point to the same object.</p>
<p dir="auto">Equal text can therefore live in two separate objects. Strings built at run time are not interned automatically, so two strings built from the same pieces are normally distinct instances: <code>==</code> returns true while <code>ReferenceEquals</code> returns false.</p>
<p dir="auto">Interning can make identity coincide through two different mechanisms:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Explicit <code>String.Intern</code>:</strong> it returns the intern pool's reference for a string with that value, adding the argument to the pool if no equal string is there yet. Equal strings passed through <code>String.Intern</code> therefore always come back as the same reference.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Automatic literal interning:</strong> identical string literals typically share one pooled instance, so <code>ReferenceEquals</code> often returns true for them. A compilation can request <code>NoStringInterning</code>, and runtime behavior may vary, so literal identity is not a dependable contract.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Because identity depends on how each string was produced, <code>ReferenceEquals</code> is not a test of content. Content comparisons belong to <code>==</code> or <code>string.Equals</code>, with an explicit <code>StringComparison</code> stating the rule the data needs: ordinal comparison (<code>Ordinal</code> or <code>OrdinalIgnoreCase</code>) for protocol keys and identifiers, and culture-aware comparison for natural-language text shown to users.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.referenceequals?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.referenceequals?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Object.ReferenceEquals</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.op_equality?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.op_equality?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: String equality operator</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.intern?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.intern?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: String.Intern</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/best-practices-strings" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/best-practices-strings" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Best practices for comparing strings</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Strings.md" class="internal-link">Strings</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why might changing a struct inside <code>foreach</code> not update the collection, and how can it be fixed?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">In an ordinary (non-<code>ref</code>) <code>foreach</code>, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.</li>
<li dir="auto">Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code>, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.</p>
<p dir="auto">The stored elements can be updated in two ways:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Indexed write-back:</strong> a loop by index reads <code>items[i]</code> into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to <code>items[i]</code>, replacing the whole element value.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>ref</code> iteration:</strong> when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as <code>Span&lt;T&gt;</code> does, <code>foreach (ref var item in span)</code> makes <code>item</code> an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Structure types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Value types</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types.md" class="internal-link">Types</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Where does boxing commonly happen, and how can it be reduced?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to <code>object</code> or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated <code>int?</code> boxes its underlying <code>int</code> value, and an empty one converts to a <code>null</code> reference without allocating.</p>
<p dir="auto">Common places:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>object</code>-typed variables, collections and parameters:</strong> <code>object o = 42;</code>, adding an <code>int</code> to a <code>List&lt;object&gt;</code> or an <code>ArrayList</code>, or passing a struct to a parameter of type <code>object</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Interface-typed variables and parameters:</strong> assigning a struct to an <code>IComparable</code> variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.</p>
<p dir="auto">Ways to reduce boxing:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generic collections and APIs:</strong> a generic collection such as <code>List&lt;int&gt;</code> is specialized for <code>int</code>, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to <code>object</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:</strong> a method such as <code>Max&lt;T&gt;(T a, T b) where T : IComparable&lt;T&gt;</code> can call <code>CompareTo</code> on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types.md" class="internal-link">Types</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a type be a <code>struct</code>, <code>class</code>, or <code>record class</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A <code>struct</code> fits a small value that is copied field by field, a <code>class</code> fits an object with its own identity, and a <code>record class</code> fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th><code>struct</code></th>
<th><code>class</code></th>
<th><code>record class</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Assignment and passing</td>
<td>Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object.</td>
<td>Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object.</td>
<td>Copies a reference, as a class does.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Default equality</td>
<td><code>Equals</code> is true when both have the same type and the same stored values.</td>
<td>Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches.</td>
<td>Compiler-generated <code>Equals</code> and <code>==</code> compare the type and member values. The generated <code>GetHashCode</code> compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Mutation</td>
<td>A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it.</td>
<td>A change is visible through every reference to the object.</td>
<td>Positional properties are init-only by default, and a <code>with</code> expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Allocation and cost</td>
<td>Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates.</td>
<td>One heap allocation per instance.</td>
<td>One heap allocation per instance, as with a class.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Inheritance</td>
<td>Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces.</td>
<td>Supports class inheritance.</td>
<td>Can inherit only from another record.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical fit</td>
<td>Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate.</td>
<td>Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior.</td>
<td>Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Structure types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Value types</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Records</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types.md" class="internal-link">Types</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Programming/NET/Runtime"><h4>Runtime</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do managed and unmanaged code differ, and why does interop require careful lifetime management?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Managed code runs under the CLR and relies on its services, such as garbage collection of managed objects, exception handling and the runtime type system. Unmanaged (native) code runs outside those services. It follows a native platform ABI and its own ownership rules, such as explicit freeing or reference counting.</p>
<p dir="auto">Interop needs careful lifetime management because the GC manages only one side of the boundary:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The GC tracks managed objects only. It cannot tell when a native handle or buffer is no longer needed.</li>
<li dir="auto">A native resource is released only when code calls its native cleanup. Disposal does this deterministically when ownership ends. A finalizer on the managed wrapper can do it later, as a fallback, if disposal was missed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>SafeHandle</code> is the usual managed owner for a native handle. It releases the handle when disposed, or during finalization if disposal never happened.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">If no code clearly owns a native resource, nothing may release it, and it leaks. Interop declarations must also match the native ABI, such as calling convention and data layout. That requirement affects whether a call works correctly, not how long a resource lives.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/native-interop/abi-support" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/native-interop/abi-support" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Native interoperability ABI support</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.safehandle" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.safehandle" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: SafeHandle class</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Common Language Runtime.md" class="internal-link">Common Language Runtime</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does .NET turn IL into machine code, and when do JIT, ReadyToRun and Native AOT each fit?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Assemblies normally contain IL, which the processor cannot run directly. By default the runtime's JIT compiler turns each method into machine code when it is first needed. ReadyToRun moves part of that work to publish time while keeping the JIT. Native AOT moves all of it to publish time and ships no JIT.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>JIT</th>
<th>ReadyToRun</th>
<th>Native AOT</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>When machine code is produced</td>
<td>At run time, as methods are first used. Tiered compilation can later recompile hot methods with more optimization.</td>
<td>At publish time for many methods. The JIT still compiles methods without usable precompiled code and can re-optimize hot ones.</td>
<td>Entirely at publish time. The app runs without a JIT.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Startup</td>
<td>Early calls pay for compilation.</td>
<td>Less compilation work at startup.</td>
<td>No JIT work at startup.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Runtime flexibility</td>
<td>Dynamic loading and runtime code generation work.</td>
<td>Same as JIT, because the IL is kept.</td>
<td>Restricted: no runtime code generation, and code must work with trimming.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main cost</td>
<td>Compilation time on first use.</td>
<td>Larger assemblies built for a specific target.</td>
<td>Compatibility constraints and platform-specific output.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">JIT is the flexible default, especially when an app loads code dynamically or generates code at run time. ReadyToRun reduces startup compilation without giving up the JIT. Native AOT fits startup- and footprint-sensitive deployments whose code and dependencies work with AOT and trimming. ReadyToRun trades larger assemblies for less startup compilation, while Native AOT trades runtime flexibility for startup and footprint benefits, so the choice rests on measured startup and footprint needs and on the runtime features the app requires. Native AOT is not a universal upgrade.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET application publishing overview</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Native AOT deployment</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Common Language Runtime.md" class="internal-link">Common Language Runtime</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the .NET garbage collector decide what managed memory it can reclaim?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The GC can reclaim any managed object that is no longer reachable from a root. Reachability alone decides: an object that is still reachable stays, even if the program will never use it again.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Start from roots.</strong> Roots are references the runtime knows about directly. They include static fields, local variables and CPU registers of running methods while the JIT reports them as live, and GC handles.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Mark reachable objects.</strong> The GC follows reference fields from the roots, then from every object it reaches. Each object found this way is live.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Treat everything else as reclaimable.</strong> An object that was not reached is eligible for reclamation. Cycles do not keep objects alive: two objects that refer only to each other are collectible once nothing reachable points to either.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Qualifications:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generations:</strong> a collection reclaims objects only in the generations it collects. A young-generation collection also inspects the older-heap ranges that CoreCLR's write barriers recorded in a card table as possibly pointing to young objects. It does not scan the whole older generation, and it does not reclaim older objects. An unreachable generation 2 object is therefore reclaimed only by a collection that includes generation 2.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Finalization:</strong> an unreachable object whose finalizer is still registered survives until its finalizer has run. A later collection normally reclaims it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Timing:</strong> eligibility does not mean immediate reclamation or memory returned to the operating system.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The reachability decision covers managed memory only. Native handles and buffers need explicit cleanup, typically through <code>IDisposable</code> and <code>using</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Fundamentals of garbage collection</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1bde9a53cb55127c1e154a2e98a7332477280abf/docs/design/coreclr/jit/GC-write-barriers.md#L25-L62" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1bde9a53cb55127c1e154a2e98a7332477280abf/docs/design/coreclr/jit/GC-write-barriers.md#L25-L62" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">dotnet/runtime: CoreCLR GC write barriers</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Garbage Collector.md" class="internal-link">Garbage Collector</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do generations make .NET garbage collection more efficient?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Generations let the GC collect the small, recently allocated part of the heap often and the large, long-lived part rarely. This pays off because most objects become unreachable soon after allocation. A collection limited to new objects reclaims much of the garbage while examining little of the heap.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generation 0:</strong> most new objects start here. It is collected most often, and a collection typically finds many of its objects already unreachable.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generation 1:</strong> objects that survived a generation 0 collection. It buffers between short-lived and long-lived objects. A generation 1 collection also collects generation 0.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generation 2:</strong> long-lived objects, such as application-lifetime services and caches. A generation 2 collection is a full collection. It includes every generation and must consider every reachable object, so its work grows with the whole live heap. Its actual cost depends on the workload, heap size and GC mode.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Survivors of a generation 0 or 1 collection usually move up one generation, although pinning and collector heuristics can keep an object in its current generation. Objects that survive a generation 2 collection stay in generation 2. Large objects, normally 85,000 bytes or more, go to the Large Object Heap, which is collected together with generation 2.</p>
<p dir="auto">The design has two consequences:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">A young collection does not walk the whole older generation, so references from old objects to young ones must be recorded separately. The runtime records them with write barriers and a card table, and the young collection inspects only the recorded older-heap ranges.</li>
<li dir="auto">An object that lives just long enough to be promoted is then reclaimed only by a less frequent collection that includes its new generation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Fundamentals of garbage collection</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1bde9a53cb55127c1e154a2e98a7332477280abf/docs/design/coreclr/jit/GC-write-barriers.md#L25-L62" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1bde9a53cb55127c1e154a2e98a7332477280abf/docs/design/coreclr/jit/GC-write-barriers.md#L25-L62" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">dotnet/runtime: CoreCLR GC write barriers</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Garbage Collector.md" class="internal-link">Garbage Collector</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the .NET GC find old-to-young references during a young-generation collection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The GC relies on write barriers that maintain a card table. When code stores a reference into a heap object, the write barrier can mark the area of the older heap that now points to young objects. A young-generation collection scans those marked areas, in addition to the roots, instead of walking the entire older generation.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is needed because a young object can be reachable only through a field of an older object. Roots alone would miss that reference, and the collector would reclaim a live object. Scanning every older object on each young collection would make it nearly as expensive as a full collection.</p>
<p dir="auto">In CoreCLR the process is:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The JIT inserts a write barrier around managed reference stores into heap objects.</li>
<li dir="auto">When a store may create a reference from an older generation to a younger one, the barrier marks the matching card-table entry. Each entry covers a small range of heap memory.</li>
<li dir="auto">A generation 0 or 1 collection scans the objects in dirty card ranges, follows the young references found there, and keeps those young objects alive.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The cost is a little extra work on reference writes, in exchange for young collections that do not walk the whole older heap. Which stores the barrier marks, how much memory each card covers and the exact scanning work are CoreCLR implementation details. They depend on runtime version and collection type and are not a .NET API contract.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1bde9a53cb55127c1e154a2e98a7332477280abf/docs/design/coreclr/jit/GC-write-barriers.md#L25-L62" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1bde9a53cb55127c1e154a2e98a7332477280abf/docs/design/coreclr/jit/GC-write-barriers.md#L25-L62" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">dotnet/runtime: CoreCLR GC write barriers</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Fundamentals of garbage collection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Garbage Collector.md" class="internal-link">Garbage Collector</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can process memory stay high after a generation 2 collection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A generation 2 collection frees space only from unreachable managed objects, and freed space is not necessarily returned to the operating system. Memory can stay high for several independent reasons:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Live retention:</strong> objects still reachable from roots, such as caches or static fields, survive every collection. The memory stays until the reference keeping the graph alive is removed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Fragmentation:</strong> pinned objects, and areas that are swept rather than compacted, can leave free gaps between survivors. The Large Object Heap in ordinary collections is one such area. The heap keeps that space, but new allocations may not fit into it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retained capacity:</strong> the GC can keep memory committed after a collection so later allocations can reuse it. Committed heap size can therefore exceed the size of live objects.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Memory outside the GC heap:</strong> native allocations and other non-GC memory in the process are not reclaimed by a managed collection.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Live object bytes, committed GC memory and process working set are different measurements, so a drop in one need not appear in another. Runtime counters and memory traces separate these causes before code or GC settings are changed. A large live heap points to retention. Much free or committed space relative to live objects points to fragmentation or retained capacity.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/performance" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/performance" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Garbage collection and performance</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Garbage Collector.md" class="internal-link">Garbage Collector</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Can a .NET application leak memory even though it has garbage collection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Yes. The garbage collector reclaims a managed object only when the object is no longer reachable, and it cannot tell that a reachable object is no longer needed. Resources outside the managed heap can also leak.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Managed retention:</strong> an object stays alive while a chain of references from a GC root, such as a static field or a local variable on a thread's stack, still reaches it. An unbounded cache held in a static field keeps its entries reachable. So does a long-lived publisher whose event still holds a subscriber's handler. The GC is working correctly here: it never reclaims data the program can still reach.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unmanaged resources:</strong> native memory and operating-system resources, such as files or network connections, must be released explicitly, and the GC does not know how to release them. If neither the owner's <code>Dispose</code> call nor a finalizable wrapper such as <code>SafeHandle</code> releases them, they stay allocated even after the managed wrapper object is collected.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Rising memory alone does not prove a leak, because heap growth, caches and allocators can keep memory high for legitimate reasons. A leak is established by the reference path that keeps unwanted objects alive, or by a native allocation that is never released.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Fundamentals of garbage collection</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Implement a Dispose method</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-memory-leak" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-memory-leak" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Debug a memory leak in .NET</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Memory Leaks.md" class="internal-link">Memory Leaks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can a suspected memory leak in a running .NET application be diagnosed?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Diagnosis first confirms a sustained growth trend, then follows the kind of memory that is growing until evidence explains why it is retained. For managed memory, that evidence is the reference path from a GC root to objects that are no longer needed.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Confirm a trend:</strong> runtime counters, for example from <code>dotnet-counters</code>, are compared across comparable workload cycles and at comparable points relative to collections. A single high reading or growth during warm-up is not yet evidence of a leak.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Locate the growth:</strong> counters indicate where to look, not the cause. Heap-size readings depend on the measurement. On .NET 9 and later, the runtime's GC heap-size metric, <code>dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.size</code>, includes fragmentation. For apps on .NET 8 and earlier, <code>dotnet-counters</code> falls back to legacy EventCounters, whose <code>gc-heap-size</code> counter is based on <code>GC.GetTotalMemory</code> and excludes fragmentation. GC committed memory also includes capacity ready for future allocations. Whichever measurement is used, a rising heap metric is a lead toward managed retention rather than proof of it. Process memory that rises without matching growth in GC committed memory is a lead toward memory outside the managed heap, such as native allocations or handles.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Managed growth, compare heap contents:</strong> dumps taken at equivalent workload points, for example with <code>dotnet-dump collect</code>, show which types grow in count or total size. In <code>dotnet-dump analyze</code>, <code>dumpheap -stat</code> summarizes the heap by type.</li>
