<li dir="auto"><strong>Managed growth, find the retaining path:</strong> for a representative instance of a growing type, <code>gcroot &lt;address&gt;</code> lists the chain of references from a GC root, such as a static field, to that object. The path names the holder, such as a cache without eviction or an event subscription that is never removed. The fix bounds or ends that ownership.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Native or handle growth:</strong> this branch needs evidence from its own layer, such as a native allocation or an operating-system handle that is never released. <code>gcroot</code> explains only managed reachability, so it cannot establish this cause.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The type that uses the most memory is only a lead until a retaining path explains it. A retaining path proves that an object is reachable. The retention is a leak only when the object is no longer useful.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-memory-leak" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-memory-leak" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Debug a memory leak in .NET</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/built-in-metrics-runtime" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/built-in-metrics-runtime" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET runtime metrics</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/available-counters" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/available-counters" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Well-known EventCounters in .NET</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.gc.gettotalmemory" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.gc.gettotalmemory" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: GC.GetTotalMemory</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/dotnet-counters" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/dotnet-counters" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: dotnet-counters</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Fundamentals of garbage collection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Memory Leaks.md" class="internal-link">Memory Leaks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is <code>using</code> needed when .NET already has garbage collection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The garbage collector frees managed memory when allocations or low system memory trigger a collection, not when code has finished with an object. Many objects also hold resources other than managed memory, such as files, network connections or database connections. Those resources are limited, and the GC does not know how to release them. At best, a finalizer releases them at an unpredictable time later, so a resource can stay open long after its last use or be exhausted.</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>using</code> makes the release deterministic. The compiler wraps the scope in <code>try</code>/<code>finally</code> and calls <code>Dispose</code> on the <code>IDisposable</code> object in the <code>finally</code> block. The resource is therefore released as soon as control leaves the scope, whether normally or through an exception. <code>await using</code> does the same for <code>IAsyncDisposable</code> by awaiting <code>DisposeAsync</code>.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token keyword">using</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> stream <span class="token operator">=</span> File<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">OpenRead</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>path<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token comment">// reads from stream</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
<span class="token comment">// stream.Dispose() has run here, even if reading threw</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">Disposal releases the resource, not the object's managed memory. The GC still reclaims that memory later, once the object is unreachable.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/using" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/using" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: using statement</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Fundamentals of garbage collection</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Implement a Dispose method</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Memory Leaks.md" class="internal-link">Memory Leaks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do <code>IDisposable</code> and a finalizer differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>Dispose</code> is deterministic cleanup that the owning code calls when it has finished with a resource. A finalizer is an optional fallback that the garbage collector runs at an unpredictable time after it finds the object unreachable, so that cleanup can still happen if <code>Dispose</code> was never called. <code>IDisposable</code> itself requires only the <code>Dispose</code> method, not a finalizer.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th><code>IDisposable.Dispose</code></th>
<th>Finalizer</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Trigger</td>
<td>Owning code calls it, directly or through <code>using</code>.</td>
<td>The GC queues it to run after finding the object unreachable.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Timing</td>
<td>Runs at a known point, so scarce resources are released promptly.</td>
<td>Runs at an unpredictable time after the object becomes unreachable. .NET 5 and later do not run finalizers when the application exits, so it may never run.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it can safely clean up</td>
<td>Managed <code>IDisposable</code> objects the type owns, plus its unmanaged resources.</td>
<td>Only unmanaged resources the object owns directly. Other managed objects may already have been finalized, because finalization order is undefined.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>An ordinary method call.</td>
<td>Each finalizable object adds an entry that the GC must process in its finalization queue.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">When a type defines its own finalizer, the two work together. <code>Dispose</code> performs the cleanup and calls <code>GC.SuppressFinalize</code>, so the finalizer runs only when disposal was missed. Most types can avoid an own-type finalizer altogether. A type whose native handle is wrapped in a <code>SafeHandle</code> needs no finalizer of its own, because <code>SafeHandle</code> already provides finalization for that handle. A custom finalizer is justified only for an unmanaged resource that the type owns directly and that no safe wrapper can hold.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Implement a Dispose method</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/finalizers" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/finalizers" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Finalizers</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.safehandle" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.safehandle" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: SafeHandle</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Memory Leaks.md" class="internal-link">Memory Leaks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the .NET dispose pattern work?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The pattern routes both cleanup paths through one method, <code>Dispose(bool disposing)</code>. Its argument tells it whether owning code called <code>Dispose</code> or a finalizer is running.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Explicit path:</strong> owning code calls the public, non-virtual <code>Dispose()</code>, which calls <code>Dispose(true)</code> and then <code>GC.SuppressFinalize(this)</code>. With <code>disposing</code> set to <code>true</code>, the method releases both the managed <code>IDisposable</code> objects the type owns and its unmanaged resources. Suppressing finalization tells the GC that cleanup is already done, so it does not run the finalizer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Finalizer path:</strong> if <code>Dispose</code> was never called and the type has a finalizer, the finalizer calls <code>Dispose(false)</code>. That call releases only unmanaged resources the object owns directly. It does not touch other managed objects, because finalization order is undefined and they may already have been finalized.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Repeated calls:</strong> <code>Dispose(bool)</code> records that disposal has happened and returns early on later calls. Calling <code>Dispose</code> more than once is therefore harmless and never releases the same resource twice.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Inheritance:</strong> in an unsealed type, <code>Dispose(bool)</code> is <code>protected virtual</code>. A derived class overrides it to release its own resources and then calls <code>base.Dispose(disposing)</code>.</li>
</ul>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">class</span> <span class="token class-name">NativeBuffer</span> <span class="token punctuation">:</span> <span class="token type-list"><span class="token class-name">IDisposable</span></span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token keyword">private</span> <span class="token class-name">IntPtr</span> _buffer <span class="token operator">=</span> Marshal<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">AllocHGlobal</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token number">1024</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>

<p dir="auto">This type needs a finalizer only because it holds a raw native pointer directly. When a <code>SafeHandle</code> owns the native resource, the type implements <code>Dispose()</code> and <code>Dispose(bool)</code> without a finalizer, and the <code>SafeHandle</code> supplies the finalization fallback.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Implement a Dispose method</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/finalizers" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/finalizers" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Finalizers</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Memory Leaks.md" class="internal-link">Memory Leaks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does the CLR do when an application starts, and why does startup behavior matter?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A native host first locates and initializes a compatible runtime and asks it to run the app. Most of the remaining work then happens on demand rather than in fixed phases. Assemblies load as code needs them. Each method runs from usable ReadyToRun precompiled code or is JIT-compiled when first needed. Static type initialization runs no later than the first use that requires it, and its exact timing depends on whether the class has an explicit static constructor. This work can add cold-start latency, so early requests can be slower than steady state. How much depends on the application, its deployment and which code paths run first.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Host:</strong> for an app running on CoreCLR, the app's executable or the <code>dotnet</code> command acts as a native host. It reads the runtime configuration, selects a compatible runtime, resolves the paths of the app's dependencies, initializes the CLR and requests that it run the app.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Assembly loading:</strong> the CLR loads the entry assembly in order to run it. Referenced assemblies load as needed, not necessarily before the entry point runs. Their exact load timing is unspecified and can vary with the runtime version and optimizations.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Code generation:</strong> a method needs native code before it runs, including the entry point. If its assembly contains usable ReadyToRun code for the method, that code runs. Otherwise the JIT compiler compiles the method's IL. Some methods still need the JIT in a ReadyToRun app, and tiered compilation can later replace frequently called code with more optimized code.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Type initialization:</strong> in C#, a class with an explicit static constructor is initialized when its first instance is created or a static member is first referenced. Without one, static field initializers run at an implementation-dependent time before the first use of a static field. Expensive static setup adds its cost to whichever operation reaches that boundary first.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These costs land on the first work that crosses each boundary. They can appear in the first requests after a deployment or scale-out, or later when a new code path first runs. ReadyToRun reduces runtime JIT work, including for code first used after startup, but produces larger binaries. Native AOT compiles the app ahead of time and has no runtime JIT, at the cost of restrictions such as no runtime code generation. Traces show which cost dominates for a particular application.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/design/features/host-components.md" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/design/features/host-components.md" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">dotnet/runtime: Host components</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/dependency-loading/loading-managed" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/dependency-loading/loading-managed" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Managed assembly loading algorithm</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/managed-execution-process" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/managed-execution-process" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Managed execution process</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/ready-to-run" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/ready-to-run" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ReadyToRun compilation</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Native AOT deployment</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# specification: Classes</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Programming/NET/Runtime/Runtime.md" class="internal-link">Runtime</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-1" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-1" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Computer Science"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Computer%20Science">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Computer%20Science"><option value="Computer Science">All Computer Science (12)</option><option value="Computer Science/Algorithms">Algorithms (7)</option><option value="Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms">Algorithms / Paradigms (7)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Computer Science questions"><h2>Computer Science</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Computer Science"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does Big O notation describe?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Big O notation describes an upper bound on how an algorithm's cost, usually running time or extra memory, grows as a function of input size <code>n</code>. It states how an approach scales, not how long it takes on a particular machine.</p>
<p dir="auto">Formally, <code>f(n) = O(g(n))</code> means positive constants <code>c</code> and <code>n₀</code> exist such that <code>f(n) ≤ c · g(n)</code> for every <code>n ≥ n₀</code>. Beyond some input size, the cost grows no faster than a fixed multiple of <code>g(n)</code>.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Upper bound, not necessarily tight:</strong> a loose bound is still true, so a linear-time algorithm is also <code>O(n²)</code>. A bound that holds from both above and below is tight and is written <code>Θ</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Defined input size:</strong> a bound is meaningful only once <code>n</code> is stated. For string processing, <code>n</code> can count strings or total characters, and the two can give different bounds.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/c6d8f06c6f11e3342633dec85498f551_MIT6_006S20_r01.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/c6d8f06c6f11e3342633dec85498f551_MIT6_006S20_r01.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006 Spring 2020: Recitation 1</a> · <a href="https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bigOnotation.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bigOnotation.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST: big-O notation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Big O Notation.md" class="internal-link">Big O Notation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does Big O notation drop constant factors and lower-order terms?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They cannot change an expression's growth class, so dropping them loses nothing that Big O expresses. Its definition only requires some fixed constant <code>c</code> and starting size <code>n₀</code> such that <code>f(n) ≤ c · g(n)</code> for every <code>n ≥ n₀</code>. A constant factor can be folded into <code>c</code>. A lower-order term grows more slowly than the dominant term. Beyond some size, it is therefore at most a fixed multiple of that term and can be folded into <code>c</code> as well.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, when <code>n ≥ 1</code>, each term of <code>n² + 100n + 500</code> is at most a multiple of <code>n²</code>:</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>n² + 100n + 500 ≤ n² + 100n² + 500n² = 601n²</code></p>
<p dir="auto">So <code>c = 601</code> and <code>n₀ = 1</code> satisfy the definition, and the expression is <code>O(n²)</code>, the same class as <code>n²</code> or <code>5n²</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">The class describes eventual growth only. The discarded parts still affect actual cost: for every <code>n</code> up to 104, <code>100n + 500</code> is larger than <code>n²</code> itself.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/c6d8f06c6f11e3342633dec85498f551_MIT6_006S20_r01.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/c6d8f06c6f11e3342633dec85498f551_MIT6_006S20_r01.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006 Spring 2020: Recitation 1</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Big O Notation.md" class="internal-link">Big O Notation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between average-case and amortized complexity?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Average-case complexity is the expected cost when inputs or random choices follow a stated probability distribution. Amortized complexity is a guaranteed bound on the total cost of a sequence of operations, spread across those operations. Amortized analysis uses no probability, so it is not a kind of average-case analysis.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Average case</th>
<th>Amortized</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What is averaged</td>
<td>The cost of an operation over possible inputs or random choices, weighted by their probability.</td>
<td>The total cost of a sequence of operations, divided by the number of operations.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Assumption</td>
<td>A stated distribution. If real inputs do not follow it, the bound does not describe them.</td>
<td>No distribution. The bound holds for every sequence the analysis covers.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What can still be slow</td>
<td>A particular unlucky or adversarial input can cost much more than expected.</td>
<td>A single operation can be expensive, but expensive steps are rare enough that the sequence total stays within the bound.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Example</td>
<td>A hash lookup is constant time on average only under suitable hashing and collision assumptions.</td>
<td>Dynamic-array append is amortized <code>O(1)</code>. A resize copies every element in <code>O(n)</code>, but growing capacity by a constant factor, such as doubling, keeps the total for <code>n</code> appends at <code>O(n)</code>.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/averagecase.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/averagecase.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST: Average-case complexity</a> · <a href="https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/79a07dc1cb47d76dae2ffedc701e3d2b_MIT6_006S20_lec2.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/79a07dc1cb47d76dae2ffedc701e3d2b_MIT6_006S20_lec2.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006 Spring 2020: Lecture 2</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Big O Notation.md" class="internal-link">Big O Notation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When can constant factors outweigh asymptotic complexity?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Constant factors can outweigh asymptotic complexity when inputs are small or bounded.</p>
<p dir="auto">Big O describes how cost grows with input size and deliberately ignores constant factors. An <code>O(n log n)</code> bound only says the cost stays below some constant times <code>n log n</code> once <code>n</code> is large enough. An algorithm with a better growth rate but more overhead can therefore be slower below some crossover size. Typical overhead includes setup work, extra bookkeeping and poorer memory access patterns. Above the crossover, the better growth rate eventually dominates.</p>
<p dir="auto">Hybrid sorting is a concrete case. The .NET 10 documentation describes <code>Array.Sort</code> as introsort, which sorts partitions of 16 or fewer elements with insertion sort. Insertion sort grows quadratically, but its low overhead suits such small partitions. The value 16 is that implementation's threshold, not a general rule.</p>
<p dir="auto">The crossover depends on the implementation, hardware and data. It is therefore established by measuring the actual workload rather than inferred from Big O alone.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bigOnotation.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bigOnotation.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST: Big-O notation</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.array.sort?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.array.sort?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Array.Sort (.NET 10)</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/df3828915ac9573c8bd0deb5d9febdd582a398c5/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/ArraySortHelper.cs#L123-L168" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/df3828915ac9573c8bd0deb5d9febdd582a398c5/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/ArraySortHelper.cs#L123-L168" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">dotnet/runtime ArraySortHelper source</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Computer Science.md" class="internal-link">Computer Science</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can the dominant operation reveal whether a performance problem needs a different data structure or algorithm?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The dominant operation is the step that accounts for most of the work, and it shows where the cost lies. If a data structure that performs that operation cheaply removes most of the work, the representation was the problem. If the operations the task requires remain too expensive even with a suitable structure, the algorithm has to change.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Repeated membership checks:</strong> checking membership in a <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code> scans the list. Checking each item of a batch against a list of similar size inside a loop therefore costs O(n²). <code>HashSet&lt;T&gt;.Contains</code> takes expected O(1) time with a good hash function, so the same batch costs expected O(n) while the surrounding logic stays unchanged.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Ordered iteration or range queries:</strong> when repeated sorting or range scanning dominates, <code>SortedSet&lt;T&gt;</code> keeps elements ordered as they are added and removed, and <code>GetViewBetween</code> returns a view of a range. The set positions an element when it is inserted, so changing the fields that determine its order in place is unsupported. Instead, the element is removed, changed and then added again.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Algorithm change:</strong> sometimes the remaining cost comes from how many operations the approach performs rather than how expensive each one is. No data structure removes that cost, so the algorithm itself has to do less work.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.hashset-1.contains?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.hashset-1.contains?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: HashSet.Contains (.NET 10)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.sortedset-1?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.sortedset-1?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: SortedSet class (.NET 10)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Computer Science.md" class="internal-link">Computer Science</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Computer Science/Algorithms"><h3>Algorithms</h3></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms"><h4>Paradigms</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does backtracking work, and how does it relate to brute-force search?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Backtracking is a form of brute-force search that builds candidates one choice at a time. It abandons a partial candidate as soon as that candidate is known to be unsuitable.</p>
<p dir="auto">The search process:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Start with an empty partial candidate.</li>
<li dir="auto">Choose one available option and add it to the partial candidate.</li>
<li dir="auto">Recursively explore the remaining choices from that partial candidate.</li>
<li dir="auto">If the candidate is complete and valid, record it. If a sound check proves the partial candidate cannot lead to a valid solution, it is a dead end and its exploration stops.</li>
<li dir="auto">Return to the previous decision point, undo the choice and try the next option. When no options remain, return to the level above.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">For example, when placing queens row by row, a placement that already attacks another queen is abandoned without filling the remaining rows.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Approach</th>
<th>How it searches</th>
<th>Consequence</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Naive complete-candidate enumeration</td>
<td>It generates every complete candidate and then checks each one.</td>
<td>Invalid candidates are fully built before they are rejected.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Backtracking</td>
<td>It extends a partial candidate one choice at a time and can check it along the way.</td>
<td>Rejecting a partial candidate skips all of its continuations.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Pruning depends on having a check that can reject partial candidates. Without such a check, backtracking still visits every complete candidate. Even with pruning, the number of branches can grow exponentially in the worst case, so backtracking does not guarantee a fast search.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs106b/cs106b.1162/preview-backtracking.shtml" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs106b/cs106b.1162/preview-backtracking.shtml" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">CS106B: Exhaustive Search and Recursive Backtracking (Stanford)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Backtracking.md" class="internal-link">Backtracking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In backtracking with shared mutable state, why undo each choice before trying the next?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Undoing restores the parent state, so each sibling choice starts from the same prefix instead of inheriting the previous branch's changes.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Pattern:</strong> choose → explore (recurse) → un-choose.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Example:</strong> permutations of A, B, C built in one shared list.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">At the root the list is <code>[ ]</code>. Choose A, giving <code>[A]</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Explore below A. The inner levels add and remove B and C, record <code>[A, B, C]</code> and <code>[A, C, B]</code>, and return with the list at <code>[A]</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>With undo:</strong> remove A, giving <code>[ ]</code>. Choose B, giving <code>[B]</code>. The B branch now explores permutations that start with B.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Without undo:</strong> A stays in the list. Choosing B gives <code>[A, B]</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The B branch should start from the root's empty prefix, but it starts from the A branch's leftover state. It therefore explores the wrong part of the search space. If A's 'used' flag also stays set, the search can record <code>[A, B, C]</code> again and never produce <code>[B, A, C]</code>. If only the list is wrong, it can record an invalid result such as <code>[A, B, A]</code>. Later sibling branches can inherit even more leftover state.</p>
<p dir="auto">Related changes, such as 'used' flags, must also be undone. A retained solution must be copied before later undo steps.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Alternative:</strong> each branch can instead receive its own copied or immutable state. Then no explicit undo is needed. Copying state adds a per-branch cost; immutable representations may share structure.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs106b/cs106b.1162/preview-backtracking.shtml" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs106b/cs106b.1162/preview-backtracking.shtml" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">CS106B: Exhaustive Search and Recursive Backtracking (Stanford)</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Collections.Immutable/src/System/Collections/Immutable/ImmutableStack_1.cs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Collections.Immutable/src/System/Collections/Immutable/ImmutableStack_1.cs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET ImmutableStack implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Backtracking.md" class="internal-link">Backtracking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What changes between memoization and tabulation if the recurrence is the same?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Memoization and tabulation evaluate the same recurrence and store one result per state. They differ in how the evaluation order is determined and which states get computed.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Memoization (top-down):</strong> starts from the requested state, recursively follows its dependencies and caches each result the first time it is computed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Tabulation (bottom-up):</strong> loops fill the stored results in an order where every dependency is already available.</li>
</ul>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Memoization (top-down)</th>
<th>Tabulation (bottom-up)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Evaluation order</td>
<td>Recursion from the target discovers dependencies as it goes, so no order has to be written down. The dependencies must still be acyclic.</td>
<td>The loops must visit states in an order that solves every dependency before any state that reads it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>States computed</td>
<td>Only states reachable from the target are computed, so unneeded states are skipped.</td>
<td>Every state in the planned table is computed, including states the target never reads.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Control cost</td>
<td>Each call costs a function call and a cache check. Recursion depth follows the longest dependency chain, so very deep chains can overflow the call stack.</td>
<td>Plain loops avoid recursive calls and their stack-depth limit.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">When both compute the same set of states with equivalent work per state, their asymptotic time is identical: the number of states times the work per state.</p>
<p dir="auto">Coin change with a <code>30¢</code> target shows the two orders. Memoization starts at <code>best(30)</code> and recurses into the smaller remaining amounts it needs. Tabulation fills <code>best[0]</code> through <code>best[30]</code> in increasing order, which works because each amount reads only smaller amounts.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/28461a74f81101874a13d9679a40584d_MIT6_006S20_lec16.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/28461a74f81101874a13d9679a40584d_MIT6_006S20_lec16.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Dynamic Programming</a> · <a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Memoization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Dynamic Programming.md" class="internal-link">Dynamic Programming</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is memoization, and when does it improve performance?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Memoization caches a function's results by argument. The first call with a given set of arguments computes the result and stores it. Later calls with the same arguments return the stored result instead of computing it again.</p>
<p dir="auto">It improves performance only when the same arguments recur. Naive recursive Fibonacci is the classic case: <code>fib(n)</code> calls <code>fib(n - 1)</code> and <code>fib(n - 2)</code>, and both branches keep recomputing the same smaller values. The number of calls therefore grows exponentially, although only <code>n + 1</code> distinct arguments exist. With memoization each argument is computed once, and the time becomes linear in <code>n</code>. In general, the time drops to roughly the number of distinct argument sets times the work per call.</p>
<p dir="auto">In a recursive function, the recursive calls must also go through the cache. Calls to the raw, uncached function bypass it and bring the repeated work back.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No repeats, no gain:</strong> if every call has distinct arguments, as with the unique subarrays in merge sort, the cache never hits and only adds lookup and storage overhead.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Memory:</strong> a long-lived cache keeps one entry per distinct argument set unless it is bounded. An evicted entry is recomputed when it is requested again.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Applied to a recurrence with overlapping subproblems, memoization is the top-down form of dynamic programming.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Memoization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Memoization.md" class="internal-link">Memoization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is dynamic programming, and what does a typical DP solution need to define?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Dynamic programming solves a problem through a recurrence over smaller subproblems. It stores each subproblem's result so later steps reuse it instead of recomputing it. In finite, one-pass DP, the dependencies between subproblems are acyclic, so each distinct subproblem is solved only once.</p>
<p dir="auto">A typical DP solution defines:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>State (subproblem):</strong> what each subproblem means, such as <code>best(a)</code>, the fewest coins that make amount <code>a</code>. The state must capture everything the remaining answer depends on, so every path that reaches the same state needs the same answer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Stored result:</strong> the value kept for each state, such as a minimum, a count or a yes/no answer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Base cases:</strong> states answered directly, such as <code>best(0) = 0</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Recurrence:</strong> how a state's result is computed from the results of the states it depends on, such as <code>best(a) = 1 + min(best(a - c))</code> over usable coins <code>c</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Evaluation order:</strong> for a finite set of states with acyclic dependencies, an order that solves every dependency before any state that reads it. Memoized recursion follows that order on demand, and tabulation writes it out as loops.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">In this one-pass form, the running time is roughly the number of distinct states times the work to compute one state from its stored dependencies.</p>
<p dir="auto">If the dependencies form a cycle, no such order exists, and a single recursive or tabulated pass cannot solve the problem. Such problems need another method that can revisit states until their values converge, such as a graph shortest-path algorithm or repeated updates.</p>
<p dir="auto">Storing results pays off when different paths reach the same state (overlapping subproblems). Optimal substructure means an optimum can be built from optimal answers to subproblems. It matters only when the goal is to choose an optimum. Counting and decision problems use the same machinery without optimizing.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/28461a74f81101874a13d9679a40584d_MIT6_006S20_lec16.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/28461a74f81101874a13d9679a40584d_MIT6_006S20_lec16.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Dynamic Programming</a> · <a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Memoization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Memoization.md" class="internal-link">Memoization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is memoizing a function call correct?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Memoizing a call is correct when returning the stored result is indistinguishable, to callers, from running the function again. Two conditions make that true:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The key determines the result.</strong> The cache key includes every input that can change the result. If an input is missing, calls that differ only in that input share one entry. A later call then receives the earlier call's answer even when its own answer would differ.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Skipping the call loses nothing required.</strong> A cache hit does not execute the function, so the function must not perform an effect that every call needs, such as sending a message or recording each request.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, and the function has no observable side effects. Purity therefore guarantees the second condition. It also narrows the first condition to the arguments, but the key must still represent every argument that affects the result. A pure two-argument function cached by its first argument alone can return wrong results. Purity with a complete key is a simple sufficient condition, not a necessary one. A function with effects that no caller requires can also qualify.</p>
<p dir="auto">When the result also depends on mutable external data, such as a price table, entries computed from the old data can become stale once that data changes. Either the data's version becomes part of the key, or affected entries are invalidated when the data changes.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Memoization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Memoization.md" class="internal-link">Memoization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why must a memoization key include every part of a subproblem’s state?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A cache hit returns whatever is stored under the key, without checking which subproblem produced it. If two different subproblems produce the same key, the later one receives the earlier one's answer. Whenever their true answers differ, the result is silently wrong rather than reported as an error. Some colliding subproblems happen to have the same answer, but an incomplete key removes any guarantee that a hit is correct.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Example: 0/1 knapsack.</strong> <code>best(i, capacity)</code> is the highest value obtainable from items <code>i</code> onward with <code>capacity</code> weight remaining, so its answer depends on both values.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">One branch reaches item 3 with 10 units of capacity left, computes the best value of the remaining items and stores it under key <code>3</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Another branch reaches item 3 with only 2 units left.</li>
<li dir="auto">The lookup for key <code>3</code> hits and returns the result for 10 units. That value can include items that do not fit in 2 units, so the second branch can receive an answer that is too high.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Keying the cache on <code>(i, capacity)</code> keeps those subproblems separate. The memo key is the DP state, so it must include everything that affects the remaining answer. History that does not affect it, such as which earlier items were chosen, can be left out. Including such history would still be correct, but it would create more distinct keys and fewer cache hits.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/28461a74f81101874a13d9679a40584d_MIT6_006S20_lec16.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/28461a74f81101874a13d9679a40584d_MIT6_006S20_lec16.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Dynamic Programming</a> · <a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/ea1cb4a29625017bdbcaf2dfd61b179e_MIT6_006F11_lec19_orig.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MIT 6.006: Memoization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Computer Science/Algorithms/Paradigms/Memoization.md" class="internal-link">Memoization</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-2" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-2" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Data Persistence"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Data%20Persistence">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Data%20Persistence"><option value="Data Persistence">All Data Persistence (31)</option><option value="Data Persistence/NoSQL">NoSQL (3)</option><option value="Data Persistence/ORMs">ORMs (6)</option><option value="Data Persistence/SQL">SQL (15)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Data Persistence questions"><h2>Data Persistence</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Data Persistence"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does ACID mean for a database transaction, and where do its guarantees stop?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">ACID names four guarantees a database gives a transaction, a group of reads and writes that ends in one commit decision. They hold only inside that database and only as strongly as its configured isolation and durability settings allow.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Atomicity:</strong> the transaction has one outcome. Either all of its writes commit or none do, so a crash or error cannot leave a partial commit.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Consistency:</strong> a correct transaction moves the data from one valid state to another. Database constraints such as foreign keys, uniqueness and <code>CHECK</code> enforce the rules the database can express. Application logic must enforce the rest.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Isolation:</strong> concurrent transactions are limited in what they can observe of each other and in which combined results can commit. The configured isolation level sets how strict this is.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Durability:</strong> once the database acknowledges a commit, the changes survive the failures its durability configuration covers, such as a crash.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The guarantees stop at these boundaries:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Configuration:</strong> weaker settings narrow the guarantees. For example, PostgreSQL asynchronous commit can acknowledge a commit before it is durably logged, so a crash can lose the most recently committed transactions.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retries:</strong> atomicity does not make an operation safe to repeat. If a client times out after the server has committed and then retries, the work is applied twice. Making the operation idempotent prevents this, for example with a unique request ID.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Other databases and services:</strong> a local commit cannot include writes elsewhere. Work that spans services needs a separate protocol, such as two-phase commit or a saga of local transactions.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cossdk/acid-properties" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cossdk/acid-properties" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ACID properties</a> · <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-async-commit.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-async-commit.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: Asynchronous commit</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ACID.md" class="internal-link">ACID</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is write skew, and why can snapshot isolation allow it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Write skew is a concurrency anomaly in which two transactions read the same data, each makes a decision that is valid for what it read, and each writes a different row. Both commit, but the combined result breaks an invariant that neither transaction broke alone.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example: a rule requires at least one doctor on call, and Alice and Bob are both on call.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Step</th>
<th>Transaction A</th>
<th>Transaction B</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Read</td>
<td>Sees Alice and Bob on call</td>
<td>Sees the same state</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Decide</td>
<td>Bob remains, so Alice may leave</td>
<td>Alice remains, so Bob may leave</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Write</td>
<td>Sets Alice off call</td>
<td>Sets Bob off call</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Commit</td>
<td>Succeeds</td>
<td>Succeeds</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">No doctor is left on call.</p>
<p dir="auto">Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a stable snapshot. Each transaction checks the rule against a snapshot that does not contain the other's change. Because they update different rows, there is no concurrent update of the same row to reject, so both commit. The problem is a read-write dependency: each transaction writes data that the other read when deciding.</p>
<p dir="auto">Preventing write skew requires protecting the whole invariant: a constraint where it can be expressed, locks covering every row or the predicate the decision read, or Serializable isolation. PostgreSQL's Serializable level detects this kind of dependency and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure. The application then retries the whole transaction.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL 18: Transaction isolation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ACID.md" class="internal-link">ACID</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should concurrency protection be chosen for a read-modify-write transaction?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Concurrency protection is chosen from the invariant the decision depends on, not from the row being written. The mechanism must protect every input that informed the decision: the rows read, any predicate such as 'at least one doctor on call', and rows whose absence mattered.</p>
<p dir="auto">Mechanisms that can cover the whole decision:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Database constraint:</strong> when the invariant can be expressed as a constraint, the database rejects any commit that would violate it, whatever the interleaving.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Serializable isolation:</strong> the database commits only results that some one-at-a-time order of the transactions could have produced. It may abort a transaction to enforce this. The whole transaction, including its reads and decisions, must then be retried. Retrying only the final write would reuse stale reasoning.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Locks:</strong> explicit locks protect the decision only when they cover every relevant row or the whole predicate.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Application-specific optimistic check:</strong> valid only when it detects a change to any decision input, not just to the updated row.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Two choices that look sufficient but are not:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Repeatable Read</strong> keeps repeated reads or the transaction snapshot stable, depending on the engine. It can still allow write skew: two transactions read the same rows, each updates a different row, and together they break the invariant.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A row-version token</strong> on the updated entity detects a concurrent change to that row only. It misses rows inserted or deleted under the predicate and changes to other rows that were read.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL 18: Transaction isolation</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: EF Core concurrency conflicts</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ACID.md" class="internal-link">ACID</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When can a larger connection pool make performance worse?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A larger pool makes performance worse once the database, rather than the pool, is the bottleneck. Until that point, more connections let more work run concurrently. After the database reaches its CPU, I/O or lock-contention limit, additional sessions add contention and queueing inside the server instead of throughput. Latency rises, and every open session still consumes client and server resources.</p>
<p dir="auto">The possible session count is also larger than one setting suggests:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The limit is per pool.</strong> A setting such as SqlClient's <code>Max Pool Size</code> caps one pool, not the whole application or fleet.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Pools fragment.</strong> Providers keep separate pools for different connection strings. Depending on the provider, they also separate pools by identity or other connection state. Per-tenant or per-user configurations can multiply connections even when each pool looks small.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Instances multiply pools.</strong> Each process owns its own pools. Fifty instances with a maximum of 100 connections each can open 5,000 sessions, even if the database can usefully run only a small fraction of them at once.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Pool size is therefore a fleet-wide budget. It starts from measured database capacity, reserves headroom for administration and background work, and divides the rest across instances. Reading pool wait time alongside database CPU, I/O and active sessions shows which side is saturated. Waits while the database is healthy point to leaks, long checkouts or an undersized pool. Waits on a saturated database are not fixed by a larger pool.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/sql-server-connection-pooling?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/sql-server-connection-pooling?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server connection pooling</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/connection-options?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/connection-options?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SqlClient connection options</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/Connection Pooling.md" class="internal-link">Connection Pooling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">With client-side connection pooling, what happens when application code opens and disposes a database connection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Opening borrows a physical connection from the pool, and disposing returns it to the pool instead of closing it. The application works with a short-lived logical connection, while the provider keeps the expensive physical connection open for reuse. Establishing a physical connection can require a socket, a security handshake, authentication and a server session, depending on the provider and connection configuration. Without pooling, every open creates a new physical connection and repeats that setup. The cost belongs to establishing the connection, not to each query sent over a connection that is already open.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Open:</strong> the provider selects the pool that matches the connection configuration. It takes an idle physical connection, or creates a new one if the pool is below its maximum size.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Exhausted pool:</strong> if every connection is checked out and the pool is at its maximum, the open call waits for another caller to return one. If none returns before the connection timeout, the open fails.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Close or dispose:</strong> the logical connection ends. The provider resets reusable session state and places the physical connection back in the pool for the next caller.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retirement:</strong> idle and maximum-lifetime settings let the provider close extra or aging physical connections later.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Failure consequence:</strong> a connection that is never closed or disposed may stay checked out. The usable pool also shrinks through leaks, long transactions and slow unrelated work while a connection is open, such as waiting for an HTTP response. Open calls then time out. Pooling therefore works best when a connection is opened just before database work and disposed as soon as that work ends, usually through <code>using</code> or <code>await using</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/sql-server-connection-pooling?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/ado-net/sql-server-connection-pooling?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server connection pooling</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/Connection Pooling.md" class="internal-link">Connection Pooling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What determines whether a service should use relational or non-relational storage?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Three needs determine the choice: the invariants the data must keep, the scope of the transactions that protect them, and the queries the service must answer. These needs are judged against a concrete engine's consistency, query, recovery and operational limits.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Relational storage</strong> is the usual default when correctness depends on constraints, joins, transactions across several records, or query combinations that keep changing. The database enforces those rules close to the data, and a new query can usually be expressed without reshaping storage.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A specialized non-relational store</strong> fits when one access pattern clearly dominates and the engine's consistency, query and recovery limits are acceptable for that workload. Typical patterns are lookup by key, reading and replacing a whole document, relationship traversal and full-text relevance.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A combination</strong> keeps a relational source of truth and adds one specialized read path, such as a search index or cache, when that path solves a measured need. Each added store brings synchronization and recovery work that must have an owner.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/data-guide/technology-choices/understand-data-store-models" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/data-guide/technology-choices/understand-data-store-models" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Understand data store models</a></p>
