</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/Data Persistence.md" class="internal-link">Data Persistence</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should a slow database-backed request be diagnosed before scaling the database?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Diagnosis measures where the slow request spends its time and fixes the smallest demonstrated cause. It moves to read offloading or larger infrastructure only when a measured limit remains.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Time breakdown:</strong> the request's latency is split into pool wait, query execution, lock wait, network, serialization and downstream calls. The same interval is correlated with database CPU, memory, I/O, connection count, rows scanned and replication lag.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Actual query and plan:</strong> the real SQL with representative parameters goes through the engine's plan tooling, such as PostgreSQL <code>EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)</code>. Estimated and actual rows, scans, joins, spills and I/O show where the work goes.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Smallest demonstrated fix:</strong> typical fixes return fewer rows or columns, remove an N+1 path, add or correct an index, shorten a transaction, or change the query or schema shape. The same trace and load are then rerun to confirm the effect.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Pool check:</strong> connection waits while the database is healthy point to leaks, long checkouts or fleet-wide pool sizing. A larger pool does not repair saturated storage or lock contention.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Read offloading:</strong> a cache, or a read model refreshed asynchronously from the source, fits only when repeated reads tolerate a declared staleness window. A materialized view that the database updates as part of each base-table write, such as a SQL Server indexed view, stays current but makes those writes more expensive. Read replicas fit when reads dominate and replica lag is acceptable.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Capacity changes:</strong> the node is scaled after the query path is sound. Partitioning or sharding is justified only when one node's measured capacity, data size or recovery boundary is still the limit.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Jumping straight to caches, replicas or shards can improve one graph while adding stale reads or duplicated writes that hide the original defect.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: Using EXPLAIN</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/views/create-indexed-views?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/views/create-indexed-views?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Create indexed views</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/Data Persistence.md" class="internal-link">Data Persistence</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Data Persistence/NoSQL"><h3>NoSQL</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why might Elasticsearch map one logical value as both <code>text</code> and <code>keyword</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Full-text search and exact-value operations need different index forms, and one field type serves only one of them well. A multi-field indexes the same source value both ways, so each query can use the form that matches its intent.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>text</code></strong> passes the value through an analyzer that splits and normalizes it into terms. A standard analyzer may index <code>Running Shoes</code> as <code>running</code> and <code>shoes</code>, so a search for <code>shoes</code> matches. The index holds separate normalized terms instead of the whole original value, so <code>text</code> is a poor basis for exact filters, sorting and aggregations.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong><code>keyword</code></strong> indexes the whole value unchanged. A term filter, a sort or an aggregation such as a facet count works on the exact value <code>Running Shoes</code>. A full-text search for <code>shoes</code> does not match it.</li>
</ul>
<pre class="language-json"><code class="language-json is-loaded"><span class="token punctuation">{</span>
  <span class="token property">"properties"</span><span class="token operator">:</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token property">"name"</span><span class="token operator">:</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token property">"type"</span><span class="token operator">:</span> <span class="token string">"text"</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token property">"fields"</span><span class="token operator">:</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token property">"raw"</span><span class="token operator">:</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token property">"type"</span><span class="token operator">:</span> <span class="token string">"keyword"</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span>
  <span class="token punctuation">}</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">With this mapping, full-text queries target <code>name</code>, while exact filters, sorting and aggregations target <code>name.raw</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/text.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/text.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Elasticsearch: text fields</a> · <a href="https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/mapping-reference/keyword" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/mapping-reference/keyword" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Elasticsearch: keyword fields</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/NoSQL/Elasticsearch.md" class="internal-link">Elasticsearch</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can a newly indexed Elasticsearch document be missing from search results for a short time?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Elasticsearch search is near real-time. A document becomes searchable only after a refresh opens the segment that contains it, so an acknowledged write can be stored before it appears in search results.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Index:</strong> the document enters an in-memory indexing buffer and the transaction log on its shard. Acknowledgement depends on the primary and replica write settings, not on search visibility.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Refresh:</strong> on a periodic interval, or when explicitly requested, buffered documents become a new immutable Lucene segment that is opened for search.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Merge:</strong> background merges combine small segments and discard obsolete document versions.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">A shorter refresh interval reduces the delay but creates more small segments and more merge work. That work consumes CPU, disk bandwidth and temporary disk space. Forcing a refresh after every write is therefore a costly default and fits only bounded workflows that truly need immediate visibility.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.elastic.co/docs/manage-data/data-store/near-real-time-search" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.elastic.co/docs/manage-data/data-store/near-real-time-search" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Elasticsearch near-real-time search</a> · <a href="https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/refresh-parameter" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/refresh-parameter" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Elasticsearch refresh parameter</a> · <a href="https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/index-settings/translog" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/index-settings/translog" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Elasticsearch translog settings</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/NoSQL/Elasticsearch.md" class="internal-link">Elasticsearch</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a non-relational store a poor fit for a service?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A non-relational store is a poor fit when the service's correctness depends on guarantees that the chosen engine cannot provide within the required scope. Those guarantees are constraints, transactions across related records, or support for a changing set of queries.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Invariants move into application code.</strong> If the database cannot enforce a rule across records, the application must enforce it, coordinate concurrent writes and repair copies that drift apart. For example, a transfer between two account records needs both balance changes to commit or fail together. An engine whose transactions are limited to one document or partition provides that atomicity only when both accounts lie inside one such scope. Under a partition-scoped transaction, two separate account documents in the same partition can still commit together. When the accounts fall outside every atomic scope the engine supports, such as in different partitions, the application must coordinate the transfer itself.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>New queries can require remodeling.</strong> Data in such stores is often shaped around known reads. A query the model was not designed for may need another index, a duplicated record or a different layout.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The label decides little.</strong> “NoSQL” names no single consistency or transaction model. Some engines provide strong reads or transactions within a bounded scope, while others offer eventual or tunable consistency. The fit therefore depends on the concrete engine and the scope of each operation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/data-guide/technology-choices/understand-data-store-models" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/data-guide/technology-choices/understand-data-store-models" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Understand data store models</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/database-transactions-optimistic-concurrency" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/database-transactions-optimistic-concurrency" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure Cosmos DB: Database transactions and optimistic concurrency</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/NoSQL/NoSQL.md" class="internal-link">NoSQL</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Data Persistence/ORMs"><h3>ORMs</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What lifetime should an EF Core <code>DbContext</code> have, and why?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An EF Core <code>DbContext</code> should live for one unit of work and serve one operation at a time. It is a session that tracks entities and coordinates <code>SaveChanges</code> for that unit of work. It is also not thread-safe, and EF Core does not support parallel operations on one instance.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Web requests:</strong> in ASP.NET Core, <code>AddDbContext</code> registers the context as scoped by default, so each request usually gets its own instance. One request can still contain several separate units of work.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Background or parallel work:</strong> each task needs its own fresh context, typically created through <code>IDbContextFactory&lt;TContext&gt;</code>, rather than a shared request instance.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Singletons:</strong> a singleton that captures a scoped context keeps one instance alive across requests, so concurrent requests can end up sharing it. This is the captive-dependency failure.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Context pooling:</strong> <code>AddDbContextPool</code> reuses reset context instances to lower setup cost. Per-request state, such as a tenant identifier, must therefore be re-established safely on each use.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/dbcontext-configuration/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/dbcontext-configuration/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core DbContext lifetime, configuration, and initialization</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/advanced-performance-topics" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/advanced-performance-topics" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core advanced performance topics and context pooling</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ORMs/Entity Framework.md" class="internal-link">Entity Framework</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does EF Core change tracking work, and when is a no-tracking query appropriate?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">EF Core change tracking records the entities that a <code>DbContext</code> loads, adds or attaches. It then compares their current values with remembered original values to decide what <code>SaveChanges</code> must write. A no-tracking query fits results that are only read and will not be updated through that context.</p>
<p dir="auto">With the default snapshot strategy, tracking works in four steps:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Track:</strong> a tracking query, the default for entity queries, attaches each returned entity to the context and keeps a snapshot of its original values. If an entity with the same key is already tracked, EF Core returns that existing instance instead of a new object. This is identity resolution.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Modify:</strong> application code changes ordinary properties. Under this strategy, assigning a property does not notify EF Core.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Detect:</strong> before <code>SaveChanges</code> writes, automatic change detection compares current values with the snapshot and marks changed entities and properties as modified.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Save:</strong> <code>SaveChanges</code> sends the inserts, updates and deletes that the tracked entity states require.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><code>.AsNoTracking()</code> skips setting up this tracking information, which usually makes read-only queries cheaper. In exchange, <code>SaveChanges</code> neither detects nor saves changes to the returned objects. A plain no-tracking query also skips identity resolution, so one row returned twice becomes two separate objects. Later use of such a detached object for an update requires attaching it, stating which entity or properties are modified and handling concurrency. The context never recorded the object's original values.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Tracking vs. no-tracking queries</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/change-tracking/change-detection" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/change-tracking/change-detection" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Change detection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ORMs/Entity Framework.md" class="internal-link">Entity Framework</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does EF Core detect that another writer changed a row between reading it and saving an update?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">EF Core detects the conflict through optimistic concurrency. The original value of a configured concurrency token is added to the <code>WHERE</code> clause of the <code>UPDATE</code> or <code>DELETE</code>. A command that then affects zero rows raises <code>DbUpdateConcurrencyException</code>. This detection does not require a database lock to span the read, the application's work and the save. Whether any lock is held during that interval depends separately on the enclosing transaction and its isolation level.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Read:</strong> EF Core loads the row and remembers the token's original value. In SQL Server, a <code>rowversion</code> column is a common token because the database changes it on every update.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Save:</strong> the generated command changes the row only if its key and token still equal the values that were read.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Conflict:</strong> if another writer updated the row in between, the token differs and the predicate matches nothing. EF Core treats the zero-row result as a conflict and throws <code>DbUpdateConcurrencyException</code>.</li>
</ol>
<pre class="language-sql"><code class="language-sql is-loaded"><span class="token comment">-- Simplified shape of the generated command</span>
<span class="token keyword">UPDATE</span> Orders
<span class="token keyword">SET</span> <span class="token keyword">Status</span> <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token variable">@newStatus</span>
<span class="token keyword">WHERE</span> Id <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token variable">@id</span> <span class="token operator">AND</span> Version <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token variable">@originalVersion</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">The application then resolves the conflict. It reloads and merges values, retries the operation from fresh state, or reports the conflict.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Limit:</strong> the check covers only the rows that the command updates or deletes. It does not detect a concurrent change to other rows that a decision relied on, such as a newly inserted overlapping booking. Protecting such a predicate needs a stronger mechanism, such as Serializable isolation.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Handling concurrency conflicts</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ORMs/Entity Framework.md" class="internal-link">Entity Framework</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the N+1 query problem, and how can it be detected?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The N+1 query problem occurs when one query loads N parent rows and code then triggers a separate query for each parent's related data. The result is N + 1 round trips instead of one or two. In EF Core it commonly comes from lazy loading: accessing a navigation inside a loop can issue a query per item.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> orders <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword">await</span> db<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Orders<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">ToListAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>   <span class="token comment">// 1 query</span>
<span class="token keyword">foreach</span> <span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> order <span class="token keyword">in</span> orders<span class="token punctuation">)</span>
    Console<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">WriteLine</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>order<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Customer<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Name<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>   <span class="token comment">// with lazy loading: can query once per order</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">Each extra query adds a round trip, so the cost grows with the number of parents. A page that seems fast with little test data can degrade as production data grows.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Detection:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Command count per operation:</strong> counting the database commands that one request or test issues reveals N+1 when the count grows with the number of parent rows.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Logged SQL:</strong> the log shows the same statement repeated many times, with only the key parameter changing.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Traces:</strong> one request contains many short, sequential database spans.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Fixes</strong> reduce the round trips. Options include a projection that selects only the related columns the result needs, an <code>Include</code> that eager-loads the navigation, or a deliberate second query that loads the related rows for all parents at once. The right choice depends on the result shape and consistency needs. No single collection-size threshold decides it.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Efficient querying</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ORMs/Entity Framework.md" class="internal-link">Entity Framework</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is raw SQL a better boundary than an ORM query?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Raw SQL is a better boundary when a query needs something the ORM cannot express, such as a provider-specific database feature. It is also a better boundary when the SQL the ORM generates has a measured performance problem that cannot be fixed predictably through the ORM. Raw SQL is not automatically faster. The reason to use it is a missing capability or a measured plan problem.</p>
<p dir="auto">Moving a query into SQL text brings its own obligations:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Data values:</strong> values are passed as database parameters, never concatenated into the SQL text. In EF Core, <code>FromSql</code> turns interpolated values into parameters (EF Core 7.0 and later; earlier versions use <code>FromSqlInterpolated</code>). A <code>FromSqlRaw</code> string built by concatenating values reintroduces SQL injection risk.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Identifiers and SQL fragments:</strong> databases do not accept column names, table names or other parts of the SQL structure as parameters. Any dynamic piece is checked against an allow-list of known values before it enters the SQL text.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Provider dependence:</strong> the SQL is written for one database engine, so its tests run against that same engine.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/sql-queries" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/sql-queries" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: SQL queries</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ORMs/ORMs.md" class="internal-link">ORMs</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can eager-loading sibling collections be expensive?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Loading two collections of the same parent in one SQL query joins both of them to the parent. Each parent row is then repeated for every combination of its matching children, so the row count multiplies instead of adding up. EF Core's documentation calls this a cartesian explosion.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, <code>Include(b =&gt; b.Posts).Include(b =&gt; b.Contributors)</code> for one blog with 10 posts and 10 contributors returns 10 × 10 = 100 rows for that blog. Each row repeats the blog's columns together with one post and one contributor. The database, the network and EF Core all process the extra rows.</p>
<p dir="auto">Two mitigations trade this cost for others:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Split query</strong> (<code>AsSplitQuery()</code>): EF Core loads the blogs and each collection with separate SQL commands, returning about 1 + 10 + 10 rows. The cost is extra round trips. The commands also run at different moments, so an update between them can produce a combined result that never existed at a single point in time. Running them in a serializable or snapshot transaction gives one consistent view, at the cost of that isolation level's own overhead.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Projection:</strong> selecting only the needed columns makes each duplicated row smaller. It does not reduce the number of rows the join produces.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/single-split-queries" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/single-split-queries" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Single vs. split queries</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/ORMs/ORMs.md" class="internal-link">ORMs</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Data Persistence/SQL"><h3>SQL</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What problem does normalization solve in a relational schema?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Normalization prevents insertion, update and deletion anomalies. These arise when one fact is stored redundantly in rows that exist for other reasons. Normalization decomposes tables according to their dependencies, so each fact is stored once, with the key that actually determines it.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, an <code>Orders</code> table that is the only place storing customer addresses repeats a customer's address on every order row. It has all three anomalies:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Update anomaly:</strong> changing the address means updating every order row for that customer. Missing one row leaves two contradictory addresses.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Insertion anomaly:</strong> a new customer's address cannot be recorded until the customer places an order.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Deletion anomaly:</strong> deleting a customer's last order also deletes the only record of the address.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Storing the address in a <code>Customers</code> table keyed by customer ID, with each order referring to that ID, removes all three. The goal is not to remove every repeated value: the customer ID repeated on each order is a reference, not a duplicated fact. The address an order was shipped to is a different, historical fact, and it belongs on the order.</p>
<p dir="auto">A valid decomposition is lossless: joining the smaller tables reproduces exactly the original rows, without losing any or inventing new ones. The constraints the business needs must also remain enforceable after the split.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://apollo.inf.upol.cz/~urbanec/teaching/2021/data2/files/codd2.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://apollo.inf.upol.cz/~urbanec/teaching/2021/data2/files/codd2.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Codd: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Normalization Denormalization.md" class="internal-link">Normalization Denormalization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does a relational schema need 4NF or 5NF rather than stopping at BCNF?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A schema needs 4NF or 5NF when redundancy remains that no functional dependency explains. 3NF and BCNF are built on functional dependencies, where one set of attributes determines a single value of another attribute. Fourth and fifth normal form handle two other kinds of dependency.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>4NF</th>
<th>5NF (project-join normal form)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Dependency removed</td>
<td>A multivalued dependency: one value determines a set of values that is independent of the table's other attributes.</td>
<td>A join dependency: the full fact is exactly the join of three or more smaller projections, and this is not implied by the candidate keys.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Example</td>
<td>A <code>{Restaurant, PizzaType, DeliveryArea}</code> table where <code>Restaurant ↠ PizzaType</code> and <code>Restaurant ↠ DeliveryArea</code> are independent. Every pizza type repeats for every area. Adding one type needs one row per area, and a missing row falsely says the pizza is unavailable there.</td>
<td>A <code>{Supplier, Product, Customer}</code> table under the rule that a supplier supplies a product to a customer exactly when the supplier offers the product, serves the customer, and the customer buys the product.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Decomposition</td>
<td><code>{Restaurant, PizzaType}</code> and <code>{Restaurant, DeliveryArea}</code>.</td>
<td><code>SupplierProduct</code>, <code>SupplierCustomer</code> and <code>ProductCustomer</code>.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Both decompositions are valid only when the dependency really holds in the domain. If pizza availability differs by delivery area, the two sets are not independent, and the three-column table is the correct fact. If a supplier offers a product only to some of its customers, joining the three pairwise tables produces combinations that never existed, so the decomposition loses information. The design follows from the dependencies that actually hold, not from a target normal-form number.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://apollo.inf.upol.cz/~urbanec/teaching/2021/data2/files/codd2.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://apollo.inf.upol.cz/~urbanec/teaching/2021/data2/files/codd2.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Codd: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model</a> · <a href="https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~lingtw/papers/fagin.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~lingtw/papers/fagin.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Fagin: Multivalued Dependencies and a New Normal Form for Relational Databases</a> · <a href="https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4735fc168eb72ef96817384aa5d40d5b6016d713&amp;repid=rep1&amp;type=pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4735fc168eb72ef96817384aa5d40d5b6016d713&amp;repid=rep1&amp;type=pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Fagin: Project-Join Normal Form</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Normalization Denormalization.md" class="internal-link">Normalization Denormalization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What conditions justify denormalizing a table, and what risks does it introduce?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Denormalization is justified when three conditions hold:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">A specific read path has a measured latency or resource problem.</li>
<li dir="auto">Cheaper fixes, such as an index or a corrected query plan, do not meet its target.</li>
<li dir="auto">Keeping a stored copy up to date costs less than recomputing the result on every read.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">High read volume alone does not justify it.</p>
<p dir="auto">The risk is that the same fact now lives in two places, and every change must reach both:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Drift:</strong> a write path that updates the source but misses the copy leaves them silently inconsistent.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Staleness:</strong> a copy updated asynchronously or on a schedule serves old data between updates. A PostgreSQL materialized view, for example, changes only when <code>REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW</code> runs.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Write cost and contention:</strong> each source change also updates the copy. A stored <code>TotalOrderAmount</code> on <code>Customers</code> adds an update to every order write, and concurrent orders for the same customer contend on that one row.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A safe design therefore names four things:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">the authoritative source;</li>
<li dir="auto">the acceptable freshness;</li>
<li dir="auto">how the copy is updated, either in the same transaction or by an asynchronous projection;</li>
<li dir="auto">a reconciliation check that detects and repairs drift.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rules-materializedviews.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rules-materializedviews.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: Materialized views</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Normalization Denormalization.md" class="internal-link">Normalization Denormalization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do 2NF and 3NF differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">2NF removes facts that depend on only part of a composite key. 3NF also removes facts that depend on another non-key attribute instead of on a key. Every relation in 3NF is also in 2NF.</p>
<p dir="auto">A <em>non-prime</em> attribute is one that is not part of any candidate key.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>2NF</th>
<th>3NF</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Problem removed</td>
<td>Partial dependency: a non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key.</td>
<td>Transitive dependency: a non-prime attribute depends on another non-key attribute, which in turn depends on the key.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Formal condition</td>
<td>The relation is in 1NF, and every non-prime attribute depends on the whole of every candidate key.</td>
<td>For every nontrivial functional dependency <code>X → A</code>, <code>X</code> is a superkey or <code>A</code> is prime.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>When it can be violated</td>
<td>For a table already in 1NF, only when a candidate key has several attributes; such a table whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF.</td>
<td>Also when the key is a single attribute.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Example violation</td>
<td>Key <code>{Make, Model}</code>: <code>Discount</code> depends only on <code>Make</code>, so the same discount repeats on every model row for that make.</td>
<td>Key <code>Model</code>: <code>Model → Store</code> and <code>Store → Phone</code>, so each store's phone number repeats on every model row for that store.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fix</td>
<td>A separate <code>{Make, Discount}</code> table holds each make's discount.</td>
<td>A separate <code>{Store, Phone}</code> table holds each store's phone number.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Each fix is a lossless decomposition: joining the new tables on the shared attribute reproduces the original rows exactly. Whether every original dependency can still be enforced within a single table is a separate design concern.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://apollo.inf.upol.cz/~urbanec/teaching/2021/data2/files/codd2.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://apollo.inf.upol.cz/~urbanec/teaching/2021/data2/files/codd2.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Codd: Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Normalization Denormalization.md" class="internal-link">Normalization Denormalization</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What evidence justifies sharding a database?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Sharding is justified by measured evidence that one database primary cannot handle the workload's write throughput or storage, after cheaper options have failed to remove that limit. A hard requirement, such as isolating tenants or keeping data in particular locations, can justify it earlier.</p>
<p dir="auto">For scale-driven sharding, the relevant ceiling is write throughput or storage, because each cheaper option addresses a different limit:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Query and index repair:</strong> removes wasted work, which may be the actual bottleneck.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Vertical scaling:</strong> adds CPU, memory or I/O to the same server.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Read replicas:</strong> add read capacity, but in a single-primary setup every write still goes to one server.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Caching:</strong> serves repeated reads without reaching the database.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Partitioning inside one database:</strong> splits a table into partitions that stay within one database and one transaction domain, so it does not spread work across independent servers.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The bar is high because sharding adds lasting costs:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Queries that need data from several shards must fan out and merge results.</li>
<li dir="auto">Transactions and constraints that span shards need extra coordination.</li>
<li dir="auto">Data must be moved when shards are rebalanced.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Sharding pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Sharding.md" class="internal-link">Sharding</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What makes a shard key viable for a workload?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A shard key is viable when four conditions hold:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The workload's common operations include it.</li>
<li dir="auto">It spreads both data and traffic evenly.</li>
<li dir="auto">Data that must change atomically shares the same key value.</li>
<li dir="auto">Its values rarely change.</li>
</ul>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Property</th>
<th>Why it matters</th>
<th>Failure when it is missing</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Present in common operations</td>
<td>The router can send each operation to the one shard that owns the key.</td>
<td>Common queries without the key must fan out to every shard and merge the results.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Even spread of data and load</td>
<td>Each shard gets a similar share of storage and requests.</td>
<td>Hot shards: skewed values, sequential ranges or one very large tenant overload a single shard even when total cluster capacity is sufficient.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Keeps atomic changes together</td>
<td>Rows that must change in one transaction live on one shard, so a local transaction is enough.</td>
<td>Those changes need cross-shard coordination or a multi-step workflow.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Stable values</td>
<td>Rows avoid moves caused by a change to their own key value. Ownership can still move when the key-to-shard mapping or shard topology changes, such as during rebalancing.</td>
<td>A changed key value can map to a different shard. When it does, the row must migrate across shards instead of being updated in place.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">For example, <code>tenant_id</code> can fit a multi-tenant service well: most requests carry it, a tenant's data usually changes together, and it does not change. It still fails if one tenant outgrows a single shard.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Sharding pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Sharding.md" class="internal-link">Sharding</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do lookup, range and hash sharding strategies differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">All three strategies map a shard key to the shard that owns the data. They differ in what decides that mapping, which in turn decides load balance, range-query efficiency and how hard rebalancing is.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Lookup (directory)</th>
<th>Range</th>
<th>Hash</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How a key is mapped</td>
<td>A stored map records which shard owns each key, tenant or virtual shard.</td>
<td>Contiguous key ranges belong to shards, such as customer IDs <code>1–9999</code> on one shard.</td>
<td>A hash of the key determines the shard, so no map has to be stored.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Load balance</td>
<td>Placement is explicit, so large tenants can be placed deliberately.</td>
<td>Can be uneven. Sequential keys, such as timestamps or increasing IDs, send new writes to the newest range and create a hotspot.</td>
<td>Usually spreads data and load evenly, although one very hot key still lands on a single shard.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Range queries</td>
<td>No inherent locality; it depends on how the map groups keys.</td>
<td>Efficient, because neighboring keys sit on the same shard.</td>
<td>Neighboring keys scatter, so a range query fans out to many shards.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rebalancing</td>
<td>Data is moved and its map entries are updated. With keys mapped to virtual shards, a virtual shard can move between physical servers without changing application code.</td>
<td>Moving or splitting a range moves its data. Rebalancing may not fix load that concentrates on adjacent keys.</td>
<td>Difficult. With a simple <code>hash(key) % N</code>, changing the number of shards changes the owner of most keys.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Routing overhead</td>
<td>A map lookup on every routed request.</td>
<td>A comparison of the key against stored range boundaries.</td>
<td>Computing the hash.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Sharding pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/Sharding.md" class="internal-link">Sharding</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In what logical order are the clauses of a SQL <code>SELECT</code> query evaluated, and why does that order matter?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Logically, a <code>SELECT</code> query is evaluated from its input outward: rows are built, filtered, grouped, filtered again as groups, projected into output columns, then sorted and limited. Each step works on the output of the previous steps, so a clause can use only what earlier steps produced.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><code>FROM</code> and joins build the input rows.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>WHERE</code> removes rows that do not satisfy its condition.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>GROUP BY</code> forms groups and computes aggregates.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>HAVING</code> removes groups.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>SELECT</code> computes the output columns and their aliases.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>DISTINCT</code> removes duplicate output rows.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>ORDER BY</code> sorts the output.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>LIMIT</code> and <code>OFFSET</code> keep a slice of the sorted rows.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Several consequences follow from this order:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><code>WHERE</code> cannot test an aggregate of its own query block, because that block's groups do not exist yet. A subquery inside <code>WHERE</code> can still compute its own aggregate for the comparison.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>WHERE</code> and <code>HAVING</code> cannot refer to an output alias defined in <code>SELECT</code>, because that alias is computed later. <code>ORDER BY</code> runs after <code>SELECT</code>, so it can.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>LIMIT</code> without <code>ORDER BY</code> returns an unpredictable subset of rows, because no order has been defined.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Alias rules vary by dialect. PostgreSQL also accepts an output column name in <code>GROUP BY</code>, while SQL Server requires the original expression there, so portable SQL repeats the expression. The order is logical: the optimizer can execute the query differently, as long as the result is the same.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: SELECT</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between <code>WHERE</code> and <code>HAVING</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>WHERE</code> filters individual rows before they are grouped. <code>HAVING</code> filters the groups that <code>GROUP BY</code> produces, so its condition can test aggregate values such as <code>COUNT(*)</code> or <code>SUM(amount)</code>.</p>
<pre class="language-sql"><code class="language-sql is-loaded"><span class="token keyword">SELECT</span> department<span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token function">COUNT</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token operator">*</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token keyword">AS</span> headcount
<span class="token keyword">FROM</span> employees
<span class="token keyword">WHERE</span> hire_date <span class="token operator">&gt;=</span> <span class="token keyword">DATE</span> <span class="token string">'2024-01-01'</span>  <span class="token comment">-- keeps recent hires only</span>
<span class="token keyword">GROUP</span> <span class="token keyword">BY</span> department
<span class="token keyword">HAVING</span> <span class="token function">COUNT</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token operator">*</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">&gt;</span> <span class="token number">5</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>                  <span class="token comment">-- keeps departments with more than five recent hires</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th><code>WHERE</code></th>
<th><code>HAVING</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it filters</td>
<td>Input rows of the query, before grouping.</td>
<td>Groups, after grouping and aggregation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Aggregates in the condition</td>
<td>Cannot use an aggregate of its own query, because no groups exist yet. A subquery inside <code>WHERE</code> can still compute its own aggregate.</td>
<td>Can use aggregates; the condition is evaluated once per group.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect on later work</td>
<td>Rows it removes never reach grouping or aggregation.</td>
<td>Groups are built and aggregated before it removes any.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A condition on a grouping column, such as <code>department = 'Sales'</code>, gives the same result in either clause. Written in <code>WHERE</code>, it expresses the cheaper logical order, because rows are removed before any grouping work.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: SELECT</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In a <code>LEFT JOIN</code>, why does putting a condition on the right table in <code>WHERE</code> instead of <code>ON</code> change the result?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A condition in <code>ON</code> decides which right-side rows match. Left rows without a match are still kept, with <code>NULL</code> in the right-side columns. A condition in <code>WHERE</code> runs after the join and keeps only the rows for which it is true. An ordinary comparison such as <code>o.total &gt;= 50</code> is not true for those <code>NULL</code>-extended rows, so <code>WHERE</code> removes them, and the query behaves like an inner join for that condition.</p>
<p dir="auto">In this example, <code>customers</code> holds Ada and Lin. Ada has orders with totals 40 and 70, and Lin has none.</p>
<pre class="language-sql"><code class="language-sql is-loaded"><span class="token comment">-- Condition in ON: every customer is kept</span>
<span class="token keyword">SELECT</span> c<span class="token punctuation">.</span>name<span class="token punctuation">,</span> o<span class="token punctuation">.</span>total
<span class="token keyword">FROM</span> customers <span class="token keyword">AS</span> c
<span class="token keyword">LEFT</span> <span class="token keyword">JOIN</span> orders <span class="token keyword">AS</span> o
  <span class="token keyword">ON</span> o<span class="token punctuation">.</span>customer_id <span class="token operator">=</span> c<span class="token punctuation">.</span>id <span class="token operator">AND</span> o<span class="token punctuation">.</span>total <span class="token operator">&gt;=</span> <span class="token number">50</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token comment">-- Ada | 70</span>
<span class="token comment">-- Lin | NULL</span>

<span class="token comment">-- Condition in WHERE: applied after the join</span> <span class="token keyword">SELECT</span> c<span class="token punctuation">.</span>name<span class="token punctuation">,</span> o<span class="token punctuation">.</span>total <span class="token keyword">FROM</span> customers <span class="token keyword">AS</span> c <span class="token keyword">LEFT</span> <span class="token keyword">JOIN</span> orders <span class="token keyword">AS</span> o <span class="token keyword">ON</span> o<span class="token punctuation">.</span>customer\_id <span class="token operator">=</span> c<span class="token punctuation">.</span>id <span class="token keyword">WHERE</span> o<span class="token punctuation">.</span>total <span class="token operator">>=</span> <span class="token number">50</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> <span class="token comment">-- Ada | 70</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<p dir="auto">In the second query, the join first produces a Lin row with a <code>NULL</code> total. <code>NULL &gt;= 50</code> evaluates to unknown rather than true, so <code>WHERE</code> removes Lin.</p>
<p dir="auto">A right-side condition that is true for <code>NULL</code> behaves differently. With the same <code>ON o.customer_id = c.id</code> join, <code>WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL</code> is true only for the <code>NULL</code>-extended row, so it keeps Lin and returns only customers without orders.</p>
<p dir="auto">The <code>ON</code> form answers 'all customers, with their large orders if any'. The <code>WHERE</code> form answers 'customers who have a large order'. The correct placement depends on which of those questions the query is meant to answer.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: SELECT</a> · <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: Table expressions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In SQL Server, how do stored procedures and user-defined functions differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A stored procedure is a database operation called as its own statement; it can change data and return several kinds of results. A T-SQL user-defined function (UDF) computes a value for use inside a query, and SQL Server forbids it from changing database state.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Stored procedure</th>
<th>T-SQL user-defined function</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How it is called</td>
<td>As a statement with <code>EXEC</code>. It cannot be used inside a <code>SELECT</code> expression.</td>
<td>Inside a query: a scalar UDF in an expression such as a <code>SELECT</code> list or <code>WHERE</code> condition, a table-valued UDF in <code>FROM</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it returns</td>
<td>Any number of result sets, output parameters and an integer return status.</td>
<td>One scalar value or one table.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Changing data</td>
<td>Can insert, update and delete data and call other procedures.</td>
<td>Cannot modify database state; only table variables declared inside the function can change.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Other restrictions</td>
<td>Can use dynamic SQL, temporary tables and <code>TRY...CATCH</code>.</td>
<td>Cannot use dynamic SQL, temporary tables or <code>TRY...CATCH</code>, and cannot call ordinary stored procedures.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Scalar UDFs carry a performance risk. Without inlining, SQL Server invokes a T-SQL scalar UDF once per qualifying row and does not run the calling query in parallel. In SQL Server 2019 (15.x) and later, at database compatibility level 150 or higher, the optimizer can inline an eligible scalar UDF by turning its body into part of the calling query's plan. Inlining applies only when the function and the calling query meet the documented eligibility requirements.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/create-procedure-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver15" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/create-procedure-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver15" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: CREATE PROCEDURE</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/user-defined-functions/create-user-defined-functions-database-engine" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/user-defined-functions/create-user-defined-functions-database-engine" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Create user-defined functions</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/user-defined-functions/scalar-udf-inlining" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/user-defined-functions/scalar-udf-inlining" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Scalar UDF inlining</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In SQL Server, when is a temp table a better fit than a CTE?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A temp table is a better fit when an intermediate result is expensive to compute and is needed more than once. It also fits when later steps need indexes or statistics on that result to be planned well. A CTE is a better fit for structuring a single statement, because it adds no storage or cleanup.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>CTE</th>
<th>Temp table</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Scope</td>
<td>A named result for the one statement that immediately follows it.</td>
<td>A real table that later statements can query until it is dropped or its session or creating procedure ends.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Materialization</td>
<td>SQL Server does not promise to store the result. If the outer query references the CTE several times, its query can run again for each reference.</td>
<td>Rows are computed once and stored, so later reads reuse them.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Optimization</td>
<td>Optimized together with the statement that uses it.</td>
<td>Can be indexed, and SQL Server keeps statistics on it that later queries' plans can use.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Inspection</td>
<td>The intermediate result cannot be examined on its own.</td>
<td>The stored rows can be queried directly, which helps debugging.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>No separate write or cleanup.</td>
<td>Writing the rows, maintaining any indexes and dropping the table add work. The rows are a copy, so later changes to the source tables do not appear in them.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Neither option is faster by default. A temp table pays off when reuse, indexing or better row estimates save more work than writing the rows costs.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/queries/with-common-table-expression-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/queries/with-common-table-expression-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: WITH common_table_expression</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do SQL Server's transaction isolation levels differ in the read anomalies they allow?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">SQL Server provides five isolation levels. From <code>READ UNCOMMITTED</code> to <code>SERIALIZABLE</code>, each lock-based level prevents more read anomalies at the cost of more blocking. <code>SNAPSHOT</code> prevents the same read anomalies as <code>SERIALIZABLE</code> by reading row versions instead of holding read locks.</p>
<p dir="auto">The anomalies are:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Dirty read:</strong> reading data another transaction has changed but not committed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Nonrepeatable read:</strong> reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different committed values.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Phantom read:</strong> re-running a range query in one transaction and getting a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows.</li>
</ul>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Level</th>
<th>How reads behave</th>
<th>Read anomalies still possible</th>
<th>Main cost</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>READ UNCOMMITTED</code></td>
<td>Reads take no shared data locks and do not wait for writers' exclusive data locks.</td>
<td>Dirty, nonrepeatable and phantom reads.</td>
<td>Results can include changes that are later rolled back.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>READ COMMITTED</code> (default)</td>
<td>Reads see only committed data. With locking, a read waits for writers and releases its shared lock soon after reading.</td>
<td>Nonrepeatable and phantom reads.</td>
<td>Readers and writers block each other.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>REPEATABLE READ</code></td>
<td>Shared locks on rows read are held until the transaction ends.</td>
<td>Phantom reads.</td>
<td>Longer-held locks increase blocking and deadlocks.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>SERIALIZABLE</code></td>
<td>Range locks also stop other transactions from inserting into ranges already read.</td>
<td>None of the three.</td>
<td>The most blocking and deadlock risk.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>SNAPSHOT</code></td>
<td>Reads see committed data as of the start of the transaction, using row versions instead of shared data locks, so reads do not block writers' data changes.</td>
<td>None of the three.</td>
<td>Row versions add overhead. An update to a row that another transaction changed after the snapshot began fails with an update conflict. The level must be enabled with the <code>ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION</code> database option.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The <code>READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT</code> database option changes how <code>READ COMMITTED</code> reads behave, but it is not a separate isolation level.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Transaction locking and row versioning guide</a></p>
