</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What changes about <code>READ COMMITTED</code> reads when SQL Server's Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI) is enabled?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">With RCSI enabled, a <code>READ COMMITTED</code> read no longer takes shared locks. It reads row versions instead, and each statement sees the data that was committed when that statement started. For data locks, readers therefore stop blocking writers, and writers stop blocking readers.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>How it is enabled:</strong> RCSI is the <code>READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT</code> database option. Sessions that use <code>READ COMMITTED</code>, the default level, get the new behavior without code changes.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Statement-level, not transaction-level:</strong> each statement takes a fresh view. Two statements in the same transaction can still see different committed data, so nonrepeatable and phantom reads remain possible. <code>SNAPSHOT</code> isolation, by contrast, keeps one view for the whole transaction.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Writes still lock:</strong> data modifications still take locks, so writers still block other writers.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost:</strong> maintaining row versions adds storage and I/O overhead.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A read no longer waits for an in-flight write. It can therefore return the last committed value of a row that another transaction is about to change. A read-then-write sequence that relied on that waiting needs explicit concurrency protection.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Transaction locking and row versioning guide</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In SQL Server, why is the <code>NOLOCK</code> hint unsafe as a general performance fix?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>NOLOCK</code> makes the read of that table behave like <code>READ UNCOMMITTED</code>. For data, the read takes no shared locks and is not blocked by other transactions' exclusive locks. It avoids waiting on concurrent writers only by giving up the guarantee that the result is correct. The hint covers only data locks: the query still takes schema-stability locks, so a concurrent schema change can still block it.</p>
<p dir="auto">While data changes concurrently, a <code>NOLOCK</code> read can return:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Uncommitted data:</strong> values written by a transaction that later rolls back, so the result contains data that was never committed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Missing or duplicate rows:</strong> the scan takes no shared data locks, so rows that concurrent changes move while it runs can be skipped or read twice. A page split is one way rows move.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These anomalies need not raise an error. A scan can sometimes fail when data moves under it, but it can also finish normally with a wrong total, a missing record or a double-counted row, and nothing signals the problem.</p>
<p dir="auto">It is also not a general speed-up. A query that is slow because of its own work, such as a large scan or a missing index, does the same work under <code>NOLOCK</code>. When the real problem is readers waiting on writers' data locks, row versioning through <code>READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT</code> or <code>SNAPSHOT</code> removes that waiting while still returning committed data.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Transaction locking and row versioning guide</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/queries/hints-transact-sql-table?view=sql-server-ver17" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/queries/hints-transact-sql-table?view=sql-server-ver17" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SQL Server: Table hints</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Data Persistence/SQL/SQL.md" class="internal-link">SQL</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-3" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-3" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Networks"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Networks">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Networks"><option value="Networks">All Networks (10)</option><option value="Networks/Protocols">Protocols (6)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Networks questions"><h2>Networks</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Networks"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the practical difference between a Layer 4 and a Layer 7 load balancer?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A Layer 4 load balancer chooses a backend once per transport connection, using connection details such as IP addresses, ports and protocol. A Layer 7 load balancer terminates and parses the application protocol, usually HTTP, so it can route each request by its content.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Layer 4</th>
<th>Layer 7</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it can see</td>
<td>Connection details only. It does not parse HTTP, so a request's host, path and headers are invisible to it.</td>
<td>The parsed request, including its host, path and headers.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Unit of balancing</td>
<td>The connection. Every request sent on that connection reaches the same backend for the connection's lifetime.</td>
<td>The individual request. Requests from one client connection can reach different backends.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Routing rules</td>
<td>Limited to connection details, so path-based or header-based routing is not possible.</td>
<td>Content-based rules, such as sending <code>/api/*</code> to one group of backends and other paths to another.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>Forwards traffic without parsing the application protocol, so it keeps little protocol state.</td>
<td>Terminating and parsing HTTP adds processing, protocol state and more ways to fail.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The unit of balancing matters for multiplexed protocols such as HTTP/2 and gRPC, where one long-lived connection carries many requests. An L4 balancer sends all of those requests to one backend. An L7 balancer that terminates HTTP/2 can spread them across backends.</p>
<p dir="auto">Request awareness does not make retries safe. When an L7 proxy is configured to retry failed requests, a retry is safe only if the application tolerates the same request being replayed.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">AWS: How Elastic Load Balancing works</a> · <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/application-load-balancers.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/application-load-balancers.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">AWS: Application Load Balancers</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9110: Idempotent methods</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/OSI Model.md" class="internal-link">OSI Model</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the OSI model map onto the TCP/IP stack?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">In the common four-layer TCP/IP view, OSI layers 5–7 are grouped as application, layer 4 maps to transport, layer 3 to Internet, and layers 1–2 to link. This is a teaching and diagnostic mapping, not a strict protocol-by-protocol equivalence: real protocols can span or blur those responsibilities. <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.html#section-1.1.3" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.html#section-1.1.3" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 1122: Internet architecture</a> · <a href="https://www.iso.org/standard/20269.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.iso.org/standard/20269.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ISO/IEC 7498-1: OSI reference model</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/OSI Model.md" class="internal-link">OSI Model</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What do a MAC address, an IP address and a port each identify?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A MAC address identifies a network interface on its local link, such as an Ethernet or Wi-Fi network. An IP address identifies a host's interface across interconnected networks, and routers forward packets by it. A port identifies an endpoint, such as a listening application, inside one host for a transport protocol such as TCP.</p>
<p dir="auto">The three work together when a packet travels to a server:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The sender addresses the IP packet to the server's IP address and the TCP segment inside it to the server's port.</li>
<li dir="auto">On each hop, the packet travels inside a link-layer frame for that link. On an Ethernet or Wi-Fi link, the frame is addressed to the MAC address of the next device on that link, usually a router.</li>
<li dir="auto">Each router reads the destination IP address, chooses the next link and places the packet in a new frame for that link. When the next link also uses MAC addressing, the new frame carries new MAC addresses.</li>
<li dir="auto">On the destination host, TCP uses the destination port to deliver the data to the right socket.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">A MAC address therefore matters only within one link, while the IP address guides the packet across networks. A port number is meaningful only within one host's, or one network namespace's, port space for that transport protocol.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.html#section-1.1.3" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.html#section-1.1.3" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 1122: Internet architecture</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9293: TCP</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/OSI Model.md" class="internal-link">OSI Model</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which values identify a TCP connection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A TCP connection is identified by four values: the local IP address and port, and the remote IP address and port. Each IP address and port pair is a socket, and the pair of sockets distinguishes one connection from every other TCP connection in the host, or network namespace, that holds it. The combination is often called the 4-tuple.</p>
<p dir="auto">Because the remote address and port are part of the identity, one local socket can take part in many connections. A server listening on port 443 can hold many connections at once, because each differs by client IP address or client port. For the same reason, one client can open several connections to the same server port by using different local ports.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9293: TCP</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/OSI Model.md" class="internal-link">OSI Model</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Networks/Protocols"><h3>Protocols</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does HTTP/2 differ from HTTP/1.1?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">HTTP/2 keeps HTTP's semantics but changes how messages travel on a connection. It replaces HTTP/1.1's text messages with binary frames, carries many concurrent exchanges as streams on one connection and compresses header fields.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>HTTP/1.1</th>
<th>HTTP/2</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Message format</td>
<td>Text messages sent one after another on the connection.</td>
<td>Binary frames, each tagged with a stream ID, so frames from different exchanges can be interleaved.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Concurrency</td>
<td>Without pipelining, one request at a time per connection. Pipelining allows several outstanding requests, but responses must return in request order, so clients commonly open several connections to deliver responses independently.</td>
<td>Many concurrent streams on one connection, and responses need not follow request order, so a client normally needs only one connection per origin.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Header fields</td>
<td>Sent as text in full with every message, so repeated fields such as cookies are resent each time.</td>
<td>Compressed with HPACK, so repeated fields cost fewer bytes.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Semantics</td>
<td>Defined by HTTP's methods, status codes and fields.</td>
<td>Unchanged, so applications and APIs keep the same meaning for every request and response.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Starting the protocol</td>
<td>Needs no negotiation and is the fallback when HTTP/2 is not agreed.</td>
<td>Negotiated: over TLS, both sides agree on <code>h2</code> through ALPN during the handshake.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Both versions run over TCP, so packet loss on an HTTP/2 connection can still delay all of its streams until TCP recovers.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9113: HTTP/2</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9293: TCP</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/Protocols/HTTP 2.md" class="internal-link">HTTP 2</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does HTTP/2 multiplexing improve over HTTP/1.1, and what head-of-line blocking remains?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">HTTP/2 multiplexing removes HTTP/1.1's response-order head-of-line blocking: a slow response no longer has to finish before later responses on the same connection can be delivered. TCP-level head-of-line blocking remains, because all streams still share one ordered TCP byte stream.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What improves:</strong> an HTTP/1.1 connection returns responses in request order. Without pipelining, the next request waits for the previous response. With pipelining, several requests can be outstanding, but a slow first response still delays the responses behind it. HTTP/2 splits requests and responses into frames tagged with a stream ID and interleaves frames from many streams on one connection, so responses no longer have to arrive in request order.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What remains:</strong> TCP delivers bytes to the receiving application strictly in order. When one TCP segment is lost, bytes that arrive after it are held back until the retransmission fills the gap, even if they belong to other streams. A lost packet can therefore stall every stream on the connection until TCP recovers.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">HTTP/2 removes this ordering dependency, not every interaction between streams. Streams still share connection-level flow control, and each block of header fields must be sent as a contiguous run of frames, so one stream can still slow another.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9113: HTTP/2</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-9.3.2" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-9.3.2" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1 pipelining</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9293: TCP</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/Protocols/HTTP 2.md" class="internal-link">HTTP 2</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When can HTTP/1.1 be necessary or perform better than HTTP/2?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">HTTP/1.1 is necessary when some hop on the path cannot negotiate HTTP/2. It can perform better on a lossy path, because with several HTTP/1.1 connections the delay caused by a lost packet stays on one connection. It is not generally faster, so the choice rests on measuring both versions on the real path.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Compatibility:</strong> HTTP/2 is used on a hop only when both ends agree to it, for example through ALPN during the TLS handshake. If the client, server or intermediary at either end of a hop supports only HTTP/1.1, that hop uses HTTP/1.1.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Loss isolation:</strong> HTTP/2 normally carries all requests to an origin on one TCP connection, so one lost packet can delay every stream until TCP retransmits it. With several HTTP/1.1 connections, the same loss delays only the requests on the affected connection.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost of extra connections:</strong> pipelining lets one HTTP/1.1 connection carry several outstanding requests, but responses must return in request order. Delivering responses independently of each other therefore takes several connections. Each needs its own TCP setup, plus TLS setup when encrypted, and its own state on clients, servers and intermediaries. Connections that share a path also compete for its capacity, and opening more of them can add to congestion.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9113: HTTP/2</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9293: TCP</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/Protocols/HTTP 2.md" class="internal-link">HTTP 2</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does HTTP idempotency guarantee about retrying a request?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An idempotent HTTP method guarantees that sending the same request several times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once. A client can therefore resend such a request after a communication failure, for example when the connection closes before the response arrives, even though the first attempt may already have succeeded.</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>PUT</code>, <code>DELETE</code> and the safe methods, such as <code>GET</code> and <code>HEAD</code>, are idempotent. <code>POST</code> is not.</p>
<p dir="auto">The guarantee is narrower than identical behavior:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Responses can differ.</strong> A retried <code>DELETE</code> leaves the resource deleted, but the second response can report that the resource no longer exists.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Only the requested effect is covered.</strong> The server can still log, audit or record history separately for each copy of the request.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Method semantics do not make a particular retry harmless.</strong> The request body must be replayable, the retry must fit within the caller's deadline and credentials must still be valid. A request that carries a single-use value, such as a one-time token, cannot simply be replayed.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For a non-idempotent method such as <code>POST</code>, an automatic retry is appropriate only when the client knows the operation is idempotent for that resource or can detect that the first attempt was never applied.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 9110: Idempotent methods</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/Protocols/HTTP.md" class="internal-link">HTTP</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is WebSocket, and how is a WebSocket connection opened?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">WebSocket is a protocol for full-duplex, message-based communication over one long-lived connection: once the connection is open, either side can send a message at any time. It starts with an HTTP handshake, which lets it use the usual web ports and work with HTTP proxies and other intermediaries.</p>
<p dir="auto">The HTTP/1.1 opening handshake defined by RFC 6455 works as follows:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The client sends an HTTP <code>GET</code> request with <code>Upgrade: websocket</code>, <code>Connection: Upgrade</code> and a random <code>Sec-WebSocket-Key</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">A server that accepts replies <code>101 Switching Protocols</code> with a <code>Sec-WebSocket-Accept</code> value computed from that key. The value shows that the server understood the request as a WebSocket handshake rather than ordinary HTTP.</li>
<li dir="auto">From then on, the same TCP connection carries WebSocket frames instead of HTTP messages. Data frames carry text or binary messages, and control frames carry ping, pong and the closing handshake.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><code>ws://</code> runs over plain TCP and <code>wss://</code> runs over TLS.</p>
<p dir="auto">The protocol provides framing and two-way delivery. It does not define request–response correlation, reconnection or resuming after a disconnect, so applications that need them build them on top.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 6455: WebSocket</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/Protocols/WebSockets.md" class="internal-link">WebSockets</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What conditions make Server-Sent Events a better fit than WebSockets?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Server-Sent Events (SSE) fit better when updates flow mainly from server to browser, client actions can travel as ordinary HTTP requests, and built-in reconnection with a resume cursor is useful. WebSockets fit better when both sides need to send messages over the same long-lived connection, or when messages are binary.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Server-Sent Events</th>
<th>WebSockets</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Direction</td>
<td>One-way: the server sends an ordered stream of events in one long-lived HTTP response. Client actions use separate HTTP requests.</td>
<td>Full duplex: either side can send messages at any time on one connection.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Message format</td>
<td>UTF-8 text events, so binary data has to be encoded as text.</td>
<td>Text or binary messages.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reconnection</td>
<td>The browser's <code>EventSource</code> reconnects automatically. If the stream has given it a nonempty event ID, the reconnection request sends that ID in a <code>Last-Event-ID</code> header.</td>
<td>Not part of the protocol. The application implements reconnection, usually with backoff.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Resuming after a disconnect</td>
<td>Works only if the server tags events with IDs, keeps recent events and replays those after <code>Last-Event-ID</code>. Clients still have to tolerate duplicates or gaps.</td>
<td>The application defines its own resume tokens, replay and acknowledgements.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Connection setup</td>
<td>An ordinary HTTP request and response. Intermediaries can drop a quiet stream, so servers often send periodic comment lines to keep it active.</td>
<td>Opens with an HTTP handshake, then exchanges WebSocket frames instead of HTTP messages.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Neither protocol guarantees a particular latency. Delivery time still depends on the server, the network and any intermediaries.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">WHATWG: Server-sent events</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 6455: WebSocket</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Networks/Protocols/WebSockets.md" class="internal-link">WebSockets</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-4" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-4" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Software Architecture"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Software%20Architecture">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Software%20Architecture"><option value="Software Architecture">All Software Architecture (104)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Application Architecture">Application Architecture (7)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Distributed Systems">Distributed Systems (8)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Message Queues">Distributed Systems / Message Queues (3)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Scalability Patterns">Distributed Systems / Scalability Patterns (3)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Patterns">Patterns (75)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns">Patterns / Architectural Patterns (5)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns">Patterns / Design Patterns (58)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral">Patterns / Design Patterns / Behavioral (25)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational">Patterns / Design Patterns / Creational (12)</option><option value="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural">Patterns / Design Patterns / Structural (15)</option><option value="Software Architecture/System Architecture">System Architecture (13)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Software Architecture questions"><h2>Software Architecture</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What factors determine whether a system should use a monolith, a modular monolith, or microservices?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The choice depends on whether real boundaries repeatedly need independent deployment, scaling or ownership, and whether the system can carry the cost of distribution. Without that pressure, one deployment is usually the better fit. A modular monolith adds clear internal boundaries without the cost of a distributed system.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Monolith</th>
<th>Modular monolith</th>
<th>Microservices</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Deployment</td>
<td>One deployable unit, so every change ships with the whole application.</td>
<td>Still one deployable unit, so all modules release together.</td>
<td>Each service deploys on its own, so one service can change without redeploying the others.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Internal boundaries</td>
<td>Code can reach across areas directly, so boundaries rely on discipline.</td>
<td>Module boundaries are explicit and enforced, so modules use each other only through public contracts.</td>
<td>Boundaries are service APIs or messages over the network.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Calls, transactions and data</td>
<td>In-process calls over a shared data layer; one local transaction can cover a whole operation.</td>
<td>The same in-process calls and local transactions as a monolith.</td>
<td>Each service owns its data. Calls cross the network and can fail or slow down. No single local transaction spans services, so consistency between them is usually eventual.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Scaling</td>
<td>The whole application scales as one unit.</td>
<td>The whole application scales as one unit.</td>
<td>Each service scales according to its own load.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Operational cost</td>
<td>Lowest: one build, deployment and runtime to monitor.</td>
<td>Close to a monolith, plus the effort of keeping boundaries enforced.</td>
<td>Highest: many deployments, network failure handling, contract versioning and monitoring across services.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Microservices fit when stable boundaries repeatedly need independent releases, independent scaling or separate team ownership, and the organization can operate the resulting distributed system. System size or expected growth alone does not justify the split.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microservices architecture style (Azure Architecture Center)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Software Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Software Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Application Architecture"><h3>Application Architecture</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is simple layering enough for a small CRUD service, and when is Clean Architecture worth it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Simple layering is usually enough when the service mainly validates input and reads or writes records, because there are few business rules to protect. Clean Architecture is worth its extra cost when substantial business rules must stay independent of the database and other infrastructure, and must be testable without them.</p>
<p dir="auto">The decision is about responsibilities and dependency direction:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Simple layering:</strong> the API calls business logic, and business logic calls data access directly. Business code refers to persistence code, so it is coupled to that code. When the logic is thin, this coupling costs little and the design stays direct.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Clean Architecture:</strong> business rules and use cases declare the interfaces they need, such as an order repository. Infrastructure implements those interfaces, and dependency injection connects them at runtime. Business code never refers to database code, but each boundary adds abstractions and configuration.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A layered design can also invert selected dependencies where a rule needs isolation. Expected future growth does not justify either choice by itself. The question is whether real business rules make isolation and independent testing worth the extra abstraction.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Common web application architectures (Microsoft Learn)</a> · <a href="https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Application Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Application Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is Clean Architecture?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Clean Architecture structures an application so its business rules sit at the center, independent of frameworks, UI and databases. Its purpose is core logic that can be understood, tested and changed independently of those details.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Entities:</strong> general business rules, such as an <code>Order</code> that rejects zero quantities.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Use cases:</strong> application-specific rules that coordinate entities, such as <code>PlaceOrder</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Adapters:</strong> translate between use cases and the outside world. Examples are controllers, presenters and repository implementations.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Frameworks and drivers (infrastructure):</strong> outer details such as ASP.NET Core, EF Core and the database.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Dependency rule:</strong> <em>inward</em> means toward the business rules. Any source-code dependency that crosses one of these boundaries must point inward, so inner code never names an outer detail. Code at the same level may still refer to its peers.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Example:</strong> <code>PlaceOrder</code> declares and calls <code>IOrderRepository</code>. <code>SqlOrderRepository</code>, a database adapter, implements that interface, and dependency injection supplies it at runtime. Control flows outward to the database, but the source dependency points inward. A fake repository therefore allows <code>PlaceOrder</code> to be tested without a database.</p>
<p dir="auto">The circles describe dependency direction. They do not require a particular number of projects or folders.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Robert C. Martin: The Clean Architecture</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Common web application architectures</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Clean Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Clean Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between traditional layered and Onion/Clean Architecture?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">In traditional layering, source dependencies usually follow the call chain downward, so business logic depends on data access. In Onion and Clean Architecture, dependencies point toward the business rules. The business and application code defines the interfaces it needs, and infrastructure implements them.</p>
<p dir="auto">In the table, A → B means that code in A refers to types in B.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Traditional layered</th>
<th>Onion/Clean</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Typical source dependencies</td>
<td>UI → business logic → data access. Business logic compiles against the data layer.</td>
<td>UI → core, and infrastructure → core. The business and application core refers to nothing outside itself.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How business rules reach storage</td>
<td>Business logic calls classes or interfaces that the data-access layer owns.</td>
<td>The core declares the interface it needs, such as IOrderRepository. Infrastructure implements it, and dependency injection supplies it at runtime.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Testing business rules</td>
<td>Isolating the rules is harder because they refer to data-access types.</td>
<td>The rules can be tested with simple fakes of core-owned interfaces, without a database.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Changing infrastructure</td>
<td>Changes to data-access types can ripple into business code.</td>
<td>Changes stay behind the core's interfaces unless the core's needs change.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Layered designs can also use dependency inversion. For example, business logic can own a repository interface that the data layer implements. Onion and Clean make that inward direction a defining rule rather than an optional technique. Onion and Clean share this rule but name their layers differently, and neither requires a particular number of projects.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Common web application architectures (Microsoft Learn)</a> · <a href="https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Layered Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Layered Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is plug-in architecture?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Plug-in architecture lets a host application gain behavior from separately built extensions through a shared contract.</p>
<p dir="auto">It has three parts:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Host:</strong> the main application. It decides where extensions can fit, then finds, loads, creates and calls them.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared contract:</strong> an interface or abstract type that both sides reference, such as <code>ICommand</code> with a <code>Name</code> and an <code>Execute</code> method.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Extensions (plug-ins):</strong> separately built implementations of the contract.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For example, an image editor can expose a filter contract and load sharpening or blur filters as extensions. The host understands how to apply a filter; each extension supplies the actual transformation.</p>
<p dir="auto">This makes supported behavior extensible, but introduces contract-compatibility and loading costs. Extensions remain limited by the host's extension points, and loading them in-process does not provide a security sandbox.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tutorials/creating-app-with-plugin-support" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tutorials/creating-app-with-plugin-support" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Create a .NET application with plugins</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Plug-in Architecture (MicroKernel).md" class="internal-link">Plug-in Architecture (MicroKernel)</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does a plug-in add behavior through an existing host extension point?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A plug-in adds behavior by implementing a contract that the host already defines. The host finds that implementation, creates it and calls it through the contract, without knowing the plug-in's concrete type.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example: the host's shared contract is <code>IExporter { string Format { get; } void Export(Document doc, Stream output); }</code>.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Implement the contract:</strong> <code>PdfExporter : IExporter</code> reports <code>pdf</code> as its format and writes PDF bytes.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Build and provide it:</strong> the extension's author compiles it separately and places it where the host looks, such as a plugins folder.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Discover:</strong> the host loads the plug-in and finds types that implement <code>IExporter</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Create:</strong> the host instantiates <code>PdfExporter</code>, either directly or through DI.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Invoke:</strong> when the user chooses PDF, the host calls <code>Export(doc, stream)</code> the same way it calls any other exporter.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Limit:</strong> a plug-in can only do what its extension point expresses. <code>IExporter</code> cannot add collaborative editing. That works only if the host already offers a suitable extension point for it. Otherwise, a suitable extension point must be added or changed first.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tutorials/creating-app-with-plugin-support" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tutorials/creating-app-with-plugin-support" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Create a .NET application with plugins</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Plug-in Architecture (MicroKernel).md" class="internal-link">Plug-in Architecture (MicroKernel)</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is plug-in architecture the wrong choice?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">It is usually a poor fit when one team owns the features and ships them with the host: dynamic discovery, loading, and extension-contract compatibility add work without enabling independent delivery. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: common web application architectures</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Plug-in Architecture (MicroKernel).md" class="internal-link">Plug-in Architecture (MicroKernel)</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the key difference between MVC and MVVM?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">In MVC, a controller receives each user action, works with the model, and then selects a view and supplies the data it renders. In MVVM, the view binds to properties and commands exposed by a view-model. The view-model changes its own state and raises change notifications, and the bindings refresh the view. The view-model never references the view.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>MVC</th>
<th>MVVM</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Handling input</td>
<td>The controller receives the request, calls application behavior and chooses the response. The path from input to output is explicit in the action code.</td>
<td>The view forwards user actions to view-model commands through bindings. The same view stays on screen and reflects the new state; navigation is handled separately.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Updating the view</td>
<td>The controller passes data to the selected view, which renders it for that response.</td>
<td>Bound controls refresh when the view-model raises a change notification, such as <code>PropertyChanged</code> from <code>INotifyPropertyChanged</code>. A missed notification leaves the screen showing stale data.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Testing</td>
<td>Controller logic can be unit-tested without rendering a view.</td>
<td>View-model state and commands can be unit-tested without creating any UI controls.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical fit</td>
<td>Request/response web applications, such as ASP.NET Core MVC.</td>
<td>Long-lived client screens on platforms with data binding, such as .NET MAUI.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The cost of MVVM is its binding infrastructure: observable properties, commands and change notifications must be implemented and kept correct.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/overview?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/overview?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Overview of ASP.NET Core MVC</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/maui/mvvm" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/maui/mvvm" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Model-View-ViewModel (.NET MAUI)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Application Architecture/Presentation Architecture Variants.md" class="internal-link">Presentation Architecture Variants</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Distributed Systems"><h3>Distributed Systems</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is two-phase commit (2PC) problematic in microservices?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Two-phase commit is a blocking protocol. Every participant that has prepared must wait for one coordinator's decision while still holding its locks, so a slow or failed coordinator or a network delay can stall other services. It also works only when every participant supports the same transaction protocol, which couples independently failing services to one shared coordinator.</p>
<p dir="auto">How the blocking arises:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Prepare:</strong> the coordinator asks each participant to make its tentative work durable and vote. A participant that votes yes keeps the locks that work needs and promises to follow the final decision.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Decide:</strong> the coordinator records commit only if every participant voted yes. Any no vote produces abort.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Complete:</strong> each participant commits or rolls back when the decision reaches it, and only then releases its locks.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Consequences for microservices:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Locks held across network delays:</strong> between steps 1 and 3, a coordinator crash or network delay leaves prepared data locked. Requests that need those rows wait or time out, so one component's failure reduces the availability and throughput of others.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared protocol requirement:</strong> each database, broker or service in the transaction must take part in the same prepare-and-commit protocol under one coordinator. A participant that cannot join that protocol cannot share the atomic commit.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This is why microservice workflows more often commit locally in each service and coordinate the remaining steps through messages, as in a saga.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare-transaction.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare-transaction.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">PostgreSQL: PREPARE TRANSACTION</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Distributed Transactions.md" class="internal-link">Distributed Transactions</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the Outbox pattern support at-least-once event delivery?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The Outbox pattern makes an event as durable as the state change it describes, then publishes it with retries. After the change commits, the event can be delayed or published more than once, but it is not lost while the relay keeps retrying.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Write atomically:</strong> the service saves the domain change and an outbox record for the event in one local database transaction. Either both commit or neither does.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Relay:</strong> a separate process reads committed outbox records and publishes them to the broker.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retry:</strong> if publishing fails, the record stays pending and the relay tries again.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Record progress:</strong> after the broker accepts the event, the relay marks the record as published.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Without an outbox, the service writes to the database and to the broker as two separate operations. A failure between them can leave one done and the other missing, for example a committed order whose event was never published.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Duplicates:</strong> if the relay crashes after the broker accepts the event but before step 4, it publishes the event again. Consumers therefore need idempotent handling or deduplication, for example by recording the IDs of events they have already processed.</p>
<p dir="auto">The atomicity covers only the local store, whose transaction must include both records. No single transaction spans the database and the broker. In Azure Cosmos DB, for example, the two writes go into one transactional batch, which must target a single logical partition.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Transactional Outbox pattern with Azure Cosmos DB</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Distributed Transactions.md" class="internal-link">Distributed Transactions</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Message Queues"><h4>Message Queues</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once message delivery?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The three guarantees describe what a failure can do to a message within a stated boundary, such as a consumer reading from a broker. At-most-once never redelivers, so a message can be lost but never repeated. At-least-once redelivers until progress is recorded, so no message is lost but one can be processed more than once. Exactly-once means each message's result is committed once, with neither loss nor duplication. It holds only inside a boundary that commits the result together with the consumer's progress. Delivery attempts can still repeat after a failure, but only one durable outcome survives.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Guarantee</th>
<th>Consumer sequence</th>
<th>After a crash</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>At-most-once</td>
<td>The consumer records its progress, by acknowledging or saving its position, and then processes the message.</td>
<td>A crash after recording progress loses the message, because it is not delivered again.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>At-least-once</td>
<td>The consumer processes the message, then records its progress.</td>
<td>A crash before progress is recorded causes redelivery, so the work can happen twice.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Exactly-once</td>
<td>The result and the consumer's progress commit atomically. Examples are output topics and consumer offsets committed in one Kafka transaction and read with <code>read_committed</code> isolation, or a database write committed in the same transaction as the message's offset or ID.</td>
<td>Either both commit or neither does. An aborted attempt leaves no visible result and is retried. After a restart, the consumer resumes from the committed position or recognizes an already recorded ID, so the result is not applied twice.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The guarantee covers only what that atomic commit includes. Kafka transactions make consuming and producing between Kafka topics exactly-once only when the output and the consumer offsets commit in one transaction and downstream consumers are configured with <code>read_committed</code>. The default <code>read_uncommitted</code> setting can expose records from aborted transactions. A database write, email or HTTP call outside the transaction is not covered. Such a side effect needs the external system's cooperation, typically an idempotency key or the message position recorded atomically with the local state change. End-to-end exactly-once across arbitrary external systems is therefore generally not available. Retry limits that move a message to a dead-letter queue, and retention or TTL expiry, are separate limits outside these guarantees.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/#message-delivery-semantics" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/#message-delivery-semantics" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Apache Kafka: Message delivery semantics</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Message Queues/Message Queues.md" class="internal-link">Message Queues</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do Kafka, RabbitMQ classic or quorum queues, and RabbitMQ Streams differ in workload fit, ordering and operational factors?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">RabbitMQ classic or quorum queues fit work items that are processed and then removed. Kafka fits high-throughput event streams that are retained so many independent consumers can read and replay them, when its partitioned log and ecosystem are central to the design. RabbitMQ Streams provide similar log-style replay and fan-out for systems that already run RabbitMQ. None of the three orders messages globally: order holds only within one queue, partition or stream partition. Operating cost and the team's experience with each platform also shape the choice.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>RabbitMQ classic/quorum queues</th>
<th>Kafka</th>
<th>RabbitMQ Streams</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>After consumption</td>
<td>An acknowledged message leaves the queue, so the queue holds only pending work. Quorum queues replicate their contents across nodes for data safety.</td>
<td>Events stay in a partitioned log for the retention period. Each consumer group tracks its own position in that log.</td>
<td>Messages stay in a replicated append-only log. Consumers read them without removing them.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Replay</td>
<td>Not built in. Reprocessing needs republishing or a copy kept elsewhere.</td>
<td>A consumer can move its offset back within retention and process events again.</td>
<td>A consumer can start reading from an offset or a timestamp.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ordering boundary</td>
<td>One queue. Redelivery and competing consumers can still change processing order.</td>
<td>One partition, not the whole topic.</td>
<td>One stream. A super stream preserves order only within each partition.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Operations</td>
<td>Health is watched through queue depth, unacknowledged messages, redelivery and node health.</td>
<td>Partitions, replication, consumer rebalances, consumer lag and retention all need planning and monitoring.</td>
<td>Streams are a RabbitMQ feature, so a team that already operates RabbitMQ gains log-style consumption without running a second broker platform.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical workload</td>
<td>Latency-sensitive commands and background jobs such as <code>GenerateInvoice</code>, with acknowledgements, retries and flexible routing through exchanges.</td>
<td>High-throughput events such as <code>OrderPlaced</code>, consumed independently by billing, analytics and rebuildable projections.</td>
<td>Large fan-out, replay or large backlogs in a system that already operates RabbitMQ.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#introduction" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#introduction" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Apache Kafka: Introduction</a> · <a href="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RabbitMQ: Quorum Queues</a> · <a href="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RabbitMQ: Streams</a> · <a href="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams#super-streams" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams#super-streams" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RabbitMQ: Super Streams</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Message Queues/Message Queues.md" class="internal-link">Message Queues</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can a message-based system keep one entity's events in order?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Most brokers order messages only within one partition or queue, not across a whole topic. One entity's events therefore stay in order only under three conditions: they all travel through the same partition, they are processed one at a time for that entity, and the consumer applies them by a per-entity sequence rather than by arrival.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Route by a stable key:</strong> the producer sends every event for the entity with the same key, such as <code>OrderId</code>. In Kafka, events with the same key go to the same partition, and consumers read each partition in the order it was written.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Process each key sequentially:</strong> concurrent handlers for one partition, or competing consumers sharing one RabbitMQ queue, can finish an entity's events in a different order than they arrived.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Apply by version or sequence number:</strong> retries, redelivery and prefetch can still deliver an event twice or late. The consumer stores the last version it applied for the entity and compares each arriving event with it:
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>At or below the applied version:</strong> a duplicate whose change is already in place, so it is acknowledged and skipped.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The next version:</strong> applied, and the stored version advances.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Further ahead:</strong> an earlier change has not arrived yet. Applying this event now would build on missing state, and discarding the earlier one when it arrives would lose its change. The consumer holds or retries the later event, or recovers the gap from the source, until the missing event is applied.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The rule differs when each event carries the entity's complete state rather than a change. A newer snapshot then supersedes every older one, so it can be applied across a gap, and a late older snapshot can be discarded without losing anything.</p>
<p dir="auto">Adding partitions increases parallelism but creates no order between partitions. RabbitMQ super streams follow the same rule and preserve order only within each partition.</p>
