<p dir="auto"><a href="https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#introduction" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#introduction" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Apache Kafka: Introduction</a> · <a href="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams#super-streams" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams#super-streams" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RabbitMQ: Super Streams</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/event-sourcing" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/event-sourcing" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Event Sourcing pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Message Queues/Message Queues.md" class="internal-link">Message Queues</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Scalability Patterns"><h4>Scalability Patterns</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Vertical scaling (scaling up) gives one instance more resources, such as a larger VM. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds instances and divides the work among them.</p>
<p dir="auto">The direction changes several practical consequences:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Vertical scaling</th>
<th>Horizontal scaling</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How capacity grows</td>
<td>A larger machine runs the same instance, so work does not have to be divided.</td>
<td>More instances share the load, which works only when work can be divided and routed among them.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Upper limit</td>
<td>The largest available instance size caps growth.</td>
<td>Shared dependencies, such as the database, become the limit rather than one machine.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Disruption while scaling</td>
<td>Resizing often makes the instance temporarily unavailable, so it is automated less often.</td>
<td>Instances can be added or removed while the application keeps running, which suits autoscaling.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect of an instance failure</td>
<td>Adds no redundancy. A failed instance takes all of its capacity with it.</td>
<td>Remaining instances can keep serving while the failed one is replaced.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>State</td>
<td>Scaling one instance up does not by itself require moving in-process state.</td>
<td>Shared state must move outside interchangeable instances, or stateful work needs explicit partition ownership.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/best-practices/auto-scaling" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/best-practices/auto-scaling" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Autoscaling guidance</a> · <a href="https://12factor.net/concurrency" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://12factor.net/concurrency" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Twelve-Factor App: Concurrency</a> · <a href="https://12factor.net/processes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://12factor.net/processes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Twelve-Factor App: Processes</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Scalability Patterns/Horizontal Scaling.md" class="internal-link">Horizontal Scaling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What architectural prerequisites must be met before horizontal scaling works?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Work must be divisible across instances, and routing must reach an instance able to own or process it. Shared durable state must live outside interchangeable workers, or stateful work needs explicit partition ownership and routing. Stateless processes are a simpler case because any replica can take the next unit; they do not mean the application has no persistent state. <a href="https://12factor.net/processes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://12factor.net/processes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Twelve-Factor App: Processes</a> · <a href="https://12factor.net/concurrency" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://12factor.net/concurrency" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Twelve-Factor App: Concurrency</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Scalability Patterns/Horizontal Scaling.md" class="internal-link">Horizontal Scaling</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can horizontal scaling fail even with many instances?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Adding instances helps only when the instances themselves are the bottleneck and work actually spreads across them. Otherwise extra replicas add load or cost without adding useful capacity.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Downstream saturation:</strong> each replica adds its own database connections and outbound calls. Twenty replicas with a pool of 100 connections each can open up to 2,000 connections, so the database, a connection limit or an external API quota saturates instead.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Instance-local state:</strong> sessions, files or locks held in one process are missing when the next request reaches another replica, so requests fail or behave inconsistently.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Uneven distribution:</strong> a hot partition key or sticky routing can overload one instance while fleet averages look healthy. More replicas do not relieve the instance that owns the hot work.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Scaling lag:</strong> an autoscaler acts on observed metrics, and new instances need startup and readiness time before they serve traffic. Capacity therefore arrives after demand has risen unless spare capacity or an earlier signal covers the delay.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When throughput barely improves after the replica count doubles, the bottleneck is elsewhere.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://12factor.net/processes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://12factor.net/processes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">The Twelve-Factor App: Processes</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/best-practices/auto-scaling" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/best-practices/auto-scaling" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Autoscaling guidance</a> · <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Kubernetes: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Distributed Systems/Scalability Patterns/Horizontal Scaling.md" class="internal-link">Horizontal Scaling</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Patterns"><h3>Patterns</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does Command-Query Separation (CQS) make code easier to reason about?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">CQS makes each operation's contract show whether it can change state. A query returns information without observable side effects; a command changes state and traditionally returns no result. Finding where the code changes state therefore only requires following command calls.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Queries:</strong> calling one causes no state change, so a query call can be added, repeated or moved, for example while debugging, without introducing a mutation.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Commands:</strong> every intended mutation goes through a command, so the paths that change state are easy to find, and retry and transaction decisions attach to those calls.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">CQS rules out state changes caused by queries, not changes in what queries observe. A side-effect-free query can return a different result when it reads the current time or data that a command or another process has changed. Its position relative to commands therefore still matters, and caching its result still needs a freshness decision.</p>
<p dir="auto">Repeating or caching a query avoids unintended state changes only when the query actually honors the contract. A query that secretly writes, such as one that updates a last-accessed timestamp, changes state on every call, and a method name alone cannot guarantee the contract.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: Command Query Separation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/CQS.md" class="internal-link">CQS</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is it pragmatic to violate Command-Query Separation (CQS)?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Violating CQS is pragmatic when reading and changing state form one coherent or atomic operation, or when a separate query would only add a round trip without adding clarity.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Atomic read-and-remove:</strong> <code>Stack&lt;T&gt;.Pop()</code> removes the top item and returns it in one call, a long-accepted exception to strict CQS. In concurrent code, separate check and remove calls would let another thread take the item in between, so <code>ConcurrentStack&lt;T&gt;.TryPop(out item)</code> does both as one atomic operation.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Create that returns its identifier:</strong> an insert can return the database-generated ID, because the caller needs it and a follow-up query would only cost another round trip.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The combined operation should still make its state change obvious and return only what the caller needs, such as an identifier or version rather than the full entity. A returned result does not show whether retrying the command is safe, so retry behavior needs its own explicit contract.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.concurrent.concurrentstack-1.trypop?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.concurrent.concurrentstack-1.trypop?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: ConcurrentStack.TryPop</a> · <a href="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: Command Query Separation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/CQS.md" class="internal-link">CQS</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between Command-Query Separation (CQS) and CQRS?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">CQS is a rule for individual operations: each method either changes state (a command) or returns data without side effects (a query). CQRS, Command Query Responsibility Segregation, applies the same distinction at the architecture level by giving the write path and the read path separate models and handlers.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>CQS</th>
<th>CQRS</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Scope</td>
<td>One method or operation at a time, usually within a single class.</td>
<td>A subsystem's whole write path and read path.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What is separated</td>
<td>Command and query signatures; both kinds of method can work on one shared model.</td>
<td>The models themselves: a write model for changes and a read model shaped for queries.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Data storage</td>
<td>Not addressed; a single shared store is normal.</td>
<td>One store can serve both sides; separate read and write stores are common but optional.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>Low; mainly a discipline for method contracts.</td>
<td>High; two models and their handlers must be built and kept consistent.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The two are independent: a CQRS system does not guarantee that every method follows strict CQS, and following CQS does not require CQRS.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: Command Query Separation</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/CQS#CQS Vs CQRS" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/CQS &gt; CQS Vs CQRS" data-tooltip-position="top">CQS vs CQRS</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/CQS.md" class="internal-link">CQS</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is dependency injection, and what problem does it solve?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Dependency injection (DI) means a class receives the objects it depends on from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself. It is a form of Inversion of Control: the class declares what it needs, and the application decides which implementations to supply.</p>
<p dir="auto">Without DI, a class that calls <code>new SmtpEmailSender()</code> is tied to that implementation. Replacing it requires editing the class, the class must also know how to build the sender's own dependencies, and a unit test cannot substitute a fake.</p>
<p dir="auto">With DI:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The class depends on an abstraction, such as <code>IEmailSender</code>, and lists it as a constructor parameter.</li>
<li dir="auto">At the composition root, typically <code>Program.cs</code>, the application chooses the implementation, either by constructing the object graph directly or by registering it in a container.</li>
<li dir="auto">When a container is used, it builds the class's dependencies recursively and manages their lifetime and disposal.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The result is explicit dependencies, implementations that can change without editing their consumers, and tests that pass collaborators directly. DI does not require a container; a container automates wiring and lifetime management.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET dependency injection overview</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Dependency Injection.md" class="internal-link">Dependency Injection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What do the <code>Transient</code>, <code>Scoped</code>, and <code>Singleton</code> service lifetimes mean in .NET dependency injection, and what is a typical use for each?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The lifetime controls how often the container creates a service and which consumers share an instance: <code>Transient</code> creates one per resolution, <code>Scoped</code> shares one within a scope, and <code>Singleton</code> shares one across the whole application.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Lifetime</th>
<th>Instances and sharing</th>
<th>Disposal of container-created instances</th>
<th>Typical use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>Transient</code></td>
<td>A new instance every time the service is resolved, even twice within the same scope.</td>
<td>When the scope that resolved it ends.</td>
<td>Lightweight stateless services, such as a mapper or formatter.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>Scoped</code></td>
<td>One instance per scope, shared by everything resolved in that scope. ASP.NET Core creates a scope for each HTTP request.</td>
<td>When the scope ends, such as at the end of the request.</td>
<td>Per-request or unit-of-work state, such as an EF Core <code>DbContext</code>, which <code>AddDbContext</code> registers as scoped by default.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>Singleton</code></td>
<td>One instance shared by every scope and every concurrent caller until the root provider is disposed.</td>
<td>When the root provider is disposed at application shutdown.</td>
<td>Services that are safe for concurrent use, such as a clock abstraction or a thread-safe, size-bounded cache.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The uses are typical fits, not guarantees from the container: a singleton is safe only if its implementation is thread-safe.</p>
<p dir="auto">Lifetimes also interact when one service holds another:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Singleton holding a scoped service:</strong> a lifetime violation, because the scoped instance would outlive its scope.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Longer-lived service holding a transient:</strong> valid, but the captured instance lives as long as the service that holds it. It must suit that effective lifetime: thread-safe if a singleton's concurrent callers use it, and acceptable to dispose only when that longer lifetime ends.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: service lifetimes</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines#thread-safety" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines#thread-safety" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET DI guidelines: thread safety</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Dependency Injection.md" class="internal-link">Dependency Injection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a captive dependency, and how can it be fixed?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A captive dependency occurs when a longer-lived service holds a shorter-lived one, so the shorter-lived instance stays in use beyond its intended lifetime. The typical case is a singleton, such as a hosted service, that receives a scoped <code>DbContext</code> through its constructor.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Consequences:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Request- or operation-specific state carries over into later, unrelated work.</li>
<li dir="auto">A scoped service that is not designed for concurrent use, such as <code>DbContext</code>, can be shared by concurrent operations and expose stale tracked state.</li>
<li dir="auto">Cleanup moves from the end of the scope to the end of the longer lifetime.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Fix:</strong> the long-lived service depends on <code>IServiceScopeFactory</code> instead of the scoped service. For each unit of work, it creates a scope, resolves the scoped service from that scope, uses it and disposes the scope. A worker that processes independent items creates a new scope per item rather than one scope for its whole lifetime.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token keyword">await</span> <span class="token keyword">using</span> <span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> scope <span class="token operator">=</span> scopeFactory<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">CreateAsyncScope</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token class-name"><span class="token keyword">var</span></span> db <span class="token operator">=</span> scope<span class="token punctuation">.</span>ServiceProvider<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token generic-method"><span class="token function">GetRequiredService</span><span class="token generic class-name"><span class="token punctuation">&lt;</span>AppDbContext<span class="token punctuation">&gt;</span></span></span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token keyword">await</span> <span class="token function">ProcessItemAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>db<span class="token punctuation">,</span> item<span class="token punctuation">,</span> cancellationToken<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Detection:</strong> when the host is built in the Development environment, scope validation rejects a scoped service injected into a singleton or resolved from the root provider. It does not catch every lifetime mistake. A transient captured by a singleton, for example, also lives as long as the singleton, and its transient registration does not make it thread-safe when concurrent callers share it.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/scoped-service" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/scoped-service" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: use scoped services within a BackgroundService</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET DI guidelines</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET service lifetimes</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET dependency injection overview</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Dependency Injection.md" class="internal-link">Dependency Injection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is Service Locator considered an anti-pattern in business code?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Service Locator hides a class's dependencies. Instead of declaring them in its constructor, the class asks a container such as <code>IServiceProvider</code> for them at runtime with <code>GetService&lt;T&gt;()</code> or <code>GetRequiredService&lt;T&gt;()</code>. In business code, this causes three problems:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Hidden requirements:</strong> the constructor no longer shows what the class needs, so its dependencies are discovered only by reading the implementation.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Late failures:</strong> a missing registration fails when that code path runs, not when the object graph is built or validated.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Harder tests:</strong> a unit test must configure a container or fake provider instead of passing collaborators to the constructor.</li>
</ul>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token keyword">sealed</span> <span class="token keyword">class</span> <span class="token class-name">CheckoutService</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token class-name">IServiceProvider</span> provider<span class="token punctuation">)</span>
<span class="token punctuation">{</span>
    <span class="token keyword">public</span> <span class="token return-type class-name">Task</span> <span class="token function">ProcessAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token operator">=&gt;</span>
        provider<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token generic-method"><span class="token function">GetRequiredService</span><span class="token generic class-name"><span class="token punctuation">&lt;</span>IOrderRepository<span class="token punctuation">&gt;</span></span></span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">SaveChangesAsync</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
<span class="token punctuation">}</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">Runtime lookup still has a narrow place in infrastructure: factories that choose an implementation at runtime, middleware or framework activation code, and background services that create explicit scopes. Application and domain services declare their collaborators in their constructors instead.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET DI guidelines</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Dependency Injection#Service Locator Anti-pattern" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Dependency Injection &gt; Service Locator Anti-pattern" data-tooltip-position="top">Service Locator anti-pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Dependency Injection.md" class="internal-link">Dependency Injection</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What evidence justifies introducing a pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A pattern is justified when the code already shows a design pressure that the pattern handles more cheaply than the direct design. That pressure takes one of three forms:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Recurring variation:</strong> the same point in the code repeatedly needs different behavior. A known structure for substituting or composing that behavior then pays off.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A responsibility boundary:</strong> one concern needs to be separated from another, and the pattern makes that boundary explicit.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A failure mode:</strong> the direct design keeps producing the same defect or cost, and the pattern makes it cheaper to handle.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The decision is a cost comparison. Every pattern adds indirection, such as extra types and interfaces, and its control flow is less direct. When the pattern answers a problem the code already has, it makes the variation or boundary easier to see. When the problem is only anticipated, the indirection is speculative. It hides simple control flow without solving anything yet.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Example:</strong> dependency injection behind an interface earns its place when implementations are actually substituted or composed. One concrete dependency with no variation is usually clearer as a direct call.</p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do the Repository and Unit of Work patterns differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Repository shapes how domain code reaches persisted aggregates, and Unit of Work controls when the changes from one business operation are committed. They solve different problems and usually work together.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Repository</th>
<th>Unit of Work</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Responsibility</td>
<td>Presents stored aggregates as a domain-oriented, collection-like interface, such as <code>IOrderRepository</code> with <code>FindAsync</code>, <code>Add</code> and <code>Remove</code>.</td>
<td>Tracks the changes made during one business operation and commits them through one transaction boundary.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it keeps out of domain code</td>
<td>Query details such as SQL, EF includes and open-ended <code>IQueryable&lt;T&gt;</code> stay in infrastructure.</td>
<td>Individual inserts, updates and deletes are gathered and written together instead of one by one.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect of a call</td>
<td><code>Add</code> or <code>Remove</code> only changes the set of pending objects; nothing is written yet.</td>
<td>One save writes the pending changes from every repository that shares the unit of work.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>EF Core counterpart</td>
<td><code>DbSet&lt;T&gt;</code> already provides collection-like access.</td>
<td><code>DbContext</code> already tracks changes until <code>SaveChangesAsync</code> commits them.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Flow:</strong> a handler creates an <code>Order</code>, adds it through <code>IOrderRepository</code>, and then calls <code>SaveChangesAsync</code> on the unit of work. Several repository operations in the same handler therefore commit through one save, inside one transaction when the provider supports it.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/dbcontext-configuration/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/dbcontext-configuration/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: DbContext lifetime, configuration, and initialization</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Using transactions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Repository &amp; UoW.md" class="internal-link">Repository &amp; UoW</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does EF Core's <code>DbContext</code> already implement the Unit of Work pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto"><code>DbContext</code> already performs the two jobs that define a Unit of Work. It records the changes made during one business operation, and it commits them together.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Tracking:</strong> the context's change tracker records entities returned by tracking queries and entities added, modified or removed through the context. Results of no-tracking queries do not enter the tracker. Tracked changes stay pending in memory until a save.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Commit:</strong> <code>SaveChanges</code> or <code>SaveChangesAsync</code> writes all pending changes. When the database provider supports transactions, EF Core applies them in one transaction by default. If any change fails, the whole save is rolled back.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Repositories that receive the same context instance therefore share one unit of work. Each repository can call <code>Add</code> or <code>Remove</code>, and one save commits all of their changes. An <code>IUnitOfWork</code> interface implemented by the context only exposes that save; the mechanism is still EF Core's.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Boundaries:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Each context instance has its own change tracker. Separate contexts are separate units of work by default, and each one's save commits on its own.</li>
<li dir="auto">With relational providers, separate contexts can join one explicit transaction by sharing the same <code>DbConnection</code> and <code>DbTransaction</code>. Their tracking stays separate, but their saves commit or roll back together with that transaction.</li>
<li dir="auto">A <code>DbContext</code> is designed for one short-lived unit of work and is not thread-safe. A singleton registration would share one long-lived tracker across concurrent requests, which is unsafe. <code>AddDbContext</code> registers the context as scoped by default, which gives one instance per request in ASP.NET Core.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Tracking vs. No-Tracking Queries</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/dbcontext-configuration/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/dbcontext-configuration/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: DbContext lifetime, configuration, and initialization</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Using transactions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Repository &amp; UoW.md" class="internal-link">Repository &amp; UoW</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a generic <code>IRepository&lt;T&gt;</code> an anti-pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A generic <code>IRepository&lt;T&gt;</code> is an anti-pattern when it serves as the domain-facing contract and its operation surface does either of two things: it lets callers bypass aggregate invariants, or it exposes operations that do not fit the aggregate. Generic typing alone is not the defect. The defect is what the contract lets callers do.</p>
<p dir="auto">The harmful case shows up in two ways:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Bypassed invariants:</strong> the contract lets callers add, update or delete objects directly instead of going through the aggregate root, whose methods enforce the rules. For example, suppose <code>Order</code> forbids changing line items after confirmation. An <code>IRepository&lt;OrderLine&gt;</code> lets code delete a line from a confirmed order without that check.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unsuitable operations:</strong> the contract gives an aggregate methods such as unrestricted update or delete even when the domain has no such operation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When every exposed operation fits and changes still go through the aggregate root, an interface is not harmful merely for being generic. A generic interface constrained to aggregate roots, for example, can be acceptable if each operation it offers is valid for those roots. An aggregate-specific interface such as <code>IOrderRepository</code> exposes only operations that make sense for <code>Order</code>. Its infrastructure implementation can still reuse a generic base class internally, as long as the generic methods do not widen the domain-facing contract.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/ddd-oriented-microservice" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/ddd-oriented-microservice" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Design a DDD-oriented microservice</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/infrastructure-persistence-layer-design" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/infrastructure-persistence-layer-design" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Design the infrastructure persistence layer</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Repository &amp; UoW.md" class="internal-link">Repository &amp; UoW</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a repository layer over EF Core worth adding instead of injecting <code>DbContext</code> directly?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A repository and unit-of-work layer over EF Core is worth adding when it protects a real domain boundary. Otherwise injecting <code>DbContext</code> directly is usually clearer. EF Core already provides collection-like access through <code>DbSet&lt;T&gt;</code>, and <code>DbContext</code> change tracking with <code>SaveChangesAsync</code> already acts as a unit of work.</p>
<p dir="auto">Reasons that justify the extra interfaces:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Domain isolation:</strong> application and domain code express aggregate operations, such as loading an order with the state its rules need, instead of EF queries.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Controlled access:</strong> aggregates are loaded only through known shapes that preserve their invariants and ownership rules.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Multiple implementations:</strong> the same domain contract genuinely has more than one persistence implementation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Reasons that do not justify it on their own:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Mirroring EF Core:</strong> interfaces that wrap every <code>DbSet&lt;T&gt;</code> with matching CRUD methods only rename EF Core and add indirection.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Testability alone:</strong> a fake repository cannot reproduce database behavior such as query translation and constraints. That behavior is better checked against the real provider.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Injecting <code>DbContext</code> keeps code simple and keeps all EF Core features available, but couples application code to EF Core. Repository interfaces give domain-oriented access and an explicit commit boundary at the cost of extra indirection. For a small CRUD service with no domain rules to isolate, direct <code>DbContext</code> is the clearer design.</p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Repository &amp; UoW.md" class="internal-link">Repository &amp; UoW</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns"><h4>Architectural Patterns</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is CQRS?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) handles state changes and reads through separate models. Commands go through a write model that enforces business rules and changes state. Queries go through a read model that returns data shaped for a screen or API and changes nothing.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Commands</strong> express a business intent, such as <code>PlaceOrder</code>. The write model validates each command against its invariants before changing state.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Queries</strong>, such as <code>GetOrderSummary</code>, only return data. Their model can be shaped for the request, for example one flat row per order summary, so the query avoids joins.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The separation lies in the models and code paths, not necessarily in storage:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared data:</strong> both models can work against the same database through separate logic. No copy has to be kept in sync.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Separate read store:</strong> a denormalized copy must be updated from write-side changes. Updating it within the same request reduces staleness, but it ties the read side's latency and failures to the write. A failure between the two updates can still leave the copy out of date unless both commit atomically. Updating it asynchronously from events removes that coupling, but reads can be stale until the projection catches up. Events then need reliable publication, such as an outbox, and an idempotent projector.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Message brokers, separate databases and Event Sourcing are optional choices, not part of the definition.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: CQRS pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns/CQRS.md" class="internal-link">CQRS</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is CQRS useful, and when does it add unnecessary complexity?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">CQRS separates command-side changes from query-side reads so each model can match different rules, shapes, or scaling needs. It is useful when a shared model has become a poor fit for both sides. If simple CRUD already handles both, separate handlers or projections add synchronization and operational cost without enough benefit. Separate databases, messaging, and event sourcing are optional; asynchronous projections can be stale. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: CQRS pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns/CQRS.md" class="internal-link">CQRS</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a bounded context in Domain-Driven Design?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A bounded context is the explicit boundary within which one domain model and its language apply. Inside it, each term has one consistent meaning. Another context can use the same word for a different concept with its own model.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, "Customer" in Sales means a prospect with contact details and deal history, while "Customer" in Billing means an account with payment terms and a credit limit. A single shared <code>Customer</code> type would collect optional fields and rules that belong to neither context.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Ownership:</strong> each context owns its model. Team organization, code bases and database schemas often mark the boundary. Contexts can still share a deployment or a physical database if table ownership keeps one model from leaking into the other.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Integration:</strong> contexts communicate through an explicit contract or translation, such as Sales publishing <code>OrderPlaced</code> and Billing creating an invoice from it, instead of using each other's internal types.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A bounded context is a model boundary, not necessarily a separate deployment.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Eric Evans: Domain-Driven Design Reference (Bounded Context)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns/Domain-Driven Design.md" class="internal-link">Domain-Driven Design</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is an aggregate in Domain-Driven Design?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An aggregate is a cluster of related domain objects treated as one consistency boundary. Outside code holds references only to its root entity and changes the cluster only through that root. The root enforces the invariants that must hold across the whole cluster.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, an <code>Order</code> root owns its order lines. Adding a line goes through <code>Order.AddLine</code>, which rejects a non-positive quantity before any state changes, and other code cannot edit the line collection directly.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Transaction scope:</strong> the aggregate boundary also scopes transactions. A transaction usually changes one aggregate, so consistency and locking stay local. Changing several in one transaction can still be correct when an immediate invariant spans them and the storage commits them atomically. If that happens often, the boundary is probably wrong.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Sizing:</strong> the boundary belongs around facts that must agree at commit time. An oversized aggregate loads and locks unrelated state. An undersized one turns an immediate invariant into coordination between transactions.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Later consequences:</strong> effects that can follow after the commit, such as updating another aggregate, are handled asynchronously, often through domain events.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Persistence:</strong> repositories load and save whole aggregates through their roots.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Eric Evans: Domain-Driven Design Reference (Aggregates)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/domain-events-design-implementation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/domain-events-design-implementation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Domain events: design and implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns/Domain-Driven Design.md" class="internal-link">Domain-Driven Design</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is full DDD the wrong choice?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Full DDD is the wrong choice when a domain has few business rules, such as a CRUD service that mainly validates and stores records. Its modeling and coordination cost then protects little, and a simple transaction script or data-centric model is easier to build and maintain.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Tactical patterns</strong> such as aggregates, value objects and repositories earn their cost where invariants must hold inside a clear consistency boundary. Without such rules, they add types and indirection without protecting anything.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Strategic patterns</strong> such as a ubiquitous language and bounded contexts can still help on their own when the same term means different things in different parts of the business, even if the code inside each context stays simple.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Effort can differ by subdomain:</strong> the core domain that differentiates the business may justify rich modeling, while supporting or generic subdomains stay simple or are bought or adopted.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The deciding factor is the amount of real domain behavior, not project size.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/ddd-oriented-microservice" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/ddd-oriented-microservice" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Design a DDD-oriented microservice</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Architectural Patterns/Domain-Driven Design.md" class="internal-link">Domain-Driven Design</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns"><h4>Design Patterns</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a design pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. It describes the problem, how a set of objects collaborates to address it, and the consequences of using it. It is not ready-made code or a fixed class diagram.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Name:</strong> a shared word for the design. Saying Strategy communicates that an algorithm varies behind a stable contract.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Problem:</strong> the pressure the pattern responds to, such as an unknown set of dependents that must be notified of state changes (Observer).</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Solution:</strong> the roles and their collaboration, adapted to each codebase rather than copied literally.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Consequences:</strong> what the pattern buys, such as replaceable behavior, and what it costs, such as extra types and indirection.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The best-known catalog is the Gang of Four book, which describes 23 object-oriented patterns grouped as creational, structural and behavioral. A pattern is justified only when its problem actually exists in the code; otherwise its indirection is pure cost.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns" data-tooltip-position="top">Design Patterns overview</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns#Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns &gt; Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" data-tooltip-position="top">Choose a pattern by intent and cost</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Design Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do the GoF categories (creational, structural, behavioral) relate to choosing a design pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The three categories group the GoF patterns by the kind of problem they address. They narrow where to look, but the concrete design pressure and each pattern's intent decide which pattern fits.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Category</th>
<th>Problem it addresses</th>
<th>Examples</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Creational</td>
<td>Where construction decisions live: which concrete class is created, how a complex object is assembled, or how instances are copied or limited.</td>
<td>Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Structural</td>
<td>How objects and types are composed into larger structures, and how interfaces are adapted or wrapped.</td>
<td>Adapter, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Proxy</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Behavioral</td>
<td>How responsibilities and communication are distributed among objects.</td>
<td>Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A category alone cannot decide, because patterns with a similar structure serve different intents. State and Strategy both delegate behavior to another object, but they differ by intent rather than by who selects the delegate: State lets behavior follow the context's current state, with transitions defined by the context or by the state objects, while Strategy makes an interchangeable algorithm a policy that a client usually supplies. The useful starting point is the pressure in the code, such as an algorithm that must vary or an interface that does not match. The pattern whose intent addresses that pressure is the candidate.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational#Patterns at a Glance" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational &gt; Patterns at a Glance" data-tooltip-position="top">Creational patterns at a glance</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns#Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns &gt; Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" data-tooltip-position="top">Choose a pattern by intent and cost</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Design Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does using a design pattern become an anti-pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A pattern becomes an anti-pattern when the indirection it adds costs more than the variation or responsibility boundary it protects. The pattern name alone never pays for the extra complexity.</p>
<p dir="auto">Every pattern adds cost:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">more types or delegates to read and maintain</li>
<li dir="auto">an extra hop between a caller and the behavior</li>
<li dir="auto">execution order, lifetime or error handling that becomes harder to follow</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Typical signs that the cost is not repaid:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No real variation:</strong> an Abstract Factory with only one product family, or a Strategy replacing a small conditional that is stable and clearer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Trivial construction:</strong> a Builder around values that a readable constructor or options record already handles.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No boundary to protect:</strong> an Adapter between two contracts that the same team controls and could simply align.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Flexibility nobody uses:</strong> a Command wrapper where nothing is delayed, logged, retried or undone, or an Observer with one required dependent that could be called directly.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When the variation that justified a pattern disappears, collapsing the abstraction back into direct code removes its cost.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns#Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns &gt; Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" data-tooltip-position="top">Choose a pattern by intent and cost</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Design Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do Adapter, Decorator, and Proxy differ despite their similar wrapper shape?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An object Adapter, a Decorator and a Proxy all wrap another object, but for different reasons. An Adapter translates an incompatible contract into the one a client expects. A Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior. A Proxy keeps the same interface and controls access to the real object. A class Adapter adapts through inheritance instead of wrapping an object, so the wrapper comparison describes the object form.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Object Adapter</th>
<th>Decorator</th>
<th>Proxy</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Interface toward the client</td>
<td>A different interface from the wrapped object's: the one the client expects.</td>
<td>The same interface as the wrapped object.</td>
<td>The same interface as the real object.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Responsibility</td>
<td>Translating calls and data between two incompatible contracts at one boundary.</td>
<td>Adding a responsibility around the call. Several decorators can be stacked at runtime, and their order affects behavior.</td>
<td>Deciding whether, when or how a call reaches the real object.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect on a call</td>
<td>It is converted into the wrapped object's operations, and results are converted back.</td>
<td>It normally reaches the wrapped object, with extra behavior before or after.</td>
<td>It may be forwarded, deferred or refused according to the access rule.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Because their class shapes look alike, the wrapper's responsibility, not its structure, identifies the pattern.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software</a> · <a href="https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1398600" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1398600" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Adapter (InformIT excerpt)</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns#Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns &gt; Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost" data-tooltip-position="top">Choose a pattern by intent and cost</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Design Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does Information Expert reduce coupling, and when should another principle override it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Information Expert assigns a responsibility to the object that already holds the information needed to perform it. This reduces coupling because callers no longer reach into that object's data to apply its rule themselves. They depend only on the result, and the rule lives in one place instead of being duplicated by each caller.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Example:</strong> <code>Order</code> owns its line items, so <code>Order.Total</code> calculates the total. An <code>OrderService</code> that summed <code>order.LineItems</code> itself would depend on the internal structure of <code>Order</code>, and other callers could repeat the same calculation.</p>
<p dir="auto">Information Expert identifies a strong candidate, not an automatic winner. Another principle should prevail when keeping the behavior on the data holder would:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Pull infrastructure into a domain object:</strong> behavior that needs I/O, such as persistence or sending email, belongs in a separate collaborator. Pure Fabrication justifies such a non-domain object, for example a mapper or a gateway.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Coordinate several aggregates:</strong> a policy that needs information beyond one object's boundary fits a separate collaborator that coordinates them.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Add a dependency across a module or layer boundary:</strong> Low Coupling favors keeping that dependency out of the object, even though the object has the data.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Give the object unrelated responsibilities:</strong> High Cohesion favors keeping its responsibilities closely related.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Behavior that depends only on the object's own state and invariants stays with that object.</p>
