<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.informit.com/content/images/0130925691/samplechapter/0130925691.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.informit.com/content/images/0130925691/samplechapter/0130925691.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Craig Larman: Applying UML and Patterns, Information Expert (sample chapter)</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#The Nine Principles" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP &gt; The Nine Principles" data-tooltip-position="top">GRASP principles</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Treating Information Expert as an Absolute" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP &gt; Treating Information Expert as an Absolute" data-tooltip-position="top">Information Expert limits</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">GRASP tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP.md" class="internal-link">GRASP</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does GRASP differ from SOLID?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">GRASP and SOLID start from different questions. GRASP, described by Craig Larman, asks which object should own a responsibility: knowing, creating, coordinating or varying a behavior. SOLID asks whether classes, interfaces and their dependencies are shaped so that change stays contained.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>GRASP</th>
<th>SOLID</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Starting question</td>
<td>Which object should be responsible for this behavior?</td>
<td>Are this class's responsibilities, interfaces, inheritance and dependency direction designed so that change stays contained?</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Focus</td>
<td>Assigning responsibilities among collaborating objects while designing how they work together.</td>
<td>Properties of individual classes and interfaces and the direction of dependencies between them.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Content</td>
<td>Nine heuristics: Information Expert, Creator, Controller, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, Polymorphism, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, Protected Variations.</td>
<td>Five principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical decision</td>
<td><code>Order</code> creates its line items and calculates its own total, because it holds that data.</td>
<td>A class that changes for several unrelated reasons is split, or high-level code depends on an abstraction rather than a concrete detail.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The two overlap in their goals: low coupling, high cohesion and protection from expected variation. For example, Polymorphism and Protected Variations in GRASP pursue the same goal as Open/Closed in SOLID. They complement each other: GRASP helps decide where behavior goes, and SOLID helps check the shape of the resulting classes and dependencies.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.informit.com/content/images/0130925691/samplechapter/0130925691.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.informit.com/content/images/0130925691/samplechapter/0130925691.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Craig Larman: Applying UML and Patterns (sample chapter)</a> · <a href="https://cleancoder.com/files/solid.md" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cleancoder.com/files/solid.md" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Robert C. Martin: SOLID course notes</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#The Nine Principles" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP &gt; The Nine Principles" data-tooltip-position="top">GRASP principles</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">GRASP tradeoffs</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Design/Principles/SOLID" aria-label="Home/Software Design/Principles/SOLID" data-tooltip-position="top">SOLID principles</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP.md" class="internal-link">GRASP</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral"><h5>Behavioral</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does ASP.NET Core middleware differ from a classical Chain of Responsibility?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both send a request through ordered handlers that can stop it early. In the classical pattern, linked handler objects pass the request along until one of them takes responsibility for it. ASP.NET Core middleware is a pipeline of delegates composed once at startup, in which each component normally does its part and calls the next, wrapping everything after it.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Classical Chain of Responsibility</th>
<th>ASP.NET Core middleware</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Handlers and links</td>
<td>Handler objects that each keep a reference to their successor.</td>
<td>Request delegates; each middleware receives the rest of the pipeline as a <code>next</code> delegate.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Building the chain</td>
<td>Links are set between objects, and an implementation may allow them to change later.</td>
<td><code>Use</code>, <code>Map</code> and <code>Run</code> registrations are composed into one request delegate when the app starts. The order is then fixed, although branches can still choose a path for each request.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Role of each handler</td>
<td>Usually either handles the request or forwards it, so typically one handler does the work.</td>
<td>Usually every component does some work and calls <code>next</code>. Not calling <code>next</code> short-circuits the rest, and a <code>Run</code> component always ends the pipeline.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Work after the next step</td>
<td>Not a focus of the pattern's intent.</td>
<td>Code after <code>await next(context)</code> runs as the response returns, so components see the response in reverse registration order.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ASP.NET Core middleware</a> · <a href="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Chain of Responsibility.md" class="internal-link">Chain of Responsibility</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Command pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The Command pattern turns a request into an object that holds the action to perform and the input it needs. An invoker triggers the command, typically through an <code>Execute</code> method, without knowing which object does the work or how.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Command:</strong> an object such as <code>PlaceOrderCommand</code> that carries the request data and knows which receiver to call.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Receiver:</strong> the object that actually performs the work, such as an <code>OrderService</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Invoker:</strong> the code that calls <code>Execute</code>, such as a button, a queue or a scheduler.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Client:</strong> creates the command and passes it to the invoker.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A restaurant ticket works the same way: it records the order, waits in the kitchen queue and tells the chef what to cook, so the waiter never cooks and the chef never takes orders.</p>
<p dir="auto">Because the request becomes an object, it can be queued, logged, retried or delayed, and a command that records enough state can also undo or compensate for its effect. Wrapping a request in an object does not make its side effects atomic or durable. An in-memory undo history disappears with the process, and steps with external effects still need durable state, idempotency keys and compensation. A plain delegate such as <code>Action</code> is enough when naming, serialization and undo are not needed.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Command: solution and limits</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command#Commands in UI, Messaging, and Data Access" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command &gt; Commands in UI, Messaging, and Data Access" data-tooltip-position="top">Command: delegates and .NET examples</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command.md" class="internal-link">Command</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does MediatR implement the Command pattern, and what does it add?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">MediatR represents a command as a request object that carries the operation's data, and <code>Send</code> dispatches it to the one handler registered for that request type. It splits classic Command into parts: the request holds the data, the handler holds the execution logic that a classic command would put in <code>Execute</code>, and the mediator acts as the invoker that finds the right handler.</p>
<p dir="auto">What it adds:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Decoupled callers:</strong> a controller or other sender depends only on the mediator and the request type, not on the handler or the services the handler uses.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Pipeline behaviors:</strong> shared policies such as validation or logging wrap every handler call without being repeated in each handler.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The cost is indirection: following a call from sender to handler requires knowing the registrations. A direct service call stays clearer for one small, fixed interaction. MediatR is one way to realize a command-style design, not a requirement of the Command pattern.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/LuckyPennySoftware/MediatR/wiki/Behaviors" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/LuckyPennySoftware/MediatR/wiki/Behaviors" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MediatR: behaviors</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command#Commands in UI, Messaging, and Data Access" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command &gt; Commands in UI, Messaging, and Data Access" data-tooltip-position="top">Command: MediatR request and handler</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command.md" class="internal-link">Command</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does EF Core use LINQ expression trees as an Interpreter?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">EF Core treats a query's lambda as a sentence in a small language. The lambda arrives as an expression tree, and EF Core walks its nodes and translates them into a query that its database provider can run, instead of running the lambda as compiled code. With a relational provider, that query is SQL.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><code>Queryable.Where</code> accepts an <code>Expression&lt;Func&lt;T, bool&gt;&gt;</code>, so the compiler builds a tree that describes the predicate. <code>Enumerable.Where</code> accepts a <code>Func&lt;T, bool&gt;</code>, which can only be executed.</li>
<li dir="auto">When the query runs, EF Core visits the supported nodes, such as member access, comparisons and <code>&amp;&amp;</code>, and the provider produces an equivalent query in its own language, which is SQL for a relational database.</li>
<li dir="auto">Captured variables, such as <code>minTotal</code> in <code>o =&gt; o.Total &gt; minTotal</code>, can become query parameters instead of literals, which are SQL parameters with a relational provider.</li>
<li dir="auto">A node with no translation, such as a call to an ordinary C# method that the provider does not map, makes EF Core 3.0 and later throw when it appears in a filter or another server-evaluated part of the query. Only the top-level projection can be partly evaluated on the client.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The tree plays the role of the Interpreter pattern's abstract syntax tree. In the classic pattern each node evaluates itself; EF Core instead translates the tree into the provider's query language, such as SQL, which the database then executes.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/expression-trees/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/expression-trees/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C# expression trees</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: client vs. server evaluation</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/how-query-works" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/how-query-works" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: how queries work</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter.md" class="internal-link">Interpreter</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the Interpreter pattern differ from the Strategy pattern when rules are chosen at runtime?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both let behavior vary at runtime, but they vary different things. Strategy chooses which already-written implementation runs. Interpreter represents the rule itself as data, such as an expression tree, and an evaluator walks that data to produce the result. Choosing an implementation at runtime is therefore not enough to make a design an Interpreter.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>Interpreter</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What varies</td>
<td>The implementation selected, such as a flat-rate or a weight-based shipping calculator.</td>
<td>The rule's structure, built from expression nodes such as <code>And(TierEquals(Silver), TotalGreaterThan(200))</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>New behavior</td>
<td>Selecting or configuring an existing implementation needs no new code; behavior that none of them provides needs a new implementation.</td>
<td>Can often be composed from existing expression types without new classes, within what the grammar can express.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Where the logic lives</td>
<td>In each strategy's code, which the caller simply invokes.</td>
<td>Split across node types that an evaluator applies to a context, such as an order and its customer.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main costs</td>
<td>Variation is limited to the implementations that exist, so uncovered behavior means new code to write, test and ship. Running a strategy is ordinary compiled code.</td>
<td>A grammar to design and maintain, slower tree evaluation and harder debugging. Rules from untrusted users also need a restricted grammar with allowlisted fields and operations.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Composing rules from data avoids new code only when the rule representation can be stored and loaded safely. Rule objects built in startup code still change only with a deployment.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Interpreter: solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Interpreter: pitfalls</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Interpreter: tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter.md" class="internal-link">Interpreter</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What should determine whether an API returns <code>IEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code>, <code>IReadOnlyList&lt;T&gt;</code>, or <code>IAsyncEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The return type should state what consumers can do with the result: enumerate it synchronously, count and index it, or await while items arrive. None of the three, by itself, promises that the data is buffered, repeatable or a snapshot.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Return type</th>
<th>Promises to consumers</th>
<th>Does not promise</th>
<th>Fits when</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>IEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code></td>
<td>Synchronous, forward-only enumeration.</td>
<td>A count, indexing or materialized data. It may be lazy, so enumerating it again can repeat the work, such as a query, and see different results.</td>
<td>Consumers only iterate, and lazy or streamed production is acceptable.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>IReadOnlyList&lt;T&gt;</code></td>
<td><code>Count</code> and access by index, with no mutation members on the interface.</td>
<td>A snapshot or immutability; a producer that keeps the underlying list can still change it.</td>
<td>Consumers need the size or random access, usually for results already in memory.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>IAsyncEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code></td>
<td>Asynchronous streaming: <code>await foreach</code> can wait between items, for example while the next page is fetched.</td>
<td>Buffering or repeatability.</td>
<td>Producing items requires I/O, and consumers should process items as they arrive rather than wait for all of them.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Buffering, repeatability and snapshot semantics form a separate contract; when they matter, the API documentation has to state them.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.ienumerable-1?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.ienumerable-1?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: IEnumerable</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/generate-consume-asynchronous-stream" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/generate-consume-asynchronous-stream" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: asynchronous streams</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Iterator.md" class="internal-link">Iterator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does the compiler generate for a <code>yield return</code> method?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The compiler rewrites an iterator method into a generated state-machine class that implements the returned iterator interfaces, such as <code>IEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code> and <code>IEnumerator&lt;T&gt;</code>. The body is split at each <code>yield return</code>, and the object records where execution stopped and keeps the values that must survive between steps.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Calling the method only creates the state-machine object. None of the body runs yet.</li>
<li dir="auto">The first <code>MoveNext()</code> runs the body from the start to the first <code>yield return</code>, stores the yielded value as <code>Current</code>, saves its position and returns <code>true</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Each later <code>MoveNext()</code> resumes just after the saved position and runs to the next <code>yield return</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Reaching the end of the body or a <code>yield break</code> makes <code>MoveNext()</code> return <code>false</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Locals and parameters used across a <code>yield return</code> are kept in the generated object, so their values survive between <code>MoveNext()</code> calls. Because the body runs only during enumeration, its work and exceptions, including argument checks, happen when the sequence is consumed rather than when the method is called. The generated type and field names are compiler implementation details.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/yield" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/yield" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C#: yield statement</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Iterator.md" class="internal-link">Iterator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Mediator pattern, and how does MediatR's request dispatch differ from it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The Mediator pattern moves the rules for how a group of objects interact into one mediator object. The participants, called colleagues, notify the mediator instead of calling each other, and the mediator decides which other colleagues react. A many-to-many web of dependencies becomes hub-and-spoke coordination, so a colleague can be changed or added without the others knowing about it. Air traffic control is the usual analogy: pilots coordinate through the tower rather than with every nearby aircraft.</p>
<p dir="auto">MediatR follows the same decoupling direction but solves a narrower problem:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Classic Mediator</th>
<th>MediatR <code>Send</code></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it connects</td>
<td>A set of peer colleagues that react to one another.</td>
<td>One sender and the single handler registered for a request type.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Where interaction rules live</td>
<td>In the mediator, which knows the colleagues and coordinates them.</td>
<td>In the handler. MediatR only locates and invokes it, with pipeline behaviors around the call.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What stops depending on what</td>
<td>Colleagues stop referring to each other.</td>
<td>The sender stops referring to the handler and the services it uses.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A MediatR handler that calls several services coordinates them itself; MediatR does not coordinate peers on its behalf.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator#In-Process Dispatch and Message Routing" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator &gt; In-Process Dispatch and Message Routing" data-tooltip-position="top">Mediator: MediatR dispatch</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator.md" class="internal-link">Mediator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What are the signs that a mediator is adding indirection without reducing coupling?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A mediator adds only indirection when it routes calls without providing a useful shared boundary: no common dispatch for several callers, no cross-cutting policy and no real coordination between participants. Typical signs:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Callers still know the participants:</strong> senders still reference concrete handlers or the services behind them, so the mediator removed no dependency.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Coordination is still duplicated:</strong> several callers repeat the same sequence around their mediator calls instead of one place owning it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Fixed two-party calls go through it:</strong> a request has one caller, one handler and no shared behavior, so the route only makes the execution path harder to find.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The mediator becomes a god object:</strong> one central mediator or handler accumulates unrelated rules instead of dispatching to focused handlers.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Moving a workflow into a handler can decouple the caller from the services it uses, but the workflow itself is no simpler. Direct calls fit simple, stable interactions. The indirection pays off when several transports share an operation or when pipeline behaviors apply shared policies.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Mediator: tradeoffs</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Mediator: duplicated coordination</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator.md" class="internal-link">Mediator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do MediatR pipeline behaviors implement the Chain of Responsibility pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Pipeline behaviors form a chain of wrappers that ends at the request handler. Each <code>IPipelineBehavior&lt;TRequest, TResponse&gt;</code> receives the request and a <code>next</code> delegate for the rest of the chain, and decides whether to pass the request on.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><code>Send</code> nests the behaviors registered for the request type around the handler.</li>
<li dir="auto">The outermost behavior runs its code before <code>next</code>, such as logging or validating the request.</li>
<li dir="auto">Calling <code>next</code> invokes the following behavior, and the innermost <code>next</code> invokes the handler.</li>
<li dir="auto">As calls return, each behavior can run code after <code>next</code>, such as recording elapsed time or adjusting the response.</li>
<li dir="auto">A behavior can short-circuit by returning a response or throwing without calling <code>next</code>, as a caching behavior does when it returns a stored result. Later behaviors and the handler then never run.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Registration order determines the nesting, so it changes what happens. A logging behavior outside a validation behavior records rejected requests; inside it, rejected requests never reach the logger. Order that matters for correctness should be explicit and covered by tests rather than left to incidental registration order.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/LuckyPennySoftware/MediatR/wiki/Behaviors" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/LuckyPennySoftware/MediatR/wiki/Behaviors" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MediatR: behaviors</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator.md" class="internal-link">Mediator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Memento pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The Memento pattern captures an object's state as a snapshot so the object can be restored to it later, without exposing the object's internals to the code that keeps the history.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Originator:</strong> the object whose state is saved, such as a shopping cart. It creates mementos and restores itself from them, so it is the only code that interprets the saved state.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Memento:</strong> the snapshot itself, ideally immutable and opaque to everything except the originator.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Caretaker:</strong> stores mementos, for example in an undo stack, without inspecting or changing them.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Undo follows from these roles: before a change, the originator produces a memento and the caretaker keeps it; to undo, the caretaker hands the memento back and the originator restores its state from it.</p>
<p dir="auto">The snapshot must be a real copy. If it shares mutable objects with live state, later edits also change the saved snapshot, so mutable nested objects need deep copies.</p>
<p dir="auto">In C#, opacity is often only a convention: a public memento record can still be read by the caretaker. A stricter design exposes an opaque interface or nests the memento type inside the originator.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Memento implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento.md" class="internal-link">Memento</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can memento history be kept from growing without limit?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Memento history is bounded by a retention limit: a maximum number of snapshots, a memory budget, or both. When a new snapshot would exceed the limit, the oldest one is discarded.</p>
<p dir="auto">Each snapshot copies the originator's state, so an unbounded history grows with every recorded change. The right limit depends on what the history is for:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Undo in an editor:</strong> a rolling window keeps the most recent steps. Steps older than the window can no longer be undone.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Large snapshots:</strong> a memory budget caps total size, because a snapshot count alone does not control memory when individual snapshots can be large.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Recovery after a crash or abandoned session:</strong> often only the latest checkpoint is needed, so earlier snapshots can be dropped.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Storing a small inverse change instead of a full copy makes each entry smaller, but it does not bound the history by itself.</p>
<p dir="auto">A full audit trail is a different requirement. It needs durable records of events or changes, as in Event Sourcing, rather than an unlimited in-memory stack of object copies.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Memento tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento.md" class="internal-link">Memento</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is Memento overkill compared to simpler approaches?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Memento is overkill when each change is small and isolated compared with the whole state. Recording how to reverse that one change, as Command-style undo does, is then cheaper and simpler than copying the entire state before every step.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Inverse change (Command-style undo)</th>
<th>Memento snapshot</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What each history entry stores</td>
<td>Only what reverses one action, such as a removed item and its former position.</td>
<td>A copy of the originator's earlier state.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost per entry</td>
<td>Grows with the size of the change, so small edits to a large object stay cheap.</td>
<td>Grows with the size of the state, so every step pays for a full copy even when little changed.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main correctness risk</td>
<td>The entry must keep enough context to reverse the change safely; a missing detail produces a wrong reversal.</td>
<td>The copy must not share mutable objects with live state; otherwise later edits also change the snapshot.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Best fit</td>
<td>Isolated, reversible edits.</td>
<td>One action that changes several interdependent values, or a need to restore a complete earlier state.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A Memento earns its cost when one action touches several related values. Restoring the snapshot resets them together, so no separate inverse logic is needed for each value.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Memento tradeoffs</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Memento implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento.md" class="internal-link">Memento</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Observer pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many relationship: a publisher keeps a list of independently registered subscribers and notifies all of them when its state changes. The publisher depends only on a notification contract, not on the subscribers' concrete types, so a subscriber can be added or removed without changing the publisher.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Publisher (subject):</strong> owns the changing state, keeps the subscription list and sends the notifications.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Subscribers (observers):</strong> register through the contract and decide how to react.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Notification contract:</strong> a callback signature or interface, such as an order's <code>StatusChanged</code> event or an <code>IOrderStatusObserver</code> interface.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">C# events provide this directly: <code>+=</code> subscribes a handler, <code>-=</code> removes it, and raising the event invokes the handlers currently subscribed. Event handlers are invoked synchronously, so asynchronous server-side subscribers fit better behind a <code>Task</code>-returning interface that keeps their completion and failures observable.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/events/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/events/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET events</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Observer implementation</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer#Events and Observable APIs in .NET" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer &gt; Events and Observable APIs in .NET" data-tooltip-position="top">Events and observable APIs in .NET</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer.md" class="internal-link">Observer</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should event subscriptions be managed to avoid retaining subscribers after their lifetime ends?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each subscription needs an owner that removes it when the subscriber's lifetime ends, usually the component that added it. Weak events are a fallback when a longer-lived publisher has no clear owner to unsubscribe.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Why retention happens:</strong> subscribing stores a delegate in the publisher, and that delegate usually references the subscriber. While the publisher stays reachable, so does the subscriber. This becomes a leak when the publisher outlives the subscriber, such as a closed view whose handler is still attached to a surviving view model.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Explicit ownership:</strong> the component that subscribes with <code>+=</code> unsubscribes with <code>-=</code> when its lifetime ends, such as when a view closes or the subscriber is disposed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Keeping the handler:</strong> unsubscribing needs the same delegate that was added, so a lambda handler has to be stored if it will be removed later.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Weak events:</strong> the publisher's reference no longer keeps the subscriber alive, so no unsubscribe owner is required. The extra machinery is worthwhile only when ownership cannot be aligned with the subscriber's lifetime.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When an owner exists, explicit unsubscription is simpler and more predictable.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/events/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/events/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET events</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Observer pitfalls</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Observer tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer.md" class="internal-link">Observer</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the State pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The State pattern moves state-dependent behavior into separate state objects that share one interface. A context object holds its current state and delegates each operation to it, so replacing the state object changes how the same operation behaves.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, <code>Order.Ship()</code> delegates to the order's current state:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><code>PendingState</code> rejects the call because the order is unpaid.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>PaidState</code> transitions the order to <code>ShippedState</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>ShippedState</code> rejects the call because the order has already shipped.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">In this example, each state decides which transitions it allows. That ownership is a design choice: either the context or a concrete state may decide which state comes next and when. In both forms, callers request domain operations such as <code>Pay()</code> or <code>Ship()</code> instead of setting a status directly.</p>
<p dir="auto">The pattern replaces the same <code>switch</code> on a status repeated across many operations. A new state becomes one new class, plus edits wherever transitions to or from it are defined. The cost is many small classes, and a new operation must be implemented in every state. A small machine with few state-dependent rules is often clearer as an enum with one transition function.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Gamma et al.: Design Patterns, State chapter</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2001/july/design-patterns-solidify-your-csharp-application-architecture-with-design-patterns" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2001/july/design-patterns-solidify-your-csharp-application-architecture-with-design-patterns" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MSDN Magazine: Solidify your C# application architecture with design patterns</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">State pattern implementation</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">State tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State.md" class="internal-link">State</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does a compiler-generated async state machine relate to the State pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both let stored state decide what happens next, but the async state machine is a compiler implementation technique, not the GoF State pattern.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Compiler-generated async state machine</th>
<th>GoF State pattern</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What the state means</td>
<td>Where the method paused, meaning which incomplete <code>await</code> it is waiting on.</td>
<td>The object's current mode in the domain, such as <code>Pending</code> or <code>Paid</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How state is stored</td>
<td>A generated state field, plus fields for the locals that must survive the <code>await</code>.</td>
<td>The context holds a reference to a state object that implements a shared interface.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How behavior changes</td>
<td>When the awaited operation completes, its continuation calls <code>MoveNext()</code>, which branches on the state field and resumes after that <code>await</code>.</td>
<td>The context delegates each operation to its current state object; replacing that object changes behavior.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Who designs it</td>
<td>The compiler generates it from an <code>async</code> method.</td>
<td>Developers design the state classes and the transitions between them.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The async machine therefore shows state-driven control flow built from generated fields and branching, not from interchangeable state objects.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C#: async scenarios</a> · <a href="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/how-async-await-really-works/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/how-async-await-really-works/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Stephen Toub: How Async/Await Really Works in C#</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State#Familiar state machines" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State &gt; Familiar state machines" data-tooltip-position="top">Familiar state machines</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">State pattern implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State.md" class="internal-link">State</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Strategy pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Strategy puts interchangeable algorithms for one step of a workflow behind a common contract. The code that runs the workflow calls the contract without knowing which algorithm it is using, so algorithms can be added or replaced independently of that workflow.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Context:</strong> owns the workflow and delegates the variable step. For example, a shipping service calls <code>IShippingCostStrategy.Calculate(order)</code> without containing any pricing rules.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Strategy contract:</strong> the interface, or a delegate for a single operation, that every algorithm implements.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Concrete strategies:</strong> the algorithms themselves, such as flat-rate, weight-based or zone-based pricing.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Selection:</strong> a client, configuration or selection policy decides which strategy the context uses.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Problem it solves:</strong> without Strategy, one conditional chain holds every variant. Adding same-day delivery then means editing the method that already carries all the other pricing rules, with a risk of disturbing them. With Strategy, a new variant is a new implementation plus its registration, and existing strategies stay unchanged.</p>
<p dir="auto">Separating the algorithms does not choose between them. When several could apply, the selection rule remains its own design decision.</p>
<p dir="auto">In .NET, <code>IComparer&lt;T&gt;</code> is a familiar example: it supplies the ordering that sorting methods use.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Strategy: Problem</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Strategy: Solution</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.icomparer-1" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.icomparer-1" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: <code>IComparer&lt;T&gt;</code></a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy.md" class="internal-link">Strategy</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What determines whether a strategy should use an interface or a <code>Func&lt;T, TResult&gt;</code> delegate?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The shape of the collaboration decides, not whether the strategy holds state. A <code>Func&lt;T, TResult&gt;</code> fits when the strategy is a single operation whose parameters and captured variables supply everything it needs. An interface is clearer when the strategy has several related members, its own dependencies, or a lifetime that must be managed.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Delegate:</strong> any lambda or method group with a matching signature can be passed without declaring a type. LINQ predicates and key selectors are strategies of this kind.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Interface:</strong> a named contract keeps related members together. Each implementation can declare constructor dependencies, which a DI container supplies with a chosen lifetime. For example, a shipping-cost strategy that exposes <code>Priority</code>, <code>AppliesTo</code> and <code>Calculate</code> and needs an <code>IZoneCalculator</code> is clearer as an interface than as three separate delegates.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">State alone does not decide the choice. A lambda can capture outer variables, and a captured variable is not collected while the delegate that references it is still reachable. A delegate can therefore carry state too.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions#capture-of-outer-variables-and-variable-scope-in-lambda-expressions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions#capture-of-outer-variables-and-variable-scope-in-lambda-expressions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Lambda capture of outer variables</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET dependency injection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy.md" class="internal-link">Strategy</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should strategy selection work when several strategies can handle the same request?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Overlaps need an explicit rule owned by the domain: a unique key, a documented precedence, or deliberate composition. The order in which a DI container returns registrations is not such a rule.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Explicit key:</strong> the request carries an identifier, such as the chosen shipping method, that maps to exactly one strategy. Overlaps cannot occur, and an unknown key fails visibly.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Documented precedence:</strong> each strategy reports whether it applies and declares a priority. The highest-priority applicable strategy wins. A tie at the top priority is a configuration error, and it is detected rather than resolved arbitrarily.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Composition:</strong> when combining is the intended behavior, such as applying several eligible discounts, every matching strategy runs under a defined combination rule.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">In .NET's built-in container, resolving a single service returns the last registration, and resolving <code>IEnumerable&lt;T&gt;</code> returns all registrations in registration order. That order is deterministic, but it reflects how the application was wired, not a business decision. Reordering registrations would silently change which strategy wins, so any intended order belongs in explicit data such as a priority.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-registration" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-registration" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Service registration</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy.md" class="internal-link">Strategy</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What should determine whether algorithm variation uses Template Method or Strategy?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The decision depends on who owns the algorithm and when the variation must be chosen. Template Method fits when a base class owns a stable sequence and subclasses vary a few steps. Strategy fits when the varying behavior is a separate collaborator that must be selected or replaced independently, including at runtime.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Template Method</th>
<th>Strategy</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Who owns the algorithm</td>
<td>The base class runs the sequence and calls hooks that subclasses override.</td>
<td>The context calls a composed object or delegate that supplies the varying behavior.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>When a variant is chosen</td>
<td>When a subclass is instantiated, so the choice is fixed for that object.</td>
<td>When a strategy is passed in or selected, so it can change at runtime.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Coupling</td>
<td>Subclasses depend on the base class's hook order and shared state, so a base-class change can affect every subtype. Inheritance also uses the class's single base-class slot.</td>
<td>Variation stays outside the class hierarchy, so the base-class slot remains free.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>Smallest design when the base genuinely owns most of the workflow.</td>
<td>Adds a separate abstraction and, with several strategies, logic to select among them.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Template Method fits poorly when behavior must change at runtime or when inheritance exists only to reuse a few lines.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Template Method tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method.md" class="internal-link">Template Method</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the "Hollywood Principle," and how does Template Method apply it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The Hollywood Principle means the framework or base class owns the control flow and calls supplied extension points. Template Method applies it by fixing the algorithm’s sequence while subclasses implement selected hooks; subclasses follow that protocol instead of driving the whole operation. <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Template Method implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method.md" class="internal-link">Template Method</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is double dispatch, and why does the Visitor pattern need it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Double dispatch chooses the code to run from the runtime types of two objects, here the element and the visitor. Visitor needs it because an ordinary virtual call dispatches on only one runtime type, and ordinary C# overload resolution picks a <code>Visit</code> overload at compile time from the argument's static type. Through an <code>ICartItem</code> reference, the concrete element type is not available for that choice.</p>
<p dir="auto">Visitor recovers it in two dispatches:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The caller invokes <code>item.Accept(visitor)</code>. Virtual dispatch on <code>item</code> runs the concrete element's <code>Accept</code>, such as <code>PhysicalProduct.Accept</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Inside that method, <code>this</code> has the static type <code>PhysicalProduct</code>, so <code>visitor.Visit(this)</code> binds to the <code>Visit(PhysicalProduct)</code> overload at compile time.</li>
<li dir="auto">That call is virtual on the visitor, so it runs the concrete visitor's implementation, such as <code>TaxCalculatorVisitor.Visit(PhysicalProduct)</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The first dispatch fixes the element type and the second fixes the operation. New operations can therefore be added as new visitor classes without changing the element classes.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Visitor implementation</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Visitor pitfalls</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor.md" class="internal-link">Visitor</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does EF Core use <code>ExpressionVisitor</code>, and what does it do?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">EF Core uses expression visitors when it translates a LINQ query for execution. A series of visitor passes walks the query's expression tree, reshapes it into a form the provider can handle, and translates the supported parts into the provider's query, such as SQL.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Traversal:</strong> <code>ExpressionVisitor</code> provides node-specific visit methods, so a pass can handle method calls, member access or constants differently.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Rewriting:</strong> a visit method can return a replacement node, so each pass hands a reshaped tree to the next. No single visitor simply emits SQL node by node.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Phases:</strong> preprocessing passes reshape the query, and translation passes then convert it into the provider's representation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Each pass is a separate operation over the same tree structure, which is the kind of variation Visitor is designed for.</p>
<p dir="auto">A translation error does not by itself show that a visit method or overload is missing. It can occur when the active provider lacks a server-side translation for that expression in that query context, but the error alone does not establish a single cause.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor#Framework examples" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor &gt; Framework examples" data-tooltip-position="top">Visitor framework examples</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: client vs. server evaluation</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/blob/main/src/EFCore/Query/QueryTranslationPreprocessor.cs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/blob/main/src/EFCore/Query/QueryTranslationPreprocessor.cs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core source: QueryTranslationPreprocessor</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor.md" class="internal-link">Visitor</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is pattern matching a better fit than Visitor?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Pattern matching is a better fit when the type set is small or when there are only a few short operations. A <code>switch</code> expression keeps the type dispatch visible in one function, without <code>Accept</code> methods or a visitor interface. A closed type set does not decide the choice by itself, because Visitor also depends on a stable element set. Visitor earns its ceremony when element types are stable, new operations are added often, and those operations benefit from carrying state across elements.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Pattern matching</th>
<th>Visitor</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Adding an operation</td>
<td>Another function with a <code>switch</code> over the types.</td>
<td>Another visitor class; element classes do not change.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Adding an element type</td>
<td>A new case in each relevant <code>switch</code>.</td>
<td>A new <code>Visit</code> method on the visitor interface, implemented in every visitor.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Detecting a missed case</td>
