<td>Over an open hierarchy with a discard <code>_</code> arm, the compiler cannot report a forgotten type; the value reaches the discard, which may throw at run time.</td>
<td>Adding the method to the visitor interface makes every visitor that lacks it fail to compile.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>State across elements</td>
<td>Awkward; a <code>switch</code> holds no state between elements, so an accumulator lives in surrounding code that the arms or the caller update.</td>
<td>Natural; a visitor accumulates results in its own fields during traversal.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Readability</td>
<td>Dispatch is explicit in one place.</td>
<td>Double dispatch through <code>Accept</code> is harder to follow.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/patterns/pattern-matching" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/patterns/pattern-matching" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">C#: pattern matching</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Visitor tradeoffs</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Visitor problem</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor.md" class="internal-link">Visitor</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational"><h5>Creational</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What should happen when an Abstract Factory gains a new product type such as <code>IFraudDetector</code>?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">It depends on whether every family must provide the new product. If so, the product is added to the abstract factory interface and implemented in every concrete factory. If the capability varies independently of the family, it belongs in a separate collaborator instead of the factory.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Required in every family:</strong> the factory interface gains a method such as <code>CreateFraudDetector()</code>, and each provider's factory returns its own implementation. A concrete factory without that method fails to compile, so no family is left incomplete. This is the pattern's known cost: each new product type changes the interface and every family.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Independent of the family:</strong> when fraud detection does not have to match the payment provider, it is injected on its own rather than forced into every family's factory.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A default no-op implementation avoids the compile errors but hides a missing required behavior. For a safety check such as fraud detection, payments would then proceed unchecked without any error.</p>
<p dir="auto">Splitting the factory interface is justified only when consumers use genuinely separate families; arbitrary splitting hides the fact that the products must vary together.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Abstract Factory pitfalls</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Abstract Factory implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory.md" class="internal-link">Abstract Factory</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is Abstract Factory overkill compared to a simpler approach?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Abstract Factory is overkill when only one product type varies, when a single provider is fixed, or when the products can be chosen independently. Injecting each product directly is simpler in those cases.</p>
<p dir="auto">The pattern adds a factory interface and one concrete factory per family. That layer pays off only when several product types must vary together. Choosing a payment provider, for example, must also choose its matching processor, receipt generator and refund handler, and the factory makes that choice once. Without such a coordinated compatibility requirement, the extra indirection buys nothing.</p>
<p dir="auto">The deciding pressure is coordinated variation, not a particular number of providers or classes.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Abstract Factory tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory.md" class="internal-link">Abstract Factory</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does Abstract Factory relate to the DI container in modern .NET?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They solve different problems and are often combined. A DI container is a general object factory that builds object graphs from registrations. An Abstract Factory is a typed creation boundary: choosing one concrete factory chooses a whole family of related products.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What the container provides:</strong> each service is resolved from its own registration. Registrations can switch several services together, but <code>IServiceProvider</code> does not check that the resolved implementations belong to the same provider, so a Stripe processor can sit next to a PayPal receipt generator by mistake.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What the factory adds:</strong> consumers depend on one interface, such as <code>IPaymentProviderFactory</code>, and each concrete factory creates all of its family's products. The compatibility decision lives in one place instead of being spread across registrations.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>How they combine:</strong> the container registers and injects the chosen concrete factory, for example with <code>AddSingleton&lt;IPaymentProviderFactory&gt;(...)</code>. One factory registered at startup fixes one family for the whole application; choosing a family per request needs a registry or strategy that selects among factories.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The factory centralizes compatibility but does not prove it. Its shared product interfaces cannot show that the returned implementations come from one provider; provider-specific types can move more of that check into the type system.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET dependency injection</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Framework examples" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory &gt; Framework examples" data-tooltip-position="top">Abstract Factory framework examples</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Abstract Factory pitfalls</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory.md" class="internal-link">Abstract Factory</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a Builder worth using instead of a constructor?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A Builder is worth its extra type when constructing the object is a process rather than one call. This holds when inputs arrive through several steps, often with many of them optional, or when the finished object needs validation or derived values that depend on the complete set of inputs. A constructor, or an object initializer with <code>required</code> members, stays clearer when the values fit in one readable call and the constructor or initializer can enforce the same invariants.</p>
<p dir="auto">What a Builder adds over a long constructor:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Named steps instead of positional arguments:</strong> calls such as <code>ShipTo(address)</code> and <code>WithGiftWrap(message)</code> replace a parameter list whose call site reads like <code>true, null, false</code>. A new option becomes another named method instead of another placeholder argument for every caller.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cross-field validation in one place:</strong> <code>Build()</code> sees the whole configuration. A rule such as requiring a shipping address and at least one item is therefore checked once, before the object exists.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Derived values and defaults:</strong> <code>Build()</code> computes values such as the order total and applies defaults. One example is using the shipping address for billing when no billing address was given. Callers no longer have to do this themselves.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The costs are an extra type that mirrors the product's API and, for any required input that is checked only in <code>Build()</code>, runtime rather than compile-time enforcement of its presence, which <code>required</code> members provide. Mandatory inputs taken through the builder's own constructor, such as the customer in <code>new OrderBuilder(customer)</code>, must still be passed when the builder is created. A builder around independent property assignments only duplicates an object initializer.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Builder tradeoffs</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Builder implementation</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/required" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/required" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: required modifier (C# reference)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder.md" class="internal-link">Builder</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does <code>WebApplicationBuilder</code> use a builder instead of a constructor with parameters?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An ASP.NET Core application is configured by many independent setup steps, not by one fixed set of arguments. <code>WebApplicationBuilder</code> collects that setup in stages, and <code>Build()</code> creates the <code>WebApplication</code> only after everything has been contributed.</p>
<p dir="auto">How the stages work:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><code>WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args)</code> creates the builder with preconfigured defaults, such as the standard configuration sources.</li>
<li dir="auto">Setup code adds to the builder's properties:
<ul>
<li dir="auto">configuration through <code>builder.Configuration</code></li>
<li dir="auto">service registrations through <code>builder.Services</code>, including registrations contributed by library extension methods</li>
<li dir="auto">host and web-server settings through <code>builder.Host</code> and <code>builder.WebHost</code></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>builder.Build()</code> creates the <code>WebApplication</code> from the accumulated configuration and registrations.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">A constructor with parameters would require callers to assemble the complete set of services and settings before a single call. That set is open-ended, because the application and its libraries both contribute to it. The builder therefore gives every contributor a shared place to add its part before anything is assembled. Staging also lets later setup steps read earlier results, such as configuration values that decide which services to register. A constructor is still used at the end: in ASP.NET Core 10, <code>Build()</code> builds the underlying host and passes it to the <code>WebApplication</code> constructor.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.builder.webapplicationbuilder?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.builder.webapplicationbuilder?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: WebApplicationBuilder class</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Configuration in ASP.NET Core</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET dependency injection</a> · <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/v10.0.0/src/DefaultBuilder/src/WebApplicationBuilder.cs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/v10.0.0/src/DefaultBuilder/src/WebApplicationBuilder.cs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ASP.NET Core 10: WebApplicationBuilder source</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder.md" class="internal-link">Builder</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do Factory Method and Abstract Factory differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both hide which concrete class is created, but they vary different things. Factory Method lets a subclass decide one product by overriding a creation hook, which inherited creator code such as a shared workflow often calls. Abstract Factory is a separate object, given to its client, that creates a whole family of related products that must work together.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Factory Method</th>
<th>Abstract Factory</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What varies</td>
<td>One product returned by an overridable creation hook, often used inside a shared workflow, such as the sender a notification workflow uses.</td>
<td>A family of compatible products, such as a whole Stripe or PayPal provider family that is swapped together.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Mechanism</td>
<td>Inheritance: the creator declares an overridable creation hook such as <code>CreateSender()</code>, and concrete creators override it to choose the product. This hook is what defines the pattern.</td>
<td>Composition: the client holds a factory object with one creation method per product and calls it without knowing which family it is.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Where creation sits</td>
<td>In the creator's overridable hook. The same creator often also runs code that uses the product, but it need not.</td>
<td>In a dedicated factory, separate from the code that uses the products.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Adding a variant</td>
<td>A new creator subclass overrides the hook to return a new product, leaving any creator code that uses it unchanged. Creator and product hierarchies grow in parallel only when each concrete product gets its own creator subclass.</td>
<td>A new factory implementation supplies a whole new family. Adding a new kind of product to the family changes the factory interface and every family implementation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it protects</td>
<td>Creator code that uses the product, when it exists, stays unchanged while one creation decision varies.</td>
<td>Products obtained from one factory belong to the same family, as long as each factory creates only matching products.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">When neither a subclass-overridable creation hook nor a product family is needed, a standalone factory function is usually smaller than both.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software</a> · <a href="https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1398599" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1398599" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Abstract Factory (InformIT excerpt)</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Factory Method solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Abstract Factory solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational#Patterns at a Glance" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational &gt; Patterns at a Glance" data-tooltip-position="top">Creational patterns at a glance</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational.md" class="internal-link">Creational</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does Factory Method become the wrong choice?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Factory Method is the wrong choice when no creator needs an overridable creation hook through which subclasses decide the product. That hook defines the pattern. A shared base workflow that uses the product is a common reason the hook pays off, but it is not required. When nothing needs a subclass creation decision, the creator hierarchy is ceremony.</p>
<p dir="auto">Simpler or better-fitting options:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Implementation chosen once at startup:</strong> a DI registration of the product interface, such as <code>INotificationSender</code> mapped to <code>EmailNotificationSender</code>, selects the implementation without a creator subclass per variant.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Plain construction:</strong> a static factory method or a constructor is smaller when creating the object needs no subclass decision. Many APIs called factory methods, such as <code>Task.FromResult&lt;T&gt;()</code>, are static functions rather than the GoF pattern.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Several related products must vary together:</strong> Abstract Factory keeps the compatible family behind one factory object instead of separate creation hooks.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When each variant gets its own creator subclass, as in the notification example, the cost being avoided is a parallel hierarchy: each new variant adds both a product class and a matching creator class, even when the creator contributes nothing beyond picking the product.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method#Related .NET factory APIs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method &gt; Related .NET factory APIs" data-tooltip-position="top">Related .NET factory APIs</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Factory Method solution</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET dependency injection</a> · <a href="https://people.csail.mit.edu/addy/pattern/pat3c.htm" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://people.csail.mit.edu/addy/pattern/pat3c.htm" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GoF: Factory Method pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method.md" class="internal-link">Factory Method</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does Factory Method support the Open/Closed Principle?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Factory Method lets a new product variant arrive as new code, in the form of a creator subclass, while the creator's existing workflow stays unchanged. That is the Open/Closed Principle at one variation point: the workflow is open to new products but closed to modification.</p>
<p dir="auto">How a new variant is added:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The base creator runs its workflow and gets the product only through the overridable factory method. In the notification example this is <code>CreateSender()</code>, which returns the product interface <code>INotificationSender</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">A new channel, such as Slack, adds a <code>SlackNotificationSender</code> and a creator subclass whose override returns it.</li>
<li dir="auto">The composition root registers the new creator. The shared workflow, the existing creators and the code that calls the workflow are not edited.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The protection covers only the anticipated variation point. A variant that needs a different product contract, or a change to the shared workflow, still requires editing existing code. The composition root that selects the creator also changes when the new creator is put into use.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://objectmentor.com/resources/articles/Principles_and_Patterns.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://objectmentor.com/resources/articles/Principles_and_Patterns.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Robert C. Martin: Design Principles and Design Patterns</a> · <a href="https://cleancoder.com/files/solid.md" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cleancoder.com/files/solid.md" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Robert C. Martin: SOLID course notes</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Factory Method solution</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method.md" class="internal-link">Factory Method</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is Prototype useful instead of constructing an object directly?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Prototype is useful when a new object should start as a copy of an existing instance rather than be built from scratch. Two situations justify it:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A configured template exists:</strong> many objects differ from a base in only a few values. Product variants, for example, share the base product's name, description, category and shipping rules. Copying the template and overriding the differences avoids manual copy code that lists every member, which silently produces incomplete objects when a newly added member is missed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The caller does not know the concrete runtime type:</strong> code that holds an object through a base type cannot call the right constructor, but the object knows its own type and can copy itself through its own copy method.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Direct construction is clearer when the type and the values are already known and no template carries useful state.</p>
<p dir="auto">A prototype still needs a defined copy contract:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">which members stay shared</li>
<li dir="auto">which are duplicated</li>
<li dir="auto">which get fresh values, such as a new identifier</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">In C#, <code>record with { }</code> makes a shallow copy with selected members replaced, and an explicit copy constructor states deeper copy rules.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Prototype solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Prototype pitfalls</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Records (C# reference)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype.md" class="internal-link">Prototype</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What separates a shallow copy from a deep copy, and which nested objects must a deep copy duplicate?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but its reference-type fields still point to the same nested objects as the original. A deep copy also duplicates nested objects, so changing them through the copy does not affect the original. A practical deep copy duplicates the mutable nested state that must evolve independently, not everything reachable.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Shallow copy</th>
<th>Deep copy</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Outer object</td>
<td>A new instance.</td>
<td>A new instance.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Value-type fields</td>
<td>Copied bit by bit.</td>
<td>Copied.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reference-type fields</td>
<td>Only the reference is copied, so both objects share the same nested instance.</td>
<td>Members covered by the copy policy get new instances.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Adding an item to a nested <code>List&lt;T&gt;</code></td>
<td>The change is visible through both objects.</td>
<td>Only the object that was changed sees it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>.NET mechanisms</td>
<td><code>Object.MemberwiseClone()</code> and <code>record with { }</code>.</td>
<td>A copy constructor or copy method that duplicates chosen members.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Where the boundary goes:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Duplicated:</strong> mutable state that the copy owns and changes independently, such as an order's line items and its shipping address.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared:</strong> immutable objects, such as immutable collections, because neither copy can change them.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared deliberately:</strong> objects that are meant to be common, such as the <code>Customer</code> an order refers to.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Left out or reset:</strong> runtime-only state such as event subscriptions, locks and caches. A cloned entity usually also needs a new identifier.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A member typed as <code>IReadOnlyList&lt;T&gt;</code> only limits the exposed API. The underlying list may still be mutable and shared.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.memberwiseclone?view=net-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.memberwiseclone?view=net-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Object.MemberwiseClone</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Records (C# reference)</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Prototype pitfalls</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype.md" class="internal-link">Prototype</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does a DI singleton differ from the classical Singleton pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A classical Singleton enforces a single instance inside the class itself and exposes it through a global static access point. A DI singleton is an ordinary class that the container creates once per root provider and injects into consumers, so its single instance is a container lifetime rule rather than a property of the type.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Classical Singleton</th>
<th>DI singleton</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Who enforces one instance</td>
<td>The type itself, through a private constructor and a static instance field, often initialized with <code>Lazy&lt;T&gt;</code>.</td>
<td>The container: after <code>AddSingleton&lt;T&gt;()</code>, the root provider creates the instance on first request and returns the same one for later resolutions.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How consumers get it</td>
<td>Through a static access point such as <code>AppConfig.Instance</code>, so the dependency is hidden inside method bodies.</td>
<td>Through constructor injection, so the dependency is visible in the consumer's constructor.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How far the single instance extends</td>
<td>Every caller of the static access point shares it.</td>
<td>One root provider and registration. A second provider, such as one created by calling <code>BuildServiceProvider</code> again, or direct construction with <code>new</code> produces another instance.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Testing and replacement</td>
<td>Consumers cannot be handed a substitute, and tests share the static state.</td>
<td>Tests pass a fake or substitute to the consumer's constructor.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Creation and disposal</td>
<td>Controlled by the type.</td>
<td>Controlled by the container, which disposes instances it created when the provider is disposed.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">In both forms, one instance serves concurrent callers, so the instance's own state must be thread-safe.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Service lifetimes</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET dependency injection</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Classical Singleton problem</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton#Singleton Lifetime in .NET" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton &gt; Singleton Lifetime in .NET" data-tooltip-position="top">Singleton lifetime in .NET</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton.md" class="internal-link">Singleton</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What must be true before choosing singleton lifetime for mutable state?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Singleton lifetime suits mutable state only when four conditions hold: sharing is intended, concurrent access is safe, retained memory is bounded, and no scoped state is captured. One instance serves every caller of its provider until the provider is disposed, usually at application shutdown, so each condition guards against a specific failure.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Sharing is intended:</strong> every request and user resolved from that provider sees the same state. If the data really belongs to one request or one user, it leaks between callers.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Concurrent access is safe:</strong> one instance serves concurrent requests. The container makes resolving the service thread-safe, but not the service's fields or dependencies, so unsynchronized mutation causes races and corrupted state.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retained memory is bounded:</strong> the singleton and its dependency graph live as long as the provider. An unbounded cache keeps growing, and failed or stale state survives far longer than intended.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No scoped state is captured:</strong> a singleton that holds a scoped service keeps that instance beyond its intended scope. This is a captive dependency. When scope validation is enabled, it rejects constructor-injecting a scoped service into a singleton.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When any condition fails, a shorter lifetime such as scoped or transient fits better, or the state needs a different owner. Singleton work that genuinely needs scoped services can create and dispose an explicit scope for each operation.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Dependency injection guidelines</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Service lifetimes</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Singleton pitfalls</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton.md" class="internal-link">Singleton</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural"><h5>Structural</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can an Adapter be distinguished from a Facade when both wrap another system?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An Adapter makes an existing component usable through a contract that a client already expects. Its defining job is compatibility. A Facade gives clients a new, simpler interface to a complex subsystem. Its defining job is simplification, which can include coordinating several subsystem calls behind one operation.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Adapter</th>
<th>Facade</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Problem it solves</td>
<td>The client depends on one interface, but the existing component exposes an incompatible one.</td>
<td>Using the subsystem directly is complex, for example because clients must know many of its components or repeat the same sequence of calls.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Interface it exposes</td>
<td>The target contract the client already uses, such as <code>IInventoryService</code>.</td>
<td>A new, higher-level interface shaped around what clients need, such as a checkout operation <code>PlaceOrderAsync</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Work inside</td>
<td>Maps method names, reshapes data, and converts results and error codes between the two contracts.</td>
<td>Hides subsystem details behind that interface. When a use case needs several steps, it calls the components in the required order and owns that workflow.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Without it</td>
<td>The two sides cannot work together unless equivalent translation is written somewhere else, such as in the client.</td>
<td>Clients can still use the subsystem directly, but each one has to handle its complexity. Where a workflow is involved, each client duplicates it, and the copies can drift in sequencing or error handling.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A Facade may also contain some translation. The defining responsibility separates the two: compatibility for an Adapter, simplification for a Facade.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/shows/visual-studio-toolbox/design-patterns-adapterfaade" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/shows/visual-studio-toolbox/design-patterns-adapterfaade" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Design Patterns: Adapter/Facade (Microsoft Learn)</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Adapter#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Adapter &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Adapter: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Facade: Problem</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Facade: Tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Adapter.md" class="internal-link">Adapter</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does the Bridge pattern add value beyond choosing one implementation behind an interface?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Bridge adds value when a design has two dimensions that vary independently, such as payment operations and payment providers, and operations must combine freely with providers. Choosing one implementation behind one interface varies only one dimension. That is ordinary polymorphism or a dependency-injection registration, or Strategy when the implementations are interchangeable algorithms for one behavior.</p>
<p dir="auto">Signals that a second dimension is real:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Both sides change:</strong> new operation variants and new providers are both being added, or are about to be.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Code multiplies by combination:</strong> methods differ only by provider, such as <code>ProcessStripeRefundAsync</code> and <code>ProcessPayPalRefundAsync</code>. Each new operation is then written once per provider, and each new provider repeats every operation.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Combinations are meaningful:</strong> every operation genuinely works with every provider. If subscriptions work with only one provider, the dimensions are coupled, and a Bridge advertises flexibility the system does not have.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">With one operation and one implementation, two hierarchies add indirection without a payoff, and a direct implementation is easier to trace.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Problem</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Pitfalls</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge.md" class="internal-link">Bridge</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Bridge pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementation into two class hierarchies joined by composition, so each hierarchy can be extended independently. The abstraction holds a reference to an implementation interface and delegates low-level work to it, instead of inheriting from a concrete implementation.</p>
<p dir="auto">Payment example:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Abstraction hierarchy:</strong> <code>PaymentOperation</code>, with variants such as <code>SingleChargePayment</code>, <code>SubscriptionPayment</code> and <code>PartialRefundPayment</code>. Each variant defines what the operation does.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Implementation interface (the bridge):</strong> <code>IPaymentGateway</code>, with primitives such as authorize, capture, refund and create subscription.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Concrete implementations:</strong> <code>StripeGateway</code>, <code>PayPalGateway</code> and <code>BankTransferGateway</code>. Each maps those primitives to one provider's API.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">An operation receives a gateway and calls its primitives. For example, a single charge authorizes and then captures. Any operation can therefore run on any provider:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">A new provider is one new <code>IPaymentGateway</code> implementation, and it works with every existing operation.</li>
<li dir="auto">A new operation built from existing primitives is one new <code>PaymentOperation</code> subclass, and it works with every provider.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Without the bridge, methods such as <code>ProcessStripeChargeAsync</code> and <code>ProcessPayPalRefundAsync</code> cover every provider-and-operation pair, and their number grows as providers × operations. If only the provider side varied, one interface with several implementations would be ordinary polymorphism. The second, abstraction-side hierarchy is what makes the design a Bridge.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Limit:</strong> Bridge prevents the cross-product, not change to the shared contract. An operation that needs a genuinely new primitive changes <code>IPaymentGateway</code> and every provider implementation.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Problem" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Problem" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Problem</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Solution</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge.md" class="internal-link">Bridge</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does Bridge differ from dependency injection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Dependency injection and Bridge answer different questions. DI is an inversion-of-control technique: a class receives its dependencies from outside instead of creating them itself. Bridge is a class structure: an abstraction hierarchy and an implementation hierarchy are separated so that each can vary independently.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What each decides:</strong> DI decides how an object obtains a collaborator. Bridge decides how a design is split into two hierarchies and where they connect.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What each requires:</strong> DI applies to any dependency, even a single one. Bridge requires two dimensions that vary independently, such as payment operations and payment providers.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>How they combine:</strong> DI can supply the bridge, for example by injecting an <code>IPaymentGateway</code> into a <code>PaymentOperation</code>. A Bridge can also be wired by hand, as in <code>new SingleChargePayment(stripeGateway)</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When DI selects one implementation behind one interface, such as one <code>IDistributedCache</code> provider, the result is ordinary polymorphism. It becomes Bridge-like only when a separate, independently changing abstraction composes with that implementation contract.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Dependency injection in .NET</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge#Related .NET Abstractions" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge &gt; Related .NET Abstractions" data-tooltip-position="top">Bridge: Related .NET Abstractions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge.md" class="internal-link">Bridge</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Composite pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Composite represents a part-whole tree so that clients treat a single object and a group of objects through the same interface. A leaf implements an operation directly. A composite implements the same operation by delegating to its children, which may be leaves or other composites, and combining their results.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example: in a product catalog, <code>SingleProduct</code> and <code>ProductBundle</code> both implement <code>IOrderComponent.GetPrice()</code>. A product returns its own price. A bundle sums <code>GetPrice()</code> over its children and applies its discount, so a bundle of bundles is priced by the same call. A caller prices any item without checking whether it is a product or a bundle.</p>
<p dir="auto">This removes repeated type checks such as <code>item is ProductBundle</code> from client code. A new leaf type, such as a subscription product, needs no changes to bundles or callers.</p>
<p dir="auto">Limits:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Child management such as <code>Add</code> and <code>Remove</code> makes sense only for composites. Putting it on the shared interface forces leaves to reject those calls.</li>
<li dir="auto">The tree must stay acyclic. A bundle that contains itself makes recursive operations overflow the stack.</li>
<li dir="auto">Composite fits a genuine part-whole hierarchy. A fixed model with two types may be clearer without it.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Composite: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Composite: Pitfalls</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Composite: Tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite.md" class="internal-link">Composite</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does Composite relate to the Visitor pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Composite and Visitor are complementary. Composite defines the structure of a part-whole tree, and Visitor defines operations over the node types in that tree, so the two can be combined.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Composite:</strong> leaves and groups share one component interface. A group implements each operation by delegating to its children, so callers treat any node the same way.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Visitor:</strong> each operation lives in a separate visitor that handles every node type, instead of being a method on every node class.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">In a plain Composite, operations such as <code>GetPrice()</code> and <code>GetItemCount()</code> are members of the shared interface, so every node class must implement each new operation. Adding Visitor moves operations out of the nodes. That combination fits when the set of node types is stable and new operations are added more often than new node types.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Composite: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Visitor: Solution</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite.md" class="internal-link">Composite</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does a Composite tree become a performance problem?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A Composite tree becomes a performance problem when recursive operations walk a large tree, or walk it very often, and measurements show that the repeated traversal is a significant cost. A call such as <code>GetPrice()</code> on a bundle visits every node below it each time it runs, so its work grows with the size of the traversed subtree.</p>
<p dir="auto">One remedy is to cache an aggregate, such as a bundle's subtotal, or to keep it updated as the tree changes. That moves cost and risk to mutation: every change below a cached value must invalidate or update it, or reads return stale results. Because the optimization adds this consistency rule and makes mutation harder, measurements of the real workload justify it, not tree size alone.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Composite: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Composite: Pitfalls</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite.md" class="internal-link">Composite</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the Decorator pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Decorator adds behavior to an object by wrapping it in another object that implements the same interface. The wrapper holds a reference to the wrapped component, normally delegates calls to it and runs its own work before or after delegating. A wrapper can also end a call without delegating, as a validation decorator does when it rejects invalid input. Because the wrapper still satisfies the original contract, clients use it exactly as they would use the component, and wrappers can be stacked.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example: a core <code>IOrderHandler</code> saves and processes an order, and separate decorators add validation, logging and metrics:</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token class-name">IOrderHandler</span> handler <span class="token operator">=</span>
    <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">ValidationOrderHandler</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>
        <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">LoggingOrderHandler</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>
            <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">MetricsOrderHandler</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>
                <span class="token keyword">new</span> <span class="token constructor-invocation class-name">CoreOrderHandler</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>repository<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span>
                metrics<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span>
            logger<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto">A call enters the outermost wrapper first and moves inward unless a layer ends it, and results return outward through the layers it passed. Each concern lives in its own class, so adding one, such as idempotency, means adding another decorator rather than editing the core handler.</p>
<p dir="auto">Order is part of the behavior. With validation outside logging, invalid orders are rejected before they are logged. With the layers reversed, every attempt is logged. The costs are more small classes and deeper call stacks to trace.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Pitfalls</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator.md" class="internal-link">Decorator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does ASP.NET Core Middleware implement the Decorator pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Middleware that delegates to the rest of the pipeline follows the Decorator shape: it wraps the remaining pipeline and adds behavior around it, while every step keeps the same request-handling contract.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared contract:</strong> each step is a request delegate that handles an <code>HttpContext</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Wrapped component:</strong> a wrapping middleware receives <code>next</code>, the delegate for the rest of the pipeline.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Added behavior:</strong> code that runs before calling <code>next</code> acts on the request, and code that runs after it acts on the response.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Composition:</strong> middleware is added in order, and each wrapping middleware can call the next. The registration order sets the request order, and the response passes back through the same middleware in reverse.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Boundary:</strong> a terminal delegate, such as one added with <code>Run</code>, receives no <code>next</code> and ends the pipeline. In the Decorator lens it is the innermost component rather than a decorator.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">As with stacked decorators, order is part of the behavior. A wrapping middleware can also end the request without calling <code>next</code>. This short-circuiting means later middleware never runs, so placement decides which middleware still sees the request.</p>
<p dir="auto">Decorator is one useful lens on this structure. The ASP.NET Core documentation describes it as a pipeline of request delegates.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ASP.NET Core middleware</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Common .NET Examples" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Common .NET Examples" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Common .NET Examples</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator.md" class="internal-link">Decorator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should Decorator replace inheritance for added behavior?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Decorator fits when the added behavior is optional, must be combined with other behaviors in a chosen order, or must wrap a type that cannot be subclassed. An example is a sealed or third-party implementation of an interface the client uses. Inheritance fits when the new type is a stable subtype of its base class rather than an add-on around it.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Decorator</th>
<th>Inheritance</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How behavior is attached</td>
<td>A wrapper implements the same interface, holds the wrapped object and runs work before or after delegating to it.</td>
<td>A subclass extends or overrides members of its base class.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Combining behaviors</td>
<td>Separate wrappers, such as validation, logging and metrics, are stacked when objects are composed, and the order is explicit there.</td>
<td>Combinations are fixed in the class hierarchy when the code is written.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Coupling</td>
<td>Depends only on the shared contract, not on a base-class implementation.</td>
<td>Ties the added behavior to the base-class implementation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>Adds an object, a delegation call and another layer to trace while debugging.</td>
<td>No wrapper object or extra delegation layer.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator.md" class="internal-link">Decorator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What's the performance cost of a deep decorator chain?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each layer can add a cost to every call that passes through it: one more method call that delegates to the inner object. That cost is not fixed. It depends on the generated code, and runtime optimizations such as devirtualization and inlining can reduce it. A wrapper written as an <code>async</code> method that awaits the inner call can also carry the bookkeeping of an asynchronous method, which suspends and resumes it when the inner task has not yet completed. The potential overhead grows with the number of layers.</p>
<p dir="auto">Whether it matters depends on the path. On a CPU-bound hot path called very often, the extra calls can be measurable. When the wrapped operation performs I/O, such as a database or HTTP call, the I/O can dominate and make the wrapper overhead small by comparison. Profiling the specific path shows whether the layers are significant. Collapsing layers without that evidence gives up the separation of concerns the decorators provide.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Asynchronous programming scenarios (C#)</a> · <a href="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/performance-improvements-in-net-10/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/performance-improvements-in-net-10/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Performance Improvements in .NET 10</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Pitfalls</a></p>
