</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator.md" class="internal-link">Decorator</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does a Facade become a "god class" anti-pattern?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A Facade simplifies access to a subsystem by coordinating its collaborators. It becomes a god class when it absorbs business rules or mutable domain state instead of delegating those responsibilities to domain services/objects. Difficulty testing it without recreating the domain is a stronger signal than line count. <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Facade tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade.md" class="internal-link">Facade</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does the Flyweight pattern reduce memory use?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Flyweight reduces memory by storing state that many objects have in common once and sharing it, instead of copying it into each object.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Intrinsic state:</strong> the shared, context-independent part, such as a product category's name, tax rate and shipping rules. It lives in the flyweight and should be immutable, because many owners see the same instance and a write to it would change what all of them observe.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Extrinsic state:</strong> the part unique to each use, such as a product's ID, SKU, price and stock. It stays with each owner or is passed in by the caller.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Factory or interning table:</strong> returns the existing flyweight for equal intrinsic state and creates one only on the first request.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Example: when 100,000 products each reference one of 50 shared category objects, the category data is stored 50 times instead of 100,000 times. <code>string.Intern()</code> applies the same idea to strings: the runtime returns one canonical instance for equal values.</p>
<p dir="auto">Flyweight is not object pooling. <code>ArrayPool&lt;T&gt;</code> lends a mutable buffer to one caller at a time and takes it back. A flyweight is shared by many owners at once.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Flyweight: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight#Common .NET Examples" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight &gt; Common .NET Examples" data-tooltip-position="top">Flyweight: Common .NET Examples</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight.md" class="internal-link">Flyweight</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is Flyweight not worth the complexity?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Flyweight is not worth its complexity when duplicated state is not a measured memory problem: the object population is modest, the shared part is small, or the state cannot be split cleanly into a shared part and a per-use part. In those cases it adds a factory, a lookup path and an extra level of indirection without relieving a real constraint. It is also a poor fit when the shared part must change per owner, because mutating a shared instance silently changes what every owner sees.</p>
<p dir="auto">It earns its cost when many objects repeat substantial immutable state and a memory profile shows that the duplication materially contributes to retained memory. The saving grows with the ratio of objects to distinct shared values. For example, 100,000 products can reference 50 shared category objects instead of each holding its own copy of the category data.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-memory-leak" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-memory-leak" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Debug a memory leak in .NET</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight#Tradeoffs" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight &gt; Tradeoffs" data-tooltip-position="top">Flyweight: Tradeoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight.md" class="internal-link">Flyweight</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What's the difference between a Proxy and a Decorator in terms of intent?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both wrap an object behind the same interface, so their structure can look identical. A Proxy exists to control access to the real subject. A Decorator exists to add a responsibility around the object it wraps.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Proxy</th>
<th>Decorator</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Intent</td>
<td>Decides whether, when or how the real subject is reached.</td>
<td>Extends what a call does by adding a responsibility around the wrapped object.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect on the real call</td>
<td>Can defer creating the subject, return a cached result or reject the call before the subject runs.</td>
<td>Normally runs added work before or after delegating to the wrapped object. It can also end a call before delegating as part of that responsibility, as validation does when it rejects invalid input.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical forms</td>
<td>Virtual (lazy creation), caching, protection (authorization) and remote proxies.</td>
<td>Logging, validation and metrics layers stacked in a chosen order.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Mixing both concerns in one wrapper makes ordering and failure behavior harder to reason about. Order matters even with separate wrappers: if a caching proxy wraps an authorization proxy, a cache hit can return data without the authorization check running.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Proxy#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Proxy &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Proxy: Solution</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Proxy#Pitfalls" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Proxy &gt; Pitfalls" data-tooltip-position="top">Proxy: Pitfalls</a> · <a class="internal-link" href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator#Solution" aria-label="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator &gt; Solution" data-tooltip-position="top">Decorator: Solution</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Proxy.md" class="internal-link">Proxy</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Architecture/System Architecture"><h3>System Architecture</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is event-driven architecture?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Event-driven architecture (EDA) is a style in which components coordinate by publishing and consuming events. An event records a fact that has already happened, such as <code>OrderPlaced</code>. A producer publishes the fact without naming the consumers, and each consumer decides what that fact means for its own state. When event communication is asynchronous, the producer also does not wait for the consumers.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Synchronous direct call</th>
<th>Event-driven</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Knowledge of the receiver</td>
<td>The caller names the service it calls.</td>
<td>The producer does not know which consumers exist, so new consumers can subscribe without changing it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Timing</td>
<td>The caller waits for the response, so both sides must be available at the same time.</td>
<td>With asynchronous delivery, consumers can react later, which removes that temporal coupling when an immediate answer is not needed.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Outcome</td>
<td>The caller learns the result before continuing.</td>
<td>With asynchronous delivery, the producer continues without learning the consumers' results. Other services update their state after processing the event, so cross-service consistency is usually eventual.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Not naming consumers does not by itself mean not waiting. In-process domain events can be dispatched synchronously, so the producing code waits for its handlers even though it does not name them.</p>
<p dir="auto">EDA is a communication model, not a synonym for using a queue. A message broker or retained log is a common transport for durable cross-process events. In-process dispatch, database change streams and HTTP webhooks can also carry events, each with different durability and coupling. Synchronous APIs remain the better fit for queries and decisions that need an immediate answer.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Event-driven architecture style (Azure Architecture Center)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/domain-events-design-implementation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/domain-events-design-implementation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Domain events: design and implementation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Event-Driven Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Event-Driven Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What determines whether an event-driven workflow uses orchestration or choreography?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The choice depends on whether one component must own the workflow's order, state and recovery. Choreography fits when services can react to published events independently and no component needs to own the whole workflow. Orchestration fits when ordered steps, current progress and failure recovery must be tracked and controlled in one place. Asynchronous messaging supports both styles, so using events does not force choreography.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Choreography</th>
<th>Orchestration</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Who decides the next step</td>
<td>Each service decides how to react to the events it receives; no component directs the others.</td>
<td>A coordinator decides which step runs next and tells the participant to perform it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Workflow state</td>
<td>Spread across the participants, so no single component knows the overall progress.</td>
<td>Held by the coordinator, which knows which steps have completed.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Failure and recovery</td>
<td>Each participant reacts to failure events itself, so recovery logic is distributed.</td>
<td>The coordinator detects a failed step and triggers retries or compensating actions.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Adding a reaction</td>
<td>A new subscriber can start consuming an event without any change to the producer.</td>
<td>A new step usually means changing the coordinator's workflow.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Example:</strong> after <code>OrderPlaced</code>, sending a confirmation email and updating analytics are independent reactions, so choreography fits. A checkout reserves stock, then takes payment, and releases the stock if payment fails. Ordered steps and compensation alone do not require an orchestrator, because a choreographed saga can also chain local transactions and compensations through events. Orchestration fits this checkout when one component must explicitly own its order, progress and recovery. Both styles can exist in one system.</p>
<p dir="auto">The number of events or services does not decide the style by itself; ownership of order, state and recovery does.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Event-driven architecture style (Azure Architecture Center)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Saga distributed transactions pattern (Azure Architecture Center)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Event-Driven Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Event-Driven Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do domain events, integration events, and event notifications differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Domain and integration events differ by boundary and contract. A domain event records a business fact inside one bounded context, while an integration event publishes a stable contract that other services depend on. Event notification is a different axis: it describes a payload and retrieval style in which the event only signals that something changed and consumers fetch the details themselves. An integration event can therefore be notification-style.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Domain event</th>
<th>Integration event</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Purpose</td>
<td>Records a business fact inside one bounded context, such as <code>InvoiceIssued</code>.</td>
<td>Shares a fact with other services as a published contract, such as <code>OrderPlacedIntegrationEvent</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Audience</td>
<td>Handlers in the same bounded context.</td>
<td>Other services.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>When it is raised or published</td>
<td>Raised by domain logic when local business state changes. It can be dispatched synchronously in process.</td>
<td>Published only after the local transaction succeeds, usually through an outbox and publisher.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Payload</td>
<td>Can follow the internal model. It typically carries rich domain data, but that richness is not what makes it a domain event.</td>
<td>A stable DTO, so consumers do not depend on the internal model.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main constraint</td>
<td>Normally stays inside the service; leaving it requires an explicit mapping to an integration event.</td>
<td>Versioning and backward compatibility become part of the contract, because consumers deploy independently.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Event notification</strong> describes what an event carries, not where it travels:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">It carries minimal identifiers and metadata, such as <code>CatalogItemChanged { ItemId, ChangedAt }</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">Consumers fetch current state from the source when they need more detail.</li>
<li dir="auto">It suits cache invalidation and broad fan-out, but couples consumers to the source's availability and read API.</li>
<li dir="auto">An integration event can use this style when other services only need to know that something changed.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The domain fact is modeled first. Only the part that another service can safely depend on is mapped into an integration event.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/domain-events-design-implementation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/domain-events-design-implementation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Domain events: design and implementation</a> · <a href="https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: What do you mean by "Event-Driven"?</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Event-Driven Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Event-Driven Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a microservices architecture?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A microservices architecture splits a system into services that can be deployed independently. Each service is built around one business capability, owns that capability's data, and works with other services only through network contracts such as APIs and events.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Independent deployment:</strong> a service can be released, rolled back and scaled without a coordinated release of the whole system. This is the property the style exists for; running code in separate processes does not by itself make it a microservice architecture.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Business-capability boundaries:</strong> services such as Orders, Inventory and Billing each contain their own rules and language, instead of the system being split by technical layer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Exclusive data ownership:</strong> only the owning service accesses its data directly, and other services go through its contract. Separate database servers are optional; exclusive ownership is not.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Contract-based integration:</strong> versioned APIs and events carry data between services, so one service's internals can change without forcing another team to release.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The cost is that calls become network calls that can fail partially, workflows that span services lose single-database transactions, and every service needs its own pipeline, monitoring and on-call ownership.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Microservices architecture style</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Microservices.md" class="internal-link">Microservices</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why do microservices create distributed data consistency problems, and what keeps a cross-service workflow reliable?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each service commits only to its own datastore, so a business operation that spans several services has no single local ACID transaction by default. One service can commit while a later step fails, which leaves partial business state. While the workflow runs, other services can also observe intermediate state, so the overall result is eventually consistent rather than atomic.</p>
<p dir="auto">A reliable cross-service workflow combines separate mechanisms, each covering a different failure:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Mechanism</th>
<th>Failure it handles</th>
<th>How it handles it</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Saga</td>
<td>A later step fails after earlier steps have committed</td>
<td>The workflow runs as a sequence of local transactions. When a step fails, compensating business actions counteract completed steps where possible, such as refunding a payment or releasing a stock reservation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Transactional outbox</td>
<td>The service crashes between committing its data and publishing the related message</td>
<td>The state change and the outgoing message are written in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes the message afterward. A committed change therefore always has a stored message waiting to be published, and a rolled-back change is never announced.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Inbox or deduplication record</td>
<td>The same message arrives again, for example after a relay retry or an unconfirmed acknowledgement</td>
<td>The consumer records which messages it has already processed and skips repeats.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Idempotent effects</td>
<td>A command or handler is retried</td>
<td>Repeating the operation leaves the same result as performing it once.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Compensation is a new business action, not a database rollback, and it has two separate limits. Some committed steps have no compensating action at all. Such noncompensable (pivot) work cannot be undone once it commits, so compensation cannot restore the earlier state. Where a compensating action does exist, it can itself fail. The outbox does not make delivery exactly-once: a message can still arrive more than once, which is why consumers need deduplication or idempotent effects.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Saga pattern</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Transactional outbox with Azure Cosmos DB</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Event-driven architecture style</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Microservices.md" class="internal-link">Microservices</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What architecture usually fits a new product, and what evidence would justify moving to microservices?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A new product is usually best served by a monolith, ideally a modular monolith with explicit internal boundaries. Moving toward microservices is justified one capability at a time, when measured evidence shows that a stable capability repeatedly needs independent deployment, scaling, ownership or isolation, and the team can operate the resulting distributed system.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Why one deployment usually fits first:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Domain boundaries in a new product are still moving. Inside one deployment, moving a boundary is an ordinary refactoring; between services, it means changing contracts, data ownership and deployments.</li>
<li dir="auto">Calls between collocated modules stay in-process, and transactions across those modules can stay local. These internal calls need no network failure handling or cross-service consistency work yet. Calls to external dependencies, such as a database or a third-party API, can still fail.</li>
<li dir="auto">One deployable unit is cheaper to operate than many services, each with its own pipeline, telemetry and on-call duty.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What counts as evidence:</strong> measured costs of the shared deployment, such as release wait time, change collisions between teams, one workload saturating while the rest of the application is idle, or incidents in one area spreading to unrelated features. A preference for microservices or an expected future scale is not evidence by itself.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Operational readiness:</strong> every extracted service adds network failure modes for its callers. A workflow whose steps commit to independently owned state also becomes eventually consistent. An extraction that only serves reads need not create such a workflow. Without distributed tracing, on-call ownership and experience with asynchronous consistency, those costs outweigh the gain.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is a conditional judgment, not a universal monolith-first rule. A monolith alongside a few extracted services can be a stable end state.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Microservices architecture style</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Microservices.md" class="internal-link">Microservices</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What evidence shows that an extracted service is independent rather than part of a distributed monolith?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An extracted service is independent when its owning team can change, deploy, roll back and operate it without a coordinated release elsewhere. A distributed monolith fails that test: its processes run separately, but its parts still change or fail together. Shared writable tables and paired deployments create that coupling directly. A mandatory synchronous call chain can create it too, when its contracts cannot evolve compatibly, its releases must be paired, or a dependency's failure is not contained. Synchronous communication alone does not force lockstep change.</p>
<p dir="auto">Evidence of independence:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unpaired release and operation:</strong> the service ships and rolls back on its own, and its team runs it with its own alerts and on-call duty.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Exclusive data ownership:</strong> only the service writes its data; other components use its contract instead of reading or writing its tables.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Versioned contract:</strong> consumers depend on a published API or event schema that can evolve compatibly, not on shared internals.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Exercised failure behavior:</strong> dependency failures have been tested, and callers reject, queue or degrade as designed instead of letting the failure spread.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Traces and reconciliation show that synchronous calls and later messages can be followed across the boundary, and that diverging state gets detected. That is useful evidence, but it does not prove independence on its own: a fully traced service can still require lockstep releases.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Microservices architecture style</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Event-driven architecture style</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Microservices.md" class="internal-link">Microservices</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a modular monolith?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A modular monolith is a single deployable application whose code and data are divided into modules, each owning one business capability behind an explicit contract. It keeps a monolith's single deployment and in-process calls while giving each module clear ownership.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Code boundary:</strong> each module exposes a small public contract, such as commands, events, DTOs and interfaces. Other modules use that contract and do not reference the module's internal domain or infrastructure types.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Data boundary:</strong> each table has one owning module, often made visible with a separate schema and <code>DbContext</code>. Other modules do not read or write those tables directly.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Runtime:</strong> modules are released together and normally run in the same process, so calls between them are in-process. With EF Core on a relational database, modules can also commit together in one local transaction when their <code>DbContext</code> instances share the same <code>DbConnection</code> and <code>DbTransaction</code>; using the same database alone is not enough.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The boundaries hold only when they are enforced. Project references, architecture tests that fail the build, and database permissions make crossing a boundary harder than using the contract. Without that enforcement, direct table reads and internal references erode the modules into ordinary folders.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.kamilgrzybek.com/blog/posts/modular-monolith-primer" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.kamilgrzybek.com/blog/posts/modular-monolith-primer" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Kamil Grzybek: Modular Monolith: A Primer</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Using transactions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Modular Monolith.md" class="internal-link">Modular Monolith</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a modular monolith a better fit than microservices, and what signals justify extracting a module?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A modular monolith fits better when strong module boundaries are valuable but one deployment, in-process calls and local transactions still serve the system well. Extracting a module is justified when it repeatedly needs independent release, scaling or isolation, and that need outweighs the cost of a new network boundary.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Module inside a modular monolith</th>
<th>Module extracted as a service</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Release</td>
<td>Ships and rolls back with every other module, so unrelated changes can delay it</td>
<td>Ships and rolls back on its own schedule</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Scaling</td>
<td>Scales only by replicating the whole application</td>
<td>Scales independently</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Calls</td>
<td>In-process, with no network between caller and module. A call can still hang, or throw after producing effects</td>
<td>Over the network, adding latency and transient failures. After a timeout or lost connection, the caller may not know whether the operation completed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Transactions</td>
<td>Can share one local transaction with another module when both <code>DbContext</code> instances use the same <code>DbConnection</code> and <code>DbTransaction</code>; using the same database alone is not enough</td>
<td>Commits only to its own store and cannot join the caller's transaction. When a local commit must also announce a change, an outbox records the message in that commit for later publication. Workflows spanning several services' commits may also need idempotent consumers and sometimes a saga</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Operations</td>
<td>Shares one pipeline and runtime with the rest of the application</td>
<td>Needs its own pipeline, telemetry and on-call ownership</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The extraction signals are recurring costs of the shared unit. The module's changes keep waiting behind unrelated releases, its load forces the whole application to scale, or its failures and resource use must be contained away from other features. Keeping the same contract interface does not make a remote call local. Deadlines, safe retries, cross-boundary observability and transaction boundaries must therefore be designed explicitly, with an outbox wherever a local commit must durably publish a message.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Microservices architecture style</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Saga pattern</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/transactions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">EF Core: Using transactions</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Transactional outbox with Azure Cosmos DB</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/retry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/retry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Retry pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Modular Monolith.md" class="internal-link">Modular Monolith</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When a modular-monolith module is extracted into a service, what must be redesigned even if its contract interface stays the same?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The interface can keep the same methods, but each call now crosses a network, which changes its latency, failure and transaction behavior. Local calls can already hang, or throw after producing an effect. The network adds another kind of uncertainty: after a timeout or lost connection, the caller may not know whether the service completed the operation. The remote call also can no longer join the caller's local transaction.</p>
<p dir="auto">What has to be redesigned:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Deadlines and cancellation:</strong> remote requests get time limits, and callers need a defined response when the service is slow or unavailable, such as rejecting, queuing or degrading.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retries:</strong> a request is retried only when repeating it is safe. Either the operation is naturally idempotent, or it carries an idempotency key that stays the same across retries of one logical request, so the service recognizes a repeat after an attempt that may already have succeeded. Retries are capped so a partial outage does not become a retry storm.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Observability:</strong> trace context crosses the boundary, and dependency latency, errors, saturation and retries are measured before traffic moves.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Transactions:</strong> the shared local transaction no longer covers both sides, so each side commits only its own state. When a local commit must also publish a message that others depend on, an outbox records the message in the same commit for later publication, so a committed change cannot lose its message. Longer workflows may also need compensation or a saga.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Data:</strong> the module's data moves to its own store through an explicit migration with backfill, reconciliation and rollback.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Good module boundaries reduce how much code changes during extraction, but they cannot make a remote operation behave like a local method call.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/retry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/retry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Retry pattern</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/guide/transactional-out-box-cosmos" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Transactional outbox with Azure Cosmos DB</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Saga pattern</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Modular Monolith.md" class="internal-link">Modular Monolith</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What evidence justifies extracting a service from a monolith?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Extraction is justified when a boundary is already able to stand alone and recurring, measured pressure requires it to. Without both conditions, extraction moves the coupling onto the network instead of removing it.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The boundary is ready:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">one team owns the capability and its changes;</li>
<li dir="auto">other code uses an explicit, stable contract instead of internal classes;</li>
<li dir="auto">the capability exclusively owns its data, and no other module reads or writes those tables directly.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><strong>There is recurring pressure for independence:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">its changes repeatedly wait for unrelated releases;</li>
<li dir="auto">its load needs to scale separately from the rest of the application;</li>
<li dir="auto">its failures or resource use need runtime isolation from other features.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">When the pressure is missing, the network hop buys no autonomy that matters. The coupling that was visible in code becomes operational coupling, with added latency, partial failure and another deployment to run. When the boundary is not ready, shared tables or paired releases make the extracted service part of a distributed monolith.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/microservices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Azure: Microservices architecture style</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Monolith Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Monolith Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does service-oriented architecture (SOA) differ from microservices?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both organize a system as services behind explicit contracts. They differ mainly in where change is controlled. Typical enterprise SOA centralizes integration and governance to connect existing systems that cannot change together. Microservices push ownership, data and deployment decisions into independently owned services.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Typical enterprise SOA</th>
<th>Typical microservices</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Main pressure</td>
<td>Make heterogeneous systems, such as SAP, mainframes and custom applications, interoperate through stable contracts</td>
<td>Let teams own, change and deploy bounded business capabilities independently</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Service size</td>
<td>Often coarse business services shared by several business units</td>
<td>Usually smaller services, each aligned to one bounded capability</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Integration logic</td>
<td>Often placed in a central ESB or orchestration layer that routes, transforms and mediates protocols</td>
<td>Kept near service endpoints or in a workflow engine, with comparatively simple transport</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Data</td>
<td>Shared enterprise stores are common</td>
<td>Each service owns its data</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Governance</td>
<td>Central contract and schema review gives controlled interoperability at the cost of slower local change</td>
<td>Teams own their contracts within platform guardrails</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Deployment</td>
<td>Services may share infrastructure and coordinate releases</td>
<td>Independent deployment is a core goal</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">These are tendencies rather than strict definitions. Many organizations use both styles: governed integration services around existing systems, and microservices for newer product capabilities.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html#MicroservicesAndSOA" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html#MicroservicesAndSOA" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Fowler and Lewis: Microservices and SOA</a> · <a href="https://soa-manifesto.org/default.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://soa-manifesto.org/default.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SOA Manifesto</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Service-Oriented Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Service-Oriented Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which part of SOA remains useful without SOAP, WSDL, or an ESB?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The durable idea is an explicit contract around a cohesive business capability: consumers depend on the published boundary, not the service’s internal code or direct writes to its data. SOAP/WSDL or an ESB were implementation/governance choices; HTTP, gRPC, or messaging can also carry the contract if compatibility is managed. <a href="https://soa-manifesto.org/default.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://soa-manifesto.org/default.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">SOA Manifesto</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Architecture/System Architecture/Service-Oriented Architecture.md" class="internal-link">Service-Oriented Architecture</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-5" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-5" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Software Design"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Software%20Design">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Software%20Design"><option value="Software Design">All Software Design (7)</option><option value="Software Design/Paradigms">Paradigms (1)</option><option value="Software Design/Testing">Testing (6)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Software Design questions"><h2>Software Design</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Design"></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Design/Paradigms"><h3>Paradigms</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What makes a function "pure" and why does purity matter for testing?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A function is pure when its result depends only on its explicit arguments and evaluating it has no observable side effects. The same inputs always give the same output. The function does not read hidden state, such as the clock, a global variable or configuration. It also changes nothing outside its return value, such as shared state, a database or a log. A call can therefore be replaced by its result without changing program behavior. This property is called referential transparency.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, <code>CalculateTax(amount, rate) =&gt; amount * rate</code> is pure. A version that reads <code>_config.TaxRate</code> and writes a log entry is impure. Its result depends on hidden state, and running it has an effect.</p>
<p dir="auto">Purity matters for testing because every dependency is an argument:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Direct checks:</strong> a test passes input values and asserts on the returned value. No database, clock or global has to be arranged, faked or reset first.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Repeatable results:</strong> the same inputs give the same result on every run and in any test order, so hidden state cannot make the test flaky.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Effects at the edges:</strong> code that reads the clock or database and writes results stays in a thin surrounding layer. The decision logic is tested with plain values, and that layer is tested separately against its real boundary.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Purity and totality are separate properties. Totality is judged against a stated input domain: a function is total on that domain when every input in it produces a result. Suppose the stated domain is every value of the parameter types. A function that deterministically fails for some of those values, for example by throwing, is then partial on that domain. The same function can still be total on a narrower stated domain that excludes those values. Haskell's semantics models such an evaluation error as bottom (⊥), like non-termination. That is a language-semantics model, not a general rule for C# exceptions. When invalid input is an expected case, it can be returned as a value, such as a <code>Result&lt;T&gt;</code>. The function then returns a result for those inputs too. The outcome stays explicit, and a test can assert it like any other result.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/linq/functional-vs-imperative-programming" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/linq/functional-vs-imperative-programming" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: Functional vs. imperative programming</a> · <a href="https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch3.html#sect3.1" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch3.html#sect3.1" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Haskell 2010 Report §3.1: Errors</a> · <a href="https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Functions/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Functions/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Lean reference: Functions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Paradigms/Functional Programming.md" class="internal-link">Functional Programming</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Software Design/Testing"><h3>Testing</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is test-driven development, and how does its red-green-refactor cycle work?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Test-driven development (TDD) builds software in short cycles. A test for the next small behavior is written first, then just enough code to pass it, and then the design is cleaned up while all tests pass.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Red:</strong> a test is written for the next behavior, usually chosen from a short list of examples still to cover. It must fail, and for the expected reason. The failure shows that the test can detect the missing behavior. A compile error because a type does not exist yet can be the first red state. It is fixed quickly so that the test fails on the behavior itself rather than on setup.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Green:</strong> the simplest production change that makes the test pass is written, without speculative extras. Behavior grows only as far as the examples require.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Refactor:</strong> with the suite green, production and test code are reviewed for naming, duplication and boundaries, and improved where that helps. The passing tests show that behavior did not change. This step is a deliberate check; code that needs no improvement is left alone.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The next example is then taken from the list and the cycle repeats. Each cycle stays small enough that the reason for a failure and the production change remain obvious. The design value depends on doing the refactor step; skipping it leaves passing tests without deliberate design improvement. TDD describes the order of work, so tests written after the implementation can be useful regression checks but are not TDD.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: Test-Driven Development</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Testing/Test-Driven Development.md" class="internal-link">Test-Driven Development</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can TDD improve design beyond increasing test coverage?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">TDD improves design by making each test the first caller of the code it specifies. Because the test is written before the implementation, construction, inputs, results and failure behavior have to be decided from the caller's side. Awkward construction or unclear results then show up while they are still cheap to change.</p>
<p dir="auto">The rest of the loop adds two more design effects:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Safe refactoring:</strong> red-green-refactor leaves a passing example for each completed behavior. Names, duplication and boundaries can then be improved while those examples show that behavior is unchanged.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Decomposition:</strong> a list of examples, worked through in small steps, breaks a large behavior into observable increments.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These benefits are conditional. They depend on choosing informative examples and actually doing the refactor step. A poorly chosen test can drive an awkward interface as easily as a good one clarifies it. Difficult test setup is a signal to investigate, for example for hidden time, global state or too many responsibilities. It does not by itself prove that a class needs splitting.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: Test-Driven Development</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Testing/Test-Driven Development.md" class="internal-link">Test-Driven Development</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is TDD not worth the overhead?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">TDD is poor value when its test-first loop yields neither useful design feedback nor lasting regression evidence. Typical cases:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Disposable spike:</strong> the goal is to learn whether an approach works, and the code is discarded or rebuilt before production. Durable tests would protect code that will not ship, and the loop adds overhead to exploration. The exception lasts only while the spike stays disposable.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Declarations the platform already guarantees:</strong> the language or framework may already guarantee a plain declaration's behavior, as with an unmodified property accessor. A test for it mostly restates that guarantee. A declaration that adds custom validation, binding or serialization is no longer in this category.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Visual rendering:</strong> when the useful feedback is how output looks, inspecting the rendered result gives that feedback more directly than a code-level red-green loop.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Skipping TDD does not remove the need to verify behavior that ships. That behavior still needs tests, written before or after the code, at the layer that can expose its realistic failure. Configuration, persistence and protocol wiring, for example, fit an integration-level test loop better than unit-level TDD. No universal coverage percentage or time-cost threshold decides the question.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET unit-testing best practices</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Testing/Test-Driven Development.md" class="internal-link">Test-Driven Development</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a unit test, and what counts as the unit?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A unit test verifies one small behavior quickly and deterministically, without crossing slow or nondeterministic process boundaries such as a database, remote HTTP, the filesystem or uncontrolled time. The unit is defined by the behavior under test, not by code size. It can be one method, one class or a small group of collaborating objects.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Kept real:</strong> ordinary in-memory collaborators can run as they are. They do not need to be mocked for the test to count as a unit test. Replacing them anyway is a design style, the mockist or London school, not part of the definition.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Replaced:</strong> process boundaries the test does not own are represented by test doubles or plain values, such as a fixed clock instead of the system time.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Result:</strong> fast, local evidence and a failure that points to a specific behavior.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A test that reaches a real database or filesystem has crossed a process boundary, whatever it is called. It becomes slower, and its failures include infrastructure state, so that behavior belongs in an integration test.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET unit-testing best practices</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Testing/Unit Testing.md" class="internal-link">Unit Testing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between a stub and a mock?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A stub supplies canned answers so the code under test can run, and the test then checks the result. A mock is set up with expected calls, and the test checks that those interactions actually happened.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Stub</th>
<th>Mock</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Role</td>
<td>Feeds inputs to the code under test, such as a repository that returns a fixed list of orders.</td>
<td>Observes outgoing calls, such as whether an email sender was asked to send a message exactly once.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What the test asserts</td>
<td>The outcome: a returned value or other observable state.</td>
<td>The interaction: which calls were made, with which arguments and how often.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Coupling to implementation</td>
<td>Lower. Internal refactoring does not break the test while the outcome and the stubbed contract stay the same.</td>
<td>Higher. Changing how collaborators are called can break the test even when the outcome is unchanged.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical fit</td>
<td>Dependencies whose answers drive the logic.</td>
<td>Commands whose observable result is the call itself, such as publishing an event.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The typical-fit row is a heuristic, not a type rule. The distinction lies in how the test uses the double, not in the tool that created it. In Moq, the same <code>Mock&lt;T&gt;</code> acts as a stub when it only configures <code>Setup(...).Returns(...)</code>, and as a mock when the test calls <code>Verify(...)</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Two related doubles complete the vocabulary. A spy records the calls it receives so the test can assert on them afterwards. A fake is a simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory repository backed by a <code>Dictionary</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Martin Fowler: Mocks Aren’t Stubs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Testing/Unit Testing.md" class="internal-link">Unit Testing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is a unit test the wrong testing layer?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A unit test is the wrong layer when the realistic failure comes from a boundary that the unit test replaces or never runs. A unit test substitutes doubles or plain values for databases, remote services and other process boundaries, so it cannot observe failures that only the real boundary produces. Using framework code does not by itself rule out a unit test. Deterministic in-memory framework behavior, such as <code>JsonSerializer.Serialize</code> turning an object into a JSON string, can run inside one. The limit applies when the test replaces that behavior or never runs the real configuration, host or wire exchange around it.</p>
<p dir="auto">Typical cases:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Provider SQL and persistence:</strong> a stubbed repository cannot show whether the database provider translates a query correctly or whether the query matches the real schema. An in-memory database provider is not a faithful substitute for relational behavior either.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Serialization and protocols:</strong> field names, formats and wire compatibility are decided by the real serializer or HTTP stack.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Dependency registration and configuration binding:</strong> a missing service registration or a misbound setting appears only when the real container and configuration are built and used.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Rendering:</strong> markup and layout come from the UI framework, not from isolated logic.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These failures need a component or integration test that exercises the boundary with a real or appropriate implementation. The guiding rule is the lowest-cost layer that can still expose the realistic failure. Deterministic domain decisions belong in unit tests, while wiring and provider behavior need integration evidence.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET unit-testing best practices</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/how-to" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/how-to" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">.NET: Serialize objects to JSON with System.Text.Json</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Software Design/Testing/Unit Testing.md" class="internal-link">Unit Testing</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-6" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-6" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="AI &amp; ML"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-AI%20%26%20ML">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-AI%20%26%20ML"><option value="AI &amp; ML">All AI &amp; ML (97)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM">LLM (91)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents">LLM / Agents (8)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Evaluation">LLM / Agents / Evaluation (3)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering">LLM / Context Engineering (30)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG">LLM / Context Engineering / RAG (28)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation">LLM / Context Engineering / RAG / Evaluation (7)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Evaluation">LLM / Evaluation (4)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering">LLM / Harness Engineering (7)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Tooling">LLM / Harness Engineering / Tooling (4)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering">LLM / Loop Engineering (8)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering">LLM / Prompt Engineering (10)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety">LLM / Safety (9)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning">Machine Learning (5)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Evaluation">Machine Learning / Evaluation (2)</option><option value="AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Types">Machine Learning / Types (2)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="AI &amp;
