ML questions"><h2>AI &amp; ML</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is classic machine learning a better fit than an LLM?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Classic machine learning is the better fit when two conditions hold. First, the task is a defined prediction with representative labeled examples and a measurable objective. Second, measurement on the actual workload shows that classic ML meets that objective with a better balance of quality, latency, cost and maintenance than an LLM. The first condition makes classic ML a strong candidate. Only the second decides.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Task and data fit:</strong> the task has a fixed output to predict, such as a class, a number or a ranking. Labeled examples represent the inputs seen in production, and a metric measures success directly. A model trained on those examples learns that mapping, and the metric checks its quality.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Why fit alone does not decide:</strong> generative models can also perform classification and regression, and an LLM can be the stronger option for some text-classification tasks. A labeled prediction task can therefore have more than one viable approach.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Measurement:</strong> both options are evaluated against the same simple, observable objective on the same data. Neither approach is inherently more accurate, faster, cheaper or easier to maintain.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Prompting can also try an LLM on a task while its requirements are still changing. Those results need the same measurement before either approach is chosen.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/ml-framing" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/ml-framing" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Google: ML problem framing</a> · <a href="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Google: Rules of Machine Learning</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/AI &amp; ML.md" class="internal-link">AI &amp; ML</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM"><h3>LLM</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is an embedding, and how does it support semantic retrieval?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An embedding is a vector of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text. The model places texts with related meaning close together, so the distance between two vectors measures how related the texts are. The vector's length is set by the model and, for some models such as OpenAI's <code>text-embedding-3</code> family, by a requested output size.</p>
<p dir="auto">Semantic retrieval relies on that geometry:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Indexing:</strong> the embedding model converts each document chunk into a vector, which is stored in a vector index.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Query:</strong> the same model, with the same output size, converts the query into a vector in the same space.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Ranking:</strong> a similarity measure, such as cosine similarity, ranks the stored vectors by closeness to the query vector. The nearest chunks become retrieval candidates.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Because matching depends on meaning rather than shared words, a query about throttling partner API traffic can find a document about rate limiting for partners. A high similarity score is only a relevance signal. It does not prove that a chunk answers the question, so retrieval quality still has to be evaluated.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Vector embeddings (OpenAI)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Vector search overview (Azure AI Search)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Embeddings.md" class="internal-link">Embeddings</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do Matryoshka embeddings reduce vector storage, and how should a shorter vector be validated?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) trains an embedding so that its first dimensions already form a useful coarse representation, and later dimensions add finer detail. A prefix of the vector, such as its first 256 values, therefore still works as a lower-dimensional embedding. Storing only that prefix reduces vector storage.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Storage:</strong> at the same data type, 256 values instead of 1536 is one-sixth of the raw vector payload. IDs, metadata and index structures do not shrink by the same factor, so the whole index shrinks less.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Search cost:</strong> shorter vectors also reduce distance-computation work.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Availability:</strong> shortening is model-specific. OpenAI's <code>text-embedding-3</code> models accept a <code>dimensions</code> parameter. A vector truncated manually is re-normalized before cosine or dot-product search.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Risk:</strong> fewer dimensions can lower retrieval quality on a particular corpus.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A shorter vector is validated by running the same labeled queries at each candidate dimension and comparing Recall@k and latency. The preferred dimension is the smallest one that still meets the recall and latency targets. A design that re-scores candidates with full-length vectors has to store them elsewhere or recompute them, which adds storage, API cost or latency.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Embeddings guide (OpenAI)</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Matryoshka Representation Learning (arXiv)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Embeddings.md" class="internal-link">Embeddings</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What happens to retrieval when queries use embeddings from a new model but the corpus still has vectors from the old model?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Retrieval quality breaks. The query vector and the stored vectors come from different vector spaces, so the distances between them do not measure relatedness, and the ranking becomes effectively arbitrary.</p>
<p dir="auto">Each embedding model learns its own coordinate system, so the same text receives unrelated vectors from two different models. If both models produce vectors of the same length, the search can still run without any error while returning poor results. That makes the mismatch easy to miss.</p>
<p dir="auto">A model change therefore requires re-embedding the whole corpus with the new model. A safe migration builds and validates the new index first and only then switches query traffic, for example by moving a collection alias. Embedding-cache keys include the model name and version, so cached vectors from the old model are not reused with the new one.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-configure-vectorizer" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-configure-vectorizer" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Configure a vectorizer (Azure AI Search)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Embeddings.md" class="internal-link">Embeddings</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is LoRA, and why is it cheaper than full fine-tuning?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tunes a pretrained model by freezing its weights and training only a small low-rank update for selected layers. Because the trainable part is a tiny fraction of the model, training needs gradients and optimizer state only for that update, and the result is a small adapter instead of a full model copy.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">A chosen weight matrix <code>W0</code> stays frozen.</li>
<li dir="auto">Its change is represented as the product of two small matrices, <code>B·A</code>. Their shared inner dimension, the rank <code>r</code>, is much smaller than the layer's dimensions.</li>
<li dir="auto">Only <code>A</code> and <code>B</code> are trained.</li>
<li dir="auto">The adapted layer computes <code>W0·x + B·A·x</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The small trainable set lowers training memory compared with updating every weight. Adapters for different tasks can share one base model and be swapped. An adapter can also be merged into <code>W0</code>, so serving needs no extra computation. Whether a LoRA adapter matches full fine-tuning on a particular task depends on its configuration, such as rank and target layers, and held-out evaluation establishes it.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hu et al.: LoRA</a> · <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/en/developer_guides/lora" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/en/developer_guides/lora" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hugging Face PEFT: LoRA</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Fine-tuning.md" class="internal-link">Fine-tuning</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can LoRA still cause capability regressions if the base weights are frozen?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Freezing the base weights fixes what is stored and updated during training, not what the deployed model computes. LoRA adds a trainable low-rank update to selected layers. While the adapter is active, each adapted layer computes the frozen weight's output plus the adapter's contribution: <code>W0·x + B·A·x</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">That added term applies to every input passing through those layers, not only to inputs that resemble the training data. Training optimizes it for the target examples alone, so it can also shift behavior the data never covered, such as instruction following, safety behavior or general reasoning. Frozen base weights therefore do not guarantee unchanged outputs. The full base-plus-adapter model needs evaluation on both the target task and broad held-out sets.</p>
<p dir="auto">Freezing does make rollback easier. A separate adapter can be disabled, which returns the model to the base behavior. Merging folds the update into the weights, so rollback after a merge depends on a supported unmerge or an unmodified copy of the base checkpoint.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hu et al.: LoRA</a> · <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/en/developer_guides/lora" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/en/developer_guides/lora" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hugging Face PEFT: LoRA</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17830" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17830" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">More Than Catastrophic Forgetting</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Fine-tuning.md" class="internal-link">Fine-tuning</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is adjusting <code>temperature</code> and <code>top_p</code> at the same time discouraged?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Both settings control sampling randomness by reshaping the same next-token distribution. When both change at once, a change in output cannot be attributed to either setting. Tuning is therefore clearer when one setting moves while the other stays at its default.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><code>temperature</code> rescales the logits before sampling. Lower values concentrate probability on the most likely tokens; higher values flatten the distribution and admit more unlikely tokens.</li>
<li dir="auto"><code>top_p</code> (nucleus sampling) samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches the threshold, cutting off the low-probability tail.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Both settings change how often low-probability tokens appear, so their effects overlap rather than controlling separate properties. OpenAI's API reference currently recommends altering one or the other, not both. This is tuning guidance, not a hard limit. Advice differs across providers, and some models fix or reject these parameters, so the deployed model's documentation and task evaluation decide the final settings.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/go/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/go/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI API reference: Create chat completion</a> · <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/text_generation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/text_generation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hugging Face Transformers: Generation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Generation.md" class="internal-link">Generation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can a response with valid citation markers still contain unsupported claims?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A citation marker only links a claim to a source location. It does not show that the cited passage supports the claim. Markers on some sentences also say nothing about sentences that have none.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Wrong support:</strong> the model generates the citation as well as the claim, so it can attach a real, on-topic passage to a statement that the passage does not entail. For example, a passage describing a refund policy may not contain the refund limit that the answer attributes to it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Missing support:</strong> a response can mix cited sentences with uncited claims drawn from the model's own memory.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Citation validity and claim support are therefore separate checks. Support is checked after generation by splitting the answer into claims and testing each claim against its cited passage, through human review or an automated verifier matched to the risk. Natural Language Inference classifiers and fact-checking models such as MiniCheck are automated options. They also make errors, so their decisions need validation against labeled examples.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic: Citations</a> · <a href="https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.499/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.499/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Tang et al.: MiniCheck</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Generation.md" class="internal-link">Generation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does an explicit execution graph define in an agent workflow?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An explicit execution graph defines an agent workflow's control flow: the units of work, the transitions allowed between them and the state carried from step to step.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Nodes</strong> do the work. A node can be ordinary code, a tool call, one model call, a complete agent loop or a nested graph.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Edges</strong> route execution. A fixed edge always leads to the same successor, a conditional edge chooses the successor from an outcome or the current state, and a terminal edge ends the run.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>State</strong> records progress. Nodes read defined state and return updates, and the runtime's merge rules decide how concurrent updates combine.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A loop can run inside one node or appear as a cycle across nodes. The graph models control flow, not relationships in data as a knowledge graph does. The framework decides when nodes run, when their updates become visible and where checkpoints are taken.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/journey/workflows" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/journey/workflows" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Agent Framework: Workflows</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/checkpoints" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/checkpoints" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Agent Framework: Checkpoints</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Graph Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Graph Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does an explicit graph not make an agentic system deterministic?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An explicit graph fixes which paths are legal, not what happens along them. Fixed edges and deterministic guards make parts of the control flow repeatable, but other sources of variation remain:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Model calls</strong> inside nodes can return different outputs, and a model-driven routing decision can choose a different legal edge.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>External services and mutable inputs</strong> can return different data on different runs.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Concurrent work</strong> can interleave differently from run to run.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The graph constrains the application's routing and makes it easier to inspect, but it does not guarantee repeatable results. Reproducing or debugging a run therefore depends on recording its inputs, state, node outputs and routing decisions.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/concepts/workflows/edges" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/concepts/workflows/edges" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Agent Framework: Workflow edges</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Graph Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Graph Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does checkpointing require idempotent node design?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Resuming from a checkpoint can run a node's work again, so any external side effect in that node must be safe to repeat. In Microsoft Agent Framework, checkpoints are taken when a superstep completes. Work done after the last saved checkpoint is not part of any saved state, so resuming can repeat it.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The checkpoint after superstep N is saved.</li>
<li dir="auto">A node in superstep N+1 sends an email.</li>
<li dir="auto">The process stops before the checkpoint after superstep N+1 is saved.</li>
<li dir="auto">Resuming from the superstep N checkpoint runs the node again, and a second email is sent.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">An idempotent operation prevents the duplicate. If the email service accepts an idempotency key, the node sends a key that identifies this one logical operation. The key stays the same on every retry or replay, so the service recognizes the repeat and does not send again. The key is built from checkpointed values, such as the run, the node and the loop iteration, rather than generated fresh inside the node, because a fresh value would differ on replay. A later send that is meant to happen, such as a reminder in a later iteration, gets a different key.</p>
<p dir="auto">When the side effect is itself a database write, atomic deduplication also works. A unique constraint on the operation's key makes a replayed insert fail instead of creating a second record. A separate check-then-write does not work, because the process can stop after the effect but before recording that it happened. Checkpointing provides resumable state, not exactly-once side effects.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/checkpoints" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/checkpoints" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Agent Framework: Checkpoints</a> · <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Amazon Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Graph Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Graph Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only transformers differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The three families differ in which transformer stacks they use, and therefore in how attention sees the input and what the model produces. Encoder-only models build contextual representations of an input. Decoder-only models generate a continuation one token at a time. Encoder-decoder models read a source sequence and generate a separate target sequence.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Encoder-only (BERT)</th>
<th>Encoder-decoder (T5)</th>
<th>Decoder-only (GPT-style)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Attention</td>
<td>Bidirectional: every token can attend to the whole input</td>
<td>The encoder reads the source bidirectionally; the decoder attends causally to its own earlier tokens and to the encoder's output</td>
<td>Causal: each position attends only to earlier positions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Pretraining objective</td>
<td>Predict masked tokens from the context on both sides</td>
<td>The encoder reads input with spans removed, and the decoder generates the missing spans</td>
<td>Predict the next token</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Output</td>
<td>One contextual vector per token, or a pooled vector, passed to a task head</td>
<td>A generated target sequence</td>
<td>A generated continuation of the prompt</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical use</td>
<td>Classification, extraction, reranking, embeddings</td>
<td>Translation, summarization and other text-to-text tasks</td>
<td>Chat, code, completion, tool-call generation</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">An encoder-only model has no autoregressive decoder, so it is not used for open-ended generation. The causal mask is what lets one decoder-only stack train on next-token prediction and then continue a prompt token by token. The typical uses describe common fits, not hard limits.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Attention Is All You Need</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">BERT</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">T5: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Language Models are Few-Shot Learners</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/LLM.md" class="internal-link">LLM</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning be chosen for an LLM system?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The choice follows the gap that evaluation reveals. A behavior gap is first addressed with clearer instructions and examples. A knowledge gap is closed by putting the facts into context. Small, stable facts can be written directly into the prompt. Large, private or changing facts are retrieved per request with RAG. Fine-tuning addresses behavior that stays inconsistent after prompt work. The techniques solve different problems and can be combined.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Technique</th>
<th>What it changes</th>
<th>Fits when</th>
<th>Main limit</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Prompting</td>
<td>The instructions, examples and any fixed reference text sent with each request</td>
<td>The model can do the task but needs a clearer specification, output format or examples, or the facts it needs are few and stable enough to write into the prompt</td>
<td>Instructions alone add no knowledge. Facts written into the prompt are fixed in advance and add tokens to every call, so this approach does not scale to large or changing knowledge</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>RAG</td>
<td>The evidence selected and placed in the context at request time</td>
<td>Answers depend on current, private or citable information that is too large or changeable to include in every prompt</td>
<td>Answer quality is limited by retrieval quality, and retrieved text does not reliably teach a new format or style</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fine-tuning</td>
<td>The model's weights, through training on examples</td>
<td>Format, style or task behavior remains inconsistent after prompt work</td>
<td>It needs training data and evaluation, and facts stored in weights are harder to update than retrieved documents</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Prompting is the usual starting point because it is the cheapest to iterate, but this is a diagnostic default, not a mandatory sequence. A fine-tuned model can still use RAG: training shapes behavior while retrieval supplies changing facts. Each change is compared on the same representative evaluation set, so an improvement can be attributed to that change.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI: Optimizing LLM accuracy</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/LLM.md" class="internal-link">LLM</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does a sparse mixture-of-experts model work, and what does sparse activation actually save?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model replaces some dense feed-forward layers with several expert networks and a learned router. Each token is processed by only a few selected experts. Compared with evaluating every expert on every token, this saves feed-forward arithmetic, so total parameter capacity can grow while per-token computation stays roughly constant. It does not shrink the parameter footprint: every expert still has to be stored and placed in device memory, and the rest of the transformer still runs for every token.</p>
<p dir="auto">Routing a token through an MoE layer:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The router scores every expert for the token's hidden state.</li>
<li dir="auto">The top-k experts are selected.</li>
<li dir="auto">The token is dispatched to those experts, possibly on other devices.</li>
<li dir="auto">Their outputs are combined using the router's weights.</li>
</ol>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Measure</th>
<th>What it reflects</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Total parameters</td>
<td>Checkpoint size and the device memory needed to hold every expert</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Active parameters per token</td>
<td>Part of the arithmetic performed for each token</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Measured latency and throughput</td>
<td>Arithmetic plus router work, cross-device dispatch, load imbalance, batching and kernels</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">If many tokens choose the same expert, its device becomes a bottleneck while others sit idle. Capacity limits and load-balancing objectives counter this. Depending on the implementation, tokens beyond an expert's capacity are dropped or rerouted.</p>
<p dir="auto">The saving is relative to evaluating all experts. It is not a guaranteed advantage over every alternative. A dense model with a similar number of active parameters can be faster than an MoE when expert traffic is communication-bound, because the MoE also pays for routing, dispatch and imbalance. Parameter counts alone cannot predict either outcome. Only measurement on the intended serving workload shows the real cost.</p>
<p dir="auto">MoE routing happens inside one model and is separate from application-level routing between different models.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://jmlr.org/papers/v23/21-0998.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://jmlr.org/papers/v23/21-0998.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Switch Transformers</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/LLM.md" class="internal-link">LLM</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should candidate LLMs be compared for a production workload?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Candidate LLMs are compared empirically. Every candidate runs on the same representative, versioned workload and is judged against the same gates for task quality, safety, latency and cost. A common decision rule then selects the least expensive candidate that clears every required gate.</p>
<p dir="auto">What the comparison measures:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Task quality:</strong> correctness, groundedness, tool-call success and failure slices, measured on a labeled set drawn from the product's own traffic and rubric.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Safety and policy:</strong> refusal behavior, data handling and provider terms.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Latency:</strong> p50 and p95 at the expected prompt size, output length and concurrency.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost per successful task:</strong> input, output and tool usage, plus retries and escalations. A model with a low price per token can still cost more per completed task if it often needs a retry or a human.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Capabilities and operations:</strong> required context length, structured outputs, tools, rate limits and version pinning.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Public leaderboards help build a shortlist, but they measure a different distribution and rubric. The evidence also expires. A change in traffic, prompts or prices invalidates earlier results, as does a new model version behind a provider alias, so the comparison is rerun when any of these occur.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI evals</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI model optimization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Model Selection and Routing.md" class="internal-link">Model Selection and Routing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do classifier routing and cascading differ when choosing an LLM for each request, and how can they be combined?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A classifier router predicts which model should handle a request before anything is generated. A cascade generates with a lower-cost model first and escalates to a stronger model only when an observable check on that output fails.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Classifier routing</th>
<th>Cascade</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>When the decision is made</td>
<td>Before generation, from request features such as task type or predicted difficulty.</td>
<td>After a first generation, from a gate on the output such as schema validation, a groundedness check, calibrated confidence or an explicit unsupported result.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Generations per request</td>
<td>One, so no request pays for a discarded attempt.</td>
<td>One when the gate passes; at least two when the request escalates.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical failure</td>
<td>A false “easy” prediction sends a hard request to a weaker model. Quality drops silently unless something downstream checks the answer.</td>
<td>Escalated requests pay for duplicate generation and extra latency, which can dominate p95. If many requests escalate, the cascade can cost more than always using the stronger model.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it depends on</td>
<td>Predictable difficulty signals, and a classifier evaluated on per-route recall for hard and safety-sensitive requests.</td>
<td>A cheap, reliable gate. A weak gate escalates too often or lets bad answers through.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Combining them:</strong> the classifier chooses the starting model, and a cascade gate checks that model's output. Requests predicted to be hard go straight to the stronger model. Requests predicted to be easy start on the cheaper model with the gate behind it. The gate then catches some misroutes that classifier routing alone would serve unnoticed.</p>
<p dir="auto">The combined policy is judged on end-to-end task success, cost per successful task and tail latency, not on classifier accuracy alone. Managed routers such as Microsoft Foundry Model Router package per-request model selection as a product feature, and they still need the same evaluation on the target workload.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">FrugalGPT (Chen et al.)</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/model-router?view=foundry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/model-router?view=foundry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Foundry Model Router</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI evals</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Model Selection and Routing.md" class="internal-link">Model Selection and Routing</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents"><h4>Agents</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does a workflow fit better than an autonomous agent?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A workflow fits better when the steps and branches can be defined in advance. Code then controls the path, and the model handles individual steps inside it. An autonomous agent is justified only when the next action must depend on intermediate results that cannot be anticipated, and that flexibility is worth its extra cost and risk.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Workflow</th>
<th>Autonomous agent</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Who chooses the next step</td>
<td>Application code follows predefined paths. The model works inside individual steps or picks one of several predefined branches.</td>
<td>The model decides its next action and tool use from the results so far.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Predictability</td>
<td>The possible paths are known before the run, so each one can be tested and reproduced.</td>
<td>The path emerges at runtime, so two runs of the same task can take different routes.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost and latency</td>
<td>Easier to predict, because the possible calls follow from the defined paths.</td>
<td>Depend on how many model and tool calls the agent decides to make.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Failure exposure</td>
<td>Failures occur at known steps, where code can add checks before the next step runs.</td>
<td>An early mistake can become the premise for later steps and compound.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The usual default is the simplest design that meets the need: a single well-prompted call first, a workflow when one call is not enough, and an agent only when no fixed path can express the task.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Building Effective AI Agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Agents.md" class="internal-link">Agents</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can errors compound during an autonomous agent run, and what controls contain them?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Errors compound because each step builds on what earlier steps produced. An agent reasons over earlier observations, acts, and feeds the new result into its next decision. A wrong assumption or misread tool result therefore does not stay one bad output: it becomes the premise for later actions. For example, an agent that looks up the wrong order can then refund, email and log against that order, with every step consistent with the original mistake.</p>
<p dir="auto">Several design controls contain this risk:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Step, cost or time limits</strong> set for the task end a run that keeps acting without converging, so drift has a bounded cost.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Checks against expected outcomes</strong>, such as tests or validation of tool results, can catch bad progress before more steps depend on it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Recovery or escalation paths</strong> define what happens when the run cannot proceed safely, such as stopping with a report or asking a human for input.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Traces</strong> of decisions, tool calls and results show where the run diverged, which makes the failure diagnosable.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These controls reduce risk; they do not guarantee that the agent recovers or reaches a correct result.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models</a> · <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Building Effective AI Agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Agents.md" class="internal-link">Agents</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What makes a task a good fit for an autonomous agent?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An agent is useful when the path cannot be fully specified in advance and intermediate results must influence the next action. The outcome still needs criteria that can eventually determine success or failure; delayed feedback can work when execution has a timeout, checkpoints, and a recovery plan. If success stays vague, the system cannot tell whether another action helped. <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Building Effective AI Agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Agents.md" class="internal-link">Agents</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer differ in who controls the next step?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They differ in how much of the control flow code fixes in advance. In prompt chaining, routing and parallelization, application code defines every possible path, and a model at most picks one predefined branch. In orchestrator-workers, a model decides the subtasks at runtime. In evaluator-optimizer, a model's evaluation decides whether the loop repeats, within a cap set in code.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Pattern</th>
<th>Who decides the next step</th>
<th>What code fixes in advance</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Prompt chaining</td>
<td>Code. Each step always follows the previous one, and programmatic gates can stop a bad intermediate result.</td>
<td>The whole sequence of steps.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Routing</td>
<td>A classifier, often an LLM, reads the input and picks one branch.</td>
<td>The set of branches and how each one is handled.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Parallelization</td>
<td>Code. It starts the calls together and aggregates them, either splitting independent sections or voting over repeated runs.</td>
<td>The subtasks and how their results are combined.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Orchestrator-workers</td>
<td>The orchestrator model decides how to split the task, what to delegate and how to synthesize the results.</td>
<td>Only the outer frame; worker count and assignments appear at runtime.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Evaluator-optimizer</td>
<td>An evaluator model decides whether a draft passes explicit criteria or returns to the generator with feedback.</td>
<td>The acceptance criteria and an iteration cap that ends the loop.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Each additional model-owned decision tends to make cost less predictable and failures harder to reproduce, so the simplest pattern that fits is usually the easiest to test.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Building Effective AI Agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Workflow Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Workflow Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is the orchestrator-workers pattern harder to operate than ordinary parallelization, even though both fan out work to several calls?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Orchestrator-workers is harder to operate because a model, not code, decides the structure of the fan-out. In ordinary parallelization, code defines the subtasks and the aggregation in advance. In orchestrator-workers, a model chooses the subtasks for each input at runtime and also synthesizes the results, so the set of calls is not known before the run.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Ordinary parallelization:</strong> application code starts a predefined set of independent calls, such as one per code-review concern, and aggregates their outputs programmatically. The split and aggregation rules can be read, reviewed and tested before any run.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Orchestrator-workers:</strong> an orchestrator model reads the input, decides how to split it and what to delegate, then synthesizes the workers' results. The worker count and assignments exist only at runtime.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Fixed rules make the structure inspectable, but they do not make outcomes repeatable. In both patterns, the workers are model calls whose outputs can differ between runs, and how well a split suits the task depends on the input. Orchestrator-workers adds model-chosen structure on top of that variability:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Work and cost vary:</strong> the number of workers, and therefore the calls and tokens spent, can change between inputs and even between runs on the same input.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The split itself can fail per run:</strong> any fan-out can miss part of the task, duplicate work or combine results poorly. With a fixed fan-out, the split and aggregation rules can be checked before deployment. With orchestrator-workers, a flawed decomposition or synthesis exists only in a particular run's decisions. It cannot be reviewed in advance and can appear for some inputs or runs but not others. It is therefore harder to reproduce and to catch with a few fixed test cases.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These are risks, not guaranteed outcomes. A trace of each run's decomposition and synthesis shows where a particular run went wrong.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Building Effective AI Agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Workflow Patterns.md" class="internal-link">Workflow Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Evaluation"><h5>Evaluation</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can one base model produce very different results on the same agent benchmark?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Because an agent benchmark scores a whole system, not the model alone. The result reflects the model together with its scaffold: prompts and policies, tool descriptions, planning and retry logic, context management, and the loop that runs it. Changing the scaffold can move the score even when the base model stays the same.</p>
<p dir="auto">Run conditions also matter. An agent can solve a task on one attempt and fail it on the next. τ-bench reports <code>pass^k</code>, the chance that all <code>k</code> trials of a task succeed, which exposes inconsistency that a single-attempt score hides.</p>
<p dir="auto">A fair model comparison therefore holds the task set, scaffold and run conditions constant and varies only the model. Comparing scaffolds is a separate experiment with the model held fixed. A leaderboard score describes one benchmark setup, not intrinsic model quality.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12045" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12045" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Evaluation/Agent Benchmarks.md" class="internal-link">Agent Benchmarks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why should tool selection and argument accuracy be measured separately?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Because they score different decisions that fail for different reasons. Tool selection asks whether the agent called the right tool for the current step, including recognizing when no call is needed. Argument accuracy asks whether a correctly chosen tool received the right values.</p>
<p dir="auto">A combined score hides which decision failed. For example, 95% selection accuracy and 70% argument accuracy average to 82.5%, and that single number no longer shows that arguments are the weak point. Separate scores point an investigation in a direction:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Selection failures</strong> often suggest unclear tool descriptions or a routing problem.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Argument failures</strong> often suggest weak grounding in the conversation or a loosely constrained schema. A call can name the right tool in schema-valid form and still send order <code>4851</code> when the conversation identifies order <code>4815</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These patterns are leads to investigate, not proof of the root cause.</p>
<p dir="auto">How argument accuracy is scored also depends on the field. Exact matching fits identifiers, enums and booleans with one defined value. Free-text fields need normalization or a semantic check, which is valid only where the tool contract accepts equivalent wording.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Evaluation/Tool-Call Evaluation.md" class="internal-link">Tool-Call Evaluation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is reference matching a better way to score an agent's trajectory than an LLM judge?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Reference matching is the better scorer when the acceptable tool-call paths are few enough to write down and the rule for comparing them is clear. It is then cheap, deterministic and repeatable. An LLM judge fits better when many different paths can be correct, because it scores the trace against a rubric instead of a list of paths. The cost is an extra model call and less deterministic scores.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Reference matching</th>
<th>LLM judge over the trace</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it needs</td>
<td>One or more known-good tool-call paths and a comparison mode.</td>
<td>A rubric describing good behavior, such as plan quality, tool choice, wasted work and recovery.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Alternative valid paths</td>
<td>Accepted only if listed or tolerated by the mode; an unanticipated correct path fails.</td>
<td>Can be accepted without being listed, because the rubric describes qualities rather than one path.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost and repeatability</td>
<td>No model call; the same trace always gets the same score.</td>
<td>A model call per scored trajectory; scores for the same trace can vary between runs.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The comparison mode sets how much variation counts as acceptable:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Strict:</strong> same calls in the same order; fits a task with one valid procedure.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unordered:</strong> same calls in any order; fits independent reads.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Subset:</strong> every agent call must appear in the reference, so unlisted tools fail. This can forbid writes in a read-only task.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Superset:</strong> every reference call must appear in the trace, and extra calls are allowed. This enforces required steps, but a wasteful trace that contains them still passes.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Several valid paths do not automatically require a judge. A richer set of references, or a hybrid rule such as a subset gate plus a judge for path quality, may be enough.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/trajectory-evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/trajectory-evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Trajectory evaluation (LangSmith)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Agents/Evaluation/Trajectory Evaluation.md" class="internal-link">Trajectory Evaluation</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering"><h4>Context Engineering</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can adding more context make answers worse instead of better?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Because a model does not use every part of a long input equally well, so extra material can bury or dilute the evidence that the answer depends on.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Position effects:</strong> in the long-context tasks evaluated in <em>Lost in the Middle</em>, some models used relevant information near the beginning or end of the input more reliably than the same information placed in the middle. The size of the effect depends on the model and task.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Dilution:</strong> irrelevant or redundant text competes with the useful evidence, so adding it can lower answer quality instead of adding information.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost:</strong> extra input tokens also add cost and can add latency, even when they do not improve the answer.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Added context is not always harmful. The aim is complete, relevant material placed deliberately, with answer quality and input cost measured on the actual workload as the context grows.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Lost in the Middle</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Latency optimization</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/Context Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Context Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can a long-running agent keep useful context within a finite window?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">By treating the context window as a working set. Each call contains the instructions, evidence and state needed for the next decision. Everything else stays outside the prompt but remains retrievable.</p>
<p dir="auto">The prompt, conversation history, tool results and space reserved for the response all draw from one finite token budget, so they are managed together:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Selection and ordering:</strong> only material relevant to the current step enters the window, and it is placed deliberately rather than replayed in full.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Trimmed tool results:</strong> tool output keeps the fields the next decision uses, and stale results that no longer matter are cleared.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Compaction:</strong> older turns are replaced by a short record of decisions, constraints and open work before history crowds out the task.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Offloading:</strong> bulky state, such as notes, files or full documents, lives outside the prompt and is reloaded by reference when needed.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Compaction trades space for possible detail loss: a summary can drop a subtle fact that later matters. Where exact recovery matters, the source material is kept outside the window instead of being trusted to the summary.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Effective context engineering for AI agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/Context Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Context Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG"><h5>RAG</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should chunking be chosen for a RAG corpus?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Chunking should be chosen from the corpus's structure, the queries it must answer and the failures that evaluation exposes. No splitter or chunk size is best for every corpus.</p>
<p dir="auto">Chunk size sets the basic trade-off:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Larger chunks</strong> keep related statements together, but they can dilute the match and spend context on irrelevant text.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Smaller chunks</strong> can match a query more precisely, but they can also separate a rule from the condition or exception that changes it.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Each chunk must also fit the embedding model's input limit. Overlap between neighboring chunks lowers the chance that a boundary cuts a statement apart, at the cost of some duplicated text.</p>
<p dir="auto">A simple rule-based splitter, such as fixed-size or recursive splitting, provides a cheap baseline. A more specialized strategy earns its extra ingestion and maintenance cost only when evaluation traces failures to the problem it addresses:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Observed failure</th>
<th>Strategy that targets it</th>
<th>Why it helps</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Tables, code blocks or clause–exception pairs are split apart</td>
<td>Structure-aware splitting</td>
<td>A format parser keeps those layout units intact.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>The right passage is found, but nearby constraints are missing from the answer</td>
<td>Parent-child retrieval</td>
<td>Small chunks are searched, and their larger surrounding section is passed to generation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Long prose without reliable headings mixes several topics in one chunk</td>
<td>Semantic splitting</td>
<td>Boundaries are placed where adjacent text stops being similar.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A change is kept only when it improves retrieval and end-to-end answers on that corpus.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Chunk large documents for vector search (Azure AI Search)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Chunking#How to Choose a Strategy" aria-label="Chunking &gt; How to Choose a Strategy" data-tooltip-position="top">Chunking: How to Choose a Strategy</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Chunking.md" class="internal-link">Chunking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does parent-child chunking change the context returned for a matching passage?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Parent-child chunking searches small child chunks but gives the generator the larger parent section that contains the match. Searching small children can keep matches precise, while generation receives surrounding text that the child alone may lack.</p>
<p dir="auto">The flow:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Ingestion splits each parent section into small child chunks and stores the parent's identifier with every child.</li>
<li dir="auto">A query is matched against the child chunks.</li>
<li dir="auto">The application maps each matched child to its parent through that identifier. This is a lookup, not another similarity search, and a parent shared by several matched children is included once.</li>
