<li dir="auto">The parent text, rather than the child alone, is assembled into the generator's context.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The parent can restore a nearby prerequisite, condition or exception that the matching child omitted, such as an exception clause that follows a retention rule. It also adds tokens. A parent that is too broad brings back the irrelevant text that small children were meant to avoid. Expansion therefore helps only when evaluation on the corpus shows better retrieval and end-to-end answers.</p>
<p dir="auto">In Azure AI Search, index projections can index child chunks with a field that links each one to its parent document. Expanding results to parent text is logic the application implements.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-how-to-define-index-projections" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-how-to-define-index-projections" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Define index projections (Azure AI Search)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Chunk large documents for vector search (Azure AI Search)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Chunking#Parent-Child Chunking" aria-label="Chunking &gt; Parent-Child Chunking" data-tooltip-position="top">Chunking: Parent-Child Chunking</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Chunking.md" class="internal-link">Chunking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a team move from recursive to structure-aware chunking?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The move is justified when evaluation repeatedly traces retrieval or answer failures to document structure that the recursive splitter breaks, and the measured gain outweighs the cost of maintaining parsers.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Recursive splitting</th>
<th>Structure-aware splitting</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How boundaries are found</td>
<td>An ordered list of separator strings is tried, such as blank lines, then newlines, then spaces. Smaller separators are used only when a piece is still too large.</td>
<td>A parser for the source format identifies headings, tables, code blocks and list items.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it keeps together</td>
<td>Paragraphs and sentences, as far as the separators match the format.</td>
<td>Logical units such as a whole table or a clause with its exception, plus metadata such as the heading path.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical failure</td>
<td>Boundaries fall wherever a separator occurs. Table rows can be separated from their header, and code blocks or clause–exception pairs can be divided.</td>
<td>A parser can misparse silently when a source changes format, and very large units still need a size limit.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>Low: rule-based, with separators configurable per format.</td>
<td>Higher: one parser per source format, plus ongoing maintenance.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A generic recursive splitter, such as LangChain's <code>RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter</code>, works on separator strings and does not parse the document format. Some failures can be fixed within recursive splitting by adding format-specific separators, or by extracting tables and code blocks as whole units first. Structure-aware splitting earns its cost when those adjustments are not enough.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/blob/master/libs/text-splitters/langchain_text_splitters/character.py" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/blob/master/libs/text-splitters/langchain_text_splitters/character.py" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">LangChain <code>RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter</code> implementation</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Chunk large documents for vector search (Azure AI Search)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Chunking#Structure-Aware Chunking" aria-label="Chunking &gt; Structure-Aware Chunking" data-tooltip-position="top">Chunking: Structure-Aware Chunking</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Chunking.md" class="internal-link">Chunking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is semantic chunking not always superior to simpler rule-based approaches?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Semantic chunking places boundaries from embedding scores and a tuned breakpoint rule. That adds ingestion cost and a setting whose behavior can shift with the model and corpus. It adds little when the document's structure already marks the topic boundaries.</p>
<p dir="auto">How a semantic splitter places boundaries:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The text is split into sentences or small groups of sentences.</li>
<li dir="auto">Each group is embedded, and the distance between neighboring groups is computed.</li>
<li dir="auto">A boundary is placed where a distance exceeds a breakpoint, such as a percentile or a number of standard deviations computed over that text's distances.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Why that is not automatically better:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost:</strong> every span needs an embedding call during ingestion, which rule-based splitters avoid.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Instability:</strong> the distribution of distances depends on the embedding model and the corpus. A breakpoint tuned in one setting can, in another, fragment text into tiny chunks or leave several topics in one chunk. It must therefore be re-evaluated after the model or corpus changes.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Redundancy:</strong> when reliable headings or markup already separate topics, a structure-aware or recursive splitter finds the same boundaries more cheaply and predictably.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Semantic splitting earns its cost for long prose that changes topic without structural markers, such as transcripts or email threads, when evaluation shows better retrieval.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain-experimental/blob/main/libs/experimental/langchain_experimental/text_splitter.py" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain-experimental/blob/main/libs/experimental/langchain_experimental/text_splitter.py" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">LangChain <code>SemanticChunker</code> implementation</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Chunk large documents for vector search (Azure AI Search)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Chunking#Semantic Chunking" aria-label="Chunking &gt; Semantic Chunking" data-tooltip-position="top">Chunking: Semantic Chunking</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Chunking.md" class="internal-link">Chunking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do offline evaluation and production monitoring work together for a RAG system?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Offline evaluation decides whether a candidate version is good enough to release. Production monitoring checks whether the released version keeps working on real traffic. Confirmed production failures are added to the offline dataset, so later releases are tested against them.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Offline evaluation</th>
<th>Production monitoring</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Data</td>
<td>A controlled, versioned dataset with relevance labels or reference answers</td>
<td>Live requests, whose query mix and source documents change over time</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Timing</td>
<td>Before release, comparing a candidate with the current baseline</td>
<td>After release, continuously</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Signals</td>
<td>Retrieval metrics against labels and answer correctness against references</td>
<td>Per-stage traces, latency, errors and cost, cheap checks on every request, and judge scores on a sample</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Blind spot</td>
<td>Query patterns and data changes that the dataset does not contain</td>
<td>Usually no reference answer, so quality scores are only as valid as the sampling and the evaluator</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The feedback loop:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">A release passes offline gates against the baseline.</li>
<li dir="auto">Monitoring flags an anomaly, such as sampled faithfulness falling for one segment or empty results rising.</li>
<li dir="auto">Traces are triaged to confirm real failures and locate the failing stage.</li>
<li dir="auto">Confirmed cases, with verified labels, join the offline dataset.</li>
<li dir="auto">The fix is evaluated offline against the expanded dataset before the next release.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Sampled quality scores need representative or stratified sampling, and a judge whose agreement with human labels is checked. Without both, monitoring can look healthy while quality falls.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/evaluation-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/evaluation-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Evaluation types (LangSmith)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Semantic conventions for generative AI systems (OpenTelemetry)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Monitoring#Sampling Bias in Quality Scoring" aria-label="Monitoring &gt; Sampling Bias in Quality Scoring" data-tooltip-position="top">Monitoring: Sampling Bias in Quality Scoring</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Monitoring#Judge Drift Without Calibration" aria-label="Monitoring &gt; Judge Drift Without Calibration" data-tooltip-position="top">Monitoring: Judge Drift Without Calibration</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Monitoring.md" class="internal-link">Monitoring</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does query translation change in a RAG retrieval pipeline, and what can it not fix?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Query translation changes only the queries sent to retrieval. A model turns the user's request into one or more retrieval inputs, such as paraphrases, a broader step-back question, sub-questions or a hypothetical answer. Each input is then searched against the existing index. Translation cannot fix problems in the corpus or in the index itself.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it can help:</strong> vocabulary mismatch, where the user and the corpus describe the same idea in different words; requests whose parts need separate searches; and questions that also need broader background. For example, “Can partners burst above limits now?” and a document titled “Partner Tier Burst Allowance” describe the same policy, and a rewrite closer to the document's wording can reach it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What it cannot fix:</strong> evidence missing from the corpus, chunks that split the needed text, a weak embedding model or a broken index. Every variant still searches the same chunks and vectors.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The work after search depends on the technique. Lists retrieved for several phrasings of one question are usually deduplicated and fused before reranking or generation. Decomposition can instead answer each sub-question from its own evidence and then synthesize the partial answers into one response. In every case, the benefit is measured against direct retrieval on the same queries.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14283" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14283" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models (Ma et al., EMNLP 2023)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2402.03367" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/html/2402.03367" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG-Fusion: a New Take on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Rackauckas, 2024)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/query_engine/sub_question_query_engine/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/query_engine/sub_question_query_engine/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Sub Question Query Engine (LlamaIndex)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Query Translation#How Each Rewrite Changes Search" aria-label="Query Translation &gt; How Each Rewrite Changes Search" data-tooltip-position="top">Query Translation: How Each Rewrite Changes Search</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Query Translation.md" class="internal-link">Query Translation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can query translation change retrieval quality, and how should that change be evaluated?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Translation can raise recall by searching wordings closer to the corpus's vocabulary. It can lower precision when a rewrite drifts from the request's entities or constraints. Its effect is measured by comparing translated retrieval with direct retrieval on the same labeled queries.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Gain:</strong> a rewrite such as “partner tier throttling policy” can match documents that use words the user did not, so relevant evidence missed by the original wording enters the results.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Loss:</strong> a rewrite can stay on topic yet change the request. When “<code>HttpClient</code> connection timeout” becomes “network timeout troubleshooting”, operating-system material can crowd out .NET-specific evidence. Fusing the result lists does not remove drift, because a document ranked highly by one bad variant can still pass the cutoff.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">How the change is evaluated:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Direct retrieval is the control, run on the same labeled queries.</li>
<li dir="auto">Results are split by query class, such as vague questions and identifier-heavy ones, because a technique can help one class and hurt another.</li>
<li dir="auto">Recall@k and Precision@k are measured at the cutoffs the pipeline actually uses. A rise in Recall@20 with a fall in Precision@5 means more relevant candidates appear within 20 results while the top five carry more noise. By itself, that result does not show what survives reranking or reaches the generator.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Two common controls limit drift: the original query stays among the searched variants, and rewrites that alter entities, identifiers, versions or other material constraints are rejected.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14283" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14283" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models (Ma et al., EMNLP 2023)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2402.03367" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/html/2402.03367" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG-Fusion: a New Take on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Rackauckas, 2024)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/ai-ml/guide/rag/rag-solution-design-and-evaluation-guide" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/ai-ml/guide/rag/rag-solution-design-and-evaluation-guide" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG solution design and evaluation guide (Azure Architecture Center)</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Query Translation.md" class="internal-link">Query Translation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a RAG system decompose a question instead of generating multiple query phrasings?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Decomposition fits a request whose parts need different evidence. Multiple phrasings fit a single, clear information need whose wording may not match the corpus.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Decomposition</th>
<th>Multi-query</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Fits when</td>
<td>Parts of the request need separate evidence, as in comparing two systems or assembling a timeline</td>
<td>One intent is clear, but the corpus may describe it in other words</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What is generated</td>
<td>Different sub-questions, each retrieving its own evidence</td>
<td>Several phrasings of the same question</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main failure</td>
<td>Sub-questions drop constraints from the original request, so retrieval returns generic evidence that synthesis cannot make specific again</td>
<td>Paraphrases drift from the intent and pull in related but wrong material</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Execution</td>
<td>Independent sub-questions can run concurrently. Multi-hop sub-questions depend on earlier answers and run in sequence.</td>
<td>Variants can run concurrently, and their result lists are merged and deduplicated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Added work</td>
<td>Generating sub-questions, one retrieval per sub-question and a synthesis step that combines the partial answers</td>
<td>Generating variants and one retrieval per variant</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Example: “How does <code>Task</code> compare to <code>ValueTask</code> for high-throughput API endpoints?” needs evidence on <code>Task</code> allocation, <code>ValueTask</code> constraints and throughput behavior, which a single passage is unlikely to contain. Decomposition fits, provided each sub-question keeps the high-throughput constraint and the synthesis step receives the original request.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/query_engine/sub_question_query_engine/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/query_engine/sub_question_query_engine/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Sub Question Query Engine (LlamaIndex)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/retrieval-augmented-generation-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/retrieval-augmented-generation-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Retrieval-augmented generation in Azure AI Search</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Query Translation.md" class="internal-link">Query Translation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What must a RAG retrieval-cache key include to keep cache hits correct?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The key must include every input that can change the ranked candidate list, so that changing any of them produces a different key. A retrieval cache stores document IDs and scores. If a result-affecting input is missing from the key, a hit returns a list computed under different conditions.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Key field</th>
<th>Failure if it is missing</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Processed query, plus the version of the canonicalization or translation that produced it</td>
<td>After query processing changes, hits can return lists produced by the old processing.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Embedding model and its configuration</td>
<td>After an upgrade, lists ranked in the old embedding space are reused.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Index or corpus version</td>
<td>Added, changed or deleted documents stay invisible to cached queries.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tenant and authorization-context hash</td>
<td>One caller receives candidates computed for another caller's permissions, which is a data leak, not just staleness.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Filters, top-k and retriever or reranker configuration</td>
<td>A request with different settings receives a list built for other settings.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The query part of the key can be processed text or embedding bytes. Text is inspectable and stays stable while its canonicalization is versioned. Embedding bytes are deterministic only while the encoder, model and configuration are pinned. Either works when every other result-changing input is also in the key.</p>
<p dir="auto">For protected content, a complete key is necessary but not sufficient. A read still checks the caller's current access, because permissions can change after an entry is stored.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Cache-Aside pattern (Azure Architecture Center)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/architecture/cache-aside-azure-managed-redis-postgresql" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/architecture/cache-aside-azure-managed-redis-postgresql" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Cache-aside with Azure Managed Redis and PostgreSQL (Azure Architecture Center)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="RAG Caching#Retrieval Cache" aria-label="RAG Caching &gt; Retrieval Cache" data-tooltip-position="top">RAG Caching: Retrieval Cache</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG Caching.md" class="internal-link">RAG Caching</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do caches help a RAG pipeline, and what makes a cache hit safe?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each cache layer skips a different expensive step: an embedding cache skips the embedding call, a retrieval cache skips search and reranking, and a response cache skips generation. A hit is safe only when three conditions hold: the key or a validation check covers every input that could change that stage's result, the caller is currently allowed to see the value, and the entry is fresh enough for its sources.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Layer</th>
<th>Stores</th>
<th>Work skipped on a hit</th>
<th>Key must cover</th>
<th>Main risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Embedding</td>
<td>The vector for a processed text</td>
<td>The embedding call, at ingestion or query time</td>
<td>Text hash, embedding model, dimensions and preprocessing version</td>
<td>Vectors from an old model mixed with new ones, which makes similarity scores meaningless</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Retrieval</td>
<td>Ranked document IDs and scores</td>
<td>Vector search and reranking</td>
<td>Processed query, index version, filters, top-k, retriever settings, tenant and authorization context</td>
<td>Stale lists after an index update, or results computed for another tenant</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Response</td>
<td>The final answer</td>
<td>Generation</td>
<td>The retrieval inputs plus prompt template, selected evidence, generation model and settings, and any conversation state that changes meaning</td>
<td>Answers grounded in outdated evidence, or served to a caller who may not see that evidence</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Freshness follows the sources. A time-to-live bounds staleness, and known source or permission changes invalidate entries before it expires. Fast-changing evidence can justify caching embeddings and retrieval results while not caching final answers.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Cache-Aside pattern (Azure Architecture Center)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="RAG Caching#Flow" aria-label="RAG Caching &gt; Flow" data-tooltip-position="top">RAG Caching: Flow</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG Caching.md" class="internal-link">RAG Caching</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What kind of RAG question can justify adding a knowledge graph to vector retrieval?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A knowledge graph can be justified when the answer depends on explicit relationships between entities, or on synthesis across much of a corpus, rather than on a few passages that resemble the question. A question such as <em>What are the main themes across these documents?</em> is an example: no small set of similar chunks contains its answer.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Vector retrieval</strong> returns the top-k chunks closest to the query. That suits direct fact lookup, where one or a few passages hold the answer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>GraphRAG</strong> uses a language model to extract entities and relationships into a graph, groups closely related entities into communities and pre-generates a summary of each community. Corpus-wide questions can then be answered from those summaries instead of from isolated chunks. Questions about dependencies or impact can follow explicit edges between entities.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The graph adds model-driven extraction, indexing and maintenance cost, and extraction or linking errors become wrong edges. Microsoft Research evaluated GraphRAG on corpus-wide, query-focused summarization, so its benefit for other question types has to be measured. The decision therefore rests on a comparison with a vector-retrieval baseline on representative questions.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/from-local-to-global-a-graph-rag-approach-to-query-focused-summarization/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/from-local-to-global-a-graph-rag-approach-to-query-focused-summarization/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization (Microsoft Research)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG Patterns.md" class="internal-link">RAG Patterns</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers a request in two steps. It first retrieves relevant evidence from an external corpus, then gives that evidence to a language model, which generates an answer grounded in it. Knowledge therefore comes from the corpus at request time, not only from what the model learned in its weights.</p>
<p dir="auto">A typical request passes through these stages:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Query processing:</strong> the question is used as is or rewritten into a better search query.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retrieval:</strong> a search over an index of document chunks returns candidate passages. The search can use vector similarity, keywords or both.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Reranking (optional):</strong> a second stage reorders the candidates so the most relevant come first.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Context assembly:</strong> the best passages are placed into the prompt within a token budget.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generation:</strong> the model answers from that context, ideally citing the passages it used.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Compared with relying on the model's weights alone, RAG changes two things. Knowledge can be updated by changing the corpus and its index instead of retraining, and an answer can point back to its sources. Each stage also limits the next: generation cannot use evidence that retrieval never returned.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (Lewis et al.)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG.md" class="internal-link">RAG</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should an advanced RAG stage, such as reranking or query rewriting, be introduced and evaluated?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An advanced stage is introduced as a controlled experiment. It targets a specific failure measured on the current pipeline, and it stays only if it beats that baseline by enough to justify its added latency, cost and maintenance.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Baseline:</strong> the current pipeline is measured on representative cases, and the failure the new stage should fix is identified. An example is relevant evidence ranked too low to reach the prompt.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Isolated change:</strong> where practical, only that stage changes. A broad change to several stages can hide which component helped and which one regressed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Same comparison:</strong> baseline and candidate run on the same cases. They are measured on the targeted metric, on end-to-end answer quality and on operational measures such as p95 latency and cost per query.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Decision:</strong> the stage is kept only when its quality gain outweighs its latency, cost and maintenance burden. Otherwise the simpler pipeline remains.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Changing exactly one thing is not always feasible. A feature flag, a controlled rollout or an ablation that removes one component at a time can still attribute an effect to a specific stage.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Rules of Machine Learning (Google)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG.md" class="internal-link">RAG</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When a RAG answer is wrong, how can the failing pipeline stage be located?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The diagnosis starts from the exact context and request the model received for that answer. Whether the needed evidence was there decides which part of the pipeline to examine, and tracing backward from there finds the stage that failed.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Actual model input:</strong> the logged prompt and assembled context for the failing request are inspected, rather than assumptions about what retrieval probably returned.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Evidence missing or unsuitable:</strong> the fault is upstream of generation. Tracing back through context assembly, ranking, filtering, retrieval and query transformation shows where the evidence was lost. It may have been retrieved but cut by the final top-k, removed by a filter, or never retrieved because a rewritten query changed the intent.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Evidence present but misused:</strong> the relevant evidence reached the model, but the answer ignored, contradicted or went beyond it. That points to generation: the prompt, the model or its settings.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Measurement itself:</strong> citation handling and the reference answer or evaluator are checked too, because a broken citation mapping or a wrong label can make an answer look wrong.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Component metrics, such as retrieval relevance and groundedness, narrow the hypotheses. End-to-end evaluation then confirms whether a fix improves the task outcome.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG evaluators (Microsoft Foundry)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG.md" class="internal-link">RAG</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does a RAG pipeline retrieve candidates first and then rerank them with a cross-encoder?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The two stages split the work between a fast scorer that can cover the whole corpus and a slower, finer-grained scorer that can only afford a short list. First-stage retrieval cheaply finds candidates across the corpus. A cross-encoder then rescores only those candidates; running it over every document would be far too slow.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Bi-encoder (first-stage retrieval)</th>
<th>Cross-encoder (reranker)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How it scores</td>
<td>Embeds the query and each document separately. Document vectors are computed once at indexing time and compared with one query vector</td>
<td>Reads the query and one candidate together in a single model pass and outputs a relevance score</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Relevance judgment</td>
<td>Coarser, because query and document are encoded without seeing each other</td>
<td>Can be finer, because attention spans both texts, so a qualifier or negation in the query can change the score. This often ranks better, but the gain depends on the model and the domain</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost per query</td>
<td>One query encoding plus a fast index search</td>
<td>One model inference per candidate</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Role</td>
<td>Recall: getting the relevant evidence into a candidate list, often tens of items</td>
<td>Precision: putting the best candidates into the small top-k that reaches the prompt</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Keyword search such as BM25 can also fill the first-stage role. Whatever the first stage is, the reranker only reorders what it returned: if the relevant document is not among the candidates, no reranker can recover it. Because the ranking gain is not guaranteed, it is confirmed on domain queries against the first-stage order before the reranker is adopted.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Retrieve &amp; Re-Rank (Sentence Transformers)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Re-ranking.md" class="internal-link">Re-ranking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can a reranker improve retrieval metrics without improving the generated answer?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A retrieval metric can improve in ranking positions that never reach the generator. Even when better evidence does reach the generator, the model still has to use it correctly.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Outside the final cutoff:</strong> a ranking metric is often computed over more results than the pipeline puts into the prompt. In this example, only the top 5 reranked chunks are assembled. Moving a relevant chunk from position 15 to position 8 raises a rank-sensitive metric such as nDCG@20, but the model input stays identical.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generation-side limits:</strong> retrieval and generation fail independently. If the needed evidence was already in the prompt, reordering it may not change the answer. If the model ignores, misreads or contradicts the evidence, better retrieval does not fix that.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Finding where the gain lands therefore requires following the same queries through each stage. The stages are candidate Recall@N before reranking, the ranking after reranking at the cutoff actually used, and the assembled context. Answer quality is then evaluated on representative queries. A retrieval metric gain alone does not establish a user-visible benefit.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Retrieve &amp; Re-Rank (Sentence Transformers)</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Optimizing LLM accuracy (OpenAI)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Re-ranking.md" class="internal-link">Re-ranking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When can reranking worsen retrieval quality, and when can it fail to improve it?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A reranker trained on short web passages may misjudge long technical documents or unfamiliar terminology. It can then worsen results by pushing relevant evidence from inside the first-stage top-k to below that cutoff. A small candidate set or low first-stage recall causes a different failure. A reranker only reorders the candidates it receives, so it cannot add relevant evidence that is missing from them.</p>
<p dir="auto">Domain queries tell these cases apart when <a class="internal-link" href="Monitoring#Retrieval Quality Metrics" aria-label="Monitoring &gt; Retrieval Quality Metrics" data-tooltip-position="top">recall and precision</a> are measured at matched points:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Missing candidates:</strong> low candidate Recall@N before reranking means the evidence was absent before reranking began. That is a first-stage limit.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Demotion:</strong> the comparison cuts the first-stage order and the reranked order at the same final k. Demotion means relevant evidence was inside the first-stage top-k but falls outside the reranked top-k. A net drop in Recall@k between the two orders signals it in aggregate. A low absolute Precision@k does not show demotion. With one relevant document ranked first in both orders, Recall@N and Recall@10 are both 1.0, yet Precision@10 is only 0.1, and nothing was demoted.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No promotion into top-k:</strong> when relevant candidates fall outside top-k in both orders, their ranks in the two orders show whether reranking helped. A move from rank 50 to rank 11 at k = 10 is a partial improvement that still misses the final cutoff. An unchanged or worse rank means the reranker did not help that evidence. Exclusion in both orders does not by itself show that k is too small. Cutoff capacity matters only when the query needs more distinct relevant pieces than k can hold.</li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Re-ranking.md" class="internal-link">Re-ranking</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why does hybrid retrieval combine keyword search and vector search?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Hybrid retrieval combines them because they fail in complementary ways. Keyword search matches the exact terms in a query, while vector search matches meaning even when the wording differs. Running both covers queries that either one alone would miss.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Keyword search, such as BM25</th>
<th>Vector search</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it matches</td>
<td>Documents that share the query's terms, with rarer terms counting more</td>
<td>Documents whose embeddings are close to the query's embedding, so related meanings match</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Strong on</td>
<td>Exact identifiers such as error codes, product names and version numbers</td>
<td>Paraphrases and natural-language questions worded differently from the source</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Weak on</td>
<td>Synonyms and rephrasing with no word overlap, such as <em>credential validation error</em> for <em>authentication failure</em></td>
<td>Exact tokens, which can blur inside the embedding and surface topically similar but wrong chunks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it needs</td>
<td>A lexical (inverted) index</td>
<td>An embedding model and a vector index</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">In a hybrid search, both queries run in parallel and their ranked lists are merged, commonly with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). RRF scores documents by their rank positions, so the two incompatible score scales never need to be normalized. For a query about <em>error 429 behavior for the partner tier</em>, keyword search can catch <code>429</code> while vector search finds rate-limiting passages phrased differently.</p>
<p dir="auto">Hybrid is a common starting point rather than a guaranteed improvement over either mode alone.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hybrid search overview (Azure AI Search)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Retrieval.md" class="internal-link">Retrieval</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When can hybrid retrieval perform worse than single-mode retrieval?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Hybrid retrieval can perform worse when one retrieval path is much weaker on a particular corpus and query mix. Fusing its results pulls poor candidates into the top results. There they displace good results that the stronger path would have returned on its own.</p>
<p dir="auto">The mechanism:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Keyword search, such as BM25, and vector search run in parallel for the same query.</li>
<li dir="auto">Their ranked lists are merged, commonly with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which scores each document from its rank positions rather than from raw scores.</li>
<li dir="auto">Standard RRF gives each list equal influence. For documents that appear in only one list, rank 1 in the weak list scores the same as rank 1 in the strong list, and higher than rank 3 in the strong list.</li>
<li dir="auto">With a small final cutoff, those weak candidates push relevant results out.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Whether this happens depends on the workload. In a homogeneous corpus where one mode clearly dominates, the other mode has little useful to add. A large top-k can also carry weak tail candidates into the context when no reranking or deduplication follows.</p>
<p dir="auto">Hybrid is therefore justified by measurement rather than assumed. Keyword-only, vector-only and hybrid retrieval are compared on representative queries, using the retrieval or end-to-end metric that matches the product goal. When hybrid loses, the fusion can be weighted toward the stronger path, or the extra path can be dropped.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hybrid search overview (Azure AI Search)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Retrieval.md" class="internal-link">Retrieval</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What role does a vector database play in a RAG system?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An embedding model creates numeric representations; a vector database or search index stores and indexes them, then retrieves nearby vectors for a query. The service can return associated IDs or fields and apply metadata filters; application code resolves the results to source text and assembles prompt context. Vector similarity finds candidates, but does not prove relevance or replace an authorization check. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Vector search overview</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Vector Databases.md" class="internal-link">Vector Databases</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why do vector indexes use approximate nearest-neighbor search instead of exact search?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Exact search must compare the query with every stored vector, so its work grows with the size of the collection. An approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index examines only a promising subset of vectors. This often cuts query work sharply, at the cost of sometimes missing true nearest neighbors.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Exact (flat) search:</strong> one distance computation per stored vector, about N × d arithmetic for N vectors of dimension d. The results are exact, and the cost is acceptable for small collections.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>ANN search:</strong> the index structure limits which vectors are compared. An IVF index clusters the vectors and searches only the clusters nearest the query. An HNSW index walks a proximity graph toward closer neighbors. Parameters such as <code>nprobe</code> for IVF or <code>efSearch</code> for HNSW control how much is examined, trading latency for recall.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Missed neighbors raise no error. Recall is therefore measured against exact-search results as ground truth, on realistic queries and filters, and the index settings are chosen to meet both the recall and the latency targets. The N × d figure describes arithmetic work, not a guaranteed wall-clock time.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Faiss indexes (Faiss wiki)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Vector Databases.md" class="internal-link">Vector Databases</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation"><h6>Evaluation</h6><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do Recall@k, Precision@k, HitRate@k, MRR and nDCG@k differ as retrieval metrics?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">All five compare a ranked result list with labeled relevant documents, but each rewards something different: coverage, low noise, any success, an early first hit or a well-ordered ranking.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>What it measures</th>
<th>Effect of rank within the top k</th>
<th>What it misses</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Recall@k</td>
<td>Share of a query's relevant documents that appear in the top k</td>
<td>None</td>
<td>How high the relevant documents rank and how much noise surrounds them</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Precision@k</td>
<td>Share of the top k results that are relevant</td>
<td>None</td>
<td>Relevant documents that were never retrieved</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>HitRate@k</td>
<td>Share of queries with at least one relevant result in the top k</td>
<td>None</td>
<td>Every missing document after the first hit</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>MRR</td>
<td>Mean, across queries, of <code>1 / rank</code> for the first relevant result, counting <code>0</code> when none is found</td>
<td>Strong, but only for the first hit</td>
<td>Everything after the first relevant result</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>nDCG@k</td>
<td>Sum of the relevance grades in the top k, each discounted by its position, divided by that sum for the ideal ordering</td>
<td>Applies across the whole top k</td>
<td>Whether a low score comes from missing documents or from poor ordering</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Example: a query has four known relevant documents, and its top five results are <code>[irrelevant, relevant, relevant, irrelevant, relevant]</code>.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Recall@5 is <code>3/4 = 0.75</code>, because three of the four relevant documents appear.</li>
<li dir="auto">Precision@5 is <code>3/5 = 0.6</code>, because three of the five results are relevant.</li>
<li dir="auto">The query counts as a hit for HitRate@5.</li>
<li dir="auto">Its reciprocal rank is <code>1/2 = 0.5</code>, because the first relevant result is at rank 2.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Recall sets a ceiling for generation, because the generator cannot use evidence it never receives. Precision matters when context space or token cost is tight. MRR fits a generator that reads only the top one or two chunks. nDCG@k fits a generator that uses all k chunks and benefits from seeing the strongest evidence first.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG evaluators and document retrieval metrics (Microsoft Foundry)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Monitoring#Retrieval Quality Metrics" aria-label="Monitoring &gt; Retrieval Quality Metrics" data-tooltip-position="top">Monitoring: Retrieval Quality Metrics</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Evaluation Metrics.md" class="internal-link">Evaluation Metrics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can aggregate retrieval metrics hide regressions, and when is a segment drop actionable?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An aggregate metric averages over all queries, so a gain on large, healthy segments can outweigh a serious loss on a small one. A segment drop is actionable when it matters to that segment's users and is too large to explain as sampling noise.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example: a change raises overall Recall@5 by 2%, while recall for one tenant's query cluster falls by 15%. A gate on the global average passes, yet that tenant now receives worse evidence.</p>
<p dir="auto">Slicing results by dimensions that change the retrieval problem, such as tenant, language, query class or document source, exposes such losses. Slicing has its own risk. A small segment has few labeled queries, so its score depends heavily on which queries happen to be in the set. A segment drop is credible and actionable when:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">the segment has enough labeled queries, representative of its real traffic, for its score to be meaningful;</li>
<li dir="auto">the drop exceeds the uncertainty that comes from that limited query sample, for example by falling outside a confidence interval computed over the segment's queries;</li>
<li dir="auto">it crosses a threshold set in advance from the product's risk for that segment.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Rerunning the same evaluation on the same queries does not satisfy the second condition. Repeated runs show whether scores stay stable when retrieval or judging is nondeterministic. They add no queries, and they do not make the existing queries more representative.</p>
<p dir="auto">A material, credible segment regression remains a regression even when the global average improves.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Rules of Machine Learning (Google)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Evaluation Metrics#Aggregate Metrics Mask Segment Regressions" aria-label="Evaluation Metrics &gt; Aggregate Metrics Mask Segment Regressions" data-tooltip-position="top">Evaluation Metrics: Aggregate Metrics Mask Segment Regressions</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Evaluation Metrics.md" class="internal-link">Evaluation Metrics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In a RAGAS evaluation, what does high Faithfulness with low Context Recall suggest, and what should be checked first?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">It suggests that the answer stays consistent with the context it received, but that context lacks evidence the reference answer needs. The first check is the measurement itself: the reference answer, the captured context and the metric configuration. Retrieval is investigated once those are confirmed sound.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Faithfulness:</strong> the share of claims in the response that the supplied context supports. It does not show whether that context was complete.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Context Recall:</strong> the share of claims in the reference answer that the retrieved context supports. It requires a reference and measures coverage of the evidence an answer needs.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Together, the scores fit a generator that stays within limited evidence, which can produce a grounded but incomplete answer.</p>
<p dir="auto">The order of investigation:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Measurement:</strong> the reference answer is correct, the scored context is what the generator actually received, and the metric variant, judge model and inputs are as intended. A flawed reference or a logging gap can produce the same pattern.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retrieval path:</strong> missing or unindexed documents, metadata filters, the candidate cutoff and context assembly.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Generation:</strong> changed only after the retrieval path is ruled out, because a prompt cannot make use of evidence that never arrived.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Neither score alone proves the cause. The combination is a hypothesis to test on representative samples.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Context Recall (Ragas)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.2.5/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.2.5/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Faithfulness (Ragas v0.2.5)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Evaluation Metrics#Diagnostic Combinations" aria-label="Evaluation Metrics &gt; Diagnostic Combinations" data-tooltip-position="top">Evaluation Metrics: Diagnostic Combinations</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Evaluation Metrics.md" class="internal-link">Evaluation Metrics</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What do retrieval, response, and end-to-end evaluations each show about a RAG system?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each evaluation answers a different question, so separate results show where a RAG system failed rather than only that it failed.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Evaluation</th>
<th>Question it answers</th>
<th>A failure points toward</th>
<th>What it cannot show</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Retrieval</td>
<td>Was relevant evidence found, ranked well and selected for the context?</td>
<td>Indexing, chunking, query handling, search or ranking</td>
<td>Whether the answer then used good evidence correctly</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Response</td>
<td>Given the supplied evidence, is the answer grounded in it, relevant to the question and, when a reference exists, correct?</td>
<td>The prompt or the generator's use of the evidence</td>
<td>Whether better evidence existed and was missed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>End-to-end</td>
<td>Did the complete system meet the task's outcome criteria?</td>
<td>A user-visible miss somewhere in the pipeline</td>
<td>Which stage caused the miss</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Combined, the results localize a likely cause. A grounded answer built on poor or incomplete context points upstream to retrieval. Good context paired with a wrong answer points to generation.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example: a support bot retrieves the correct policy but misreads its date constraint. Retrieval passes and the response check fails, so more search tuning cannot fix that answer.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG evaluators (Microsoft Foundry)</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Evaluation.md" class="internal-link">Evaluation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which evaluation concerns are specific to RAG, and which can reuse general LLM evaluation methods?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">RAG adds retrieval to evaluation: whether relevant evidence was found, ranked well and supplied in sufficient quantity. Retrieval metrics that score against labeled relevance judgments need relevance labels that other LLM tasks do not. Reference-free retrieval evaluation does not use such labels. Answer-quality checks and the evaluation methods themselves are largely reusable.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Specific to RAG</th>
<th>Reusable from general LLM evaluation</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What is measured</td>
<td>Retrieval relevance, ranking quality and whether the context covers the evidence an answer needs</td>
<td>Correctness, relevance to the question, safety and format. Groundedness also applies to any answer constrained by supplied text, such as a summary of a given document.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ground truth</td>
<td>For label-based retrieval metrics, relevance labels per query, which must allow several acceptable chunks or require a set of complementary ones</td>
<td>Reference answers and rubrics, built as for any task</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Methods</td>
<td>Ranked-retrieval metrics, such as Recall@k or nDCG, over those labels</td>
<td>Golden datasets, deterministic checks, LLM judges, human review and online evaluation of production traces</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Any evaluator must match the claim being measured. Its limits need checking, as do any labels it uses. A judge reused from another task is not automatically valid for a new one.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/built-in-evaluators" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/built-in-evaluators" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Built-in evaluators (Microsoft Foundry)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://aclanthology.org/2024.eacl-demo.16.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://aclanthology.org/2024.eacl-demo.16.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (EACL 2024)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/evaluation-types" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/evaluation-types" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Evaluation types (LangSmith)</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Evaluation.md" class="internal-link">Evaluation</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should retrieval metrics and cutoffs be chosen when a query has several relevant chunks?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The metric depends on how the relevant chunks contribute to the answer, and the cutoff must match what each pipeline stage actually passes on.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Relevance shape</th>
<th>Success means</th>
<th>Fitting metric</th>
<th>Misleading metric</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Substitutable: any one chunk answers, as with duplicated policy text</td>
<td>At least one valid chunk appears, ideally early</td>
<td>HitRate@k, plus MRR when the first relevant rank matters</td>
