<td>Strict Recall@k, which penalizes missing copies the generator never needed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Complementary: the answer needs the whole set, as in a comparison</td>
<td>Every required chunk appears</td>
<td>Recall@k or RAGAS Context Recall</td>
<td>HitRate@k, which passes after the first hit and hides the missing pieces</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Graded: some chunks are more useful than others</td>
<td>The most useful chunks rank highest</td>
<td>nDCG@k with graded labels, such as <code>2</code> for direct evidence, <code>1</code> for support and <code>0</code> for irrelevant</td>
<td>Binary recall or precision, which discard the grades</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Example: “How do plans A and B differ on refunds?” needs one policy chunk per plan. A result containing only plan A has <code>HitRate@5 = 1</code> but complementary recall of <code>1/2</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Cutoffs:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The final k equals the number of chunks the generator receives. A larger k credits evidence that never reaches the model.</li>
<li dir="auto">For complementary evidence, k must be at least the size of the required set. Otherwise recall cannot reach <code>1.0</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto">In a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline, first-stage Recall@N shows whether the evidence entered the candidate set, and the final top-k shows what reaches generation. Either measurement alone can hide a loss at the other stage.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators?view=foundry" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAG evaluators and document retrieval metrics (Microsoft Foundry)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Retrieve &amp; Re-Rank (Sentence Transformers)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Context Recall (Ragas)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Retrieval Evaluation Sets#When One Query Has Several Relevant Chunks" aria-label="Retrieval Evaluation Sets &gt; When One Query Has Several Relevant Chunks" data-tooltip-position="top">Retrieval Evaluation Sets: When One Query Has Several Relevant Chunks</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Retrieval Evaluation Sets.md" class="internal-link">Retrieval Evaluation Sets</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can chunk-generated questions produce misleading retrieval evaluation labels?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A question generated from one chunk is labeled with only that chunk as relevant. That label can miss other valid answers, and the question can be easier to retrieve than real user queries.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Missing positives (false negatives):</strong> a duplicate, an overview section or another passage may answer the question equally well. If it is not labeled, a retriever that returns it is scored as wrong, and comparisons between retrievers can be distorted.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Lexical leakage:</strong> the question may copy distinctive phrases from its source chunk. Exact-term overlap then makes keyword retrieval look stronger than it would on real queries.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Both are risks to check, not certainties. Common controls:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">A second retrieval pass runs each generated question, and the top candidates are judged. Other valid chunks are added to the labels, or questions that stay ambiguous are dropped.</li>
<li dir="auto">Generation prompts ask for paraphrased, realistically incomplete wording, and the token overlap between each question and its source chunk is inspected.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Sources:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/test_data_generation/rag/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/test_data_generation/rag/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Test data generation (Ragas)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.3.1/getstarted/rag_testset_generation/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.3.1/getstarted/rag_testset_generation/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Generate a synthetic test set for RAG (Ragas v0.3.1)</a></li>
<li dir="auto"><a class="internal-link" href="Retrieval Evaluation Sets#How Synthetic Questions Distort Labels" aria-label="Retrieval Evaluation Sets &gt; How Synthetic Questions Distort Labels" data-tooltip-position="top">Retrieval Evaluation Sets: How Synthetic Questions Distort Labels</a></li>
</ul>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/Evaluation/Retrieval Evaluation Sets.md" class="internal-link">Retrieval Evaluation Sets</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Evaluation"><h4>Evaluation</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a team add human-labeled evaluation cases instead of relying only on synthetic generation?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Human-labeled cases become necessary when synthetic cases can no longer be trusted to represent the workload or to label it correctly. That happens when correctness depends on expert judgment, when failures are costly, or when production inputs differ from the generated ones.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What synthetic generation does well:</strong> a model writes plausible requests from source material with known provenance. Coverage and a working evaluation harness therefore arrive quickly and cheaply.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Where it falls short:</strong> generated cases share the generator's phrasing and preferred difficulty, so ambiguous, messy or adversarial real inputs are under-represented. Generated labels can also miss subtle domain distinctions.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What human labels add:</strong> reviewed cases ground the evaluation in real inputs and expert judgment. They also show whether synthetic labels and automated judges agree with people. ARES, for example, pairs synthetic training data with a small human-annotated set that corrects its automated estimates.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A practical evaluation set often combines synthetic breadth, human-reviewed cases and regression cases taken from real failures. The balance depends on the task's risk and on how closely synthetic cases match production traffic.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09476" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09476" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems (arXiv)</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Evaluation best practices (OpenAI)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Evaluation/Building an Evaluation Set.md" class="internal-link">Building an Evaluation Set</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which deterministic checks should run before and after a tool-using agent calls a tool?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Before a tool runs, deterministic checks confirm that the caller is allowed to perform the requested action and validate the arguments against the tool's contract. After the call, they validate any returned data against the schema the next step expects.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Before execution:</strong> a permission or allowlist rule rejects an action the caller may not take. Argument validation rejects missing, malformed or out-of-range inputs. These checks must come first because later validation cannot undo a side effect: an agent can call <code>delete_record</code>, receive a success result and still return perfectly valid JSON.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>After execution:</strong> result validation stops malformed or unexpected data from reaching the next step.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A strict function schema constrains the shape of arguments. Schema validity neither authorizes the action nor shows that it was the right action. A schema-valid request can still choose the wrong permitted action, such as <code>search</code> when the case required <code>escalate</code>. The product's risks determine which further checks are needed and whether a failure is rejected outright or routed to review.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI: Function calling</a> · <a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP: LLM06 Excessive Agency</a> · <a href="https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">JSON Schema Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Evaluation/Deterministic Checks.md" class="internal-link">Deterministic Checks</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does an LLM judge fit better than a deterministic check?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An LLM judge fits when acceptance depends on meaning or quality that cannot be written as an exact rule, such as whether an answer is correct for the case, grounded in its sources, relevant or clear. A deterministic check fits any property that can be stated exactly, such as schema validity, an allowed action or a length limit. For those properties it remains the better tool even when a judge is available.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Deterministic check</th>
<th>LLM judge</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What it can decide</td>
<td>Exactly stated properties such as format, structure, allowed actions and hard policy rules</td>
<td>Open-ended qualities that a rubric can describe but code cannot fully specify</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Repeatability</td>
<td>The same rule and input always give the same result</td>
<td>Verdicts can change with the judge model, prompt and sampling settings</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cost</td>
<td>Local parsing or scanning</td>
<td>A model call for every judgment</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How it fails</td>
<td>Exact for schemas and allowlists; heuristic scanners such as PII detectors can misclassify</td>
<td>It can misread the rubric or the answer, or favor irrelevant features such as length</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The two approaches combine. Deterministic checks run first, so a malformed output or a forbidden action fails immediately without the cost of a judge call. A good semantic score cannot rescue a failed hard rule. The judge then evaluates the remaining semantic criteria, and its verdicts are trusted only after calibration against human labels.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI: Evals guide</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Zheng et al.: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena</a> · <a href="https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">JSON Schema Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Evaluation/LLM-as-a-Judge.md" class="internal-link">LLM-as-a-Judge</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What evidence supports trusting an LLM judge's verdicts?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An LLM judge earns trust through measured agreement with human judgment on representative cases. It also needs tests showing that its verdicts do not depend on irrelevant features such as answer order. This evidence supports the judge's reliability; it does not prove that the rubric measures the right thing.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Agreement with human labels:</strong> the judge scores a fixed set of cases that humans have already labeled, and its agreement with those labels is measured. Disagreements are inspected because they reveal whether the rubric is ambiguous, the reference is incomplete or the judge is biased.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Order-swap consistency:</strong> in pairwise comparison, each pair is judged twice, once in each order. A consistent judge prefers the same underlying answer both times, so its A/B label switches along with the answers. A judge that keeps choosing the same position instead follows position rather than content, which is position bias. A pair whose preferred answer changes with the order is treated as a tie or sent to human review.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Bias probes:</strong> calibration cases set concise correct answers beside padded or repetitive ones to expose verbosity bias. They also include outputs from the judge's own model family to expose self-preference.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Recalibration after changes:</strong> the judge model, prompt, rubric and sampling settings together define the measurement. A change to any of them can make scores stricter or looser, so the calibration set is rerun before new scores are compared with old ones.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">High agreement shows only that the judge matches the labelers on those cases. A judge that consistently applies a flawed rubric is stable but still measures the wrong thing.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Zheng et al.: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI: Evals guide</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Evaluation/LLM-as-a-Judge.md" class="internal-link">LLM-as-a-Judge</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering"><h4>Harness Engineering</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do context, harness, and loop engineering differ in what they control?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The three disciplines own different decisions about the same agent run. Context engineering decides what the model sees. Harness engineering decides what the model's proposed actions can reach and do. Loop engineering decides whether and how the work continues across turns.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Discipline</th>
<th>Decision it owns</th>
<th>Typical controls</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Context engineering</td>
<td>Which information the model receives on each call</td>
<td>Selecting and compacting instructions, retrieved evidence, history and tool results</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Harness engineering</td>
<td>What the runtime allows a proposed action to do once the model emits it</td>
<td>Which tools exist, their permissions and credentials, call validation, sandboxing and approval gates</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Loop engineering</td>
<td>Whether another turn happens and when the run stops</td>
<td>Progress and verification checks, iteration and cost budgets, and termination</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The boundaries touch. Tool schemas take up context and tool results feed later turns, so context engineering decides how much of them the model sees. Whether a tool such as <code>delete_branch</code> exists at all, and which policy approves its use, remains a harness decision.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Harness Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Harness Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a tool remain an in-process function instead of being exposed through an MCP server?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A tool should stay an in-process function when only one application uses it, especially when it works directly on that application's private state or business logic. An MCP server is worth its extra moving parts when several compatible clients need the same capability, managed and secured separately from any one application.</p>
<p dir="auto">The choice concerns where the tool lives, not how the model calls it. With function calling, the model returns a structured request and the application executes it. MCP is a client/server protocol through which a server advertises tools and other capabilities to any compatible client. A host can discover an MCP tool and present it to its model as a function definition. That translation is done by the host or its SDK, not by function calling itself.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>In-process function tool</th>
<th>Tool behind an MCP server</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Reuse</td>
<td>Belongs to one application; other applications reuse it only through shared code or services</td>
<td>Any compatible MCP client can discover and call it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Application state</td>
<td>Reads the application's in-memory state directly</td>
<td>Cannot see the host application's memory; needed context arrives in each request, for example as an explicit handle that the server must authorize</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Runtime cost</td>
<td>A local method call</td>
<td>A separate process or network hop, plus deployment and lifecycle for the server</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Trust</td>
<td>Runs inside the application's own security context</td>
<td>Runs as a separate server that each host must configure and trust</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI: Function calling</a> · <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MCP specification 2026-07-28: Tools</a> · <a href="https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MCP 2026-07-28 update</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Model Context Protocol.md" class="internal-link">Model Context Protocol</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which security checks must an MCP server still perform after HTTP authorization admits a caller?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">HTTP authorization admits a caller only as far as its access token allows: the token must be issued for this MCP server and carry the scopes the request requires. The server still decides, in its own code, whether that caller may perform the operation on the specific object and tenant involved. It also validates every tool input before using it.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Covered by MCP authorization for HTTP-based transports:</strong> the server accepts only an OAuth access token issued for itself as the intended audience, and it can require particular scopes, such as a write scope for a tool that changes data. Audience and scopes decide who may reach the server and which kinds of operation the token permits.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Left to application-defined authorization:</strong> whether this caller may act on this particular object or tenant, such as deleting a specific record or reading another tenant's data. A write scope permits writing in general but does not say which records. The server also validates tool arguments, rate-limits tool calls and sanitizes tool output.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Tool names, descriptions and results are text placed in the model's context. They can influence what the model requests, but they enforce nothing, so permission checks belong in server code.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MCP specification 2026-07-28: Authorization</a> · <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">MCP specification 2026-07-28: Tools</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Model Context Protocol.md" class="internal-link">Model Context Protocol</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Tooling"><h5>Tooling</h5><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why use path-specific instruction files for coding agents, and what must be checked before relying on them?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Path-specific instruction files apply guidance only to files whose path matches a pattern. An agent working on those files receives the local constraints it needs, while guidance for unrelated parts of the repository stays out of its context. Before relying on them, the selected agent's documented rules for loading, precedence and conflict handling must be checked, because those rules are tool-specific.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Example:</strong> in GitHub Copilot CLI, a path-specific file declares an <code>applyTo</code> pattern. When the agent works on a matching file, those instructions are combined with the repository-wide instructions.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Precedence:</strong> GitHub's documentation describes this combination but does not define a general precedence order for conflicting instructions. If two files name different test commands, the outcome depends on runtime behavior rather than on a documented rule.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Maintainability rule:</strong> local files written as refinements of the root guidance, rather than reversals, do not depend on how a runtime resolves conflicts. This is a maintenance discipline, not a portable precedence guarantee.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/add-custom-instructions" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/add-custom-instructions" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GitHub Copilot CLI custom instructions</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Tooling/Agent Instructions.md" class="internal-link">Agent Instructions</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What controls reduce risk when a coding agent can change a repository?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The main controls are a bounded task and budget, restricted permissions, runtime-enforced approval or denial of consequential actions, and CI plus review of the resulting change. They work because the runtime and delivery process enforce them; instructions alone depend on the model complying.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Control</th>
<th>What it does</th>
<th>Risk it reduces</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Narrow task, limited tools, step or iteration budget</td>
<td>Restricts what the agent attempts and how long it can keep retrying</td>
<td>Broad diffs that are hard to review, and costly retry loops that repeat the same failure</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sandbox and permissions</td>
<td>Limits filesystem, network and command access, where the platform provides these controls</td>
<td>Actions outside the intended workspace or network reach</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Runtime approval or denial</td>
<td>Requires approval for consequential actions or blocks them before execution; in GitHub Copilot, a hook that runs before a tool call can deny that call</td>
<td>Dangerous actions that the model was only told to avoid</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>CI and code review</td>
<td>Check the resulting change before it merges</td>
<td>Defects and boundary violations in the produced code</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Each control covers specific paths and failure modes. Passing tests and review reduce risk but do not prove that every tool call or behavior was safe. A change can pass the suite and still violate an architectural boundary that the tests do not encode.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GitHub Copilot hooks reference</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Tooling/Coding Agents.md" class="internal-link">Coding Agents</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should repeated agent failures be fixed in a tool contract instead of the prompt?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A failure belongs in the tool contract when it recurs across different requests that use the same tool: the wrong tool is selected, arguments are malformed, or errors are not recovered from. A pattern that repeats across requests points to the interface, not to one request's wording. The contract is part of every call to that tool, so a change there reaches all later calls. A prompt workaround works only when the model remembers and follows the exception.</p>
<p dir="auto">Reaching every call does not guarantee that the failure stops. Rerunning representative tool tasks and comparing selection, argument and recovery failures before and after the change shows whether it actually helps.</p>
<p dir="auto">Contract-level fixes include:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Names and descriptions</strong> that state what the tool does, what it returns and when a different tool fits.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Parameters</strong> with explicit formats, enums and required fields, leaving fewer ways to produce a call that parses but means nothing.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Errors</strong> that say what failed and how to correct the call, so the next attempt has a concrete repair.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Results</strong> that contain the fields the next step needs, including identifiers a later call may use.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For example, Anthropic reported that its SWE-bench agent made mistakes with relative file paths after moving out of the root directory. It also reported that those mistakes stopped once the tool was changed to always require absolute paths.</p>
<p dir="auto">The prompt remains the place for task intent and for instructions specific to one request.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Writing effective tools for AI agents (Anthropic)</a> · <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Building effective agents (Anthropic)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Tooling/Tool Design.md" class="internal-link">Tool Design</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What determines whether related operations should use one broad tool or several narrower tools?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The deciding factor is whether the operations share one contract. Operations that need different permissions, input schemas or descriptions belong in separate tools. Closely related actions that share context, permissions and arguments can stay in one tool.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Signal</th>
<th>Points toward</th>
<th>Reason</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Different permission checks</td>
<td>Separate tools</td>
<td>Each tool can be authorized and exposed on its own.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One schema collecting unrelated optional fields</td>
<td>Separate tools</td>
<td>Fewer argument combinations remain that are valid JSON but meaningless as a request.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Actions sharing context, permissions and arguments</td>
<td>One tool</td>
<td>A single description and schema cover them without unrelated options.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Many similar or overlapping tools already exposed</td>
<td>Fewer, clearer tools</td>
<td>Each additional tool is another option the model must tell apart, so selection errors can rise.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Narrower tools usually simplify each call's arguments but enlarge the set the model chooses from. The net effect depends on the real task mix and the whole exposed catalog, so it is measured rather than assumed. Tracking tool-selection accuracy and argument correctness separately on representative tasks shows which failure a change actually reduces.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Writing effective tools for AI agents (Anthropic)</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Tooling/Tool Design.md" class="internal-link">Tool Design</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering"><h4>Loop Engineering</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does ReAct add to language-model reasoning when a task needs external information or computation?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">ReAct adds acting to reasoning. The model interleaves reasoning steps with actions such as a search, an API call or a calculation, and each action's result returns as an observation that informs the next reasoning step.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Reason:</strong> the model determines what is missing and which action could supply it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Act:</strong> the model requests a tool call, and the runtime executes it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Observe:</strong> the result is added to the model's context.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Continue or answer:</strong> the model reasons over the new evidence, then requests another action or gives a final answer.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Reasoning alone draws only on the model's internal knowledge and the initial prompt, so an invented fact early in a reasoning chain can carry through to the answer. Observations ground each next step in external evidence, while reasoning decides which action is worth taking and how to interpret its result.</p>
<p dir="auto">ReAct does not guarantee a correct answer: a tool can return poor evidence, and the model can misread it. Each sequential cycle also adds a model call and more context, although a runtime can batch or parallelize independent actions.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models</a> · <a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Claude: How tool use works</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Agent Loop.md" class="internal-link">Agent Loop</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In a tool-using agent loop, which safeguards must be enforced outside the model, and what failure does each contain?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Hard limits on iterations, time and spending, plus validation of every tool call before it executes, must be enforced by the runtime. The model cannot be relied on to stop itself or to request only valid actions, so these checks live in code the model cannot override.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Safeguard</th>
<th>Failure it contains</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Iteration cap per request</td>
<td>A loop that keeps calling tools and never reaches a final answer</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Time limit</td>
<td>A slow or hanging call that never finishes its iteration, so an iteration cap alone would never trigger</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Token and cost budget</td>
<td>Context growth that overflows the window, or spending that exceeds its limit</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Repetition detection</td>
<td>The same call repeated, or two states alternating, without progress</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tool-call validation</td>
<td>Unknown tools, schema-invalid arguments or unauthorized requests reaching a side-effecting operation; a precise error lets the next iteration correct the call</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Frameworks expose some of these limits directly; the OpenAI Agents SDK, for example, bounds a run with <code>max_turns</code>. Prompt instructions can reinforce the limits but cannot replace them, because none may depend on the model obeying.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI Agents SDK: Running agents</a> · <a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Claude: How tool use works</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Agent Loop.md" class="internal-link">Agent Loop</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does a tool-using model need from a runtime to operate as a loop?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The runtime executes requested tools, returns observations to the model, and decides whether another turn runs. It owns the completion check and operational bounds; the model’s final text alone does not prove the task succeeded. A one-call tool request becomes a loop only when the runtime sends its result back for another decision. <a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Claude tool-use loop</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Loop Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Loop Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What should a runtime report when its loop budget expires before the task is complete?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The runtime reports that the run stopped incomplete, not that it succeeded. The report names the limit that was reached, the completion condition that is still unmet, and the partial result or state produced so far.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Why it matters:</strong> budget exhaustion is not success. If partial output is presented as a final answer or silently truncated, callers treat unfinished work as done and the failure stays hidden.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What follows:</strong> where the application configures it, the partial state and the unresolved work pass to a continuation run or to a person. Otherwise the run ends with an explicit error.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Platform behavior differs. The OpenAI Agents SDK treats reaching <code>max_turns</code> as an error condition and supports a handler for that case. With Anthropic task budgets, a task that exceeds its budget can end with a partial result.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI Agents SDK: Running agents</a> · <a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/task-budgets" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/task-budgets" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic task budgets</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Loop Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Loop Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In a long-running agent, how is compaction work split between deciding what context to keep and deciding when to compact?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Compaction needs two separate decisions. The content decision, owned by context engineering, determines what the model still needs and what a summary must preserve. The timing decision, owned by loop engineering, determines when to compact, offload an artifact or stop. Compaction typically runs at a token threshold, before the next request would overflow the window.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Decision</th>
<th>What it settles</th>
<th>Failure when it is neglected</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Content (context engineering)</td>
<td>Which goals, decisions, open issues and references a summary keeps</td>
<td>The summary drops a constraint, and later turns proceed without it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Timing (loop engineering)</td>
<td>When to summarize, when to move large artifacts to external storage behind lightweight references, and when to stop</td>
<td>The window overflows, and truncation removes old messages that may still matter</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Durable state sits outside both decisions. A plan or progress log stored by the application can be reread after compaction, which keeps a long run tied to its original goal. OpenAI Responses API compaction, for example, carries prior state forward as smaller, opaque compaction items. Plans and artifacts that the application must rely on remain application-managed.</p>
<p dir="auto">This split is a convention for assigning responsibility, not a boundary defined by an API.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI: Compaction</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Loop Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Loop Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is multi-agent coordination worth its added complexity?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Multi-agent coordination is worth its cost when at least one of these pressures exists and evaluation shows an improvement in a required outcome over a single agent:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Context isolation:</strong> a large subtask would fill the main context with material the coordinator does not need. A separate agent explores it and returns a condensed result.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Parallel work:</strong> independent paths can run at the same time, and latency matters.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Specialization:</strong> part of the task needs a different tool set, or instructions that conflict with the rest of the task.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The cost is real. Each split adds handoffs, duplicated context, more traces and new coordination failures. Agents can also pass work back and forth, so the whole run needs turn and token limits, not just each agent. Anthropic reported that its multi-agent research system used about 15 times as many tokens as ordinary chat interactions. That multiplier describes one workload, but the direction of the cost is general.</p>
<p dir="auto">A useful split gives each agent a bounded body of context that it can summarize back as an artifact or decision. Closely related work, such as implementing a feature and testing it, stays with one agent, which can reuse its evidence and decisions instead of rebuilding them after a lossy handoff. Without one of the pressures above, a single agent with well-designed tools is usually cheaper and easier to debug.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Multi-Agentic Systems.md" class="internal-link">Multi-Agentic Systems</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When one agent hands work to another, how much prior context should the receiving agent get?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The receiving agent should get the context its assignment needs, not automatically everything that came before. More history preserves detail but dilutes focus and exposes more data. Less history keeps focus but can drop an edge case the next agent needed.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Handoff content</th>
<th>Benefit</th>
<th>Risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Full conversation history</td>
<td>Nothing is lost, and it is the simplest option to wire up</td>
<td>Irrelevant turns compete with the assignment, and all prior data is exposed to the receiver</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Scoped assignment or summary</td>
<td>The receiver sees only its task, which keeps it focused and limits data exposure</td>
<td>A summary can omit or distort a detail; in a chain of handoffs each summary summarizes the previous one, so loss compounds</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Small assignment plus references to durable artifacts</td>
<td>Focus is kept while exact source material stays retrievable, and structured outputs can be validated before use</td>
<td>Requires shared storage and an agreed artifact format</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a handoff gives the receiving agent the previous conversation history by default. An <code>input_filter</code> can change what is passed, for example by removing earlier tool calls. Reducing that history is a deliberate decision about focus and data exposure.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI Agents SDK: Handoffs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Multi-Agentic Systems.md" class="internal-link">Multi-Agentic Systems</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What evidence makes failures across multi-agent handoffs traceable?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Failures become traceable when a run records who produced each piece of work, what crossed each handoff, and why routing and tool decisions were made, all linked to the same run.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Run-level correlation:</strong> every agent's activity in one workflow belongs to a single trace, so a failure in a later agent can be followed back to earlier steps.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Artifact provenance:</strong> each artifact records the agent that produced it and the evidence behind its key claims, so an unsupported premise can be found where it entered.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Handoff contents:</strong> the assignment, summary or references passed to the receiving agent show whether a detail was lost or distorted at the transfer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Decisions:</strong> routing choices and tool calls are recorded with their arguments and results.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Forwarding every raw message to every agent is not required. Structured artifacts with provenance preserve the chain of evidence with less context and less data exposure. The retained trace is kept under the system's access and retention policy. The OpenAI Agents SDK, for example, records agent runs, model generations, tool calls and handoffs as spans within a trace.</p>
<p dir="auto">Source: <a href="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tracing/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tracing/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI Agents SDK: Tracing</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Multi-Agentic Systems.md" class="internal-link">Multi-Agentic Systems</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering"><h4>Prompt Engineering</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When should a prompt move from zero-shot to one-shot or few-shot?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A prompt moves beyond zero-shot only when evaluation shows a gap that examples can close. Each added example stays only if it improves results on a representative evaluation set.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Zero-shot:</strong> instructions without examples. This is enough when the instruction and allowed labels already define the task, and it is the cheapest baseline that later prompts must beat.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>One-shot:</strong> one complete input-output pair. This fits when the task is understood but the output shape is not, such as JSON keys or field order.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Few-shot:</strong> several diverse examples. These fit when they show decision boundaries better than prose can, such as classes that are easy to confuse. Near-duplicate easy examples add tokens without adding information.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The evaluation gate matters because examples are not free. Each one consumes context on every request. Example choice, order and formatting can also change behavior, so a model upgrade or a reordering can require reevaluation. When inconsistent output comes from an ambiguous instruction or conflicting example formats, more examples can amplify the problem, so fixing the instruction and format comes first.</p>
<p dir="auto">Examples make a format likely, not guaranteed. A strict output shape still needs structured outputs or schema validation.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12837" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12837" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Min et al., Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI Structured Outputs</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/In-Context Learning.md" class="internal-link">In-Context Learning</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How does in-context learning work, and how does it differ from fine-tuning and retrieval?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">In-context learning adapts a pretrained model to a task through instructions and examples placed in the prompt. The model still predicts the next token, and the examples shift that prediction by showing the task structure, the label space and the output format. No weights change, so the effect applies only to requests that include the examples.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>In-context learning</th>
<th>Fine-tuning</th>
<th>Retrieval</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What changes</td>
<td>The prompt of one request.</td>
<td>The model's weights, through a training run.</td>
<td>The context, filled at request time with passages from an external store.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What it mainly supplies</td>
<td>How to perform the task: format, labels and boundary cases.</td>
<td>Stable learned behavior that no longer has to fit in every prompt.</td>
<td>Evidence the model lacks, such as current or private documents.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How long the effect lasts</td>
<td>Only while the examples are in the prompt.</td>
<td>Until the model is retrained or replaced.</td>
<td>It reflects whatever the index contains when the request runs.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main cost</td>
<td>Context tokens on every request, plus sensitivity to example choice and order.</td>
<td>Training data, training runs and a model lifecycle to maintain.</td>
<td>Indexing and retrieval quality; poor retrieval caps answer quality.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The mechanisms combine: one prompt can contain retrieved passages and a few examples and be sent to a base or fine-tuned model. Examples are still not a reliable substitute for current or private source material, because they demonstrate behavior rather than serving as a dependable store of facts.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12837" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12837" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Min et al., Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI prompt engineering</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/In-Context Learning.md" class="internal-link">In-Context Learning</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What can few-shot examples clarify, and what problems do they not solve?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Few-shot examples clarify how a task should be performed. They show the output format, the allowed labels, conventions such as casing and field order, and the boundary between easily confused cases. They are not a dependable source of facts and cannot enforce permissions or runtime limits. Their own effect also depends on how they are chosen.</p>
<p dir="auto">What they do not solve:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Missing or changing facts:</strong> examples condition the response to the current prompt without updating model weights. They demonstrate behavior, so they are not a reliable store for facts absent from the model and the supplied context. Current or private evidence comes from trusted context supplied with the request, such as provided documents or retrieved passages.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Permissions and runtime limits:</strong> prompt text cannot enforce authorization, budgets or loop termination in a multi-step workflow. Those controls run in the runtime, outside the model.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Their effect is also sensitive and costly. Example choice, format and order, as well as the model itself, can change the result, so a change to any of them needs reevaluation. A long example block also uses context needed for the request and its source material.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12837" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12837" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Min et al., Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI prompt engineering</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/In-Context Learning.md" class="internal-link">In-Context Learning</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is prompt chaining a better fit than one large prompt?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Prompt chaining fits better when a task has real stages and an intermediate result must be checked before later work can trust it, or when that result determines what happens next. One prompt fits better when no intermediate result needs separate treatment. Each extra call adds latency, token cost and another boundary where errors can propagate.</p>
<p dir="auto">A chain earns its cost only when its boundaries are real:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Each stage has one narrow job and an explicit output contract, such as entities as JSON or an intent label from a closed set.</li>
<li dir="auto">A deterministic check runs before the next stage uses that output. A missing required field or an unknown label stops the chain instead of corrupting later steps.</li>
<li dir="auto">Failures can be localized, because each stage's input and output can be inspected separately.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For example, a support assistant extracts entities, validates them against a schema, classifies intent into an allowed set and only then writes the reply. If the error code <code>ERR-42</code> comes back as <code>error_code: null</code>, a required-field check stops the chain. Without that check, the classifier may route the request as a general inquiry.</p>
<p dir="auto">Splitting one vague prompt into several vague prompts adds failure points without adding control. For that reason, the complete chain is evaluated end to end against a simpler single-prompt baseline.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic, Building effective agents</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI evals</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Composition.md" class="internal-link">Prompt Composition</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a practical meta-prompting workflow for improving a weak prompt?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A practical workflow treats a model-drafted prompt revision as a candidate that must beat the current prompt on held-out cases before it ships.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Collect failures:</strong> the starting evidence is observed failures from real outputs, such as incident summaries that omit the timeline and root cause.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Group by cause:</strong> failures are grouped by likely cause, such as a missing output requirement or an ambiguous instruction. One revision then targets a cause instead of patching single cases.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Draft a candidate:</strong> a model receives the current prompt, the grouped failures and the required output contract, and proposes a revision. In the incident example, the revision can require <code>timeline</code>, <code>root_cause</code> and <code>actions</code> as mandatory JSON keys.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Compare on held-out cases:</strong> the candidate and the current prompt are both scored on the known failures and on representative cases that were not used to write the revision.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Version and gate:</strong> the prompt is versioned together with its evaluator, and a rollback threshold is set before deployment.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The held-out comparison is the check for meta-prompt overfitting, where a revision fixes the remembered failures but silently breaks ordinary inputs. It can reveal that regression before release, which reduces the risk without ruling it out. Inputs that the evaluation set does not represent can still regress, so the rollback threshold limits the damage after deployment. A model-drafted revision is a hypothesis to test, not a reliability guarantee.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI model optimization</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI evals</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Composition.md" class="internal-link">Prompt Composition</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why must prompt instructions and generation settings be evaluated together?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The prompt and the generation settings control different parts of the result, and neither can compensate for a defect in the other. The prompt defines the task, context, constraints and requested output. Where the selected model and endpoint support them, generation settings control sampling and output limits.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">A low-randomness setting, such as a low temperature, makes output more repeatable but cannot resolve an ambiguous instruction. It can just produce the same misreading more consistently.</li>
<li dir="auto">A clear prompt cannot make an unsupported setting take effect. Parameter support differs across models and endpoints, so values tuned on one model may not carry over to another.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Because the result depends on the combination, prompt and settings are evaluated together on a task-specific set for the selected model and endpoint. A change to either one, or a switch to another model, calls for reevaluation.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI prompt engineering</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI reasoning best practices</a></p>
