</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Prompt Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can an output-token cap limit cost without truncating valid answers?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An output-token cap limits cost as a hard ceiling against runaway generation, not as a way to shorten normal answers. Normal length and cost are reduced through the prompt. The cap is sized from the measured total of generated tokens plus headroom, within the room the context window leaves after the input.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Prompt first:</strong> repeated instructions, irrelevant context and redundant examples are removed, and the desired answer shape is stated directly, such as a label, a fixed set of fields or a length limit. This lowers cost without risking a cut-off answer.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cap as a ceiling:</strong> generation stops when the cap is reached, whether or not the answer is complete. A cap is not a reliable request for concise wording, so a cap set near typical length truncates longer valid answers. A truncated JSON object, for example, no longer parses.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Total generated tokens:</strong> the cap is sized from the generated-token counts of valid responses on the evaluation set, plus headroom. Where a model's reasoning or other non-visible tokens count toward the output limit, they belong in that total. Hidden reasoning can then use up the cap before a short visible answer is finished, or before any visible output appears.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Context capacity:</strong> input and generated tokens share the model's context window. A long input leaves less room for output, so generation can stop at the context limit before it reaches the cap.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Detecting truncation:</strong> a response that stopped at a limit is identified from the stop or incomplete reason that the API returns. It is handled as truncated rather than complete.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Parameter names and limit reporting are endpoint- and model-specific. In OpenAI's APIs, Responses uses <code>max_output_tokens</code> and Chat Completions uses <code>max_completion_tokens</code>. On OpenAI reasoning models, reasoning tokens count toward that limit and are billed as output tokens. A Responses call that hits the limit returns an <code>incomplete</code> status with the reason <code>max_output_tokens</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/token-counting" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/token-counting" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI token counting</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI reasoning models</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Engineering.md" class="internal-link">Prompt Engineering</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When can Chain-of-Thought prompting help, and when can it add risk or waste?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Chain-of-Thought prompting can help when a task carries intermediate state across several steps, such as multi-step arithmetic, and the model is large enough to use worked reasoning. It can waste tokens when the task has little intermediate state. It can also waste them on models that already reason internally and whose provider advises against explicit step-by-step prompts. It adds risk when the visible trace is trusted as proof.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Where it helped:</strong> in Wei et al. (2022), chain-of-thought demonstrations improved some tested arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic benchmarks, and the gains depended on model scale. Writing out intermediate steps can turn one hard generation into a sequence of smaller continuations. These are results for the tested benchmarks and models, not a universal rule.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Where it can add risk or waste:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost:</strong> longer outputs add tokens and latency. That cost is waste whenever the reasoning does not improve the answer on the selected model and task.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Error propagation:</strong> a longer trace has more steps in which an early wrong assumption can carry forward, and a fluent explanation does not show that the answer is right.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Little intermediate state:</strong> simple extraction or lookup has few steps to make explicit, so extra reasoning tokens are unlikely to improve the result.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Internally reasoning models:</strong> OpenAI's reasoning best practices advise against explicit “think step by step” instructions for its reasoning models, because those models already reason internally. Other providers and models need their own guidance and evaluation.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Whether CoT helps is settled by comparing it with a direct prompt on the selected model and task, with the final answer checked independently of the trace.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI reasoning best practices</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Reasoning Techniques.md" class="internal-link">Reasoning Techniques</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does Tree of Thoughts justify its search cost over a single reasoning path?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Tree of Thoughts justifies its cost when a problem has a real search space. That means meaningful alternatives at intermediate steps, consequences that appear only later, and partial states that can be evaluated usefully. Without those, a single reasoning path or a direct call is cheaper.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How it works:</strong> ToT wraps the model in a search procedure.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The model proposes several candidate next states, or thoughts, from the current state.</li>
<li dir="auto">An evaluator judges how promising each state is. The evaluator can be the model itself.</li>
<li dir="auto">A search strategy such as breadth-first or depth-first search keeps and expands the promising branches.</li>
<li dir="auto">When a branch is judged a dead end, it is abandoned and the search backtracks to an earlier state. This replaces continuing one irreversible completion.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Costs and limits:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Work grows with branching and depth, because each expanded state needs generation and evaluation calls.</li>
<li dir="auto">The evaluator is the weak point. A poor evaluator can keep a bad branch or prune the one that leads to the solution.</li>
<li dir="auto">Straightforward extraction has no useful search tree, and plain arithmetic is cheaper with a calculator.</li>
<li dir="auto">The reported gains come from the tasks tested in the original paper and are not a general guarantee.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Self-consistency sits between a single path and ToT. It samples complete paths independently and votes on their final answers, without evaluating intermediate states or backtracking from them.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Yao et al., Tree of Thoughts</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Wang et al., Self-Consistency</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Reasoning Techniques.md" class="internal-link">Reasoning Techniques</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does self-consistency help, and when can majority aggregation fail?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Self-consistency helps when independent samples tend to make different mistakes and their final answers can be normalized and compared, so the correct answer is likely to be the most common one. Majority aggregation fails when errors are correlated, so that most samples share the same mistake. It also fails when correct answers cannot be matched reliably.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How it works:</strong></p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The same prompt is sampled several times, producing different reasoning paths instead of one greedy path.</li>
<li dir="auto">Each path's final answer is extracted and normalized, so <code>67</code>, <code>67.0</code> and “sixty-seven” count as the same answer.</li>
<li dir="auto">Equivalent answers are grouped, and the most frequent one is selected.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">For example, three sampled paths for an age puzzle answer <code>67</code>, <code>67</code> and <code>35</code>, and the vote returns <code>67</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Where it fails or costs too much:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Correlated errors:</strong> if most samples repeat the same misconception, the wrong answer wins the vote.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Open-ended outputs:</strong> two correct summaries rarely match word for word, so literal string voting splits the correct answers. A meaningful comparison rule is needed, and that rule must itself be tested.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Cost:</strong> calls and tokens grow roughly with the number of samples. Parallel calls reduce elapsed time but still consume capacity.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A comparison against a single-path baseline on the target task shows whether the extra calls pay off.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Reasoning Techniques.md" class="internal-link">Reasoning Techniques</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety"><h4>Safety</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Which guardrails keep unsafe model output from becoming an unsafe action?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The controls that stop unsafe output from becoming an unsafe action sit between the model and the action. They are least-privilege access to tools and data, authorization enforced in application code, strict validation of structured output before dispatch, and bounds on requests and loops. They assume that a bad output or a successful injection can occur, and they limit what it can do.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Least-privilege tools and data:</strong> only the operations and data the current task needs are exposed. An injected instruction cannot call a tool the dispatcher never exposed. Data is contained only if no model-visible path can reach it, including the prompt, conversation history, retrieved context and every exposed tool. Leaving a document out of one retrieval result is not, by itself, a confidentiality guarantee.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Authorization in application code:</strong> the executor checks whether this caller may perform the requested operation on this resource, regardless of what the model asked for.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Validation before dispatch:</strong> output is parsed against a strict schema of allowed fields and values, then mapped to fixed operations. If the model emits the action <code>refund</code>, the schema only confirms that <code>refund</code> is an allowed action name. The permission check still decides whether this refund may happen.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Budgets and bounds:</strong> rate limits, token budgets and loop-iteration caps limit runaway or abused loops.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Classifiers, monitoring and human approval for high-impact actions such as payments or account changes are added where the potential harm justifies their cost. Prompt-injection screening can flag familiar attack wording but can miss novel, obfuscated and indirect instructions, so it cannot replace least privilege. Together these controls form a defense-in-depth baseline, not a security or compliance guarantee.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet</a> · <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI safety best practices</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/Guardrails.md" class="internal-link">Guardrails</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is an LLM hallucination, and why does it happen?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">An LLM hallucination is generated content that the available evidence does not support. It happens because a language model produces plausible continuations of text rather than checking each claim against reality, so fluent, confident output can carry unsupported claims.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>What happens</th>
<th>How it can be detected</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Intrinsic</td>
<td>The answer contradicts the source, such as naming Dickens when the passage names Austen.</td>
<td>Comparing the answer with the supplied context can expose the contradiction.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Extrinsic</td>
<td>The answer adds a claim the source never states, such as a plausible date or citation. The claim may even be true, but nothing supports it.</td>
<td>The context alone cannot settle it. Another source or an abstention policy is needed.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Several causes can produce the same symptom:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Weak evidence:</strong> sparse or outdated training data gives the model little to draw on.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Preference tuning:</strong> it can reward confident, agreeable answers over accurate ones.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Sampling:</strong> generation can select an invented detail from several plausible continuations.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Polished prose does not reveal which cause applies. Claims are therefore checked against evidence rather than judged by how convincing they sound.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03629" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03629" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Ji et al., Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation</a> · <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic sycophancy research</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/Hallucinations.md" class="internal-link">Hallucinations</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why can retrieval-augmented generation still produce a hallucinated answer?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Retrieval supplies evidence, but it does not guarantee that the evidence is sufficient or that the generated answer stays within it. The hallucination itself is an unsupported claim in the generated answer. A retrieval defect is a separate failure, although it can leave the gap that the model then fills.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Retrieval defect:</strong> the corpus may lack the fact, or retrieval may miss it or return weak or irrelevant passages. This is a retrieval failure, not yet a hallucination. It leads to one when the answer goes on to state claims the passages do not support instead of abstaining.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unsupported generation:</strong> even with good passages, the model can contradict them or add a plausible date, number or citation that they never mention.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Retrieval quality and answer faithfulness are measured separately so that a wrong answer can be traced to the stage that caused it. Separate measurement does not mean the failures are independent: a retrieval gap can be the reason for an unsupported claim, and both can affect the same answer. A faithfulness score checks only whether the answer's claims are supported by the supplied context. It does not show that the context is true, current or complete, and a faithful answer cannot recover evidence that retrieval never supplied. Automated faithfulness judges need calibration against reviewed examples.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.2.5/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.2.5/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAGAS faithfulness metric</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RAGAS paper</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/Hallucinations.md" class="internal-link">Hallucinations</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How can preference tuning make an answer more agreeable without making it more factual?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Preference tuning optimizes a model toward answers that human raters or preference models score highly. When those scores reward agreeing with the user or sounding convincing, optimization can make answers more agreeable without making them more correct. This includes accepting a false premise in the question.</p>
<p dir="auto">The mechanism:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Raters, human or model, compare candidate responses and mark the preferred one.</li>
<li dir="auto">The model is optimized to produce responses that earn higher preference scores.</li>
<li dir="auto">When raters sometimes prefer a convincingly written agreeable answer over a correct one, that preference is reinforced along with the useful ones.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Research on sycophancy found that in the studied RLHF settings, human and preference-model judgments sometimes favored sycophantic responses over correct ones. This is a risk, not an inevitable result of every preference-tuning setup.</p>
<p dir="auto">A higher preference score does not imply higher factual accuracy. Factual accuracy and calibration are therefore evaluated separately from preference scores, with test prompts that contain false premises so that agreement is not mistaken for quality.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Anthropic, Towards understanding sycophancy in language models</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/Hallucinations.md" class="internal-link">Hallucinations</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is prompt injection, and how does indirect prompt injection differ from direct prompt injection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Prompt injection is input that changes a language model's behavior or output in a way the application did not intend. Direct and indirect injection differ in where that input enters the model's context.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Direct injection</th>
<th>Indirect injection</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Entry point</td>
<td>The user's own message to the model.</td>
<td>External content that the model processes, such as web pages, files, retrieved documents or tool results.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Who can supply it</td>
<td>The person interacting with the system.</td>
<td>Anyone who can influence that content, without access to the conversation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Example</td>
<td>A chat message telling the model to ignore its instructions and reveal hidden rules.</td>
<td>A web page with hidden instructions that make a summarizing assistant leak the conversation through a link.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The input can be deliberate or accidental, because ordinary content can also conflict with instructions. Injected text does not have to be visible to people as long as the model parses it, and multimodal systems can receive it through images or other media. Its impact depends largely on what the manipulated model can reach. Access to protected context, or to tools that act, is what turns a manipulated answer into a data leak or a damaging action.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/OWASP vulnerabilities on AI LLM.md" class="internal-link">OWASP vulnerabilities on AI LLM</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is prompt injection harder to prevent than SQL injection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Prompt injection is harder to prevent because SQL has a code/data boundary that the database enforces, and language models have no established equivalent. A model receives its instructions and untrusted text through the same natural-language input, so untrusted text can still act as instructions.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>SQL injection</th>
<th>Prompt injection</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How code and data reach the interpreter</td>
<td>A parameterized query defines the SQL code first and passes values separately. The database treats each bound value as data, whatever it contains.</td>
<td>System instructions, user messages, retrieved documents and tool results all enter the same model context. No mechanism forces the model to treat any part of that context only as data.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect of marking the data</td>
<td>Binding a value stops it from changing the query's structure.</td>
<td>Delimiters, labels on untrusted content and input filters lower the risk. The model may still follow instructions inside the marked content, and new phrasings can slip past filters.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Resulting defense</td>
<td>Prevention: a correctly bound value cannot become SQL code.</td>
<td>Containment: bypass is assumed possible, so controls outside the model limit what a manipulated model can do. These controls include least-privilege tools, validation of model output, authorization of each consequential action and human approval for high-risk actions.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">OWASP's 2025 guidance states that it is unclear whether foolproof prevention methods for prompt injection exist. That statement describes current techniques. It does not prove that a stronger boundary can never be built.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet</a> · <a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/OWASP vulnerabilities on AI LLM.md" class="internal-link">OWASP vulnerabilities on AI LLM</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why should a system prompt not be treated as a secret or authorization boundary?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A system prompt can be disclosed, and the model follows its instructions only probabilistically. It therefore cannot keep secrets or reliably decide what a caller is allowed to do.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Not a secret:</strong> adversarial queries can reveal the prompt. Any API keys, database credentials or other sensitive data placed in it can leak with it. Revealed internal rules, filtering criteria or role descriptions can also help an attacker plan further attacks.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Not an authorization boundary:</strong> an instruction such as "only administrators may delete records" does not stop a manipulated or mistaken model from requesting a deletion. Enforcement belongs in deterministic code or the downstream service, which checks each requested action against the caller's actual permissions.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Secure designs keep credentials and authorization decisions outside the prompt and assume that the prompt may be exposed. That assumption does not make every prompt harmless to publish. It means that the system stays protected if the prompt leaks.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage</a> · <a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/OWASP vulnerabilities on AI LLM.md" class="internal-link">OWASP vulnerabilities on AI LLM</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do security failures and reliability failures differ, and why does the distinction matter?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A security failure breaks a protection boundary: data is disclosed, or an access or action happens that should not be allowed. An attacker can cause it, and so can an ordinary model mistake. A reliability failure is incorrect or unsupported output, and it can occur with no attacker at all. The distinction matters because each type of failure is limited by different controls, and neither set of controls replaces the other.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Security failure</th>
<th>Reliability failure</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>What goes wrong</td>
<td>Unauthorized disclosure, access or action.</td>
<td>An incorrect, unsupported or confabulated answer.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical cause</td>
<td>Prompt injection or other hostile input, or a model error in a system that gives the model too much authority.</td>
<td>Generation itself; no adversary is needed.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Controls</td>
<td>Least privilege, authorization enforced outside the model, and isolation. They limit the damage whatever produced the bad request.</td>
<td>Grounding in evidence, checking claims against sources, and evaluating answer quality.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What those controls do not fix</td>
<td>A tightly permissioned system can still give a wrong answer.</td>
<td>Grounding and claim checks do not stop a manipulated or mistaken request from running a privileged action.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">One incident can be both. A hallucinated tool call is a reliability failure. It also becomes a security incident when an overprivileged agent executes it and the result is unauthorized disclosure or access, or a damaging action. If the agent lacked permission for that action, enforcement outside the model would refuse the call, and the error would stay a reliability failure.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency</a> · <a href="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST AI 600-1</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/Safety.md" class="internal-link">Safety</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why are prompt-level guardrails insufficient on their own?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Prompt-level guardrails are insufficient on their own because a prompt only influences what the model generates. The prompt cannot enforce anything at the point where that output is used. The model also follows instructions probabilistically, so prompt injection or an ordinary model error can make it ignore a rule such as "never call <code>delete</code>".</p>
<p dir="auto">Enforcement therefore happens in deterministic code at the points where model output takes effect:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Output handling:</strong> the code that consumes model output treats it as untrusted input. It validates or encodes the output for its destination, for example with parameterized SQL, context-aware HTML encoding or schema checks on tool arguments.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Authorization:</strong> application code or the downstream service checks each requested action against the caller's permissions. The model does not make that decision.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Impact limits:</strong> least-privilege tools and isolation such as sandboxing limit the damage when a bad request passes the other checks.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Human approval:</strong> reserved for actions whose consequences justify the delay, such as irreversible operations.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Prompt instructions still help by guiding normal behavior and reducing mistakes. They are a useful layer, not an enforcement mechanism.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm052025-improper-output-handling/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm052025-improper-output-handling/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling</a> · <a href="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/LLM/Safety/Safety.md" class="internal-link">Safety</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning"><h3>Machine Learning</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Data drift, in its narrow sense, is a change in the input distribution P(X). Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, P(Y|X). After concept drift, the same input tends to have a different correct answer.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What changes:</strong> with input (covariate) drift, the mix of feature values shifts, for example when a new user segment with different demographics arrives. With concept drift, the mapping from inputs to outcomes changes, for example when spam patterns change as spammers adapt.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Effect on the model:</strong> input drift may or may not reduce quality. It matters when the shift reaches features the model relies on or regions where the model generalizes poorly. Concept drift means the learned mapping is out of date, so predictions can be wrong even for inputs that look familiar.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Evidence needed:</strong> input drift can be measured from unlabeled production inputs by comparing feature distributions with a baseline. Confirming concept drift needs outcome labels, because unlabeled inputs cannot show whether the relationship between inputs and outcomes has changed.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The term "data drift" is used inconsistently, sometimes for any change in distribution. Stating which distribution is monitored, such as P(X) or P(Y|X), avoids that ambiguity. An input-distribution alert neither proves that model quality fell nor rules out concept drift. Recent labeled outcomes, which often arrive late, are the stronger check.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/2523813" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://doi.org/10.1145/2523813" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Gama et al., A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Data Drift.md" class="internal-link">Data Drift</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Evaluation"><h4>Evaluation</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does ROC-AUC show about a classifier?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">ROC-AUC shows how well a binary classifier's scores rank positive cases above negative cases, summarized across all decision thresholds.</p>
<p dir="auto">The ROC curve comes from sweeping the threshold from strict to permissive. Each threshold gives one point on the curve. The point plots the true-positive rate (the share of positives flagged) against the false-positive rate (the share of negatives wrongly flagged).</p>
<p dir="auto">The area under this curve has a direct ranking meaning. An AUC of 0.8 means that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative about 80% of the time, with ties counted as half. Random ranking gives about 0.5, and perfect ranking gives 1.0.</p>
<p dir="auto">Because it summarizes ranking over every threshold, ROC-AUC does not:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>choose an operating threshold:</strong> that choice still depends on error costs, review capacity or a required precision or recall;</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>show calibration:</strong> a model with a high AUC can give a case a score of 0.9 without that score meaning a 90% probability of the event.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">scikit-learn: ROC and model evaluation</a> · <a href="https://doi.org/10.1148/radiology.143.1.7063747" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://doi.org/10.1148/radiology.143.1.7063747" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Hanley and McNeil: The meaning and use of the area under a ROC curve</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Evaluation/ROC-AUC and PR-AUC.md" class="internal-link">ROC-AUC and PR-AUC</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is PR-AUC especially useful alongside ROC-AUC?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">PR-AUC is especially useful when positives are rare and the system acts on positive predictions, as with fraud alerts or review queues. ROC-AUC still describes overall ranking. PR-AUC adds whether the predicted positives are mostly correct, which ROC-AUC can hide.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Why ROC-AUC can look strong:</strong> the false-positive rate divides false positives by all negatives. With many negatives, even a large number of false alarms gives a small rate. For example, with 100 positives and 100,000 negatives, catching 80 positives while flagging 1,000 negatives gives a false-positive rate of 1%, yet only 80 of the 1,080 alerts, about 7%, are correct.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>What PR shows:</strong> precision is the share of alerts that are correct, and recall is the share of positives found. Both measures focus on the positive class, so false alarms that consume review capacity stay visible.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Two qualifications apply when reading a PR-AUC value:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The baseline depends on prevalence:</strong> a random ranker's expected precision equals the positive rate. A PR-AUC value is therefore meaningful only next to that rate. Comparing values across datasets with different positive rates mixes model quality with dataset composition. The evaluation set needs to match the production population and workload.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Implementations differ:</strong> average precision, trapezoidal areas and interpolated areas under the PR curve can give different values. A reported PR-AUC is comparable only when the calculation method is known.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/1143844.1143874" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://doi.org/10.1145/1143844.1143874" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Davis and Goadrich: The Relationship Between Precision-Recall and ROC Curves</a> · <a href="https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">scikit-learn: average_precision_score</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Evaluation/ROC-AUC and PR-AUC.md" class="internal-link">ROC-AUC and PR-AUC</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Types"><h4>Types</h4><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Supervised learning trains on inputs paired with known targets and learns to predict those targets. Unsupervised learning trains on inputs without targets. It finds structure defined by a chosen objective, such as groups of similar examples.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Supervised learning</th>
<th>Unsupervised learning</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Training data</td>
<td>Examples with labels, such as tickets paired with their owning team or houses paired with their sale price.</td>
<td>Examples without labels, such as merchant transaction histories.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What training optimizes</td>
<td>Error between predictions and the known targets.</td>
<td>An objective that defines structure, for example how close examples are to their cluster centers in k-means, or how much variance PCA keeps.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical tasks</td>
<td>Classification, regression and ranking.</td>
<td>Clustering, dimensionality reduction and anomaly detection.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>How results are evaluated</td>
<td>Directly, by comparing predictions with held-out labels the model did not see during training.</td>
<td>Training gives no answers to compare against, and a good objective score is only a proxy. Usefulness needs external evidence, such as whether the structure explains different behavior or improves a real decision. That evidence can be label-free or use labels collected only for evaluation.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Common failure</td>
<td>Label errors, held-out data that does not represent production, or distribution shift.</td>
<td>Structure that is mathematically tidy but useless. Feature choice, scaling and random initialization can change the result substantially.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A cluster is therefore not a discovered truth. It is the output of a chosen objective and feature space.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/glossary" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/glossary" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Google Machine Learning Glossary</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Types/Types.md" class="internal-link">Types</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do supervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning differ in their learning signal, even when all three use neural networks?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">The three paradigms differ in where the training signal comes from. Supervised learning uses a target supplied for each example. Self-supervised learning derives targets automatically from the input data. Reinforcement learning uses rewards that an environment returns in response to actions, and it optimizes expected cumulative reward.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Paradigm</th>
<th>Learning signal</th>
<th>Example</th>
<th>What training optimizes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Supervised</td>
<td>A label for each example, provided by people or by another system.</td>
<td>Support tickets paired with the team that owns them.</td>
<td>Agreement between predictions and the given labels.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Self-supervised</td>
<td>A proxy target derived from the data itself, with no human annotation.</td>
<td>Predicting the next token, or a hidden one, in text.</td>
<td>Performance on the proxy task, usually to learn representations that are reused for other tasks.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reinforcement</td>
<td>A reward from the environment after an action. The reward may arrive immediately or only after later actions.</td>
<td>A routing policy rewarded when tickets get resolved.</td>
<td>A policy with high expected cumulative reward (return) over time.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The architecture does not determine the paradigm: similar neural-network components can be trained with any of these signals. The signal determines what training can optimize and how the result is evaluated. Taxonomies differ on where self-supervised learning belongs. It is sometimes described as turning an unsupervised problem into a supervised one by creating surrogate labels from unlabeled data.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/glossary" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/glossary" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Google Machine Learning Glossary</a> · <a href="https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/spinningup/rl_intro.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/spinningup/rl_intro.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenAI Spinning Up: Key Concepts in RL</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/AI &amp; ML/Machine Learning/Types/Types.md" class="internal-link">Types</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-7" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-7" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Security"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Security">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Security"><option value="Security">All Security (14)</option><option value="Security/Authentication">Authentication (3)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="Security questions"><h2>Security</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Security"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How are symmetric and asymmetric cryptography used together in a real system?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography handles the small jobs that establish trust: authenticating a party with a signature, and establishing or protecting a shared key. Symmetric authenticated encryption then protects the bulk data with that key, because it is efficient and detects tampering as well as hiding content. Real systems combine the two instead of choosing one family for everything.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>TLS 1.3 with certificate authentication:</strong></p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">Client and server run an ephemeral (EC)DHE key agreement. Both sides derive fresh shared secrets without ever sending the key itself.</li>
<li dir="auto">The server signs the handshake transcript with its certificate's private key. The client validates the certificate and checks the signature with the certificate's public key, which authenticates the exchange as coming from that server.</li>
<li dir="auto">Keys derived from the shared secrets drive a symmetric AEAD cipher, such as AES-GCM, that protects all application data.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">In this handshake, the certificate key only signs. It never encrypts a session key.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Envelope encryption for stored data:</strong></p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">A random data-encryption key (DEK) encrypts the payload with symmetric authenticated encryption.</li>
<li dir="auto">A key-encryption key held in a key service, or a recipient's public key, encrypts (wraps) the DEK.</li>
<li dir="auto">The wrapped DEK is stored with the ciphertext. Decryption first unwraps the DEK, then decrypts the payload.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Rotating the key-encryption key or adding a recipient then rewraps only the small DEK instead of re-encrypting the bulk data.</p>
<p dir="auto">Public-key encryption suits only small payloads such as keys, so it is not applied to bulk data directly. Combining the families also does not remove key management. Public keys still need authentication, for example through certificates, and private keys and key-encryption keys still need protection.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: Recommendation for Key Management</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 8446: TLS 1.3</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Encryption.md" class="internal-link">Encryption</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is a cryptographic hash function, and what security properties does it provide?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A cryptographic hash function maps input of any length to a fixed-length digest, such as 256 bits for SHA-256. It uses no key and has no decryption operation. It is designed so that the digest can represent the data in comparisons and integrity checks:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Deterministic:</strong> the same bytes always produce the same digest, so anyone can recompute and compare it.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Preimage resistance:</strong> given a digest, finding any input that produces it is computationally infeasible.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Second-preimage resistance:</strong> given one input, finding a different input with the same digest is infeasible, so a known file cannot be replaced by a different file with a matching digest.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Collision resistance:</strong> finding any two different inputs with the same digest is infeasible. Signatures and attacker-facing file identities rely on this property. An attacker who could produce such a pair could get one input approved and then substitute the other.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These properties do not hide a value drawn from a small or predictable set. Passwords, phone numbers or IDs can be recovered by hashing likely candidates and comparing digests. Once practical collisions are found, as they have been for MD5 and SHA-1, the function no longer suits uses that depend on collision resistance, such as signatures.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST FIPS 180-4: Secure Hash Standard</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Hashing.md" class="internal-link">Hashing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is SHA-256 alone unsuitable for password storage?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">SHA-256 is unsuitable because it is designed to be fast. An attacker who steals the stored digests can test password guesses offline at very high speed, and nothing in SHA-256 makes each guess costly. Without a salt, identical passwords also produce identical digests. Precomputed tables, and every digest the attacker cracks, therefore apply to every account with the same password.</p>
<p dir="auto">Password storage instead uses a purpose-built password-hashing function:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Deliberately expensive, adjustable cost:</strong> Argon2id, scrypt or PBKDF2 make each guess slow. Argon2id and scrypt also need substantial memory per guess, which raises the cost of cracking on massively parallel hardware. The cost parameters are tuned to current production hardware and raised over time.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A unique random salt for each stored password:</strong> the salt is stored with the hash, so equal passwords produce different hashes and precomputation cannot be reused across accounts.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These measures raise the cost of every guess. They do not make a weak or common password safe, because it can still be guessed, only more slowly.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Hashing.md" class="internal-link">Hashing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do a hash, an HMAC, and a digital signature differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">All three produce a value that detects changes to a message. They differ in their keys, and therefore in who can create a valid value and who can check it.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Hash, such as SHA-256</th>
<th>HMAC</th>
<th>Digital signature</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Key</td>
<td>None.</td>
<td>One secret key shared by everyone who creates or verifies tags.</td>
<td>A private signing key and a matching public verification key.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Who can create a valid value</td>
<td>Anyone, including an attacker who changes the message and recomputes the digest.</td>
<td>Any holder of the shared key.</td>
<td>Only the holder of the private key.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Who can verify</td>
<td>Anyone who has a trusted expected digest.</td>
<td>Only holders of the shared key, who could also have created the tag.</td>
<td>Anyone who has the public key.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What a successful check shows</td>
<td>The data matches the expected digest. This stops deliberate tampering only if the expected digest arrived through an authenticated channel.</td>
<td>The message was not altered and came from some holder of the key, but not from one identifiable holder.</td>
<td>The message was not altered and was signed with that private key. Linking the key to a person or organization depends on a trusted key binding, such as a certificate.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical use</td>
<td>Fingerprints, download checks against accidental corruption, and a building block for HMAC and signatures.</td>
<td>Webhook signatures, HS256 JWTs and messages between parties that already share a secret.</td>
<td>Software and certificate signing, signed tokens and messages that many parties must verify.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">A signature does not prove non-repudiation by itself either. That depends on how the private key is held, how a compromise is handled and what audit evidence connects the key to an act.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST FIPS 180-4: Secure Hash Standard</a> · <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/198-1/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/198-1/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST FIPS 198-1: The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC)</a> · <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/186-5/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/186-5/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST FIPS 186-5: Digital Signature Standard</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Hashing.md" class="internal-link">Hashing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What does a salt protect against, and why must it be unique per user?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A salt protects against attacks that reuse one computation across many stored password hashes. With a unique random salt for each stored password, the same password produces different hashes. As a result, precomputed lookup or rainbow tables do not apply, cracking one hash does not reveal every account with that password, and the stored hashes do not show which accounts share a password.</p>
<p dir="auto">That protection depends on each salt being unique:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Shared salt:</strong> equal passwords again produce equal hashes. Each guess, hashed once with the shared salt, can be checked against every account at once, and a table built for that salt covers the whole database.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Unique salt:</strong> each guess must be hashed separately for each account, so attacking many accounts requires many separate efforts.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The salt is not secret and is stored next to the hash. It does not slow down guessing against one stolen hash, so it does not protect a weak password by itself. That per-guess cost comes from a deliberately slow password-hashing function such as Argon2id.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Hashing.md" class="internal-link">Hashing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between hashing, encryption, and encoding?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Encoding changes how data is represented, encryption hides data from anyone without the key, and hashing produces a fixed-size fingerprint that cannot be turned back into the data. Only encryption both protects a secret and allows authorized recovery.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Encoding, such as Base64</th>
<th>Encryption, such as AES-GCM</th>
<th>Hashing, such as SHA-256</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Purpose</td>
<td>Represents bytes in a form a channel or syntax accepts, such as an HTTP header.</td>
<td>Keeps data confidential. Authenticated encryption also detects tampering.</td>
<td>Produces a fingerprint for comparison and integrity checks, and serves as a building block for HMAC, signatures and password hashing.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reversal</td>
<td>Anyone who knows the encoding can decode the value.</td>
<td>Only a holder of the decryption key can recover the plaintext.</td>
<td>There is no decryption operation. A guessable input can only be found by hashing candidates and comparing digests.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Secret involved</td>
<td>None.</td>
<td>A key. Whoever can obtain the key can read the data.</td>
<td>None for a plain hash.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Security provided</td>
<td>None. The encoded value is the original data in another form.</td>
<td>Confidentiality against anyone without the key.</td>
<td>Detects changes when the expected digest is trusted. It does not hide inputs from a small or predictable set.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Choosing the wrong operation causes predictable failures. A Base64-encoded password, as in HTTP Basic authentication, is readable by anyone who sees it. Data that must be read later is lost if it is only hashed.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST FIPS 180-4: Secure Hash Standard</a> · <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: Recommendation for Key Management</a> · <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 7617: The 'Basic' HTTP Authentication Scheme</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Hashing.md" class="internal-link">Hashing</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should a .NET application prevent SQL injection?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A .NET application prevents SQL injection by keeping untrusted input out of the SQL text. Values are bound as parameters, and any dynamic part of the query structure is chosen from a fixed allowlist.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Why parameters work:</strong> when input is concatenated into a query, the database parses it as SQL. An email value such as <code>x' OR '1'='1</code> then closes the string literal and adds a condition that is always true. A parameterized query contains only a placeholder, and the value is bound to it as data. Whatever characters the value contains, it cannot close a literal or add a clause.</p>
<pre class="language-csharp"><code class="language-csharp is-loaded"><span class="token comment">// Unsafe: the input becomes part of the SQL text</span>
context<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Users<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">FromSqlRaw</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token string">"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = '"</span> <span class="token operator">+</span> email <span class="token operator">+</span> <span class="token string">"'"</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>

<span class="token comment">// Safe (EF Core 7.0+): the interpolated value becomes a DbParameter</span>
context<span class="token punctuation">.</span>Users<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token function">FromSql</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token interpolation-string"><span class="token string">\$"SELECT \* FROM Users WHERE Email = </span><span class="token interpolation"><span class="token punctuation">{</span><span class="token expression language-csharp">email</span><span class="token punctuation">}</span></span><span class="token string">"</span></span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> </code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>

<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Library calls:</strong> an ORM or data-access helper protects only when it actually creates parameters. The two calls above look similar, but only <code>FromSql</code> turns <code>email</code> into a parameter. <code>FromSqlRaw</code> sends the concatenated text as written.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Identifiers and structure:</strong> parameters represent values, not table names, column names or sort direction. A dynamic sort column is therefore mapped from user input to known SQL through a closed allowlist, such as <code>"name"</code> → <code>Name</code>, and any other input is rejected.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Least privilege:</strong> a database account with narrow permissions limits what injected SQL can do, but the injected SQL still runs. It reduces impact and does not replace parameterization.</li>
</ul>
