<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/sql-queries" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/sql-queries" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: SQL queries in EF Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/OWASP.md" class="internal-link">OWASP</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How should a service store and verify user passwords?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A service stores each password as a verifier produced by a slow, salted password-hashing function. It never stores plaintext, reversibly encrypted text or a fast general-purpose hash. The service only needs to check a password, not recover it, and the function's deliberate cost makes each guess against a stolen table expensive.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Storing:</strong> OWASP currently recommends Argon2id with at least 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and a parallelism of 1. That configuration is a floor, and the cost is raised as far as the authentication servers can sustain. When Argon2id is unavailable, scrypt is the next option, and PBKDF2 fits systems that require FIPS-140 compliance. A maintained library generates a unique random salt for every password. It encodes the algorithm, its cost parameters, the salt and the derived output in one record:</p>

// Questions index — Datacore port of the former DataviewJS aggregation (issue #69).
// Walks every note under this folder, pulls out Question/Qard callouts, and
// presents one selected topic or subtopic at a time. Root topic order comes from
// FolderNote frontmatter, matching the Home dashboard; Tabsdown owns the tabs.
//
// Loading is parallel + progressive: the ~300 note reads run through a bounded
// worker pool, and partial results are flushed into the view in batches. Stable
// per-callout keys let Preact reuse already-rendered callouts. The chosen scope
// remains in state while an index refresh rebuilds the tree.
// Every topic's questions render during this initial scan; selection only hides
// existing panels and sections, so topic switches never start another read.
//
// The `dc-questions-index` wrapper class is a deliberate strip-target: on the
// published Quartz site this page is rendered by the QuestionsIndex component
// (fed by the question-collector transformer), so SyncerFixups removes this
// block's frozen output by that class to avoid a double render. In Obsidian the
// class is inert.
// Tabsdown moves its panels. Restore them before Preact patches this subtree,
// then mount again without leaving Datacore's Markdown rendering context.
class QuestionTopics extends dc.preact.Component {
  host = dc.preact.createRef();
  controller = null;
  focusedTopic = null;

plugin() {
return dc.app.plugins?.getPlugin("tabsdown");
}

mount() {
const host = this.host.current;
const plugin = this.plugin();
if (!host || typeof plugin?.mountTabs !== "function") return;
this.controller = plugin.mountTabs(host, {
label: "Question topics",
selection: this.props.selection,
tabs: this.props.topics.map((topic) => ({
id: topic.name,
label: `${topic.label} (${topic.count})`,
panel: Array.from(host.children).find((panel) => panel.dataset.topic === topic.name),
})),
onSelectionChange: (selection, previous) => {
if (selection === null) this.controller.setSelection(previous);
else this.props.onSelect(selection);
},
});
if (this.focusedTopic) {
const index = this.props.topics.findIndex((topic) => topic.name === this.focusedTopic);
host.querySelectorAll(".tabsdown\_\_tab")\[index]?.focus();
this.focusedTopic = null;
}
}

componentDidMount() {
this.mount();
}

componentWillUpdate() {
const host = this.host.current;
const active = host.getRootNode().activeElement ?? host.ownerDocument.activeElement;
const index = Array.from(host.querySelectorAll(".tabsdown\_\_tab")).indexOf(active);
this.focusedTopic = this.props.topics\[index]?.name ?? null;
this.controller?.destroy();
this.controller = null;
}

componentDidUpdate() {
this.mount();
}

componentWillUnmount() {
this.controller?.destroy();
this.controller = null;
}

render({ children }) {
return ( <div class="dc-qi-tabs" ref={this.host}>
{typeof this.plugin()?.mountTabs !== "function" ? ( <p class="dc-qi-empty">Enable Tabsdown to switch topics.</p>
) : null}
{children} </div>
);
}
}

// Keep the previous tree visible until the first new batch arrives.
const root = { children: {}, items: [] };
const targets = pages.filter(
  (page) => page.$path.split("/").pop().replace(/\.md$/, "") !== "Questions",
);

const insert = (path, name, callouts) => {
  const folder = path.slice(0, path.lastIndexOf("/"));
  const parts = folder
    .replace(new RegExp("^" + ROOT + "/?"), "")
    .split("/")
    .filter(Boolean);
  let node = root;
  for (const key of parts) {
    if (!node.children[key]) node.children[key] = { children: {}, items: [] };
    node = node.children[key];
  }
  callouts.forEach((block, index) =>
    node.items.push({ block, source: name, path, id: `${path}#${index}` }),
  );
};

const flush = () => {
  if (cancelled) return;
  treeRef.current = root;
  setVersion((current) => current + 1);
};

(async () => {
  const CONCURRENCY = 24;
  const FLUSH_EVERY = 24;
  let cursor = 0;
  let processed = 0;

  const worker = async () => {
    while (!cancelled && cursor < targets.length) {
      const path = targets[cursor++].$path;
      const name = path.split("/").pop().replace(/\.md$/, "");
      const file = dc.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(path);
      if (file) {
        try {
          const content = await dc.app.vault.cachedRead(file);
          if (content) {
            const callouts = questionCallouts(content);
            if (callouts.length) insert(path, name, callouts);
          }
        } catch (error) {
          // Keep the rest of the index usable when one file cannot be read.
        }
      }
      processed++;
      if (processed % FLUSH_EVERY === 0) flush();
    }
  };

  await Promise.all(
    Array.from({ length: Math.min(CONCURRENCY, targets.length) }, worker),
  );
  flush();
  if (!cancelled) setDone(true);
})();

return () => {
  cancelled = true;
};

  setVersion((current) => current + 1);
};

(async () => {
  const CONCURRENCY = 24;
  const FLUSH_EVERY = 24;
  let cursor = 0;
  let processed = 0;

  const worker = async () => {
    while (!cancelled && cursor < targets.length) {
      const path = targets[cursor++].$path;
      const name = path.split("/").pop().replace(/\.md$/, "");
      const file = dc.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(path);
      if (file) {
        try {
          const content = await dc.app.vault.cachedRead(file);
          if (content) {
            const callouts = questionCallouts(content);
            if (callouts.length) insert(path, name, callouts);
          }
        } catch (error) {
          // Keep the rest of the index usable when one file cannot be read.
        }
      }
      processed++;
      if (processed % FLUSH_EVERY === 0) flush();
    }
  };

  await Promise.all(
    Array.from({ length: Math.min(CONCURRENCY, targets.length) }, worker),
  );
  flush();
  if (!cancelled) setDone(true);
})();

return () => {
  cancelled = true;
};

```lt;output>
</code><button class="copy-code-button"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-copy" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect ry="2" rx="2" height="14" width="14" y="8" x="8"/><path d="M4 16c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V4c0-1.1.9-2 2-2h10c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2"/></svg></button></pre>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Verifying a login:</strong></p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto">The algorithm, parameters and salt are read from the stored record.</li>
<li dir="auto">The same function runs on the submitted password with those stored settings.</li>
<li dir="auto">The library's constant-time verification routine compares the result with the stored output.</li>
<li dir="auto">After a successful match, the password is rehashed with current settings if the record uses an older algorithm or a lower cost.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Because each record carries its own settings, old and new records can be verified side by side, and accounts move to stronger settings as their users sign in. Accounts that never sign in again keep the old verifier, so an expiry or forced-reset policy is needed for them.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP: Password Storage Cheat Sheet</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Password Storage.md" class="internal-link">Password Storage</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">In password storage, what protection does a pepper add, and what does it cost?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A pepper is a secret key that is applied in addition to each password's salt. It is shared by all password records and stored outside the database. It protects against theft of the database alone: without the key, a stolen verifier cannot be tested against guessed passwords. In exchange, the system must protect and keep available one more critical secret, and rotation becomes harder. The pepper also does not replace a slow password-hashing function.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How it protects:</strong> a salt is stored next to its verifier, so a thief who copies the table has everything needed to hash a guess and compare the result. A pepper is kept elsewhere, such as in a secrets vault or an HSM, and serves as the key for an extra step after password hashing. OWASP describes hashing the password as usual and then applying HMAC to the result, with the pepper as the key. NIST describes that extra secret-key step as either a keyed hash or an encryption operation. Without the key, a thief cannot compute the stored value for any guess.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What it costs:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A critical secret:</strong> every login needs the pepper. If it leaks along with the table, for example when the application host is compromised, the extra protection is gone. If it is lost, no existing verifier can be checked, and every user must reset their password.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Harder rotation:</strong> how existing records move to a new pepper depends on the construction. With a one-way keyed hash such as HMAC, a record can be rebuilt only from the password: at the user's next successful login or through a reset. With reversible encryption, stored values can instead be decrypted with the old key, while it is still available, and re-encrypted under the new key. Re-encryption changes only the records currently stored. A copy of the table already stolen together with the compromised key remains open to offline guessing.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>No substitute for the hashing function:</strong> once the pepper leaks, only the cost of the salted password-hashing function slows offline guessing. A fast hash combined with a pepper therefore remains weak.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OWASP: Password Storage Cheat Sheet</a> · <a href="https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#passwordver" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#passwordver" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">NIST SP 800-63B-4: Password verifiers</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Password Storage.md" class="internal-link">Password Storage</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What should happen when a secret is accidentally committed and pushed?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">A pushed secret is treated as compromised. The response replaces and revokes the credential at its issuer, confirms that the old value no longer works, and checks whether it was used. Cleaning the repository comes afterward and is not a fix by itself, because copies that already exist cannot be recalled.</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Assume exposure:</strong> once pushed, the value may already exist in clones, forks, caches, CI logs and notifications. Deleting it from Git does not make it secret again.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Rotate and revoke:</strong> a replacement credential is issued, every service that uses the secret moves to it, and the old value is revoked where it is accepted. Until revocation, anyone holding a copy can still use the old value. Revoking before consumers move stops misuse sooner but breaks those consumers, so the window is kept as short as the rollout allows.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Verify:</strong> an attempt with the old value is rejected, and the dependent services work with the new one.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Investigate:</strong> the issuer's access or audit logs are reviewed for use of the credential while it was exposed.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Clean up the repository:</strong> removing the value from current files, and optionally rewriting history, reduces future discovery. Neither step revokes the credential or recalls copies already made.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">The common failure is treating deletion as remediation. A later commit that deletes the line leaves the value in history, and the credential stays valid wherever it was copied.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/remediate-leaked-secrets/remediating-a-leaked-secret" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/remediate-leaked-secrets/remediating-a-leaked-secret" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">GitHub: Remediating a leaked secret</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Secrets Management.md" class="internal-link">Secrets Management</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do authentication and authorization work together when handling a request?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Authentication runs first and establishes who is calling. It validates a credential, such as a cookie or bearer token, and produces a principal with claims. Authorization then uses that principal to decide whether this caller may perform this action on this resource in the current context. A valid identity is an input to the authorization decision, not permission for every operation.</p>
<p dir="auto">In ASP.NET Core, one request flows as follows:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Authenticate:</strong> the handler for the configured scheme validates the credential and sets <code>HttpContext.User</code> to the resulting principal. This step does not reject a request that lacks a valid credential. Such a request continues without an authenticated identity.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Authorize the endpoint:</strong> policies on the endpoint are evaluated against the principal before the action runs. Examples are requiring an authenticated user, a role or a claim.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Authorize the resource:</strong> an endpoint policy cannot see a record that the action has not loaded yet. When the decision depends on the record, such as whether the caller owns invoice 42, the action loads it and calls <code>IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, invoice, "CanReadInvoice")</code>.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Handle a denial:</strong> an unauthenticated caller receives a <em>challenge</em>, which asks for credentials. An authenticated caller without permission receives a <em>forbid</em>. The scheme decides the actual response:
<ul>
<li dir="auto">JWT bearer authentication returns 401 for a challenge and 403 for a forbid.</li>
<li dir="auto">Cookie authentication returns 401 or 403 to XHR requests and, from ASP.NET Core 10, to recognized API endpoints by default.</li>
<li dir="auto">Other cookie-authenticated requests are redirected to a sign-in page or an access-denied page.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: ASP.NET Core authentication</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resource-based?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resource-based?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: Resource-based authorization</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/breaking-changes/10/cookie-authentication-api-endpoints?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/breaking-changes/10/cookie-authentication-api-endpoints?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft: .NET 10 cookie authentication change for API endpoints</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Security.md" class="internal-link">Security</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Security/Authentication"><h3>Authentication</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why is Basic Auth unsafe over HTTP?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Basic Auth sends a reusable username/password value encoded with Base64; Base64 is reversible and provides no confidentiality. Without TLS, an observer on the path can recover credentials and replay them. TLS protects only up to its termination point, so logs and trusted intermediaries remain separate exposure boundaries. <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 7617: Basic authentication</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Authentication/Basic Auth.md" class="internal-link">Basic Auth</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When is Basic Auth acceptable in production?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Basic Auth is acceptable in production only for a narrow, controlled integration that needs it. A typical case is a legacy or machine-to-machine interface whose protocol requires Basic. Its coarse credential lifecycle must be acceptable, and the credential must be protected on every hop.</p>
<p dir="auto">Basic itself provides none of this protection, so the deployment must supply it:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>TLS on every hop:</strong> without it, anyone on the path can read the Base64 credential.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>A distinct credential per client:</strong> one client can be disabled without rotating every other client.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Narrow authorization:</strong> the credential can perform only the operations its integration needs.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Rotation and revocation:</strong> the password is long-lived and reusable. It is therefore kept in a secret store and replaced on a schedule and after any suspected exposure.</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Redaction and abuse controls:</strong> the <code>Authorization</code> header stays out of logs and traces, and repeated failed attempts are rate-limited.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Basic is a poor default for interactive login and broad external APIs. Every request presents the primary secret, and revocation means disabling the account or changing its password. Workload identity, mutual TLS or OAuth client authentication usually give a better credential lifecycle. Being on an internal network does not make Basic safe either.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">RFC 7617: The 'Basic' HTTP Authentication Scheme</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Authentication/Basic Auth.md" class="internal-link">Basic Auth</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between role-based and resource-based authorization?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Role-based authorization decides whether a principal holds a broad capability, such as being an editor. Resource-based authorization decides whether the principal may perform an operation on one specific resource, using facts from that resource such as its owner, tenant or current state.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Role-based</th>
<th>Resource-based</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Question answered</td>
<td>Whether the principal may perform this kind of operation at all.</td>
<td>Whether the principal may perform the operation on this particular instance.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Facts evaluated</td>
<td>The principal's assigned roles. A conventional role check does not need the target object.</td>
<td>Data from the loaded resource, such as owner, tenant, project or classification, compared with the principal's identity and claims.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>When the check can run</td>
<td>Before the action executes, for example declaratively with <code>[Authorize(Roles = "Editor")]</code>.</td>
<td>Only after the resource is loaded. The code passes the resource to <code>IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, document, "DocumentOwner")</code> before returning data or applying a change.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Limit</td>
<td>A global role cannot express ownership or tenancy of one object. An <code>Editor</code> role alone lets every editor edit every document.</td>
<td>The resource must be loaded before the decision, and every code path that reads or changes the instance needs the check.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The two work together. A role check can act as a coarse early gate, and the resource check makes the final decision for the instance. Resource-based authorization is an evaluation shape rather than a separate model: the handler that receives the resource can apply role, attribute or relationship rules to it. When permission depends on the instance but only a role check runs, an authenticated user can change an identifier and reach another owner's or tenant's object. This flaw is called an insecure direct object reference.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sources: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resourcebased?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resourcebased?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Resource-based authorization in ASP.NET Core</a> · <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/roles?view=aspnetcore-10.0" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/roles?view=aspnetcore-10.0" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Microsoft Learn: Role-based authorization in ASP.NET Core</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/Security/Authentication/Resource-based Auth.md" class="internal-link">Resource-based Auth</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-8" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-8" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="Cloud"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-Cloud">Subtopic</label><select class="dc-qi-empty">No questions in this topic yet.</p><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="Cloud"></section></section></section><section aria-labelledby="tabsdown-mount-18-tab-9" id="tabsdown-mount-18-panel-9" class="dc-qi-topic-panel tabsdown__panel" hidden="" data-topic="DevOps"><div class="dc-qi-controls"><label for="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-DevOps">Subtopic</label><select id="dc-qi-subtopic-fc209b79-1f91-4f43-934a-379f31d75991-DevOps"><option value="DevOps">All DevOps (6)</option><option value="DevOps/Deployment Strategies">Deployment Strategies (2)</option></select></div><section class="dc-qi-results" aria-label="DevOps questions"><h2>DevOps</h2><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="DevOps"><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What separates continuous delivery from continuous deployment?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They differ only in the final step to production. Continuous delivery keeps every change that passes the pipeline releasable, but a separate authorized decision releases it. Continuous deployment has no routine approval step: each change that passes all required gates is released to production automatically.</p>
<p dir="auto">Both build on continuous integration, in which small changes are merged frequently and each one is built and verified automatically.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Continuous delivery</th>
<th>Continuous deployment</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Production release decision</td>
<td>A person or business process approves the release of an already verified artifact.</td>
<td>The pipeline releases the artifact as soon as the required gates pass.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Release timing</td>
<td>Verified changes can wait, so a release can follow business timing such as a planned launch.</td>
<td>Each qualifying change reaches production shortly after it is verified, without waiting for an approver.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Role of automated gates</td>
<td>They show that an artifact is ready to release; the approval adds the decision to release it.</td>
<td>They make the whole release decision, so their evidence must be trustworthy enough to stand in for an approver.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">The gates are broader than tests. They can include security and policy checks, environment checks, and health checks during a progressive rollout.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/practicing-continuous-integration-continuous-delivery/what-is-continuous-integration-and-continuous-deliverydeployment.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/practicing-continuous-integration-continuous-delivery/what-is-continuous-integration-and-continuous-deliverydeployment.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">AWS: Continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/DevOps/CI CD tools.md" class="internal-link">CI CD tools</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What is the difference between a Pod, Deployment, and Service?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">They separate three concerns. A Pod runs containers. A Deployment declares the desired set of Pods, drives the cluster toward it and rolls out changes to it. A Service gives clients a stable way to reach the Pods behind it while those Pods change.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Object</th>
<th>Responsibility</th>
<th>Identity and lifetime</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Pod</td>
<td>The smallest unit Kubernetes schedules onto a node: one or more containers that share networking and can share storage.</td>
<td>Replaceable. A replacement is a new Pod, usually with a different IP, so Pod addresses are not durable identity.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Deployment</td>
<td>Declares how many Pods should run from a Pod template and reconciles actual state toward that count through a ReplicaSet. A template change rolls out through a new ReplicaSet.</td>
<td>A long-lived declaration; the individual Pods it manages come and go.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Service (typical selector-based ClusterIP)</td>
<td>Selects Pods by label, puts a stable name and virtual IP in front of them and distributes traffic among them.</td>
<td>Stays the same while its set of backend Pods changes.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How they work together:</strong> a Deployment with <code>replicas: 3</code> and the Pod label <code>app: myapi</code> declares three desired replicas. If one Pod is deleted or its node fails, the ReplicaSet creates a replacement Pod, usually with a new IP, to converge back toward three. The count is a target, not a guarantee: unschedulable Pods, insufficient quota, image pull errors or failing readiness checks can leave fewer Pods ready to serve. A Service that selects <code>app: myapi</code> keeps its name and address throughout. Normally only Pods that pass their readiness check receive Service traffic, so the replacement starts receiving requests once it becomes ready. Clients never have to track Pod IPs.</p>
<p dir="auto">A Deployment never routes traffic, and a Service never creates Pods. In this selector-based setup, they are connected only through the labels on the Pods. A Service without a selector relies on separately managed endpoints, and a headless Service has no virtual IP.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Kubernetes: Pods</a> · <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Kubernetes: Deployments</a> · <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/service-resources/service-v1/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/service-resources/service-v1/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Kubernetes: Service API</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/DevOps/Kubernetes.md" class="internal-link">Kubernetes</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">How do metrics, logs, and traces answer different observability questions?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each signal answers a different question. Metrics show whether the system is healthy and how large a problem is. Logs record exactly what happened at a point in time. Traces show where one operation spent its time or failed as it crossed services.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Signal</th>
<th>What it records</th>
<th>Question it answers</th>
<th>Main limit</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Metrics</td>
<td>Numeric measurements aggregated over time, such as request rate, error count or a latency distribution.</td>
<td>Is something wrong, since when, and how widespread is it?</td>
<td>Aggregation discards per-request detail, and label values must stay bounded.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Logs</td>
<td>Discrete, timestamped events, ideally with structured fields that describe state or errors.</td>
<td>What exact error or state change occurred?</td>
<td>High volume, sensitive data and inconsistent fields make them costly and hard to query.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Traces</td>
<td>A tree of timed spans for one operation, linked by a trace ID that is propagated across process boundaries.</td>
<td>Which step or dependency made this request slow or fail?</td>
<td>Every boundary must propagate the trace context, and sampling can drop the trace that matters.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Correlation turns a symptom into an explanation. A metric alert identifies the affected time window and scale. A trace from that window shows the failing or slow dependency. Logs that carry the same trace ID supply the application state that the spans do not contain. Each signal still needs its own retention and access policy.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Prometheus: Instrumentation</a> · <a href="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenTelemetry Logs data model</a> · <a href="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenTelemetry traces</a> · <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">W3C Trace Context</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/DevOps/Observability.md" class="internal-link">Observability</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">Why should request or user IDs not be metric labels?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Each distinct combination of label values creates a separate time series. Request IDs take a new value for every request and user IDs one for every user, so the number of series grows with traffic instead of staying bounded. Memory, storage and query cost grow with it.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example, an <code>http_requests_total</code> counter labeled by <code>route</code> and <code>status</code> has one series per route and status pair, such as one that counts all failed <code>/checkout</code> requests. Adding a <code>request_id</code> label creates a new series for every request, each used once. Even a simple total then has to be computed across an ever-growing number of series.</p>
<p dir="auto">Metric labels suit bounded dimensions such as service, route template, method and status class, where each value is worth aggregating. Per-request identifiers belong in logs or traces, which record individual events. Trace IDs connect those records to each other, so an investigation can move from a metric spike in a time window to the matching traces and logs. That link does not grant access: the logs and traces still need their own access controls.</p>
<p dir="auto">The exact cost of high cardinality depends on the metrics backend, but an unbounded label sets no upper limit on the number of series.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/#do-not-overuse-labels" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/#do-not-overuse-labels" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Prometheus: Do not overuse labels</a> · <a href="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">OpenTelemetry Logs data model</a> · <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">W3C Trace Context</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/DevOps/Observability.md" class="internal-link">Observability</a></em></p></span></div></div></section><section class="dc-qi-section" data-scope="DevOps/Deployment Strategies"><h3>Deployment Strategies</h3><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">What are the main deployment strategies, and how do they differ?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Deployment strategies differ in how the new version replaces the old one and how quickly users are exposed to it. Recreate stops the old version before starting the new one. Rolling replaces instances in batches. Blue-green switches traffic to a fully prepared copy. Canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first. They trade spare capacity and rollout complexity against downtime, the number of users a defect can reach, and how fast a release can be reversed.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>Mechanism</th>
<th>User exposure</th>
<th>Main cost</th>
<th>Reversal</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Recreate</td>
<td>All old instances stop, then the new ones start.</td>
<td>Downtime, then every user gets the new version at once.</td>
<td>An outage during each release.</td>
<td>Redeploying the old artifact the same way.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rolling</td>
<td>Instances are replaced in batches while the rest keep serving.</td>
<td>Grows batch by batch; old and new versions usually serve side by side during the rollout.</td>
<td>Compatibility between adjacent versions while they overlap, and capacity that dips or surges during the rollout.</td>
<td>Rolling the previous version back through the fleet.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Blue-green</td>
<td>A complete new environment runs and is tested beside the live one, then traffic switches to it.</td>
<td>All traffic moves at the switch.</td>
<td>Near-duplicate capacity while the decision is open.</td>
<td>Switching traffic back while the old environment still runs.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Canary</td>
<td>A small representative share of traffic goes to the new version, and exposure expands as health evidence allows.</td>
<td>Starts with a small cohort and grows in steps.</td>
<td>Fine-grained traffic routing and telemetry separated by version.</td>
<td>Removing the canary from traffic.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Kubernetes Deployments offer the first two directly as the <code>Recreate</code> and <code>RollingUpdate</code> strategies. For rolling updates, <code>maxUnavailable</code> limits how many desired Pods may be unavailable, and <code>maxSurge</code> allows temporary extra Pods. These settings and the replica count shape how much the old and new versions overlap.</p>
<p dir="auto">Rolling, blue-green and canary commonly involve a period in which old and new versions run at the same time. Whenever they coexist, shared schemas, messages and data must work for both. If the new version writes data the old one cannot read, moving traffic back does not restore the previous system.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#strategy" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#strategy" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Kubernetes: Deployment strategy</a> · <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/practicing-continuous-integration-continuous-delivery/deployment-methods.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/practicing-continuous-integration-continuous-delivery/deployment-methods.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">AWS: Deployment methods</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/DevOps/Deployment Strategies/Deployment Strategies.md" class="internal-link">Deployment Strategies</a></em></p></span></div></div><div class="dc-qi-question"><span><div class="callout is-collapsible is-collapsed node-insert-event" data-callout="qard" data-callout-fold="" data-callout-metadata=""><div dir="auto" class="callout-title"><div class="callout-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" height="16" width="16"/></div><div class="callout-title-inner">When does canary fit better than blue-green deployment, and what does each approach cost?</div><div class="callout-fold is-collapsed"><svg class="svg-icon lucide-chevron-down" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="m6 9 6 6 6-6"/></svg></div></div><div style="display: none;" class="callout-content">
<p dir="auto">Canary fits better when a small, representative share of production traffic can be routed to the new version and its health measured before exposure grows. Blue-green fits better when a complete candidate environment can be tested before traffic is switched to it. Canary costs traffic control and reliable per-cohort telemetry; blue-green costs near-duplicate capacity plus a safe cutover and switch-back path.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Canary</th>
<th>Blue-green</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How the release proceeds</td>
<td>A small cohort gets the new version first, and exposure expands only while its health evidence stays acceptable.</td>
<td>The candidate runs and is tested beside the live environment, then traffic moves to it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Direct exposure to the new version</td>
<td>Only the current cohort's requests run the new version until the next expansion step, so a missed defect directly reaches only that cohort.</td>
<td>With a single switch, all requests are routed to the new version at once, so a missed defect can affect any request that exercises the defective code path.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Main cost</td>
<td>Routing a controlled share of traffic, telemetry separated by version, and a phase in which both versions serve live traffic.</td>
<td>Close to a second full environment while the decision is open, plus a reliable traffic switch.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reversal</td>
<td>Removing the canary from traffic.</td>
<td>Switching traffic back, which works only while the old environment is still running and compatible.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p dir="auto">Routing limits direct exposure, not total impact. The canary and the old version can share databases, caches, queues and downstream services. If the canary corrupts shared data or overloads a shared dependency, requests still served by the old version can fail too. A small cohort therefore contains a defect only as far as its failure domain is isolated.</p>
<p dir="auto">A canary is only as useful as its evidence. Expanding exposure needs a metric, a threshold and an observation window long enough to show the failure that matters. A fixed pause is not evidence by itself, and very low traffic can leave a small cohort inconclusive.</p>
<p dir="auto">Neither strategy removes compatibility requirements. While both versions exist, shared schemas, messages and external side effects must work for both. If the new version writes data the old one cannot read, moving traffic back does not restore the previous system.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/practicing-continuous-integration-continuous-delivery/deployment-methods.html" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/practicing-continuous-integration-continuous-delivery/deployment-methods.html" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">AWS: Deployment methods</a> · <a href="https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/#dependencies_and_isolation" class="external-link" rel="noopener nofollow" aria-label="https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/#dependencies_and_isolation" data-tooltip-position="top" target="_blank">Google SRE Workbook: Canarying releases</a></p>
</div></div></span><div class="dc-qi-source"><span><p dir="auto"><em>Source: <a href="Home/DevOps/Deployment Strategies/Deployment Strategies.md" class="internal-link">Deployment Strategies</a></em></p></span></div></div></section></section></section></div></div></div></div>
```
